title: 1. Business positioning statement
body: Write a one-paragraph positioning statement for my BUSINESS TYPE targeting AUDIENCE. We solve SPECIFIC PAIN POINT with PRODUCTSERVICE. Our tone is TONE and we operate in LOCATION. Make it punchy, specific, and memorable — no corporate jargon.
whatItIsFor: Use when setting up your business profile or briefing a new AI session. Run this once and save the output to reuse across all other prompts.
howToUseIt: Replace all caps tokens with your real details. If you're unsure about tone, describe three brands you admire and ask Claude to match that style.
exampleOutput: Example output: "We help overwhelmed freelancers in Manchester win back 10 hours a week by turning messy admin into clean automated workflows — without hiring staff or learning code."

title: 2. Ideal customer profile builder
body: I run a BUSINESS TYPE serving AUDIENCE in LOCATION. Build a detailed ideal customer profile with: demographics, psychographics, daily frustrations, buying triggers, objections, and where they spend time online. Format as a one-page reference card I can reuse in every marketing prompt.
whatItIsFor: Use before writing any marketing copy, ads, or emails. A sharp ICP makes every other prompt 5x more effective.
howToUseIt: After the first output, ask: "Now write this as a first-person narrative — as if the customer is describing their own life." That version is often better for ad copy.
exampleOutput: Example: Demographics: 34–45, female, urban, self-employed. Pain: never enough time, feels behind. Trigger: a viral post about automation. Objection: "I'm not technical."

title: 3. Core offer clarity statement
body: Help me write a crystal-clear offer statement for PRODUCTSERVICE aimed at AUDIENCE. Include: what it is, who it's for, what result they get, how long it takes, and what makes it different from competitors. Write 3 versions: one-liner, one paragraph, one full page.
whatItIsFor: Use when you feel your offer description is vague or prospects keep asking "but what exactly do you do?" Run before building a website, pitch deck, or sales page.
howToUseIt: Take the one-liner version and test it on someone outside your industry. If they need to ask a follow-up question, keep simplifying.

title: 4. Brand voice guide
body: Create a brand voice guide for BUSINESS TYPE targeting AUDIENCE with a TONE personality. Include: 5 voice pillars with one-line descriptions, 10 words we use, 10 words we never use, 5 before/after rewrites showing the voice in action, and a one-paragraph summary I can paste into prompts.
whatItIsFor: Use once, then paste the output into every content and copy prompt to keep your AI-generated content sounding like you.
exampleOutput: Example pillar: "Real over polished — we use contractions, short sentences, and plain English. Never use 'leverage', 'synergy', or 'utilise'."

title: 5. Competitor analysis brief
body: I'm a BUSINESS TYPE in LOCATION. My main competitors are COMPETITOR NAMES OR TYPES. Analyse their positioning: what do they claim, what do they ignore, what complaints do customers leave in reviews, and where is the gap I can own? Give me 3 positioning angles they haven't claimed.
whatItIsFor: Use before launching a campaign or updating your positioning. Understanding what competitors say (and don't say) reveals your whitespace.
howToUseIt: Paste in actual competitor homepage copy or Google review snippets for sharper output. The more raw material you give, the better the analysis.

title: 6. Pricing strategy review
body: I sell PRODUCTSERVICE to AUDIENCE at CURRENT PRICE. My main competitors charge COMPETITOR PRICE RANGE. Review my pricing strategy and recommend: whether to raise, lower, or restructure, a 3-tier pricing model if applicable, and how to justify my prices in one sentence. Include psychological pricing tactics relevant to my market.
whatItIsFor: Use when you suspect you're undercharging, overcharging, or losing deals due to pricing confusion.

title: 7. Mission and values statement
body: Write a mission statement and 4 core values for BUSINESS TYPE. Context: we serve AUDIENCE, our founder started this because FOUNDING REASON, and we believe BELIEF ABOUT INDUSTRY. Make the values actionable — each should have a one-sentence behaviour that brings it to life. Avoid generic words like "excellence" or "integrity" without explaining what they mean in practice.
whatItIsFor: Use for website About pages, investor decks, staff onboarding, or whenever you need to articulate why the business exists beyond making money.

title: 8. SWOT analysis for small business
body: Run a SWOT analysis for my BUSINESS TYPE in LOCATION. Context: AUDIENCE, PRODUCTSERVICE, TONE, current annual revenue roughly REVENUE RANGE, biggest current challenge SPECIFIC CHALLENGE. For each quadrant give 5 specific points — not generic ones. Then suggest 3 strategic actions that turn strengths into opportunities or neutralise threats with strengths.
whatItIsFor: Use quarterly or before a major decision. A structured SWOT is the foundation of any strategic planning session.

title: 9. 90-day business plan
body: Create a 90-day business plan for my BUSINESS TYPE. I want to achieve SPECIFIC GOAL by the end of the quarter. My resources: AVAILABLE TIME PER WEEK hours per week, budget BUDGET, team TEAM SIZE. Break it into three 30-day sprints with specific weekly actions, KPIs to track, and red flags that signal I'm off track.
whatItIsFor: Use at the start of each quarter. A 90-day plan beats a 12-month plan — it's concrete enough to act on and short enough to stay relevant.

title: 10. Niche clarity statement
body: I'm a BUSINESS TYPE and I'm currently trying to serve CURRENT BROAD AUDIENCE. Help me identify 3 profitable niches I could own within that audience. For each niche give: specific descriptor, estimated market size, pain intensity score 1-10, how crowded the space is, and one sentence of positioning I could use. Then recommend the best one and explain why.
whatItIsFor: Use when you're trying to stop being everything to everyone. Niching down increases prices, reduces competition, and makes marketing far easier.

title: 11. Tagline generator
body: Write 10 tagline options for BUSINESS TYPE targeting AUDIENCE with a TONE voice. Our biggest promise is CORE PROMISE. Make them: punchy (under 8 words), benefit-focused (not feature-focused), and distinctly ours — not something a competitor could use. Mark your top 3 picks and explain why.
whatItIsFor: Use for website headers, business cards, social bios, and anywhere you need a memorable short line that captures what you do.

title: 12. About page copy
body: Write an About page for my BUSINESS TYPE. Include: founder story (why I started — FOUNDING REASON), who we serve (AUDIENCE), what makes us different (UNIQUE ANGLE), and a soft CTA inviting visitors to NEXT STEP. Tone: TONE. Length: 250–350 words. Make it feel human, not corporate.
whatItIsFor: Use when building or refreshing your website. Your About page is often the second most visited page — it needs to convert, not just inform.

title: 13. Elevator pitch — 30 seconds
body: Write a 30-second elevator pitch for BUSINESS TYPE. I help AUDIENCE who SPECIFIC PROBLEM to DESIRED OUTCOME without COMMON OBJECTION OR FEAR. Tone: TONE. Write 3 versions: casual (like talking to a friend), professional (for a business event), and bold (for someone who appreciates directness).
whatItIsFor: Use for networking events, discovery calls, podcast intros, or any time someone asks "what do you do?"

title: 14. LinkedIn bio rewrite
body: Rewrite my LinkedIn summary for BUSINESS TYPE. Current version: PASTE CURRENT BIO OR DESCRIBE WHAT YOU DO. Target audience: AUDIENCE. I want people to feel DESIRED EMOTION when they read it, and take action by DESIRED CTA. Max 220 words. Open with a hook, not "I am". End with a soft CTA. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use when updating your LinkedIn profile. A strong LinkedIn summary generates inbound enquiries even when you're not actively posting.
tokens: PASTE CURRENT BIO OR DESCRIBE WHAT YOU DO

title: 15. Brand story — one-page version
body: Write a one-page brand story for BUSINESS TYPE using the StoryBrand framework. Hero: AUDIENCE. Problem: SPECIFIC PAIN POINT. Guide: my business. Plan: PRODUCTSERVICE. Call to action: NEXT STEP. Avoid failure: WHAT THEY LOSE WITHOUT US. Success: TRANSFORMATION. Keep it under 400 words, first-person perspective, TONE voice.
whatItIsFor: Use for pitch decks, grant applications, partnership proposals, and anywhere you need to tell the human story behind the business in a structured way.

title: 19. Annual marketing strategy
body: Create a one-page annual marketing strategy for BUSINESS TYPE targeting AUDIENCE with a budget of BUDGET. Include: 3 primary channels and why, monthly content themes aligned to YEAR calendar, key campaigns (launches, seasonal, evergreen), KPIs for each channel, and a quarterly review trigger. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use at the start of the year or when entering a new market. A strategy doesn't need to be complicated — a one-page version you actually use beats a 30-page one you don't.

title: 20. Revenue growth plan
body: I run a BUSINESS TYPE generating CURRENT REVENUE annually. I want to reach TARGET REVENUE in TIMEFRAME. Analyse my three growth levers — more customers, higher prices, and more purchases per customer — and for each give 2 specific tactics I can implement this quarter. Then prioritise them by impact vs effort using a 2x2 matrix.
whatItIsFor: Use when revenue has plateaued or you want to intentionally plan a growth leap. Most small businesses ignore this until they're in trouble — proactive planning wins.

title: 29. Instagram caption — educational
body: Write an Instagram caption for BUSINESS TYPE teaching AUDIENCE about TOPIC. Format: hook line (stop the scroll), 3–5 value bullet points, a relatable closing line, and a CTA to DESIRED ACTION. Tone: TONE. Max 220 words. Include 5 relevant hashtags at the end.
whatItIsFor: Use for your value-driven posts — teaching AUDIENCE something useful. Educational content drives the most saves and shares, which boosts algorithmic reach.
howToUseIt: For the hook, ask Claude to "write 5 alternative opening lines" and pick the strongest. The hook is 80% of the post's success.
exampleOutput: Example hook: "3 things every [audience] gets wrong about [topic] (and what to do instead)"

title: 30. Instagram carousel — 7 slides
body: Write a 7-slide Instagram carousel for BUSINESS TYPE on the topic: TOPIC. Audience: AUDIENCE. Slide 1: bold hook promise. Slides 2–6: one actionable point each (headline + 2-line explanation). Slide 7: summary and CTA to DESIRED ACTION. Tone: TONE. Keep each slide under 40 words.
whatItIsFor: Carousels get 3x more reach than single image posts on Instagram. Use for tutorials, listicles, or before/after content.

title: 31. Instagram Reel script — 30 seconds
body: Write a 30-second Instagram Reel script for BUSINESS TYPE. Topic: TOPIC. Audience: AUDIENCE. Structure: 3-second hook (visual action + spoken line), 20-second value (3 quick points), 7-second CTA. Tone: TONE. Include on-screen text suggestions in brackets. Keep language conversational — this is spoken, not written.
whatItIsFor: Short-form video is the fastest organic reach driver in YEAR. Use for product demos, quick tips, or opinion content.

title: 32. Social proof post
body: Write a social media post for BUSINESS TYPE sharing this result: SPECIFIC RESULT OR TESTIMONIAL. Platform: PLATFORM. Turn the result into a story: the situation before, what we did, the outcome, and a bridge connecting the result to what AUDIENCE wants. End with a soft CTA. Tone: TONE. Don't make it braggy — make it inspiring.
whatItIsFor: Use after receiving a strong testimonial or case study result. Social proof posts consistently outperform other content types for converting followers into buyers.

title: 33. 30-day content calendar
body: Create a 30-day social media content calendar for BUSINESS TYPE. Platforms: PLATFORMS. Audience: AUDIENCE. Mix: 40% educational, 30% entertaining/relatable, 20% promotional, 10% personal/behind-the-scenes. Include for each post: day, platform, content type, hook idea, and CTA. Align with any relevant dates in SPECIFIC MONTH YEAR.
whatItIsFor: Use at the start of each month. A content calendar removes decision fatigue and ensures you're mixing content types (educate, entertain, convert) in the right ratio.

title: 34. Viral hook generator
body: Generate 20 scroll-stopping hooks for BUSINESS TYPE content targeting AUDIENCE. Use these formats: contrarian statement, surprising statistic, "X mistakes" opener, personal confession, bold claim, and direct question. Topic area: TOPIC. Tone: TONE. Mark your top 5.
whatItIsFor: Use when your content isn't getting saves or shares. The hook is the single most important line — it determines whether anyone reads the rest.

title: 43. LinkedIn thought leadership post
body: Write a LinkedIn post for BUSINESS TYPE sharing a genuine insight about TOPIC. Audience: AUDIENCE. Open with a 1-line hook that challenges a common assumption. Share the insight in 3–4 short paragraphs. End with a question that invites comments. Tone: TONE. Max 250 words. No hashtag spam — 2–3 relevant ones max.
whatItIsFor: Use for building authority with AUDIENCE. LinkedIn organic reach for text posts is still exceptionally high compared to other platforms — especially for professional niches.

title: 44. LinkedIn article outline — SEO-optimised
body: Create a full outline for a LinkedIn article on TOPIC for BUSINESS TYPE. Target audience: AUDIENCE. Include: SEO title (include SPECIFIC KEYWORD), meta description (160 chars), introduction hook, 5–7 section headings with 2-bullet sub-points each, expert quote placeholder, CTA section, and 5 tags to use on publication.
whatItIsFor: LinkedIn articles rank in Google and position you as the go-to authority on a topic. Use monthly for sustained organic visibility.

title: 45. Cold connection request message
body: Write a LinkedIn connection request message from BUSINESS TYPE to IDEAL PROSPECT TYPE. Mention: I noticed SPECIFIC REASON FOR REACHING OUT. Keep it under 300 characters. Sound human and curious — not salesy. No pitch. No "I'd love to connect." Write 5 variations.
whatItIsFor: Use when reaching out to prospects, collaborators, or press contacts on LinkedIn. A personalised request gets 5x the acceptance rate of a blank one.

title: 46. Authority content series — 5 posts
body: Write a 5-post LinkedIn content series for BUSINESS TYPE on TOPIC. Audience: AUDIENCE. Post 1: define the problem. Post 2: common mistake. Post 3: my framework/approach. Post 4: case study or example. Post 5: actionable checklist. Each post: under 200 words, strong opening hook, one key insight, light CTA. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use to establish expertise on a single topic over 5 consecutive posts. Consistency on one topic builds faster authority than jumping between subjects.

title: 89. Blog post — full draft
body: Write a full SEO blog post for BUSINESS TYPE on the topic: TOPIC. Target keyword: SPECIFIC KEYWORD. Audience: AUDIENCE. Structure: H1 title (include keyword), 120-word intro (hook + promise + keyword), 4–5 H2 sections with 150–200 words each, practical examples, internal link placeholders, and conclusion with CTA to DESIRED ACTION. Tone: TONE. Length: 900–1200 words.
whatItIsFor: Use for monthly SEO content. A well-optimised blog post generates traffic for years after publishing — unlike social content that disappears in hours.

title: 90. Meta title and description — 5 variations
body: Write 5 meta titles and meta descriptions for a page about TOPIC for BUSINESS TYPE targeting AUDIENCE. Target keyword: SPECIFIC KEYWORD. Each title: 50–60 chars, includes keyword, has a power word (Best, Free, Proven, etc.). Each description: 140–160 chars, benefit-led, includes a soft CTA.
whatItIsFor: Use for every piece of content you publish online. Meta descriptions don't directly affect rankings but they determine click-through rate — which does.

title: 91. Keyword research brief
body: Act as an SEO strategist. I'm a BUSINESS TYPE targeting AUDIENCE in LOCATION. My core service is PRODUCTSERVICE. Generate: 10 high-intent keywords (buyer-ready), 10 informational keywords (educate and attract), 5 local keywords (include LOCATION), and 5 competitor gap keywords I might be missing. Group by search intent and note estimated difficulty for each.
whatItIsFor: Use before writing any new content. Understanding search intent stops you writing content no one is looking for.

title: 92. Content repurposing plan
body: I've just created: DESCRIBE CONTENT PIECE (type, topic, length). Create a complete repurposing plan that turns it into content for: Instagram (3 captions + 1 carousel outline), LinkedIn (2 posts), TikTok/Reels (1 script hook), email newsletter (subject line + intro paragraph), Twitter/X (3 tweets), and a Pinterest pin description. Keep all versions consistent in message but native to each platform.
whatItIsFor: Use after creating any pillar piece of content. One blog post or podcast episode should generate 10–15 pieces of content across multiple platforms.

title: 114. Lead magnet concept generator
body: Generate 10 lead magnet ideas for BUSINESS TYPE targeting AUDIENCE. For each: title, format (checklist/template/video/quiz/calculator), promise (what they get in 60 seconds), and estimated conversion appeal score 1–10. Prioritise quick-win formats — AUDIENCE don't have time for 40-page ebooks. Flag the top 3 you'd recommend and explain why.
whatItIsFor: Use when building your email list. A well-matched lead magnet converts 5–20x better than a generic "sign up for updates" offer.

title: 115. Opt-in landing page copy
body: Write opt-in landing page copy for a free LEAD MAGNET TYPE for BUSINESS TYPE. Audience: AUDIENCE. Structure: headline (big benefit promise), subheadline (who it's for + what they get), 3 bullet point outcomes (specific and tangible), social proof placeholder, and a CTA button label. Also write an A/B headline variant. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use when building a lead capture page. The average opt-in page converts at 2–5% — a well-written one hits 15–40% for warm traffic.

title: 116. 5-email welcome sequence
body: Write a 5-email welcome sequence for BUSINESS TYPE. New subscriber just downloaded: LEAD MAGNET. Audience: AUDIENCE. Email 1 (day 0): deliver the lead magnet + warm welcome. Email 2 (day 2): share one unexpected insight. Email 3 (day 4): address the #1 objection AUDIENCE have. Email 4 (day 6): share a relevant case study or result. Email 5 (day 8): soft pitch of PRODUCTSERVICE. Tone: TONE. Subject line + body for each.
whatItIsFor: Use when someone joins your email list. The first 5 emails set the relationship — they determine open rates, trust, and whether people ever buy from you.

title: 117. Quiz funnel concept
body: Design a lead generation quiz for BUSINESS TYPE targeting AUDIENCE. Topic: SPECIFIC TOPIC OR PROBLEM AREA. Include: quiz title, 6–8 questions (multiple choice), 3 result types with titles and descriptions, a one-email follow-up for each result type recommending PRODUCTSERVICE, and opt-in copy to capture email before showing results. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use when you want to segment leads and personalise follow-up. Quiz funnels generate extremely high opt-in rates (30–50%) because people love self-discovery.

title: 118. Free consultation booking page
body: Write a booking page for a free CONSULTATION TYPE consultation for BUSINESS TYPE. Audience: AUDIENCE. Include: bold headline (benefit of the call, not "book a call"), 3 bullet points of what we'll cover, 3 bullet points of who it's NOT for (pre-qualifies leads), testimonial placeholder, "What happens next" 3-step visual, and FAQ section with 3 common questions. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use for service businesses offering discovery calls. Most booking pages are dull and don't pre-sell the call — this prompt changes that.

title: 136. Meta (Facebook/Instagram) ad — primary text
body: Write 3 Meta ad primary texts for BUSINESS TYPE promoting PRODUCTSERVICE to AUDIENCE. Ad objective: CAMPAIGN OBJECTIVE. For each version use a different angle: pain-agitate-solve, social proof led, and curiosity/question led. Keep each under 125 words. Include a strong CTA. Tone: TONE. Note which audience temperature (cold/warm/retargeting) each version suits best.
whatItIsFor: Use for paid social campaigns. Well-written primary text reduces your cost per click by signalling relevance to the platform algorithm.

title: 137. Google Ads — 3 responsive search ads
body: Write a Google Responsive Search Ad for BUSINESS TYPE targeting the keyword: SPECIFIC KEYWORD. Audience: AUDIENCE in LOCATION. Write: 15 unique headlines (max 30 chars each), 4 descriptions (max 90 chars each). Include the keyword in at least 3 headlines. Mix benefit headlines, urgency headlines, and credibility headlines. Include a display path suggestion.
whatItIsFor: Use when setting up Google Search campaigns. Responsive search ads need 15 headlines and 4 descriptions — this prompt fills them fast.

title: 138. Retargeting ad sequence — 3 stages
body: Write a 3-stage retargeting ad sequence for BUSINESS TYPE promoting PRODUCTSERVICE. Stage 1 (visited website, no action): remind and add value. Stage 2 (viewed pricing page): overcome objections. Stage 3 (abandoned enquiry or cart): urgency + offer. For each stage: ad headline, primary text (under 100 words), CTA, and recommended offer or hook. Audience: AUDIENCE. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use when you have website traffic but no conversions. Retargeting converts 10x better than cold traffic — most small businesses leave this money on the table.

title: 144. Market research summary
body: Act as a market research analyst. I'm a BUSINESS TYPE planning to SPECIFIC PLAN. Summarise the market for PRODUCTSERVICE in LOCATION: market size estimate, 3 key trends affecting the market in YEAR, 3 buyer behaviour shifts, top 3 competitor types and their weaknesses, and 3 risks I should plan for. Base your analysis on publicly available patterns. Flag your confidence level for each section.
whatItIsFor: Use before launching a new product, entering a new market, or pitching to investors. Good decisions need good data — and this prompt helps you structure what you already know.

title: 154. Cold outreach email — first contact
body: Write a cold outreach email from BUSINESS TYPE to IDEAL PROSPECT TYPE. Our offer: PRODUCTSERVICE. Their likely pain: SPECIFIC PAIN POINT. Keep it under 120 words. Open with a relevant observation about their business (leave a COMPANY NAME placeholder). One line on who we are. One line on what we've done for similar businesses (leave a RESULT placeholder). One soft CTA: a 15-minute call or reply. Tone: TONE. Write 3 subject line options.
whatItIsFor: Use when prospecting new clients directly. The best cold emails are short, specific, and make the prospect feel understood — not sold to.

title: 155. Proposal introduction — executive summary
body: Write a one-page executive summary for a proposal from BUSINESS TYPE to PROSPECT TYPE. Context: they need SPECIFIC NEED. Our solution: PRODUCTSERVICE. Investment: approximately PRICE RANGE. Write: headline (their goal, not our service name), problem statement (their words, not ours), proposed solution in 3 bullet points, expected outcome with timeframe, and next step CTA. Tone: TONE — confident and clear.
whatItIsFor: Use for any formal proposal or quote document. The executive summary is the only section many decision-makers read — make it count.

title: 156. Follow-up email after no reply
body: Write a follow-up email for BUSINESS TYPE following up on a previous email about PRODUCTSERVICE sent to PROSPECT TYPE. No response received after DAYS SINCE FIRST EMAIL days. Keep it under 80 words. Don't apologise for following up. Add one new piece of value (a relevant stat, tip, or resource). End with a lower-commitment CTA than the first email. Tone: TONE. Write 2 versions: gentle and direct.
whatItIsFor: Use 3–5 days after a first email gets no response. Most deals are closed on follow-up 3, 4, or 5 — not the first email.

title: 157. Objection handling script
body: I sell PRODUCTSERVICE to AUDIENCE. The most common objections I face are: SPECIFIC OBJECTION 1, SPECIFIC OBJECTION 2, SPECIFIC OBJECTION 3. For each objection write: the underlying fear behind it, a validation statement (acknowledge it first), a reframe, a proof point or example, and a bridge back to the sale. Keep each response under 100 words. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use in sales calls, discovery calls, and email follow-ups. Prepare your responses before the objection comes — improvised rebuttals almost always lose.

title: 158. Testimonial request email
body: Write an email requesting a testimonial from a satisfied client of BUSINESS TYPE. The client received PRODUCTSERVICE and achieved SPECIFIC RESULT. Keep it short and warm. Include: genuine thanks, specific result to remind them of the win, a 3-question format they can just fill in (what was the problem before, what happened after, who would you recommend this to), and a note that one sentence is fine too. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use 2–4 weeks after delivering great results. Most clients are happy to give a testimonial — they just need a prompt and a simple format to make it easy.

title: 169. Sales page — full structure
body: Write a complete sales page structure for PRODUCTSERVICE by BUSINESS TYPE targeting AUDIENCE at a price of PRICE. Include: hero headline (transformation promise), subheadline, agitation section (make the pain real), solution reveal, features as benefits (rewrite each feature as the outcome it delivers), social proof section (3 testimonial formats), FAQ (5 common objections), pricing section with anchor, and closing CTA. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use for any paid product or service with a dedicated sales page. Most small business sales pages fail because they lead with features, not transformation.

title: 170. Pricing page copy
body: Write pricing page copy for BUSINESS TYPE with PRODUCTSERVICE. Create a 3-tier pricing structure: Starter (PRICE 1), Core (PRICE 2), and Pro (PRICE 3). For each tier: tier name, one-line promise, 5 included features as outcomes not features, who it's best for, and a CTA. Add an FAQ section addressing: "Can I change plans?", "Is there a contract?", and SPECIFIC OBJECTION. Highlight the Core tier as "most popular". Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use when building or refreshing your pricing page. A well-structured pricing page pre-handles objections and guides the right buyer to the right plan.

title: 189. Launch offer — limited time
body: Write launch offer copy for BUSINESS TYPE promoting PRODUCTSERVICE at a limited-time price of LAUNCH PRICE (normally REGULAR PRICE). Duration: OFFER DURATION days. Audience: AUDIENCE. Include: urgency headline, what's included (make it feel like a lot of value), what's NOT included at this price (creates clarity), deadline CTA, and an email subject line for the launch day and last-chance day. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use for product launches, relaunches, or seasonal campaigns. Scarcity and time limits increase conversions — but only if the offer is genuinely strong.

title: 209. Customer complaint response
body: Write a professional response to this customer complaint for BUSINESS TYPE: PASTE COMPLAINT OR DESCRIBE SITUATION. The issue was caused by WHAT HAPPENED. Our resolution is WHAT WE WILL DO. Goals: acknowledge fully, avoid being defensive, offer a clear resolution, and end positively. Keep it under 150 words. Tone: TONE — warm but professional.
whatItIsFor: Use whenever a customer raises an issue — by email, review, or social media. How you respond to complaints matters more than the complaint itself.
howToUseIt: Never argue in the response. Even if the customer is factually wrong, lead with empathy. Save the facts for a private follow-up call if needed.

title: 210. Onboarding email sequence — new client
body: Write a 4-email onboarding sequence for new clients of BUSINESS TYPE who just purchased PRODUCTSERVICE. Email 1 (day 0): warm welcome, what happens next, who to contact. Email 2 (day 2): quick-start tip to get first result fast. Email 3 (day 5): address the most common early struggle (SPECIFIC EARLY CHALLENGE). Email 4 (day 14): check-in, invite to share progress, soft upsell mention. Tone: TONE. Subject lines + full email body each.
whatItIsFor: Use immediately after a client signs up or makes a purchase. A great onboarding sequence reduces buyer's remorse, increases product usage, and cuts cancellations in the first 30 days.

title: 211. FAQ document — comprehensive
body: Create a comprehensive FAQ document for BUSINESS TYPE about PRODUCTSERVICE. Audience: AUDIENCE. Generate 20 questions and answers covering: before purchase (5), during setup or onboarding (5), ongoing use (5), billing and policy (3), and troubleshooting (2). Write the answers in a warm, clear TONE voice. Flag the 3 questions that come up most often and suggest featuring them at the top.
whatItIsFor: Use for your website, client portal, or support inbox. A good FAQ page reduces support load by 40–60% and improves SEO by capturing long-tail question searches.

title: 224. Google review request — post-service
body: Write a short, warm SMS or email to request a Google review for BUSINESS TYPE sent to a client who just received PRODUCTSERVICE. Keep it under 80 words. Include: thanks, one specific reference to the work done (leave a SPECIFIC PROJECT placeholder), a direct link placeholder, and a note that it takes under 60 seconds. Don't beg — make it feel like a natural next step. Tone: TONE. Write an SMS version and an email version.
whatItIsFor: Use 24–48 hours after completing a service or delivering a product. Timing is everything — catch the customer at peak satisfaction, before life moves on.

title: 225. Negative review response
body: Write a professional public response to this negative review for BUSINESS TYPE: PASTE THE REVIEW TEXT. Tone: TONE — empathetic, non-defensive. Structure: acknowledge the frustration, briefly explain what happened (without making excuses), state what we've done or will do, and invite them to contact us directly. Keep it under 100 words. Do not offer refunds publicly. Do not name other customers or staff.
whatItIsFor: Use within 24 hours of a negative review appearing. A well-handled negative review actually builds more trust than a page full of 5-stars — buyers know bad reviews happen, they're watching how you respond.

title: 232. Re-engagement email — inactive customers
body: Write a re-engagement email for BUSINESS TYPE targeting customers who haven't purchased in INACTIVE PERIOD. Product/service: PRODUCTSERVICE. Include: a reference to what they previously bought (leave a PREVIOUS PURCHASE placeholder), one new reason to come back (new product, improvement, or offer), a time-limited incentive (SPECIFIC OFFER), and a soft "if you'd rather not hear from us" opt-out that feels human not legal. Subject line + body. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use for customers who haven't bought in 60–180 days. Re-engaging a lapsed customer costs 5–7x less than acquiring a new one.

title: 233. Loyalty programme concept
body: Design a loyalty programme for BUSINESS TYPE serving AUDIENCE with PRODUCTSERVICE. Include: programme name, 3-tier structure (names, entry criteria, rewards at each level), how to communicate it to existing customers, how to promote it to new customers, and the tech tools needed to run it. Make it simple enough to launch in one week. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use when retention is a business priority. A loyalty programme doesn't need to be complex — even a simple referral reward or VIP status can dramatically increase repeat purchases.

title: 252. Project kickoff brief template
body: Create a project kickoff brief template for BUSINESS TYPE delivering PRODUCTSERVICE to AUDIENCE. Include sections for: project overview, objectives and success metrics, scope (in scope / out of scope), timeline with milestones, communication plan (who, how often, which channels), sign-off process, and a risk register with 3 common risks pre-filled. Format as a fillable document with placeholder labels in square brackets.
whatItIsFor: Use at the start of every client engagement. A clear kickoff brief prevents scope creep, miscommunication, and wasted time on both sides.

title: 272. Weekly business review template
body: Create a weekly business review template for BUSINESS TYPE. Include sections: wins this week (3 minimum), numbers check (revenue, leads, enquiries — leave metric placeholders), what slowed me down, next week's top 3 priorities, one thing to stop doing, and one thing to start doing. Format for a 20-minute review. Add a monthly summary trigger for the last week of each month. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use every Friday or Monday morning. A 20-minute weekly review is the most high-leverage habit for small business owners — it prevents drift and surfaces problems early.

title: 273. SOP — standard operating procedure
body: Write a standard operating procedure (SOP) for BUSINESS TYPE for the task: SPECIFIC TASK. Include: purpose, trigger (what starts this process), tools required, step-by-step instructions (numbered, action verbs), decision points and how to handle them, quality checks, and common errors to avoid. Write it so a new team member with no context could complete the task correctly on day one. Tone: clear and direct.
whatItIsFor: Use to document any repeatable task. SOPs are the foundation of delegation — you can't hire help for a task that only exists in your head.

title: 274. Task prioritisation — Eisenhower matrix
body: Here is my current task list for BUSINESS TYPE: PASTE TASK LIST. Apply the Eisenhower matrix: categorise each task as Urgent+Important (do now), Important+Not Urgent (schedule), Urgent+Not Important (delegate), or Neither (delete). Then give me my top 3 priorities for today and one task I should stop doing entirely. Be direct — I need clarity, not more options.
whatItIsFor: Use when feeling overwhelmed or when your to-do list is out of control. The Eisenhower matrix forces you to decide what actually matters vs what just feels urgent.

title: 299. Cash flow forecast — plain language
body: Help me build a simple 3-month cash flow forecast for BUSINESS TYPE. Monthly revenue: REVENUE RANGE. Fixed costs: FIXED COSTS. Variable costs: VARIABLE COSTS. Upcoming one-off payments: UPCOMING EXPENSES. Identify: my break-even point, months where cash may be tight, and 3 ways to improve cash flow without taking on debt. Present as a table I can paste into a spreadsheet.
whatItIsFor: Use monthly. Cash flow problems kill more profitable businesses than anything else — running a simple forecast takes 30 minutes and can prevent crisis.

title: 300. Invoice overdue — chaser sequence
body: Write a 3-email chaser sequence for BUSINESS TYPE for an overdue invoice of INVOICE AMOUNT issued DAYS OVERDUE days ago. Tone progresses from friendly reminder to firm. Email 1: gentle reminder, assume oversight. Email 2 (7 days later): polite but clear, reference payment terms. Email 3 (14 days later): formal notice, mention late payment policy. Each under 100 words. Tone baseline: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use when a client is late paying. Most overdue invoices are resolved by the third chaser — and the best chasers are firm but never hostile.

title: 324. Job description — attract the right candidate
body: Write a job description for BUSINESS TYPE hiring a ROLE TITLE. This is a FULL TIME PART TIME FREELANCE position, SALARY RANGE. Core responsibilities: CORE DUTIES. Must-have skills: REQUIRED SKILLS. Nice-to-have: BONUS SKILLS. Our culture: CULTURE DESCRIPTION. Format: headline that sells the role, 3-bullet "why join us", responsibilities (8 bullets), requirements (5 must-have + 3 nice-to-have), and application instructions. Tone: TONE — make it sound like somewhere worth working.
whatItIsFor: Use when hiring. Most job descriptions attract the wrong candidates because they read like a legal document instead of a compelling opportunity.

title: 347. Weekly newsletter — full draft
body: Write a weekly email newsletter for BUSINESS TYPE. Audience: AUDIENCE. This week's theme: TOPIC. Include: subject line (curiosity + benefit, under 50 chars), preview text (under 90 chars), personal opening paragraph (brief, warm, relevant to TOPIC), main value section (one insight, tip, or story — 150–200 words), quick links or resources section (3 items), and a soft CTA to DESIRED ACTION. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use for your regular email newsletter. Consistent newsletters build audience trust faster than any social platform because you own the list and the inbox is personal.

title: 348. Email subject line split test
body: Write 10 email subject line options for BUSINESS TYPE sending an email about TOPIC to AUDIENCE. Use these different techniques: curiosity gap, numbered list, direct benefit, question, controversy, personalisation token [First Name], urgency, one-word, and emoji-led. Mark which approach you'd recommend for a cold list vs a warm engaged list. Preheader text suggestion for each.
whatItIsFor: Use before every email send. A 5% improvement in open rate compounds dramatically over thousands of emails — always test subject lines.

title: 349. Promotional email — product launch
body: Write a promotional email for BUSINESS TYPE launching or promoting PRODUCTSERVICE to AUDIENCE. Price: PRICE. Offer details: OFFER DETAILS. Deadline: DEADLINE. Structure: subject line (urgency + benefit), hook (story or surprising statement), what it is and who it's for, what they get (3 specific outcomes), the offer and deadline, objection buster (one line), CTA button copy (not "click here"), and P.S. line. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use for new product launches, seasonal sales, or special offers. Promotional emails work best when they're rare — if every email is a pitch, none of them land.

title: 367. Trend analysis for YEAR
body: Act as a market trends analyst for BUSINESS TYPE in LOCATION serving AUDIENCE. Identify the top 5 trends affecting INDUSTRY in YEAR. For each trend: what it is, what's driving it, how it affects AUDIENCE buying behaviour, what opportunity it creates for my business, and one specific action I can take in the next 90 days. Flag one trend that most small businesses are ignoring.
whatItIsFor: Use at the start of each year or quarter. Understanding trends early lets you position your business in front of demand before competitors catch up.

title: 368. Customer survey design
body: Design a customer survey for BUSINESS TYPE. Audience: AUDIENCE. Goal: understand SPECIFIC QUESTION OR DECISION. Write 10 survey questions: mix of multiple choice (7) and open text (3). Include: a satisfaction score question (NPS), a question that reveals why they chose us over competitors, a question about their biggest ongoing challenge, and a question about future purchase intent. Keep it completable in under 4 minutes. Suggest the best tool to send it.
whatItIsFor: Use before a product update, rebrand, or strategic pivot. The fastest way to understand your customers is to ask them — most businesses never do.

title: 387. Partnership outreach email
body: Write a partnership outreach email from BUSINESS TYPE to PARTNER BUSINESS TYPE. Context: our audiences overlap — we serve AUDIENCE and they serve THEIR AUDIENCE. Proposed collaboration: COLLABORATION IDEA. Keep under 150 words. Open with a genuine compliment about their work (leave a SPECIFIC THING placeholder). Explain the overlap briefly. Propose one specific, low-commitment first step. Tone: TONE — peer to peer, not supplier to client.
whatItIsFor: Use when approaching a potential referral partner, collaborator, or co-marketing partner. The best partnerships are win-win — make that explicit in your outreach.

title: 443. Product description — convert browsers to buyers
body: Write a product description for BUSINESS TYPE for the product: PRODUCT NAME. Audience: AUDIENCE. Price: PRICE. Key features: LIST KEY FEATURES. Write: a headline (benefit promise, not product name), 60-word opening paragraph (paint the before/after), bullet features as benefits (5 bullets), a short paragraph for the sceptic addressing the top objection, and a CTA. Tone: TONE. Include a meta description (155 chars) for SEO.
whatItIsFor: Use for every product on your e-commerce store. Product descriptions are your silent salesperson — they work 24/7 and a good one outperforms a bad one by 3–5x in conversion rate.

title: 486. Consulting engagement proposal
body: Write a consulting proposal for BUSINESS TYPE offering PRODUCTSERVICE to IDEAL CLIENT TYPE. Scope: SPECIFIC SCOPE. Duration: PROJECT DURATION. Investment: PRICE. Quantify the ROI: if they achieve EXPECTED OUTCOME, what is that worth to their business (leave THEIR REVENUE placeholder)? Structure: executive summary, problem diagnosis, proposed solution, deliverables, timeline, investment and ROI, about us, and next steps. Tone: TONE — expert and direct.
whatItIsFor: Use for high-ticket consulting engagements. A proposal that clearly quantifies the value of the engagement closes faster and at higher rates than one that just lists deliverables.

title: 487. SaaS onboarding checklist
body: Create a 7-day onboarding checklist for a SaaS product PRODUCTSERVICE targeting AUDIENCE. For each day: the single most important action, why it matters (outcome, not task), the in-app prompt or email trigger, and a success indicator. Design it so users hit their "aha moment" — the moment they first see real value — by day 3. Include a day-7 check-in survey (3 questions).
whatItIsFor: Use for any software or subscription product. The first 7 days of a SaaS subscription determine whether the customer stays — most churn comes from users who never achieved their first win.

title: 488. Churn prevention email sequence
body: Write a 3-email churn prevention sequence for BUSINESS TYPE with product PRODUCTSERVICE. Trigger: customer has not logged in for INACTIVE DAYS days. Email 1 (gentle check-in): ask if everything is okay, share one quick win they could get today. Email 2 (value reminder): showcase a feature or result they may not be using. Email 3 (save offer): a personal offer — upgrade, discount, or expert help call. Subject + body for each. Tone: TONE — human and concerned, not desperate.
whatItIsFor: Use for subscription businesses when usage drops or a cancellation is attempted. Preventing churn is always cheaper than finding a replacement customer.

title: 501. Messaging ladder
body: Build a messaging ladder for BUSINESS TYPE targeting AUDIENCE with PRODUCTSERVICE. Include four levels: Problem (what pain they feel), Promise (the transformation we offer), Proof (evidence it works), and CTA (next step). For each level write: a one-line version for social, a 3-sentence version for email, and a paragraph version for long-form content. This becomes the foundation for all our marketing. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use to create a consistent messaging hierarchy you can pull from across all content, ads, and sales conversations. A messaging ladder means you never start from blank again.

title: 502. Value proposition — 5 angles
body: Write 5 distinct value proposition angles for BUSINESS TYPE targeting AUDIENCE with PRODUCTSERVICE. Each angle should lead with a different benefit or outcome the customer cares about. Angles to explore: time saved, money made or saved, risk reduced, status or identity gained, and ease of use. For each: a one-line headline and a 2-sentence supporting statement. Then recommend which angle to lead with for cold traffic and which for warm traffic.
whatItIsFor: Use when testing different angles in ads or emails. Most businesses only know their value proposition from one angle — usually the one the founder believes in, not the one the market responds to.

title: 503. Website homepage — full rewrite
body: Rewrite the homepage for BUSINESS TYPE. Audience: AUDIENCE. Product/service: PRODUCTSERVICE. Price range: PRICE RANGE. Sections to write: Hero (headline + subheadline + CTA), Social Proof bar (5 logo placeholders + trust stat), Problem section (agitate their frustration in their words), Solution section (introduce us as the guide), How It Works (3 steps), Results section (3 outcome statements), Testimonials (3 placeholder formats), FAQ (5 questions), and Final CTA. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use when refreshing your website or building a new one. Most homepage copy fails because it describes the business rather than speaking to the visitor's situation.

title: 504. AI assistant system prompt — for your business
body: Write a system prompt that configures an AI assistant for BUSINESS TYPE. It should know: what the business does (PRODUCTSERVICE), who it serves (AUDIENCE), the brand voice (TONE), what it should never say, common questions it will be asked, 3 example responses that demonstrate the voice, and a fallback response for questions outside its scope. Make it specific enough that two different AI sessions would produce consistent-sounding output.
whatItIsFor: Use to create a custom GPT or Claude project that sounds like you and knows your business. Save this prompt as a system prompt in your AI tool of choice.

title: 530. Delegation plan — what to hand over first
body: I run a BUSINESS TYPE and I'm spending HOURS PER WEEK hours per week on tasks that aren't generating growth. Here is my current task list: PASTE TASK LIST. Analyse these tasks and recommend: which to delegate first (highest time cost, lowest skill requirement), which to automate, which only I should do (founder-level decisions), and the profile of the first hire or contractor I need. Include a 30-day delegation timeline. Tone: direct.
whatItIsFor: Use when you're overwhelmed and know you need help but don't know where to start. Most founders delegate the wrong things first — this prompt helps you get it right.

title: 531. Team culture document
body: Write a one-page team culture document for BUSINESS TYPE. We believe CORE BELIEF ABOUT WORK. Our values in practice: how we treat each other, how we make decisions, how we handle mistakes, how we celebrate wins, and what we never compromise on. Write it as a living document — conversational, not corporate. Tone: TONE. Include a section: "You'll thrive here if..." and "This probably isn't for you if..."
whatItIsFor: Use when you make your first hire or when you want to codify how your team works. Culture documents aren't just for big companies — a one-pager shapes behaviour from day one.

title: 550. Business systems audit
body: Run a systems audit for BUSINESS TYPE. I need to assess: sales process, client onboarding, service delivery, invoicing and finance, marketing content production, customer support, and team communication. For each area: rate the current state (manual/semi-automated/fully systematised), identify the biggest risk if this person leaves or the process breaks, and recommend the single most impactful system to build first. Present as a table with a priority ranking.
whatItIsFor: Use before hiring, scaling, or selling. You can't scale what isn't systematised — this audit reveals your weakest operational links.

title: 551. Automation opportunities map
body: Identify the top 10 automation opportunities for BUSINESS TYPE. For each task: describe the current manual process, the trigger and action in automation terms, the recommended no-code tool (Zapier, Make, n8n, or other), estimated time saved per week, and difficulty to implement (Easy/Medium/Hard). Sort by time saved. Highlight the top 3 I should build this month.
whatItIsFor: Use when you want to reduce time on repetitive tasks. Automation doesn't require technical skills — most small business automation uses no-code tools like Zapier, Make, or n8n.

title: 570. New product validation brief
body: Help me validate a new product idea for BUSINESS TYPE. The idea: PRODUCT IDEA. Target customer: AUDIENCE. Assumed problem it solves: SPECIFIC PROBLEM. Give me: 5 validation questions to ask potential customers, a minimum viable version I could test in 2 weeks, signals that would confirm strong demand, signals that would tell me to stop, and one competitor who has done something similar with the lesson to learn from them.
whatItIsFor: Use before investing significant time or money into a new product idea. Validation is faster and cheaper than building — most products fail because founders skip this step.

title: 571. Productised service design
body: Help me design a productised service for BUSINESS TYPE. Current custom service: CURRENT SERVICE DESCRIPTION. Audience: AUDIENCE. Design a fixed-scope package: name, one-line description, what's included (specific deliverables), what's excluded (to prevent scope creep), timeline, price, delivery process (5 steps or fewer), and how to say no to out-of-scope requests. Make it something I can sell from a single landing page. Tone: TONE.
whatItIsFor: Use when you want to package a service into a repeatable, scalable product. Productised services are faster to sell, easier to deliver, and simpler to delegate than custom projects.

title: 610. White-label service pitch
body: Write a white-label partnership pitch from BUSINESS TYPE offering PRODUCTSERVICE to PARTNER AGENCY TYPE. Include: what we offer (keep it short and clear), why it fits their business model, what they handle (client relationship) vs what we handle (delivery), margins or pricing structure (leave a MARGIN PLACEHOLDER), a 3-step onboarding process, and a one-paragraph success story placeholder. Tone: TONE — peer-level business conversation. Keep it under one page.
whatItIsFor: Use when approaching agencies or businesses that could resell your service under their brand. White-label partnerships can multiply your revenue without marketing spend.

title: 611. Franchise model concept
body: Help me design a franchise or licensing concept for BUSINESS TYPE. The core model: BUSINESS MODEL DESCRIPTION. What we'd licence: WHAT IS LICENSABLE (brand, system, training, territory?). For the framework include: what a licensee gets, ongoing obligations (fees, standards, reporting), typical licensee profile, training and onboarding plan, how we protect quality, and an estimated revenue model for both parties. Flag the 3 biggest risks and how to mitigate them.
whatItIsFor: Use when considering franchising or licensing your business model. Most franchise opportunities are overengineered — a lean model that anyone can follow is worth more than a 200-page operations manual no one reads.

title: Code Review Assistant
body:
Act as a senior [LANGUAGE] engineer performing a professional code review.

**Code context**
- Language / runtime: [LANGUAGE]
- Framework or library: [FRAMEWORK or "None"]
- What this code does: [ONE SENTENCE DESCRIPTION]
- Special constraints or requirements: [CONSTRAINTS or "None"]

**Code to review**
```[LANGUAGE]
[PASTE YOUR CODE HERE]
```

**Review instructions**
Work through each dimension below in order. For every issue you find, provide:
- **Location** — function name or line reference
- **Severity** — Critical | High | Medium | Low
- **Problem** — one sentence explaining what is wrong and why it matters
- **Fix** — a corrected code snippet (not just a description)

Dimensions to cover:
1. Critical bugs and logic errors
2. Security vulnerabilities (SQL injection, XSS, insecure input handling, hardcoded secrets, improper error exposure, [ADDITIONAL SECURITY CONCERNS or "standard OWASP issues"])
3. Performance and efficiency (unnecessary loops, missing indexes, memory leaks, blocking calls)
4. Readability and naming (unclear variable names, missing type hints, overly complex conditionals)
5. Edge cases and error handling (null/undefined inputs, empty collections, network failures, race conditions)

After the issue list, write a one-paragraph **Executive Summary** that: (a) gives an overall quality rating out of 10, (b) names the single most important improvement, and (c) notes any genuinely strong patterns worth keeping.

Do not include compliments, filler sentences, or unsolicited disclaimers. Be direct, specific, and actionable.
whatItIsFor: Get a thorough, structured code review covering bugs, security, performance, and style — with severity ratings and ready-to-use fixes — by pasting any function, class, or diff into Claude.ai or ChatGPT.
howToUseIt: Replace every [PLACEHOLDER] with your real values — at minimum fill in LANGUAGE, a one-sentence description of what the code does, and paste your code. The more context you provide (framework, constraints, specific security concerns), the more targeted the feedback will be. You can omit dimensions you don't care about by removing them from the numbered list.
exampleOutput: [CLAUDE] Works best as-is. You can wrap the code block in XML tags and the instructions in for even stricter adherence. Claude handles large files (500+ lines) well. If Claude adds unsolicited caveats, append: 'Provide fixes directly without disclaimers.' [CHATGPT] Remove the XML tag suggestions and keep the Markdown formatting as shown. GPT-4o handles large pastes well; for files over ~400 lines consider splitting by logical section. ChatGPT's Code Interpreter (Advanced Data Analysis) can execute simple snippets — mention this in your prompt if you want runtime verification. [PERPLEXITY] Shorten the prompt: keep the role, code context, code block, and the top 2-3 dimensions most relevant to your review. Perplexity's web search is a bonus — add 'check current documentation for [LIBRARY] if relevant' to leverage it. Avoid XML tags; plain Markdown works best.

title: Code Review Assistant — Security Audit

**Code context**

End with a one-paragraph risk summary. Be direct and specific — no filler.

title: Code Review Assistant — PR Diff Review
body:
Act as a senior [LANGUAGE] engineer reviewing a pull request.

**PR context**
- Language / runtime: [LANGUAGE]
- What this PR does: [ONE SENTENCE DESCRIPTION]
- Ticket or requirement reference: [TICKET ID or "None"]

**Diff to review**
```diff
[PASTE YOUR GIT DIFF HERE]
```

**Review instructions**
Focus only on changed lines and their immediate context. For each issue:
- **Location** — file and function/line reference
- **Severity** — Critical | High | Medium | Low
- **Problem** — one sentence
- **Fix** — corrected code snippet

Cover in order:
1. Correctness — does the change do what the description says?
2. Regressions — could this break existing functionality?
3. Security implications of new code paths
4. Missing tests for new behaviour

Ignore formatting-only changes. End with a one-line merge recommendation: Approve / Request Changes / Needs Discussion.
whatItIsFor: Reviewing git diffs or pull requests where you want focused feedback only on what changed, including a clear merge recommendation.

You can omit dimensions you don't care about by removing them from the numbered list.

title: Customer Support Ticket Triage & Draft Response
body:
You are an experienced customer support specialist with deep knowledge of handling customer issues with empathy and efficiency. Your job is to triage incoming support tickets and draft professional first responses.

Analyse the customer message below and produce exactly the following sections in order. Do not add commentary between sections.

**CATEGORY**
Classify the ticket into exactly one of: Billing & Payments | Technical Issue | Account Access | Product Question | Shipping & Delivery | Feature Request | Bug Report | Complaint | General Enquiry

**URGENCY**
Assign one of: Critical / High / Medium / Low
Critical = service completely broken, legal/financial risk, or major data issue. High = significant impact on customer's work or business. Medium = inconvenience but workaround exists. Low = question or minor annoyance.
Then write one sentence explaining your urgency decision.

**SENTIMENT**
Describe the customer's emotional state in one sentence (e.g. frustrated and losing patience, anxious about a deadline, neutral and informational, satisfied but has a question).

**ESCALATE**
Yes or No. If Yes, write one sentence explaining what makes this ticket require escalation to a senior agent or specialist team.

**DRAFT REPLY**
Write an empathetic 2–3 paragraph reply the agent can send or lightly edit. Rules:
- Open by acknowledging the specific issue described — do not use hollow phrases like "I understand your frustration" alone.
- Match your tone to the detected sentiment (e.g. warm and reassuring for anxious customers; direct and action-focused for frustrated ones).
- In the second paragraph, explain the next step or resolution path clearly.
- Close with a specific offer of further help and the agent's name.
- Keep the reply to 100–180 words.
- Sign off as: [AGENT NAME] from the [COMPANY NAME] Support Team.

---

<ticket>
[CUSTOMER MESSAGE]
</ticket>

Company name: [COMPANY NAME]
Product or service: [PRODUCT OR SERVICE]
Agent name: [AGENT NAME]
whatItIsFor: A support agent pastes a raw customer message to get an instant triage (category, urgency, sentiment, escalation flag) plus a ready-to-send empathetic draft reply — all in one output.
howToUseIt: Replace [CUSTOMER MESSAGE] with the full text of the incoming ticket (copy-paste the customer's email or chat message). Fill in [COMPANY NAME], [PRODUCT OR SERVICE], and [AGENT NAME] with your real values. Paste the entire prompt into Claude.ai or ChatGPT and send — you will get a structured triage plus a draft reply you can copy, lightly edit, and send.
exampleOutput:
[CLAUDE]
Works best as-is. Use the XML <ticket> delimiter — Claude handles it natively and it reduces prompt injection risk from customer message content. Claude reliably produces all five sections in order without drifting. No extra formatting instructions needed.

[CHATGPT]
Works well with GPT-4o. Add 'Use markdown ## headers for each section label' if you want cleaner rendering in the chat UI. If ChatGPT adds filler text between sections, append 'Do not add any commentary or transitions between sections' to the prompt. The role statement ('experienced customer support specialist') measurably improves tone quality.

[PERPLEXITY]
Perplexity may attempt to pull in web search results about the product or issue mentioned in the ticket. To prevent this, add 'Do not search the web. Analyse only the text I have provided.' at the top of the prompt. The Quick Triage Only variation works better on Perplexity than the full version with a draft reply, as Perplexity is optimised for research rather than long-form generation.

title: Customer Support Ticket Triage & Draft Response — Full Context with SLA and Previous Interaction
body:
You are an experienced customer support specialist. Triage the ticket below, taking into account the customer's history and SLA tier.

Analyse and produce exactly these sections in order. Do not add commentary between sections.

**CATEGORY** — one of: Billing & Payments | Technical Issue | Account Access | Product Question | Shipping & Delivery | Feature Request | Bug Report | Complaint | General Enquiry
**URGENCY** — Critical / High / Medium / Low + one sentence reason (factor in the SLA tier)
**SENTIMENT** — one sentence describing the customer's emotional state
**ESCALATE** — Yes or No + one sentence reason if Yes
**DRAFT REPLY** — 2–3 paragraphs, empathetic, action-focused, 100–180 words. Acknowledge the specific issue. Reference any relevant previous interaction if provided. Sign off as [AGENT NAME] from the [COMPANY NAME] Support Team.

---

<ticket>
[CUSTOMER MESSAGE]
</ticket>

Company name: [COMPANY NAME]

title: Interview Question Generator
body:
Act as an experienced [SENIORITY_LEVEL] hiring manager in the [INDUSTRY] sector.

I am preparing to interview candidates for the role below. Read the job description carefully and generate a complete, structured interview question bank I can use immediately.

<job_description>
[PASTE_FULL_JOB_DESCRIPTION_HERE]
</job_description>

**Candidate seniority level:** [ENTRY / MID-LEVEL / SENIOR / LEAD / EXECUTIVE]
**Interview stage:** [PHONE SCREEN / FIRST ROUND / PANEL / FINAL]
**Team context (optional):** [E.G. "Fast-paced startup, remote-first" OR leave blank]

---

Produce the following sections in order:

**SECTION 1 — KEY COMPETENCIES**
List the 4–6 core competencies this role requires, drawn directly from the job description. One sentence per competency explaining why it matters for this role.

**SECTION 2 — BEHAVIOURAL QUESTIONS (STAR format expected)**
Write 3 behavioural questions tied to the competencies above.
For each question provide:
- The question itself
- One follow-up probe to dig deeper
- Ideal answer framework: what a strong answer includes, what a weak answer looks like

**SECTION 3 — SITUATIONAL / SCENARIO QUESTIONS**
Write 2 scenario-based questions that present a realistic situation this person would face in the role.
For each question provide:
- The scenario and question
- Key things to listen for in the response
- One red-flag indicator

**SECTION 4 — TECHNICAL / FUNCTIONAL QUESTIONS**
Write 2 questions that test specific technical or functional skills listed in the job description.
For each question provide:
- The question
- What a correct or strong answer demonstrates
- An acceptable minimum standard for this seniority level

**SECTION 5 — CULTURE & VALUES QUESTION**
Write 1 question that explores alignment with the team or company values mentioned in the job description (or general professional values if none are stated).
Provide: the question, what to listen for, and why it matters.

---

**Output rules:**
- Numbered list format within each section
- No preamble, no summary at the end
- Concise and direct — each answer framework should be 2–4 sentences
- Do NOT include questions that ask about age, family status, nationality, religion, or any other protected characteristic
- All questions must be grounded in the job description provided — do not invent requirements not present in the JD
whatItIsFor: A hiring manager or recruiter pastes a job description and receives a structured, role-specific interview question bank with behavioural, situational, technical, and culture-fit questions — each with ideal answer frameworks and difficulty calibration.
howToUseIt: Replace every [PLACEHOLDER] with your specific details, then paste the full job description inside the <job_description> tags. Copy the completed prompt into Claude.ai, ChatGPT, or your preferred AI chat tool and send it as a single message. The output is ready to paste into your interview guide or ATS notes field.

title: Product Requirements Writer
body:
You are an experienced senior product manager helping draft a Product Requirements Document (PRD) for an engineering team.

**Product context:**
- Product name: [PRODUCT_NAME]
- Target users: [USER_PERSONA — e.g., 'B2B SaaS ops managers' or 'consumer fitness app users']
- Company / product stage: [STAGE — e.g., 'early-stage startup', 'growth-stage, 50k MAU']

**Feature idea (1–3 sentences):**
[FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]

**Core problem this solves:**
[PROBLEM_STATEMENT — what pain does the user have today, and why does it matter?]

**Any known constraints or non-negotiables:**
[CONSTRAINTS — e.g., 'must work offline', 'no changes to the billing system', or 'none yet']

---

Using the information above, write a PRD draft with the following sections:

1. **Problem Statement** — Describe the user problem clearly. Include who is affected, how often, and what the current workaround is.
2. **Proposed Solution** — High-level description of the feature. No implementation detail — focus on what the user experiences, not how it is built.
3. **User Stories** — Write 3–5 user stories in the format: *As a [user type], I want [action], so that [benefit].* Cover the primary flow and at least one secondary or edge-case scenario.
4. **Acceptance Criteria** — For each user story, list 2–3 acceptance criteria. Each must be specific and testable: state a condition, an action, and a measurable or observable outcome. Avoid vague language like 'should be fast' or 'user-friendly'.
5. **Edge Cases & Failure States** — List at least 4 scenarios where the feature might behave unexpectedly or fail, and describe the expected graceful handling.
6. **Out of Scope** — Explicitly state what this feature does NOT include in this version. This is as important as what it does include.
7. **Success Metrics** — Define 2–3 metrics that would indicate the feature is working. Use [METRIC_PLACEHOLDER] for any metric that requires real baseline data you don't have yet. Explain why each metric was chosen.
8. **Open Questions & Assumptions** — List every assumption you made while writing this PRD, and flag any questions that must be answered before engineering can begin.

**Constraints for your output:**
- Do not invent statistics or benchmark numbers. Use [DATA_NEEDED] if a real figure is required.
- Keep the document focused — equivalent to 1–2 pages. Do not pad sections.
- Write for an engineering audience, not executives. Be specific and unambiguous.
- If the feature idea is too vague for you to write a section with confidence, say so explicitly rather than guessing.
whatItIsFor: Turn a rough product idea or feature brief into a structured PRD draft with user stories, acceptance criteria, and edge cases — ready for engineering review.
howToUseIt: Fill in all five [PLACEHOLDER] fields before pasting: your product name, who your users are, your company stage, a 1–3 sentence description of the feature, and the core problem it solves. Paste the completed prompt into Claude.ai or ChatGPT and treat the output as a first draft — use follow-up messages to refine specific sections, challenge assumptions, or add missing context.
exampleOutput:
[CLAUDE]
Claude.ai is the recommended platform for this prompt. Claude follows structural formatting instructions very precisely, producing clean section-by-section output. Use Projects to maintain context across iterations — paste your company background or existing PRD template as a Project document so Claude already knows your format. Claude is also reliably responsive to 'flag all assumptions' instructions.

[CHATGPT]
Works well in GPT-4o and later. ChatGPT tends to produce slightly wordier output and may add unrequested sections (e.g. Executive Summary) — if this happens, follow up with 'Remove the Executive Summary section and keep only the 8 sections I specified.' Use Custom Instructions to pre-load company context so you don't need to repeat it in every prompt.

[PERPLEXITY]
Perplexity is not recommended as the primary PRD drafting tool — it is optimised for research synthesis, not structured document generation. Best use: run a Perplexity search first ('What are the main approaches competitors use for [feature type]?') and paste the findings into the [CONSTRAINTS] or [PROBLEM_STATEMENT] field before running this prompt in Claude or ChatGPT.

title: SQL Query Generator
body:
You are an expert SQL developer. Your task is to write a single, correct, optimised [SQL_DIALECT] query that answers the business question below.

## Schema

[PASTE_YOUR_TABLE_DEFINITIONS_HERE]

Example format:
```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT,
  amount DECIMAL(10,2),
  status TEXT,
  created_at TIMESTAMP
);
```

## Business Context (optional but recommended)

[DEFINE_ANY_DOMAIN_TERMS_HERE — e.g. "Active user = a user who logged in within the last 30 days", "Completed order = orders with status = 'completed'"]

## Question

[YOUR_PLAIN_ENGLISH_QUESTION]

## Requirements

- Use [SQL_DIALECT] syntax only (e.g. PostgreSQL, MySQL, BigQuery, SQL Server, SQLite)
- Do NOT use SELECT * — alias all returned columns with clear, readable names
- Add a short comment above each major clause (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, etc.)
- If a CTE would improve readability, use one
- Handle NULLs explicitly where relevant

## Output format

1. **Approach** (2–3 sentences): explain the join strategy, aggregation logic, or filtering approach before writing any SQL
2. **Query**: a clean SQL code block
3. **Verification**: one sentence confirming the query handles edge cases (NULLs, empty results, date ranges)
whatItIsFor: Convert a plain-English business question into a correct, optimised SQL query with a brief explanation. Designed for data analysts and developers who have a database schema and want a working query they can run immediately.
howToUseIt: Replace [SQL_DIALECT] with your database type (e.g. PostgreSQL), paste your CREATE TABLE statements into the Schema section, fill in the Question with your plain-English request, and optionally define any business terms in the Business Context section. title: Startup Board Update Writer
body:
You are an experienced board communications advisor — part CFO, part board secretary — helping a startup founder write a structured monthly or quarterly board update. Your readers are experienced investors and operators who have seen hundreds of these documents. They will notice vague language, softened misses, and missing asks immediately.

This is a governance document, not an investor newsletter. Its primary purpose is to surface decisions that require board input, present performance with complete honesty, and give the board what they need to fulfil their fiduciary role.

Write the board update using the data below. Follow all instructions exactly.

--- COMPANY CONTEXT ---
Company name: [COMPANY_NAME]
Period covered: [e.g. April 2025 / Q1 2025]
Stage: [e.g. Seed, Series A]
Board audience: [brief description e.g. 2 investors, 1 independent chair, 1 observer]

--- FINANCIALS ---
Revenue this period (actual vs. target): [e.g. £82k actual vs. £95k target]
ARR or MRR (actual vs. target): [e.g. £984k ARR vs. £1.1M target]
Gross margin: [e.g. 71%]
Net burn this period: [e.g. £118k]
Cash in bank: [e.g. £740k]
Runway at current burn: [e.g. 6.3 months]
Notes on financials (optional): [any context — one-off costs, timing effects, etc.]

--- KPI TABLE ---
List 3–6 key metrics in this format, one per line:
Metric name | Target | Actual | vs. Last Period | G/A/R
[example: New MRR | £45k | £31k | -£8k | R]
[example: Churn rate | <2% | 1.8% | -0.3pp | G]
[add your metrics here]

--- WINS ---
List 2–3 specific wins with numbers. Avoid vague statements.
[WIN 1: e.g. Closed Hartwell Group at £18k ARR — our largest deal to date, 3 months shorter sales cycle than average]
[WIN 2: e.g. Launched self-serve onboarding; activation rate lifted from 34% to 61% in the first two weeks]
[WIN 3 — optional]

--- LOWLIGHTS ---
List 1–2 misses. For each, state: what missed, why it missed, and what you are doing about it.
Do not soften, hedge, or minimise. State the facts plainly.
[LOWLIGHT 1: What missed — Why — Remediation]
[LOWLIGHT 2 — optional]

--- DECISIONS NEEDED ---
List each decision the board needs to make or weigh in on. For each, state:
- The decision as a direct question
- Brief context (2–3 sentences)
- Management's recommendation
[DECISION 1]
[DECISION 2 — if applicable]

--- 30-DAY PRIORITIES ---
List 3–5 specific priorities for the next 30 days with an owner where relevant.
[PRIORITY 1]
[PRIORITY 2]
[PRIORITY 3]
[PRIORITY 4 — optional]
[PRIORITY 5 — optional]

--- OPTIONAL: TEAM AND HIRING ---
[Any headcount changes, key hires closed, open roles, or org changes — or leave blank]

---

OUTPUT INSTRUCTIONS:

Produce the board update with exactly these 8 sections in this order:

1. TL;DR
Three bullets only. Cover: (1) overall health signal in plain language, (2) the single most significant positive development this period, (3) the single most significant risk or the most urgent decision needed. No more than 20 words per bullet. Do not pad or qualify.

2. Financial Summary
A table with these columns: Metric | Target | Actual | Variance | Signal
Rows: Revenue, ARR/MRR, Gross Margin, Net Burn, Cash, Runway. Use Green / Amber / Red in the Signal column. Follow with a maximum of 3 sentences of plain-language commentary on the financials. Do not repeat what the table already shows.

3. KPI Dashboard
A table with these columns: Metric | Target | Actual | vs. Last Period | Signal (G/A/R)
Convert the G/A/R inputs to full words: Green, Amber, Red. Add one sentence below the table noting the most critical metric requiring attention.

4. Wins
2–3 bullet points. Each must include a specific number or quantified outcome. Do not use superlatives or promotional language ('crushed', 'incredible', 'huge'). Write as a CFO reporting facts, not a founder celebrating. Maximum 40 words per bullet.

5. Lowlights and Mitigations
For each lowlight: state the miss as a fact (metric or event), state the root cause directly, state the specific remediation action and who owns it and by when. Do not use hedging language ('somewhat', 'slightly', 'unfortunately we fell short of'). Do not bury a miss in passive voice. Maximum 150 words total for this section.

6. Decisions Needed
For each decision: write the question as a direct, unambiguous sentence ending in a question mark. Follow with 2–3 sentences of context. Close with 'Management recommendation:' and state it clearly. If there are no decisions to bring to the board this period, write: 'No board decisions required this period. This update is for information only.'

7. Team and Hiring
If input was provided: max 75 words, factual and specific. If input was blank: omit this section entirely.

8. Priorities: Next 30 Days
3–5 bullet points. Each should be a specific, outcome-oriented action — not a vague intent. Include the owner in parentheses where provided.

TONE CONSTRAINTS — apply throughout:
- Professional and direct. Not formal legal language. Not casual.
- No hedging verbs on bad news: forbidden phrases include 'somewhat underperformed', 'fell slightly short', 'unfortunately we missed', 'we are working to address'
- No promotional language on good news: forbidden phrases include 'crushed it', 'incredible results', 'the team really delivered', 'super excited'
- No filler phrases: 'it is worth noting', 'needless to say', 'as you know', 'at the end of the day'
- If any input placeholder appears to contain vague or unquantified data (e.g. a win with no number), add a parenthetical note: '[Note: add a specific metric here before sending]'
- Write as a mature CFO drafting on behalf of the founder — not a founder writing about themselves
whatItIsFor: A startup founder pastes this into Claude.ai or ChatGPT to generate a structured, governance-quality board update covering financials, KPIs, wins, honest lowlights, decisions needed, and next-period priorities. Produces a consistent, reusable document — not an investor newsletter — that builds board trust through radical transparency and a clear decision-forward structure.
howToUseIt: Fill in every section between the --- markers before pasting into the chat. Replace every [PLACEHOLDER] with your real data. The more specific your inputs — particularly for Lowlights and Decisions Needed — the more useful the output will be. For Wins, include at least one number per bullet or the AI will flag it. For KPIs, use the exact format shown (pipe-separated, with your G/A/R rating). After the AI generates the update, read the Lowlights section first: if it sounds softer than the raw facts you typed in, ask the AI to 'rewrite the lowlights section with no hedging — state each miss as a plain fact'. The document is designed to be reused monthly — keep a copy of your filled-in input template and update the numbers each period.
exampleOutput:
[CLAUDE]
Claude is the strongest platform for this use case. It handles multi-section structured documents reliably, respects per-section word limits, and follows nuanced constraints like 'no hedging language' consistently throughout a long output. Claude is particularly good at the Decisions Needed section — it tends to produce well-reasoned 'management recommendation' language that sounds like a CFO, not a founder. If your lowlights input is vague, Claude will flag it with a parenthetical note rather than inventing detail. Recommended workflow: paste the filled prompt into a new Claude.ai conversation, review the output, then use follow-up messages to refine specific sections ('rewrite section 5 with sharper language on the root cause').

[CHATGPT]
ChatGPT (GPT-4o) produces solid first drafts quickly and follows the fill-in-the-blank structure well. Two known tendencies to watch for: (1) it runs 20–30% longer than the word guidance specifies — if sections are too long, add 'Tighten each section to the word limit specified. Cut anything that does not add new information.' (2) it tends toward slightly promotional language in the Wins section even with tone constraints — if you see phrases like 'the team delivered exceptional results', add: 'Rewrite the Wins section. Remove any superlatives or team-praise language. Report the facts only, as a CFO would.' GPT-4o handles markdown tables reliably; if you are using an older model, the KPI table may need manual formatting.

[PERPLEXITY]
Perplexity is not suited to generating this document — its strength is web search and citation, not structured document drafting. Use Perplexity only as a pre-step: if you need industry benchmark KPIs to contextualise your own metrics (e.g. 'What is typical SaaS net revenue retention at $1M ARR?'), ask Perplexity first, then paste those benchmarks as additional context into the KPI section before running this prompt in Claude or ChatGPT. Do not attempt to generate the full board update in Perplexity.
