title: Startup Board Update Writer — Pre-Fundraise Board Update (Investor-Ready)
body:
You are an experienced board communications advisor helping a startup founder write a board update in the 1–2 months before a fundraise. This update will be seen by existing board members and may be shared with prospective investors during due diligence. It must therefore be both governance-quality and fundraise-ready: honest about the current state, clear on trajectory, and framed around the narrative an investor needs to build conviction.

In addition to the standard 8 sections, add a 9th section at the end:

9. Fundraise Update
- Round details: amount, structure, timeline
- Pipeline status (number of investors engaged, stages they are at — no names unless appropriate)
- Key open questions or risks in the raise
- What the board can do to help

--- COMPANY CONTEXT ---
Company name: [COMPANY_NAME]
Period covered: [PERIOD]
Stage: [STAGE]
Board audience: [BOARD_COMPOSITION]

--- FINANCIALS ---
[REVENUE] | [ARR] | [MARGIN] | [BURN] | [CASH] | [RUNWAY]

--- KPI TABLE ---
[Metric | Target | Actual | vs. Last Period | G/A/R]

--- WINS ---
[2–3 wins with numbers]

--- LOWLIGHTS ---
[1–2 misses: what, why, remediation]

--- DECISIONS NEEDED ---
[Include any decisions related to the fundraise]

--- 30-DAY PRIORITIES ---
[3–5 priorities — include fundraise milestones]

--- FUNDRAISE DETAILS ---
Amount raising: [AMOUNT]
Round structure: [e.g. SAFE at £6M cap / Priced seed round]
Target close date: [DATE]
Investors engaged: [NUMBER and rough stage — e.g. '8 VCs, 3 at term sheet stage, 2 passed']
Board asks: [What specifically do you need from the board to close the round]

Tone: same governance standards as a standard board update. Do not inflate or 'sell' the fundraise section — present the pipeline with the same directness as the lowlights section.
whatItIsFor: The 1–3 board updates immediately before or during an active fundraise, where the board update doubles as a data room document that prospective lead investors may review
howToUseIt: Fill in every section between the --- markers before pasting into the chat. Replace every [PLACEHOLDER] with your real data. title: Startup Brand Messaging Guide
body:
You are a senior brand strategist and copywriter with 15 years of experience helping early-stage B2B and B2C startups build brand messaging from scratch. Your job is to produce a complete, usable brand messaging guide — not a framework essay, not a list of questions, and not generic advice. Write the guide itself.

--- COMPANY BRIEF ---
Company name: [COMPANY_NAME]
What it does: [PRODUCT_OR_SERVICE — one sentence describing what it does and for whom]
Target customer: [TARGET_CUSTOMER — job title, description, or type of person/business]
The problem it solves: [SPECIFIC_PAIN_POINT — what frustration or cost does this remove?]
Key differentiator vs. [COMPETITOR_NAME]: [WHAT_YOU_DO_THAT_THEY_DON'T_OR_DO_DIFFERENTLY]
Brand voice direction — 3 to 5 adjectives: [VOICE_ADJECTIVE_1], [VOICE_ADJECTIVE_2], [VOICE_ADJECTIVE_3], [VOICE_ADJECTIVE_4 — optional], [VOICE_ADJECTIVE_5 — optional]
Things to avoid sounding like: [E.G. corporate, hype-y, overly technical, consultant-speak]

--- TASK ---
Write a complete brand messaging guide as a working reference document. Cover every section in the checklist below, in order. Do not add commentary, preamble, or framework explanations — just write the guide. Do not use generic corporate language (leverage, synergy, innovative, cutting-edge, disruptive, at the intersection of, best-in-class, world-class, holistic, scalable solutions, empower, revolutionise).

--- OUTPUT CHECKLIST ---

1. BRAND VOICE
Define 3 to 4 voice characteristics based on the adjectives provided. For each one:
- Name the characteristic (one word or short phrase)
- Explain what it means in practice for this company specifically (2 sentences)
- Write a DO sentence: a real example of copy that embodies it
- Write a DON'T sentence: a real example of copy that violates it

2. TONE BY CHANNEL
Produce a table with these six rows: Homepage hero, About page, Cold outreach email, LinkedIn post, Job description, Sales one-pager.
Columns: Channel | Tone setting (3–4 words) | Vocabulary register (formal/plain/conversational/technical) | Sample opening line
The sample opening line must be specific to [COMPANY_NAME] — not a generic template.

3. ELEVATOR PITCH
One tight paragraph, 40–55 words, written for verbal use (a conversation, not a slide). It must name the problem, name the solution, name who it is for, and state what makes it different from [COMPETITOR_NAME]. Do not start with "We are" or the company name.

4. TAGLINES
Five options:
- Two short (5 words or fewer)
- Two medium (6–12 words)
- One question format
Each tagline must be differentiated from [COMPETITOR_NAME]'s positioning — no tagline should work equally well for a competitor.

5. MESSAGING HIERARCHY
Format as an indented tree:

Core Brand Promise (one sentence — the single idea the whole company stands behind)
  Pillar 1: [one sentence — first strategic reason to believe the promise]
    → Proof point A (specific, concrete claim or example)
    → Proof point B (specific, concrete claim or example)
  Pillar 2: [one sentence — second strategic reason to believe the promise]
    → Proof point A
    → Proof point B
  Pillar 3: [one sentence — third strategic reason to believe the promise]
    → Proof point A
    → Proof point B

6. WORD BANK
Two lists:
- USE THESE: 8–10 words or short phrases that fit the brand voice and feel specific to this company's world
- AVOID THESE: 6–8 words or phrases that would undermine the voice, including any that would make [COMPANY_NAME] sound like a generic startup or like [COMPETITOR_NAME]
whatItIsFor: An early-stage founder pastes this into Claude.ai, ChatGPT, or Perplexity to generate a complete brand messaging reference document — covering brand voice, tone by channel, elevator pitch, taglines, messaging hierarchy, and a word bank. Output is ready to hand to a copywriter, contractor, or new hire on day one.
howToUseIt: Fill in every [PLACEHOLDER] before pasting. The more specific your inputs — especially the differentiator and the pain point — the more distinctive and usable the output will be. After the AI generates the guide, read the elevator pitch aloud: if any sentence trips you up or sounds like a press release rather than a person talking, ask the AI to rewrite it. For the taglines, shortlist two or three and test them on someone outside your company — the one they remember 60 seconds later is usually the winner. If the output feels too long for one session (common on ChatGPT free tier), split it: request sections 1–3 first, then follow up with 'now write sections 4–6 using the same company brief'.

[CLAUDE]
Claude handles long, structured prompts well and will produce all six sections in a single response without truncating. Explicit section headers in the prompt (1. BRAND VOICE, 2. TONE BY CHANNEL, etc.) map directly to output headers — Claude treats the numbered checklist as a contract and works through it in order. If any section feels shallow, follow up with 'Expand section [X] — add more specificity to the [COMPANY_NAME] context'. Claude is particularly strong at the 'do / don't' sentence pairs in the Brand Voice section and will write examples that feel genuinely specific rather than generic.

[CHATGPT]

Here is your brand messaging guide…' — add 'Skip any preamble and go directly to section 1' to prevent this; (2) it may truncate on long outputs if using GPT-4o mini or the free tier — if it stops early, reply 'Continue from section [X]' to resume. title: Startup Cash Flow Narrative
body:
You are a fractional CFO who specialises in translating startup finances into plain English for founders, boards, and investors. Your job is not just to analyse numbers — it is to help me tell a clear, honest story about our cash position and what we are doing about it.

Define any financial term the first time you use it. Do not soften bad news. Be honest, but always frame the position with what we control and what we are doing about it.

**Audience**
My audience for this narrative is: [AUDIENCE — e.g. seed investors / our board of directors / my co-founders / myself for internal planning]

Adapt the tone, framing, and emphasis to what this audience cares about most:
- Investors: signals of control, trajectory, and a clear path to the next milestone
- Board: accountability, scenario awareness, and decision inputs
- Co-founders / internal: direct operational clarity, no investor framing needed

**Business Context**
- Business type: [BUSINESS_TYPE — e.g. B2B SaaS, marketplace, e-commerce, services]
- Stage: [STAGE — e.g. pre-revenue, seed, Series A]
- Funding history: [FUNDING_HISTORY — e.g. bootstrapped / raised $800k seed 10 months ago]
- What has changed recently: [RECENT_CHANGES — e.g. hired two engineers last month, lost our largest customer, closed a new enterprise deal, launched a new pricing tier]

**Cash Position**
- Cash in bank right now: [CASH — e.g. $340,000]
- Monthly net burn (cash out minus cash in): [NET_BURN — e.g. $52,000/month]
- Runway at current burn: [RUNWAY — e.g. ~6.5 months]
- Key drivers of spend this month: [COST_DRIVERS — e.g. payroll $38k, cloud hosting $7k, contractor fees $4k, marketing $3k]
- Key drivers of revenue or inflows: [REVENUE_DRIVERS — e.g. MRR $18k from 45 customers, one-off consulting $5k]
- Any expected changes to burn or revenue in the next 90 days: [UPCOMING_CHANGES — e.g. two new hires starting next month adding $14k/month, enterprise deal worth $8k/month expected to close in 6 weeks]

**Please produce the following:**

1. **Plain-English Position Summary** (2–3 paragraphs)
Write a flowing, human-readable narrative of our current cash position: where we are, why we are here, and what we are doing about it. Write it so the audience above would fully understand it without any financial training. Do not use bullet points in this section — prose only.

2. **What Is Driving This** (decomposition)
For each major item in our cost or revenue picture, explain:
- What is causing it
- Whether it is structural (recurring and permanent), a timing issue (temporary), or an investable spend (expected to generate return)
Keep each explanation to 2–3 sentences. Use plain English, no jargon.

3. **Levers to Extend Runway** (ranked by impact and speed)
List the top 4 levers available to us. For each lever:
- Name the action clearly
- Estimate the impact in weeks or months of additional runway, or in dollars of monthly burn reduction
- State how quickly this lever could realistically take effect (e.g. immediately, within 2 weeks, within 60 days)
- Note whether it is low-risk or involves a meaningful trade-off
Rank them: most impactful first. If a lever is fast but small, note that. If a lever is large but slow, note that too.

4. **90-Day Scenarios**
Write three short scenarios (3–5 sentences each) — no tables:
- **Base case**: current trajectory with no major changes
- **Upside case**: if [UPCOMING_CHANGES or the most likely positive assumption] plays out as hoped
- **Downside case**: if a realistic risk materialises (name the specific risk based on our context)
For each scenario, state where we would end up at the 90-day mark in plain English.

5. **One-Sentence Answer**
Write one sentence I can use verbally to answer the question "How long is your runway?" honestly and confidently when speaking directly to [AUDIENCE]. It should be factual, calm, and forward-looking — not defensive.
whatItIsFor: A non-finance founder pastes their cash position, burn rate, runway, and cost context into Claude.ai, ChatGPT, or Perplexity and receives a plain-English narrative about their current cash position, what is driving the numbers, the highest-impact levers to pull, and a 90-day scenario (base, upside, downside) — all adapted to the specified audience (investor, board, or co-founder).
howToUseIt: Fill in every [PLACEHOLDER] with your actual information before pasting. If you do not have an exact number, use your best estimate and note it — write 'approximately $45k' rather than leaving the field blank. The more specific your RECENT_CHANGES and UPCOMING_CHANGES, the more accurate the narrative and scenarios will be. Paste the completed prompt into Claude.ai, ChatGPT, or Perplexity as a single message. If your situation is complex (e.g. a bridge round alongside a runway crisis), add 'Ask me any clarifying questions before writing the narrative' at the end of the prompt.

[CLAUDE]
Claude is the strongest platform for this prompt. It handles long structured prompts with mixed narrative and numbers well, maintains prose coherence across sections, and will proactively flag inconsistencies — for example, if the stated runway does not match the cash and burn figures you provided. Claude is also the most likely of the three platforms to ask a clarifying question if your data is ambiguous, which matters when financial errors are high-stakes. Use the prompt as written in a single message. For a deeper dive on any section, follow up with 'Expand on the levers section' or 'Rewrite the position summary for a co-founder audience instead.'

[CHATGPT]
Works well with GPT-4o or later. ChatGPT produces polished, investor-ready prose and responds well to explicit tone direction. If you want candid rather than diplomatic framing, add 'Do not soften bad news — be direct' at the end of the prompt, as GPT-4o has a tendency to hedge negative findings. If you have Advanced Data Analysis enabled, you can upload your actual spreadsheet or accounting export directly rather than transcribing numbers manually — this eliminates transcription errors and allows the model to work from real data. For the narrative sections specifically, GPT-4o's prose quality is excellent.

[PERPLEXITY]
Perplexity is not the primary tool for this prompt, but it is highly effective as a pre-step. Before running the main prompt, ask Perplexity: 'What is a healthy burn rate, burn multiple, and runway for a [stage] [business type] startup in 2026?' The cited benchmarks give you real market context to paste into your RECENT_CHANGES or UPCOMING_CHANGES fields, and they help you frame whether your numbers are at, above, or below market — which matters significantly when the audience is investors or a board.

**Numbers**
- Cash available: [CASH]
- Monthly burn (net): [NET_BURN]
- Runway: [RUNWAY]
- Main things we are spending on: [COST_DRIVERS]
- Main sources of revenue or income: [REVENUE_DRIVERS]
- Anything expected to change in the next 90 days: [UPCOMING_CHANGES]

Please produce:
1. A 2-paragraph plain summary of where we stand — written as if you are speaking directly to us around a table, not presenting to an outsider.
2. The top 3 levers we should discuss as co-founders. For each: what the action is, how much runway it adds or burn it cuts, and what the real trade-off is (e.g. slower growth, team morale, product delays).
3. A recommendation on which lever to pull first and why — your honest opinion, not a balanced 'it depends' answer.
4. One sentence capturing what we need to agree on by the end of this conversation.

Quantify everything in weeks or dollars. Do not use percentages unless they are more intuitive than the absolute number.
whatItIsFor: Co-founding teams who need to align on their cash reality and make operational decisions together, without investor-facing polish.
howToUseIt: Fill in every [PLACEHOLDER] with your actual information before pasting. The more specific your RECENT_CHANGES and UPCOMING_CHANGES, the more accurate the narrative and scenarios will be. Paste the completed prompt into Claude.ai, ChatGPT, or Perplexity as a single message. If your situation is complex (e.g. a bridge round alongside a runway crisis), add 'Ask me any clarifying questions before writing the narrative' at the end of the prompt.

title: Startup Cold Sales Email
body:
You are an outbound sales copywriter helping a startup founder write a personalised cold email to a prospective customer.

Write a cold outreach email using the details below. Do not invent details I have not provided.

---

WHAT WE DO
[PRODUCT] — one sentence describing what it does and who it is for

OUTCOME / PROOF POINT
[OUTCOME] — a specific result or metric, e.g. "cut customer onboarding time by 40%" or "used by Acme and BuildCo"

PROSPECT
Name: [PROSPECT NAME]
Role: [PROSPECT ROLE]
Company: [PROSPECT COMPANY]

PERSONALISATION TRIGGER
[TRIGGER] — one specific, real detail about this prospect: a recent hire, funding round, LinkedIn post, job listing, product launch, or press mention

ASK
[ASK] — what you want from this email, e.g. "a 15-minute call to see if there is a fit"

---

CONSTRAINTS
- Under 120 words (body only, not subject line)
- Open with the personalisation trigger or the outcome we deliver — not with any generic greeting
- Tone: direct, human, confident — not salesy, not enthusiastic
- Frame the value as a business outcome, not a feature list
- One CTA only, phrased as a yes/no question the prospect can answer in one reply
- Subject line under 8 words
- Do NOT use any of these phrases: "just wanted to reach out", "I hope this finds you well", "I came across your profile", "game-changing", "revolutionary", "disruptive", "cutting-edge", "innovative", "excited to share", "thrilled to", "synergies", "value-add", "best-in-class", "would love to connect", "let me know your thoughts", "touch base", "circle back", "at the end of the day", "move the needle"
- Return only the subject line and email body. No commentary, no alternatives, no explanation.

OUTPUT FORMAT
Subject: [subject line — under 8 words]

[email body]
whatItIsFor: A startup founder doing outbound sales needs a personalised cold email draft — under 150 words, value-led, with a low-friction CTA — that they can generate quickly for each prospect by filling in five fields.
howToUseIt: Copy the entire prompt into Claude.ai, ChatGPT, or Perplexity.
Replace each [PLACEHOLDER] with your real details. Fill in all five fields — do not leave any blank.
For [TRIGGER], use one specific, real detail about this prospect. If you do not have one, use Perplexity first to find recent news, hires, or LinkedIn posts for the prospect's company.
For [OUTCOME], use a number or a named customer if you have one. 'We help companies grow' is not an outcome.
Submit the prompt and receive a subject line and email body.
Read the output and rewrite one or two lines in your own voice before sending — AI-generated copy is easy to spot when sent unedited.

[CLAUDE_AI]
Claude follows multi-part structured prompts reliably — word limits, tone rules, banned phrases, and output format are all respected in a single turn. If your value proposition is vague, Claude may ask a clarifying question rather than inventing details; treat this as useful feedback and tighten the [PRODUCT] or [OUTCOME] field. Paste the full prompt as a single block. You do not need role-play framing ('act as a founder') — direct instruction works better.

[CHATGPT]
ChatGPT (GPT-4o) produces fluent first drafts quickly and is good for generating variants. Add 'Return only the email. No commentary, no alternatives, no explanation.' at the end of the prompt — this is already included but emphasise it if you get meta-output. If the output runs over 120 words, follow up with: 'Cut this to under 100 words. Keep the trigger, the outcome, and the CTA. Remove everything else.' Role framing ('You are an outbound sales copywriter') helps anchor directness.

[PERPLEXITY]
Perplexity is best used as a research step, not a writing step. Use it to find the personalisation trigger (recent news, hires, LinkedIn posts) for each prospect, then paste that output into the main prompt in Claude or ChatGPT. The variation 'Two-step: Perplexity research then write' documents this workflow. If you use Perplexity for the full prompt, keep your inputs short and expect to trim the output significantly — it tends toward an informational rather than persuasive register.

title: Startup Competitive Analysis
body:
Act as a senior strategy analyst preparing competitive intelligence for a startup investor pitch.

- Product: [PRODUCT_DESCRIPTION — 2-3 sentences on what it does and how]

- Stage: [STAGE — e.g. pre-seed, seed, Series A] | Geography: [GEOGRAPHY — e.g. US, global, UK]

Competitors to analyse (add or remove as needed):
- Direct: [COMPETITOR_1], [COMPETITOR_2], [COMPETITOR_3]
- Indirect / substitutes: [INDIRECT_COMPETITOR_1], [INDIRECT_COMPETITOR_2]

For each competitor, analyse these dimensions:
1. Pricing model (how they charge and approximate price points if known)
2. Core features / capabilities
3. Primary target segment
4. Go-to-market motion (how they acquire customers)
5. Positioning / messaging angle (how they describe themselves)
6. Known weaknesses or customer complaints
7. Funding stage / scale

Then provide:
**A. Competitive Landscape Table** — format as a markdown table with competitors as rows and the 7 dimensions as columns.

**B. Strategic Narrative** (3-4 paragraphs) — summarise the competitive landscape, identify how competitors cluster, and explain where the meaningful whitespace lies.

**C. My Differentiation Opportunity** — in 3-5 bullet points, describe the most defensible positioning gap my startup can credibly occupy and why.

**D. Top 3 Competitive Threats** — the most likely scenarios where a competitor could undercut or outflank my position in the next 18-24 months.

Important: If you are not confident about specific data points (e.g. exact pricing, funding amount, specific features), say so explicitly rather than inventing details. Use "[unconfirmed]" to flag uncertain information.

title: Startup Competitive Analysis — Jobs-to-Be-Done Whitespace Finder
body:

title: Customer Discovery Interview Question Generator
body:
You are an expert startup researcher trained in the Mom Test (Rob Fitzpatrick) and the Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD) framework. Your job is to generate sharp, behaviour-anchoring customer discovery interview questions — the kind a trained qualitative researcher would be proud to ask.

Here is my hypothesis:
- Target customer: [TARGET_CUSTOMER] (be specific — e.g. "solo freelance designers billing under $10k/month", not just "designers")
- Assumed problem: [ASSUMED_PROBLEM] (what you believe they struggle with)
- My proposed solution: [SOLUTION_DESCRIPTION] (what you're building or considering)
- Current stage: [STAGE] (e.g. pre-product, MVP, post-launch)

Generate 12–15 customer discovery interview questions I can use in a 30–45 minute call. Follow these rules without exception:

1. Ask only about PAST BEHAVIOUR — never about hypothetical future behaviour. Use "the last time" or "tell me about a time when" framing.
2. Do NOT reveal, hint at, or reference my solution in any question.
3. No leading questions. No opinion questions. No compliment-fishing.
4. Prefer "how" and "what" questions over "why" questions.
5. Every question must be capable of producing a surprising or invalidating answer.

Format your output as follows:

**RAPPORT & CONTEXT (2 questions)**
[Questions to open the call and establish the customer's relevant context]

**PROBLEM EXPLORATION (5–6 questions)**
[Questions that surface the depth, frequency, and emotional weight of the problem]

**CURRENT SOLUTIONS & WORKAROUNDS (3–4 questions)**
[Questions that reveal how they solve this today, what they've tried, what they've paid for]

**CLOSING (1–2 questions)**
[Questions to surface anything unexpected and close warmly]

After the questions, add a brief section: **INTERVIEWER NOTES** — 3 bullet points reminding me what to watch for during the call (signals of a real problem vs. polite interest).
whatItIsFor: Generate a tailored set of 12–15 customer discovery interview questions for a startup founder preparing to validate (or invalidate) their core hypothesis about a target customer, problem, and solution.
howToUseIt: Fill in the four [PLACEHOLDER] values with specifics about your startup hypothesis — the narrower your target customer description, the sharper the questions. Paste the completed prompt into Claude.ai or ChatGPT and copy the generated questions into your interview guide. Before each call, re-read the INTERVIEWER NOTES section at the bottom of the output.

Claude follows explicit constraints faithfully — the numbered rules and strict formatting instructions work especially well here. If you want Claude to be even more rigorous, add: 'If any question you generate is hypothetical or leading, rewrite it before showing it to me.' You can also paste in prior interview notes and ask Claude to adjust questions based on what you've already learned.

[CHATGPT]
ChatGPT (GPT-4o) may generate more questions than requested — add 'Stop at exactly 14 questions, no more' if you need a hard cap. It handles follow-up conversation well, so after the initial output try: 'Rewrite question 7 so it probes the emotional cost more directly.' ChatGPT also performs well if you ask it to roleplay as an interviewer and test the questions against a synthetic persona.

[PERPLEXITY]
Perplexity is less suited to generating the questions themselves. Use it in the research phase instead: search 'customer complaints about [problem area] site:reddit.com' to validate your problem hypothesis before writing the prompt. Then switch to Claude or ChatGPT for question generation.

title: Startup Customer Persona Builder (ICP)
body:
Act as a senior B2B customer research analyst. You have spent a decade building Ideal Customer Profiles for early-stage startups using the Jobs-to-be-Done framework and the trigger-event model. Your job is to take the raw data a founder provides about their early customers, synthesise it into a structured ICP document, fill gaps with reasoned inference, and be explicit about which is which.

Anything you state that is not directly supported by the data I provide below must be marked [inferred]. Do not present invented details as facts.

---

## WHAT I KNOW ABOUT MY CUSTOMERS

**My product:**
[PRODUCT — 2-3 sentences: what it does, how it works, and what problem it solves]

**Who I've sold to so far (describe your best 2-5 customers — anonymise if needed):**
[CUSTOMERS — e.g. "A 40-person logistics SaaS company in the US, seed-funded. Their ops director found us via LinkedIn. Deal closed in 3 weeks at $8k/year."]

**Market / industry:**
[MARKET — e.g. "B2B SaaS companies at seed to Series A, 10-100 employees, US and UK"]

**Pain points I know they had before buying:**
[PAIN_POINTS — what were they struggling with? Quote real words if you have them.]

**What triggered them to look for a solution when they did:**
[TRIGGER — e.g. "hired a new head of sales", "just closed a funding round", "lost a big deal due to slow response times"]

**Objections they raised before buying:**
[OBJECTIONS — what did they push back on? Price, timing, trust, integration, ROI?]

**Anything else you know (optional):** deal sizes, sales cycle length, who else was in the buying decision, where they heard about you, early churn signals
[ADDITIONAL_CONTEXT]

---

## OUTPUT FORMAT

Produce the following sections in order:

### ONE-SENTENCE ICP SUMMARY
A single crisp sentence usable in a pitch deck or job description: "[My product] is the right fit for [specific company type] when [trigger event or condition], typically sold to [buyer role]."

### SECTION 1 — IDEAL CUSTOMER PROFILE (Company)
Describe the company that is most likely to buy, stay, and succeed. Cover:
- **Firmographics:** industry, company size (headcount and revenue range), geography, funding stage, tech stack signals
- **Organisational triggers:** the specific events or changes that make them urgently ready to buy right now (rank the top 3)
- **Deal economics:** typical deal size, sales cycle length, budget authority, who else is in the buying decision
- **Strategic fit signals:** 3-5 characteristics that make a prospect a strong fit beyond the basics

### SECTION 2 — BUYER PERSONA (The Person)
Create a named persona — give them a realistic first name, job title, and a one-line company context. Then cover:
- **A day in their life:** 3-4 sentences describing their typical workday and the pressures they face
- **Top 3 goals** (professional outcomes they are measured on or care about most)
- **Top 3 daily frustrations** (the specific pains your product addresses)
- **Fears and risks:** what could go wrong for them personally if they choose your product and it fails
- **Trusted sources:** where they go to learn, stay current, and evaluate tools (publications, communities, influencers, events)
- **Buying process:** how they typically discover, evaluate, and approve a new tool — who else is involved
- **What makes them champion this internally:** what they need to feel confident presenting this to their manager or team

### SECTION 3 — TOP OBJECTIONS AND HOW TO ADDRESS THEM
List the 3 most common objections this persona raises before buying, and for each:
- The underlying concern behind the objection
- The most credible response a founder can give

### SECTION 4 — DISQUALIFIERS (Bad-Fit Signals)
List 5 characteristics of prospects that look like the ICP on paper but consistently fail to convert, struggle with the product, or churn early. These are the signals a founder or salesperson should use to exit a deal early.

### SECTION 5 — WHERE TO FIND AND REACH THEM
- Top 3 channels where this persona discovers new tools
- Top 3 communities or watering holes (subreddits, Slack groups, LinkedIn communities, events, newsletters)
- One sentence on the message framing most likely to resonate at first contact

---

Keep each section tight and scannable. Use bullet points within sections. Mark every claim not supported by the data I provided with [inferred].
whatItIsFor: A founder who has made their first sales but has never formalised who their ideal customer is pastes this into Claude.ai, ChatGPT, or Perplexity to get a complete ICP document — company profile, named buyer persona, trigger events, objections, and disqualifiers — ready to hand to a new salesperson, drop into a pitch deck, or use to qualify leads.
howToUseIt: Fill in all [PLACEHOLDER] fields before pasting. The quality of the output is directly proportional to the quality of what you put in — even rough notes about your real customers will dramatically outperform leaving fields blank. If you have not yet made any sales, fill in your hypotheses and the AI will frame the output as a hypothesis to test rather than a confirmed profile. After generating, use the [inferred] markers to build your customer interview agenda: those are exactly the gaps your next 5 conversations should fill.
exampleOutput:
[CLAUDE]
This is the recommended platform for this prompt. Claude follows the [inferred] flagging instruction reliably throughout long outputs — a constraint that ChatGPT occasionally drops by the end of a long response. Claude's large context window means you can paste substantial raw material directly into the ADDITIONAL_CONTEXT field: interview transcripts, CRM export snippets, competitor G2 review excerpts, or email threads with early customers. Claude will synthesise all of it. For best results, paste real quotes from customers into the PAIN_POINTS and TRIGGER fields — Claude will anchor on specific language and produce more grounded output.

[CHATGPT]
Works well and produces vivid, narrative-rich personas that are easy to share with a team. **Market / category:**
[MARKET — e.g. "personal finance apps for millennials", "fitness products for new parents"]

**What they were struggling with before:**
[PAIN_POINTS — what was the problem they were living with? Use their own words if possible.]

**What triggered them to act when they did:**

title: Startup Financial Model Explainer
body:
You are a startup CFO and advisor who specialises in explaining finances to non-finance founders. Your job is to take my numbers, calculate the key metrics, explain what they mean in plain English, and tell me what an investor will think when they see them.

Please define any financial term the first time you use it.

**My Startup Context**
- Business type: [BUSINESS_TYPE — e.g. B2B SaaS, marketplace, e-commerce, services]
- Stage: [STAGE — e.g. pre-revenue, seed, Series A]
- Funding status: [FUNDING_STATUS — e.g. bootstrapped, raised $500k seed, raising Series A]
- All numbers below are monthly unless stated otherwise

**My Numbers**
- Monthly Revenue (MRR): [MONTHLY_REVENUE]
- Monthly Operating Costs: [MONTHLY_COSTS]
- Cash in Bank: [CASH_IN_BANK]
- Number of Paying Customers: [CUSTOMER_COUNT]
- New Customers Acquired Last Month: [NEW_CUSTOMERS_LAST_MONTH]
- Marketing/Sales Spend Last Month: [ACQUISITION_SPEND]
- Average Revenue Per Customer Per Month: [ARPU]
- Monthly Customer Churn Rate: [CHURN_RATE — e.g. 3%]
- Gross Margin: [GROSS_MARGIN — e.g. 65%]
- MRR Growth Rate (Month-over-Month): [MOM_GROWTH_RATE]

**Please do the following:**

1. **Calculate these metrics from my numbers** (show the formula and result for each):
   - Net Burn Rate
   - Runway (months)
   - Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)
   - Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)
   - LTV:CAC Ratio
   - CAC Payback Period (months)

2. **Plain-English health check**: In 3–5 sentences, summarise the overall financial health of my business. Use a traffic-light rating (Green / Amber / Red) for each metric and explain why.

3. **Investor perspective**: List the 5 most likely questions a seed or Series A investor would ask about these numbers. For each question, briefly tell me what answer they are hoping to hear and whether my numbers support that answer.

4. **Warning flags**: Identify any metrics that are concerning or critical. Explain the risk in plain English and give a rough sense of how urgent it is.

5. **Top 3 actions**: Based on these numbers, what are the three most important things I should do in the next 90 days to improve my financial position? Be specific and prioritised.

Format your response with clear headers for each section. Keep explanations concise — I want insight, not a textbook.
whatItIsFor: A non-finance founder pastes their basic startup numbers (revenue, costs, cash, customer metrics) into Claude.ai or ChatGPT and receives a plain-English explanation of their financial health, key metrics, investor red flags, and prioritised actions.
howToUseIt: Fill in every [PLACEHOLDER] with your actual numbers before pasting. If you do not have a number (e.g. churn rate is not yet tracked), write 'unknown' or 'not tracked yet' — the AI will note what it cannot calculate and why that gap matters. Paste the completed prompt directly into Claude.ai, ChatGPT, or another AI chat interface and send as a single message.

title: Startup Go-to-Market Strategy
body:
Act as a senior GTM strategist and Head of Growth who has taken five early-stage startups from zero to their first 50 paying customers. You are opinionated — you make choices, not lists — and you calibrate advice directly to the resources available. A plan for a solo founder with no budget looks completely different from one for a five-person team with runway to spend.

My startup:
- Product: [PRODUCT — 2 sentences: what it does and who it's built for]
- GTM motion: [MOTION — choose one: B2B sales-led / B2B product-led / B2C / marketplace]
- Target customer (your best guess): [ICP_HYPOTHESIS — be specific, e.g. "ops managers at logistics companies with 50-500 employees"]
- Core problem solved: [PROBLEM — 1 sentence: the painful status quo your product replaces]
- Current traction: [TRACTION — choose one: no users yet / waitlist only / 1-5 paying customers / 6-20 paying customers / 20+ paying customers]
- Team size: [TEAM_SIZE — e.g. solo founder / 2 people / 5 people]
- Monthly acquisition budget: [BUDGET — e.g. $0 / $500 / $2,000 / $10,000]
- Geography: [GEOGRAPHY — e.g. US only / UK / global English-speaking]

Using this context, produce a structured GTM plan in the following sections. Work through them in order — ICP before channel, channel before messaging, messaging before plan.

---

**SECTION 1: BEACHHEAD ICP**
Define the single most winnable customer segment to focus on first. Include:
- Firmographic or demographic profile (industry, company size, role, or consumer profile — match to GTM motion)
- The trigger event that makes them actively looking for a solution right now
- Their current workaround and why it fails them
- Why this segment, not a broader or adjacent one, is the right beachhead for this stage

**SECTION 2: CORE MESSAGING**
- One-sentence value proposition (written for the buyer, not the product team — outcome-first, no jargon)
- Three proof points that back the value proposition (use placeholders if real data doesn't exist yet: "[INSERT: X% reduction in Y from beta user Z]")
- Primary objection this buyer will raise and a one-paragraph rebuttal

**SECTION 3: PRIMARY ACQUISITION CHANNEL**
Choose exactly ONE primary channel for the next 90 days. Do not list options — make the call and defend it based on the team size and budget provided.
- Primary channel: [name the channel and the specific tactic, e.g. not "outbound" but "cold LinkedIn DMs to VP Ops at 50-200 person logistics companies"]
- Why this channel fits this ICP, stage, and resource level
- What "good" looks like in 30 days on this channel (a leading metric with a specific target)
- One secondary channel to run in parallel at low effort
- Two channels to defer and why they don't fit right now

**SECTION 4: 90-DAY PHASED PLAN**
Three phases with concrete milestones and measurable KPIs. Calibrate ambition to the team size and budget provided — do not write a plan a solo founder cannot execute.

Phase 1 — Days 1-30: Foundation
- 3 priorities
- KPIs: [2-3 leading indicators with specific numeric targets]

Phase 2 — Days 31-60: First Traction
- 3 priorities
- KPIs: [2-3 metrics mixing leading and lagging indicators]

Phase 3 — Days 61-90: Optimise and Commit
- 3 priorities
- KPIs: [2-3 lagging indicators tied to revenue or retention]

**SECTION 5: PRICING ENTRY POINT**
What to charge the first 10 customers and why — including whether to offer a discount, pilot, or free tier at this stage, and what pricing signal to avoid sending.

**SECTION 6: FIRST-WEEK ACTION LIST**
Exactly 7 concrete tasks the founder can start on Monday morning. Number them. Each task must be completable in a single day or less. No vague actions — every item must name a specific deliverable or action (e.g. not "research competitors" but "list 20 companies matching the ICP in a spreadsheet using LinkedIn Sales Navigator filters").
whatItIsFor: A founder with a product ready to launch — or a handful of early customers — pastes this into Claude.ai, ChatGPT, or Perplexity to get a structured, prioritised 90-day GTM plan: a tight ICP definition, a single primary acquisition channel, phased milestones with KPIs, and a first-week action list they can execute immediately.
howToUseIt: Fill in every [PLACEHOLDER] before pasting — the more specific your inputs, the more actionable the output. The GTM motion field (B2B sales-led, B2B product-led, B2C, marketplace) is the single most important input: leave it vague and the plan will blend strategies that don't fit together. If your budget is genuinely zero, say so — the plan will shift to founder-led tactics that cost only time. After getting the initial output, use follow-up prompts to go deeper: 'Rewrite Section 2 assuming the buyer is a CFO, not an ops manager' or 'Give me 10 specific LinkedIn DM scripts for the primary channel in Section 3'.
exampleOutput:
[CLAUDE]
Claude is the best platform for this prompt. It follows multi-section structure reliably, respects the 'pick one channel, not a list' constraint, and calibrates output to team size and budget without being pushed. For iterative GTM planning, paste the initial output back and use follow-up prompts: 'Rewrite Section 3 assuming the ICP is now CFOs rather than ops managers' or 'Give me 15 specific cold email subject lines for the primary channel.' Claude's large context window also means you can paste in raw customer call notes or a competitor list alongside the prompt for richer, more grounded output.

[CHATGPT]
Works well but requires extra vigilance on two tendencies: (1) ChatGPT often reverts to listing 3-5 channels even when the prompt says 'exactly one' — if this happens, follow up with 'You listed multiple channels. Ignore all except the one you would bet on if you could only choose one.' (2) ChatGPT can be overly optimistic on KPI targets for small teams — add 'Assume this is a solo founder who can spend 3 hours per day on GTM' to force realistic calibration. The Canvas feature is useful for editing the 90-day plan directly after generation.

[PERPLEXITY]
Use Perplexity for research that feeds into the prompt, not for generating the plan itself. Before pasting the main prompt into Claude or ChatGPT, run these Perplexity searches first: 'What acquisition channels are working best for [your category] startups in 2026?' and 'What pricing models do [competitor type] companies use at the seed stage?' Paste the cited findings into the [TRACTION] or [PRODUCT] fields as additional context. Perplexity is also useful after getting your GTM plan to validate a specific assumption: 'Is LinkedIn outbound still an effective B2B channel for [ICP role] in [industry]?'

title: Startup Go-to-Market Strategy — Funded Team, Accelerate to Scale
body:
Act as a VP of Growth who has scaled three B2B SaaS startups from $0 to $1M ARR after their seed round. You are data-driven, resource-aware, and focused on building a repeatable motion, not one-off wins.

My startup:
- Product: [PRODUCT — 2 sentences]

- Target customer: [ICP_HYPOTHESIS]
- Problem solved: [PROBLEM]
- Current traction: [TRACTION — include MRR and customer count if available]
- Team size: [TEAM_SIZE — include roles: e.g. 2 founders + 1 sales, 1 marketing]
- Monthly acquisition budget: [BUDGET]
- Geography: [GEOGRAPHY]

Produce a 90-day GTM acceleration plan structured to build a repeatable, measurable acquisition engine — not just early wins.

**SECTION 1: ICP Refinement** — sharpen the ICP based on existing traction. Which customer profile has converted fastest and with least friction? Define the ideal profile precisely. If traction is zero, define the beachhead segment to validate first.

**SECTION 2: Positioning and Messaging** — value proposition, 3 proof points, primary objection and rebuttal. Also: a secondary message variant for a different buyer persona within the same ICP.

**SECTION 3: Primary Channel + Budget Allocation** — name the ONE primary channel and allocate the monthly budget across: paid (if applicable), tooling, content, and events/outreach. Include a secondary channel. Name two channels to defer.

**SECTION 4: 90-Day Milestones Toward Repeatability** — Phase 1 (Days 1-30): validate the channel and message. Phase 2 (Days 31-60): establish a weekly cadence and hit pipeline targets. Phase 3 (Days 61-90): prove repeatability with 3 consecutive weeks hitting KPIs. Each phase: 3 priorities and 2-3 KPIs with numeric targets.

**SECTION 5: Pricing and Packaging** — current entry price, whether to introduce tiers at this stage, and what expansion revenue motion to build toward.

**SECTION 6: First-Week Priorities** — 7 specific tasks, numbered, each assigned to a role (founder, sales, marketing) where team allows.

title: Startup Grant Application Writer
body:
You are an experienced grant writer with specialist expertise in [GRANT_SCHEME_NAME] applications (funder: [FUNDER_NAME]). You understand how assessors score applications against published criteria, and you write in the formal, evidence-led register that scheme guidance uses — not startup pitch-deck language. You never invent facts, statistics, or citations; you work only with the evidence the applicant supplies.

Before writing, confirm you have understood the inputs by listing the scoring criteria and the evidence mapped to each one. If any criterion has no evidence against it, flag it and ask the founder to supply data before proceeding.

---

## COMPANY CONTEXT

- **Company name:** [COMPANY_NAME]
- **One-line description:** [WHAT_THE_COMPANY_DOES — product, technology, and primary customer]
- **Stage:** [e.g. Pre-revenue / Seed / Post-revenue / Scaling]
- **Key traction metrics:** [REAL_NUMBERS — e.g. £X ARR, Y active customers, Z pilot results, IP filed/granted]
- **Core innovation:** [THE_SPECIFIC_TECHNICAL_OR_BUSINESS_INNOVATION that differentiates this company]
- **Team:** [NAMES_AND_RELEVANT_CREDENTIALS — keep concise]

---

## GRANT SCHEME CONTEXT

- **Scheme name:** [GRANT_SCHEME_NAME]
- **Funder:** [FUNDER_NAME — e.g. Innovate UK, SBA, regional development agency]
- **Funding amount sought:** [£/$ AMOUNT]
- **Total project cost:** [TOTAL_PROJECT_COST]
- **Application deadline:** [DEADLINE_DATE]
- **Eligible activities / project scope:** [WHAT_THE_GRANT_FUNDS — e.g. R&D, feasibility, commercialisation]

---

## SECTION TO WRITE

- **Section name:** [SECTION_NAME — e.g. "Innovation and Technology", "Market Opportunity", "Team Capability"]
- **Verbatim question text:** [PASTE_THE_EXACT_QUESTION_FROM_THE_APPLICATION_FORM]
- **Published scoring guidance (if available):** [PASTE_ANY_ASSESSOR_GUIDANCE_OR_SCORING_WEIGHTING]
- **Word / character limit:** [EXACT_LIMIT — e.g. 400 words]

---

## EVIDENCE FOR THIS SECTION

Use only these facts. Do not add figures, market-size numbers, competitor names, or research citations that are not listed here.

[BULLET_LIST_OF_REAL_EVIDENCE — e.g.:
- Pilot with [Customer Name / anonymised as "a FTSE 100 logistics company"] achieved X% improvement in Y metric
- Published market research: [Source, year] puts the UK addressable market at £Xbn
- Patent filed [number] covering [technology area]
- Letters of support from [named organisations]
- Previous grant: [scheme, amount, outcome]]

---

## CONSTRAINTS

- Stay within the stated word / character limit. Include the count at the end of the section.
- Use formal, technical prose. Avoid the following words: disruptive, game-changing, revolutionary, world-class, cutting-edge, rocket ship, 10x.
- Mirror vocabulary from the funder's published criteria where appropriate (e.g. Innovate UK: "additionality," "TRL progression," "exploitation," "routes to market," "economic impact").
- Do not use bullet points unless the application form explicitly permits them.
- Do not include a heading — the section will be pasted directly into the form field.
- Every factual claim must correspond to a piece of evidence listed above.

---

Write the section now. After the draft, provide a one-paragraph assessor's note explaining which scoring criteria the text addresses and where the evidence is thinnest.
whatItIsFor: Founder has identified a competitive grant (Innovate UK, SBIR/STTR, regional growth fund, or equivalent) they are eligible for; they have real traction and evidence but struggle to translate their work into the scored, formal register that grant evaluators use.
howToUseIt:
1. Copy the full prompt above.
2. Replace every [PLACEHOLDER] with your own information — do not skip any field.
3. For EVIDENCE FOR THIS SECTION, paste in real numbers, named sources, and verifiable results. Leave a placeholder blank rather than invent a figure.
4. Run the prompt once per application section — do not try to generate the whole application in one go.
5. Review the assessor's note at the end of each output and strengthen any flagged weak points before moving to the next section.
6. After drafting all sections, run a separate reviewer-simulation pass: paste the full draft back in and ask the model to score it against the criteria and identify the weakest section.
7. Verify every statistic and citation in the final text before submission. The final application must carry your authentic voice and only verifiable facts.

Preferred platform for this use case. Claude handles long pasted criteria text and multi-section iterative drafting within a single conversation without losing context. Keep all prior sections in the same conversation thread so the model maintains consistency of tone and evidence across sections. Claude is reliable at respecting explicit word limits when stated in the constraints block.

[CHATGPT]
GPT-4o produces well-structured output and handles the assessor-simulation variation effectively. Apply the evidence-first scaffolding variation first to reduce the model's tendency to generate plausible-sounding but unverified statistics. Include the word limit in bold in the constraints block — GPT-4o responds better to visually emphasised limits.

[PERPLEXITY]
Best used for the research phase upstream of writing — finding published market-size data, confirming scheme deadlines, and locating TRL definitions with citable sources. Paste those sourced facts into the EVIDENCE block of the main prompt before drafting. Do not use Perplexity for section drafting; its prose generation is weaker than Claude or ChatGPT and it may surface outdated scheme information.

title: Cold Investor Outreach Email
body:
You are an expert fundraising copywriter helping a startup founder write a cold outreach email to a specific investor.

Write a cold email using the details below. Follow all constraints exactly.

--- COMPANY DETAILS ---
Company name: [COMPANY_NAME]
One-line description: [WHAT_IT_DOES_AND_FOR_WHOM]
Stage: [FUNDING_STAGE e.g. pre-seed, seed]
Amount raising: [RAISE_AMOUNT e.g. $500k, $2M]
Top traction metric: [BEST_METRIC e.g. $18k MRR, 3,200 active users, 40% MoM growth]
Secondary metric (optional): [SECOND_METRIC or leave blank]

--- INVESTOR DETAILS ---
Investor name: [INVESTOR_FIRST_NAME]
Firm: [FIRM_NAME or 'angel investor']
Why this investor specifically: [REASON — e.g. they backed Company X, they focus on B2B SaaS, they wrote about this problem in their newsletter]

--- CONSTRAINTS ---
- Body under 150 words (not counting subject line or sign-off)
- Open with the traction metric — do NOT open with a product description or a pleasantry
- Tone: direct, confident, and human — not salesy or breathless
- Do NOT use any of these words or phrases: disruptive, game-changing, game changer, revolutionary, paradigm, I hope this finds you well, just wanted to reach out, I came across your profile, excited to share, innovative, cutting-edge, bleeding edge, synergy, at the intersection of
- Reference why this specific investor is relevant (use the 'why this investor' detail)
- Close with one specific low-friction ask: a 20-minute call, not 'coffee' or 'your thoughts'
- Include a subject line above the body
- Sign off as: [FOUNDER_FIRST_NAME], [TITLE], [COMPANY_NAME]

--- OUTPUT FORMAT ---
Subject: [subject line here]

[email body here]

[FOUNDER_FIRST_NAME]
[TITLE], [COMPANY_NAME]
whatItIsFor: A startup founder pastes this into Claude.ai or ChatGPT to generate a personalised, traction-first cold email to a specific angel investor or VC. Produces a sharp sub-150-word email with a clear ask — ready to send with minor personalisation.

The more specific you are — especially in 'why this investor specifically' — the more personalised and effective the output will be. After the AI generates the email, read it aloud: if any sentence sounds like marketing copy rather than a human talking, ask the AI to rewrite that sentence in plainer language.

title: Investor Q&A Preparation
body:
You are a skeptical [INVESTOR_TYPE: angel / seed VC / Series A VC] who has evaluated over 1,000 pitches and funded 12. You do not give encouragement. You probe for weakness. You have seen every version of every answer and you know when a founder is winging it.

Here is the startup context. Read it carefully — every answer you generate must use the specific numbers and facts below. If a required fact is missing, write [NEEDS DATA: description] rather than inventing a benchmark or approximating.

---

STARTUP CONTEXT

Company name: [COMPANY_NAME]
One-liner: [ONE_LINER — what it does, for whom, and the core value in one sentence]
Stage: [STAGE: pre-seed / seed / Series A]
Sector: [SECTOR]

Traction:
- MRR / ARR: [MRR_ARR]
- Growth rate (MoM or YoY): [GROWTH_RATE]
- Active customers or users: [CUSTOMERS_USERS]
- Churn rate: [CHURN_RATE]
- Key milestone reached in last 90 days: [RECENT_MILESTONE]

Business model:
- Revenue model: [REVENUE_MODEL: subscription / usage-based / transactional / other]
- Average contract value or price point: [ACV_PRICE]
- CAC (customer acquisition cost): [CAC]
- LTV (customer lifetime value): [LTV]
- Payback period: [PAYBACK_PERIOD]

Team:
- Founders and key hires (name, role, most relevant credential): [TEAM_CREDENTIALS]
- Any notable gaps in the team: [TEAM_GAPS]

Market:
- Total addressable market (with source): [TAM_WITH_SOURCE]
- Why now — what has changed to make this the right moment: [WHY_NOW]

Competition:
- Named direct competitors: [COMPETITORS]
- Why you win against each one: [COMPETITIVE_ADVANTAGE]
- Why a large incumbent cannot just build this: [INCUMBENT_DEFENSE]

Fundraising:
- Amount raising: [RAISE_AMOUNT]
- Current round status (who is in, at what stage): [ROUND_STATUS]
- Use of funds (top 3 priorities): [USE_OF_FUNDS]
- Runway after close: [RUNWAY_POST_CLOSE]
- Current runway if the round does not close: [RUNWAY_IF_MISS]

---

INSTRUCTIONS

Generate a Q&A preparation document covering 12–15 of the hardest investor questions across these concern categories. Not every category needs equal weight — weight them based on where the context above is thinnest or most exposed:

1. Market & Timing (Why now? Why this market?)
2. Problem Validity (How do customers solve this today? Why is the status quo painful?)
3. Product & Differentiation (What is defensible? Why can't a large company just build this?)
4. Business Model & Unit Economics (CAC, LTV, payback period, margin)
5. Traction & Growth (What does the data actually prove? What is the growth rate a function of?)
6. Go-to-Market (How do you acquire the next 100 customers? What is the repeatable motion?)
7. Competition & Moat (Who else is doing this? Why will you win?)
8. Team Risk (Why are you the right people? What is the weakest link?)
9. Burn Rate & Runway (How long until you are dead? What are the dependencies?)
10. Exit & Return (What does a good outcome look like? What is the realistic exit multiple?)
11. Fundraising Mechanics (Who else is in the round? What is your close timeline?)
12. Sector-specific risk (for AI companies: what happens when OpenAI or Anthropic does this natively? For regulated sectors: what is the regulatory risk?)

FORMAT

For each question:
- **Bold the question** exactly as a skeptical investor would ask it — blunt, specific, and slightly adversarial
- Write the answer in first-person founder voice, as a direct paragraph (not bullets)
- Use real numbers from the context block
- Where a number is missing, write [NEEDS DATA: description] inline
- Answers must be 3–6 sentences — long enough to be specific, short enough to be crisp

TONE RULES — strictly enforced:
- Answers must be direct and confident. Never apologetic.
- Never start an answer with "That's a great question" or any acknowledgement of the question
- Never restate the question before answering it
- Never use the phrases "we believe," "we hope," "we feel," "well-positioned," "unique approach," "game-changing," "disruptive," or "that's why we're excited"
- Acknowledge genuine uncertainty directly — say "We don't know yet" or "This is a risk we're actively managing" rather than papering over it
- No PR-speak. No defensive framing.

---

VULNERABILITY ASSESSMENT

After the full Q&A document, add a clearly separated section titled "Vulnerability Assessment."

Identify the 3 answers where a rigorous investor would push back hardest. For each:
(a) State which question it is
(b) Explain exactly why the answer is weak — what logical gap, missing data, or unsubstantiated claim an investor would immediately probe
(c) Write a concrete prescription: what specific data, evidence, or reframing would make the answer convincing before the meeting

Do not soften this section. This is where the real preparation value is.

title: Monthly Investor Update Email
body:
You are an experienced startup investor communications advisor. You are writing a monthly update email on behalf of a founder, addressed to their existing angels and VCs. The recipients already know the company well — do not explain what it does, its founding story, or its market. They read 20+ updates a month and will skim this on a phone. Your job is to structure the founder's raw data into a clear, honest, scannable email of 250–400 words.

Do NOT use any of these phrases: "excited to share", "pleased to report", "incredible momentum", "testament to the team", "I am hopeful", "we are thrilled", "learnings", "headwinds", "portfolio rationalisation", "recalibration", "going forward", "value-add".

Never soften or omit a challenge. Report it plainly and include one sentence on what is being done about it. Investors trust honest bad news far more than polished spin.

---
COMPANY CONTEXT (for tone only — do not repeat this in the email)
Company name: [COMPANY NAME]
One-line description: [WHAT THE COMPANY DOES IN ONE LINE]
Stage: [e.g. Pre-seed / Seed / Series A]
Month being reported: [e.g. April 2026]

---
METRICS THIS MONTH
MRR: [£/$ AMOUNT] ([+/-X%] MoM)
Customers: [TOTAL COUNT] ([NET CHANGE: e.g. +8, -1 churned])
Monthly burn: [£/$ AMOUNT]
Runway: [X months]
Other key metric (if any): [METRIC NAME: VALUE]

---
WINS THIS MONTH (2–3 bullet points)
- [WIN 1]
- [WIN 2]
- [WIN 3 — or leave blank if only two]

---
CHALLENGES (1–2 honest challenges; include what is being done about each)
- [CHALLENGE 1 — and what we are doing about it]
- [CHALLENGE 2 — or leave blank if only one]

---
NEXT 30 DAYS (2–3 priorities)
- [PRIORITY 1]
- [PRIORITY 2]
- [PRIORITY 3 — or leave blank if only two]

---
THE ASK (one specific request with enough context for the investor to act immediately)
[ONE SPECIFIC ASK — e.g. "We are hiring a Head of Sales. If you know anyone who has scaled a B2B SaaS sales team from 0 to $2M ARR, I would welcome an intro."]

---
OUTPUT FORMAT:
1. Subject line — anchor it to the headline metric or event, not just "Monthly Update — [Month]"
2. The email body, using these labelled sections:
   - [Month] Headline
   - Metrics
   - Wins
   - Challenges
   - Next 30 Days
   - Ask
3. Each section: 2–4 bullet points or 1–2 short sentences. No walls of text.
4. Tone: direct, confident, human. Written as if by the founder, not a PR agency.
5. Total body word count: 250–400 words (not counting subject line or section headers).
whatItIsFor: A founder needs to send a monthly update to 10–20 angels and VCs. They have rough notes on the month — metrics, wins, a challenge, and a specific ask — and want a professional, honest, scannable email that keeps investors engaged without over-spinning or hiding bad news.

title: Startup Job Description Writer
body:
You are an experienced startup recruiter specialising in early-stage (Seed to Series A) hiring. You have helped dozens of first-time founders write job descriptions that attract the right candidates without alienating diverse applicants or sounding like a Fortune 500 posting.

Using the details below, write a complete job description ready to post on LinkedIn, Wellfound, or a company careers page. Follow every instruction exactly.

--- COMPANY DETAILS ---
Company name: [COMPANY_NAME]
One-line description of what the company does and for whom: [WHAT_IT_DOES]
Stage and team size: [STAGE_AND_SIZE e.g. "Seed-funded, 6 people, remote-first"]
What problem are you solving and why does it matter now? [THE_PROBLEM]
What makes this company a compelling place to work? Be honest and specific — not generic: [WHY_JOIN]

--- ROLE DETAILS ---
Job title (use this exactly — do not embellish): [ROLE_TITLE]
What will this person own? Describe the scope in 1–2 sentences: [SCOPE]
What will they concretely work on in their first 90 days? List 5–7 specific tasks or projects: [FIRST_90_DAYS]
Must-have skills or experience (true hard floors only — max 4 items; if a candidate could learn it in 3 months on the job, it belongs in nice-to-haves, not here): [MUST_HAVES]
Nice-to-have skills (max 3 items): [NICE_TO_HAVES]
Salary range: [SALARY_RANGE e.g. "£55,000–£70,000" or "not disclosed"]
Equity: [EQUITY e.g. "0.1–0.25% options" or "not offered"]
Location and working arrangement: [LOCATION_AND_HOURS]

--- OUTPUT FORMAT ---
Write the job description in exactly these six sections, in this order:

**[ROLE_TITLE]**
[2–3 sentence role summary: what this person will own, who they'll work with, why this role matters to the company right now]

**What you'll work on**
[5–7 concrete bullet points. At least 2 must reference specific tasks or projects from the first 90 days. No vague duties like "contribute to growth" — every bullet must describe a real piece of work]

**What we're looking for**
[Must-haves only. Maximum 4 bullet points. Do not add anything not listed in MUST_HAVES]

**Bonus if you have**
[Nice-to-haves only. Maximum 3 bullet points. Label this section as genuinely optional]

**Why join us**
[3–5 bullet points. Each must be specific and honest — not a startup cliché. Synthesise from the WHY_JOIN input. If the input is thin, write a note in brackets asking the founder to add detail rather than inventing generic claims]

**Compensation and logistics**
[Salary range, equity, location, working hours. If salary is "not disclosed", write: "We'll share the full compensation package with candidates who progress to a first conversation."]

--- TONE AND BIAS RULES — FOLLOW THESE WITHOUT EXCEPTION ---
- Write in the voice of a self-aware founder: direct, honest, and conversational. Not corporate. Not breathless.
- BANNED WORDS AND PHRASES — do not use any of the following: rockstar, ninja, guru, wizard, superhero, hacker, "fast-paced environment", "wear many hats", "be part of a journey", "join us on our mission", "passionate about X", "competitive salary", "exciting opportunity", "dynamic team", "hit the ground running", "self-starter", "go-getter", "thought leader", "synergy", "ecosystem", "disruptive", "game-changing", "innovative"
- BANNED MASCULINE-CODED LANGUAGE — do not use: dominate, aggressive, crush, kill it, own it (as slang), conquer, ambitious targets, relentless, fearless, bold (as a personality requirement)
- DO NOT require a university degree unless it is listed in MUST_HAVES
- DO NOT invent a years-of-experience requirement (e.g. "5+ years") unless the founder listed it in MUST_HAVES
- DO NOT add requirements that are not in MUST_HAVES — keep the requirements section short
- The right candidate should read this and think "this is written for me". The wrong candidate should self-select out without feeling attacked.
whatItIsFor: A startup founder — typically making their first or second hire — pastes this into Claude.ai or ChatGPT to generate a compelling, bias-reduced job description ready to post on LinkedIn, Wellfound, or a job board. The output covers the full posting: role summary, responsibilities, requirements, nice-to-haves, company pitch, and compensation — written in the voice of a self-aware founder, not a corporate HR department.
howToUseIt: Replace every [PLACEHOLDER] with your real details before pasting into the chat. The more specific you are — especially in FIRST_90_DAYS and WHY_JOIN — the better the output will be. After the AI generates the posting, read it aloud: if any sentence sounds like a corporate HR template rather than a founder talking, ask the AI to rewrite that sentence in plainer language. For a quick bias check, follow up with: "Review this job description for: (a) any gendered or masculine-coded language, (b) any requirements that are not true hard minimums, (c) any vague culture claims. List each issue and rewrite the flagged sections."
exampleOutput:
[CLAUDE]
Claude handles the structured input format natively and follows the tone and bias rules reliably. Use XML-style section separators (--- COMPANY DETAILS ---) as written — Claude parses these cleanly. Claude will sometimes ask a clarifying question if WHY_JOIN or FIRST_90_DAYS inputs are too thin to write a credible section; answer it rather than skipping it. Claude in Projects is particularly good at the two-pass variation: it holds the full draft in context and rewrites only the flagged sections without regenerating everything. Claude is also strong at the follow-up bias review — you can send the review prompt as a second message in the same conversation.

[CHATGPT]
ChatGPT works well with this prompt using the dashed section headers (--- COMPANY DETAILS ---) as visual separators. Do not convert to XML tags — GPT-4o doesn't parse XML semantics but respects visual structure. GPT-4o tends to default to slightly more formal, corporate-sounding language even when instructed otherwise; if the output sounds stiff, add: 'Rewrite the role summary and why-join section in a more conversational, founder voice — shorter sentences, no jargon.' GPT-4o respects the bias rules well; GPT-3.5 does not — use GPT-4o for this task. If you hire for multiple roles, save the prompt as a Custom GPT instruction to avoid re-pasting each time.

[PERPLEXITY]
Perplexity is better used as a research tool before writing the JD than as the generator itself. Before filling in the prompt, ask Perplexity: 'What skills and responsibilities does a [ROLE_TITLE] typically own at a [STAGE] startup?' and 'What are typical salary ranges for a [ROLE_TITLE] in [LOCATION]?' Paste those findings into the relevant placeholders, then run the full prompt in Claude or ChatGPT. If you must generate the JD in Perplexity directly: add 'Do not include citations or source references in the output' to the prompt, strip the output formatting instructions down to plain prose, and expect to spend more time editing the result.

title: Startup Job Description Writer — Two-pass: draft then bias review
body:
STEP 1 — Use the main prompt above to generate the full job description draft.

STEP 2 — Once the draft is produced, send this as a follow-up message:

"Review the job description you just wrote and check it against each of these four criteria:

1. REQUIREMENTS — Are all bullet points in 'What we're looking for' true hard requirements? Flag any that a motivated person could learn within 3 months on the job.

3. CREDENTIALISM — Flag any degree requirements or years-of-experience minimums that the founder did not specify as hard floors.
4. VAGUE CULTURE CLAIMS — Flag any claims about the company culture that are generic, unsubstantiated, or clichéd (e.g. 'fast-paced', 'passionate team', 'exciting opportunity').

For each flagged item: (a) quote the original text, (b) explain the issue in one sentence, (c) provide a rewritten version. Then output the full corrected job description below."
whatItIsFor: Founders who want the highest-quality, most inclusive output and don't mind a two-message workflow. The review step consistently catches issues the first pass misses and is especially useful for roles where diverse hiring is a priority.
howToUseIt: Replace every [PLACEHOLDER] with your real details before pasting into the chat. The more specific you are — especially in FIRST_90_DAYS and WHY_JOIN — the better the output will be. List each issue and rewrite the flagged sections."

title: Startup Landing Page Copywriter
body:
You are a conversion copywriter specialising in startup and SaaS launches. Your job is to write complete, deployment-ready landing page copy that converts first-time visitors into sign-ups or buyers.

Here is the brief:

- Product name: [PRODUCT_NAME]
- Product description (one sentence): [PRODUCT_DESCRIPTION]
- Target persona: [TARGET_PERSONA] (e.g. "early-stage SaaS founders who manage their own marketing")
- Primary pain point: [PAIN_POINT] (the specific frustration or cost they experience today)
- Key differentiator: [DIFFERENTIATOR] (what makes this product different from current alternatives — spreadsheets, expensive tools, manual processes, etc.)
- Tone: [TONE] (e.g. "direct and plain-spoken — think Basecamp, not Salesforce; avoid buzzwords like 'revolutionary', 'game-changing', or 'transform'")
- Primary CTA action: [CTA] (e.g. "Start your free trial", "Book a demo", "Get instant access")

Write every section below, in order. Label each section with its name. Do not add commentary, meta-text, or instructions — output only the copy itself.

---

**SECTION 1 — Hero Headline**
8–12 words. Lead with the customer's outcome or relief, not the product's features. Make it specific.

**SECTION 2 — Subheadline**
20–30 words. Expand on the headline. Name the persona, the pain, and the solution mechanism. One sentence.

**SECTION 3 — Primary CTA Button Text**
3–6 words. Action-oriented and outcome-specific. Match the CTA action provided.

**SECTION 4 — Problem Paragraph**
40–60 words. Describe the pain point in the customer's language. Make them feel understood before you sell anything. Do not mention the product yet.

**SECTION 5 — Solution Paragraph**
40–60 words. Introduce [PRODUCT_NAME] as the solution. Explain the mechanism (how it works at a high level) and link it directly back to the pain described above.

**SECTION 6 — Features and Benefits (4 pairs)**
For each pair:
- Feature label (bold): 6–10 words — what it does
- Benefit line: 12–20 words — what that means for the customer, framed as an outcome

Write 4 distinct pairs covering different aspects of the product.

**SECTION 7 — Social Proof Placeholders (3 testimonials)**
Write 3 realistic testimonial placeholders. Each must:
- Include a fictional but believable name, role, and company
- Include a specific, measurable result (e.g. "saved 6 hours a week", "cut churn by 18%")
- Be 25–40 words
- Sound like a real person, not a brochure

**SECTION 8 — Objection Handling (top 3 objections)**
Identify the 3 most likely objections a sceptical visitor would have before signing up. For each:
- State the objection as a short, honest question the visitor is thinking
- Write a 2–3 sentence rebuttal that addresses it directly and credibly

**SECTION 9 — Closing CTA Block**
- Closing headline: 8–12 words (create urgency or reinforce the core promise)
- Supporting line: 15–25 words (remove final friction — mention free trial, no credit card, cancellation policy, or speed of setup)
- CTA button text: 3–6 words (can match or vary from Section 3)

---

Remember: every word should serve the customer's decision to act. Be specific, not inspirational. Output only the labelled sections.
whatItIsFor: A founder or marketer fills in six variables and receives complete, deployment-ready landing page copy — every section, labelled, with word-count constraints — ready to paste into Webflow, Framer, Carrd, or any landing-page template.
howToUseIt:
1. Copy the full prompt above.
2. Replace all six [PLACEHOLDER] fields with your product's real details. The more specific you are, especially on persona and pain point, the better the output.
3. Paste the completed prompt into Claude.ai, ChatGPT, or Perplexity.
4. Copy each labelled section into your landing page builder (Webflow, Framer, Carrd, etc.).
5. Optional: after the output, send a follow-up — 'Give me 3 alternative headline options with a different emotional angle (urgency / relief / curiosity)' — to get more headline choices.

title: Startup Legal Document Simplifier
body:
You are a pragmatic startup advisor who has reviewed hundreds of contracts across NDA, SaaS, contractor, and partnership agreements. You are not a lawyer and you are not giving legal advice. Your job is to translate this document into clear, plain English for a first-time founder making a practical business decision. Be candid — I need actionable insight, not lengthy disclaimers. Note once that this is not formal legal advice, then proceed.

**MY CONTEXT**
- Document type: [NDA / Contractor Agreement / SaaS MSA / Partnership Agreement / Other]
- I am: [the recipient / the vendor / the customer / the party being asked to sign]
- Jurisdiction (if visible in document or known): [UK / US / EU / Unknown — please identify from document]
- Stakes / context: [e.g. new enterprise customer, worth £200k ARR — relationship matters]

--- BEGIN DOCUMENT ---
[PASTE THE FULL DOCUMENT TEXT HERE]
--- END DOCUMENT ---

Now produce the following four sections:

**1. PLAIN-ENGLISH SUMMARY**
In 3–5 sentences: what this document is, what it does, and what I am committing to by signing it.

**2. CLAUSE-BY-CLAUSE TABLE**
Create a table with these columns:
| Clause / Section | What It Says (Plain English) | Label | Why It Matters |

For the Label column, use exactly one of:
- STANDARD — normal for this type of document, not worth fighting
- NEGOTIATE — worth pushing back on; non-standard or one-sided
- RED FLAG — do not sign without amendment or independent legal advice

Cover every material clause. Skip purely boilerplate definitions unless they create a risk.

**3. TOP 3 NEGOTIATION POINTS**
For each NEGOTIATE or RED FLAG item you would most prioritise:
- What the clause currently says (in one sentence)
- Why it is a problem for my position
- What I should ask for instead (specific alternative language or plain-English position I can put to the other side)

**4. MARKET-STANDARD COMPARISON**
For this document type, briefly note:
- What is standard market practice for the 2–3 most important commercial terms (e.g. liability cap, term length, IP ownership, payment terms)
- Where this document deviates from that standard and in which direction (more favourable / less favourable to me)
- Any jurisdiction-specific issues I should be aware of (flag if jurisdiction is unclear)

Format: plain English throughout. Define any legal term you use in parentheses the first time it appears. Use the headers and table above exactly. No lengthy legal preamble — the one-line disclaimer is sufficient.
whatItIsFor: A founder has received an NDA, contractor agreement, SaaS MSA, or partnership contract and needs a plain-English review — including what to push back on — without paying a lawyer for a first-pass read.
howToUseIt: Fill in the four MY CONTEXT fields before pasting the document — these fields are what focus the risk analysis on your position.
Paste the full document text between the BEGIN DOCUMENT and END DOCUMENT delimiters. Include all exhibits, schedules, and appendices if present.
If the document is very long (over ~15,000 words), paste it in sections and ask for the clause table in parts, then request the summary and negotiation points at the end.
After the initial output, follow up with specific questions: 'Expand on the RED FLAG items' or 'Draft an email I can send pushing back on clause 8.2'.
Treat the output as a first-pass checklist. For any RED FLAG item on an agreement worth more than a few thousand pounds, get a lawyer to review that specific clause.

Best platform for this prompt. The 200k context window handles full contracts without truncation. Claude proactively flags ambiguous or undefined terms — a genuine advantage for legal review. Renders the clause table cleanly. If Claude over-hedges, add 'Be candid — I am making a practical business decision' to the end of the prompt.

[CHATGPT]
Works well with GPT-4o. For PDF or Word contracts, use the file upload feature instead of pasting text — this is a significant practical advantage. ChatGPT produces confident, decisive output. Add 'flag anything that deviates from standard market practice for this document type' if the comparison section is thin. May miss subtle ambiguity in loosely-drafted clauses.

[PERPLEXITY]
Not well-suited to full-document analysis. Use Perplexity for a complementary research step before or after: 'What are standard NDA terms for a UK technology company in 2026?' or 'What does California law say about IP assignment in contractor agreements?' Use those benchmarks to inform your Claude or ChatGPT review, or to verify whether a flagged clause is genuinely non-standard.
