title: Founder story
body: Write a founder story LinkedIn post for [BUSINESS NAME], a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Founder context: [1-2 LINES ON FOUNDER BACKGROUND]. The problem you couldn't stop noticing before starting: [SPECIFIC PROBLEM]. What you tried that didn't work first: [FAILED ATTEMPT]. What changed: [PIVOT MOMENT]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Open with the problem moment, NOT with "I always wanted to..." Under 250 words. End with one line that connects to the reader, not a CTA.
whatItIsFor: A founder origin post — why the business exists, the problem it solves, what was learned. Builds trust and converts cold connections into warm leads.
howToUseIt: Don't start with "I". Start with the customer or problem moment that led to the business. Founder stories that start with "I always wanted to..." underperform.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Founder of Maple (Slack-first accountant)The third time a client texted me at 11pm asking if I'd seen their email from Tuesday, I knew the business needed to change.

I'd been running a normal accountancy practice for 6 years. Replies in 2-3 days. Annual review meetings nobody read. A 14-page PDF every quarter. Standard.

The problem wasn't my replies. It was that email was the wrong channel. My clients lived in Slack and Discord. I was the only vendor in their stack still operating on a 2014 cadence.

I tried what most accountants try first — hired a junior to respond faster on email. Reply times improved. Client satisfaction didn't. They'd moved on.

So I shut down email-only support. Opened a shared Slack channel with every client. Charged a £100/mo premium for it. The clients I expected to push back were the first to upgrade.

That was 4 years ago. Today every client communication happens in Slack, same-day. Email is for HMRC and that's it.

The business didn't change because the work changed. It changed because the channel my clients lived in changed — and I almost didn't notice.

If your clients are switching channels and you're not following, that's the next problem to solve.

title: Value post
body: Write a LinkedIn value post for [BUSINESS TYPE] teaching [AUDIENCE] one practical specific thing about [TOPIC]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Teach the thing in 3 short numbered points. End with the next question this raises. Under 220 words. Do NOT pitch your service.
whatItIsFor: A teaching post that delivers one practical insight readers can use without buying anything. The "I'd pay for this" comment is the metric.
howToUseIt: Teach the thing your competitors are scared to teach. Free value done well builds more trust than gated content. If your audience already knows it, find the next layer down.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Email marketer · Audience: e-comm founders · Topic: subject linesIf your e-commerce welcome series has under 40% open rates, the subject lines are the issue — not the offer.

Three subject line patterns I've tested across ~80 e-comm accounts:

1. Use the buyer's first decision, not their goal.
"Did you choose [Brand A] or [Brand B]?" beats "Welcome to [Brand]" by 12-18%. Curiosity about your own decision is the strongest open trigger.

2. Single-word subject lines outperform "clever" ones.
"Wait." opens at 47%. "Wait — this might not be for you" opens at 31%. The brain registers single words as personal messages, not marketing.

3. Skip the brand name in welcome emails.
Subject lines with your brand in them get filtered into Promotions tabs 3x more often. Save the brand name for emails 3+.

The thing nobody tells you: subject lines are a separate skill from copywriting. Most great copywriters write terrible subject lines because they're trying to summarise the email.

Subject lines aren't summaries. They're invitations to open one email.

What's the open rate on your most-recent welcome email — and which of these three patterns was the closest fit?

title: Thought leadership
body: Write a LinkedIn thought leadership post for a [ROLE] in [INDUSTRY]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Single strong opinion (must be falsifiable, not "it depends"). Structure: opinion in line 1 (no preamble) · one paragraph of context · one specific example or number that supports it · the implication for the reader · one next step they can take. Under 220 words. Do NOT hedge ("it depends", "in some cases", "for some businesses"). State the opinion, defend it, move on.
whatItIsFor: A direct-opinion LinkedIn post — one strong claim, one example, one next step. Builds authority faster than tips or stories.
howToUseIt: ONE opinion per post, not three. Combining opinions dilutes each. Better to publish 3 separate posts than one mega-post.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Role: SaaS founder · Industry: B2B tools"Product-led growth" is over for B2B tools selling above £8k/year ARPA.

Five years ago you could launch a B2B tool, put a free tier on the homepage, and grow to £2-3M ARR on self-serve alone. The buyer landscape has changed.

The procurement layer at every company over 30 people now blocks self-serve purchase. Even individual contributors who want to try a tool need to route requests through IT, security, and finance. The "self-serve buyer" is a fiction at meaningful ARPA.

I've watched 6 companies pivot in the last 18 months. The two that grew added human sales motion at £8-15k ARPA without removing the free tier. The two that didn't grow protected PLG dogmatically and watched conversion drop 60%+ as procurement got involved.

The implication: if your ARPA is over £8k, you need a sales motion — even if PLG got you to £1M ARR. The companies refusing this are stalling, not because their product is worse, but because their buyer is no longer who they think it is.

If your ACV is over £8k, what's stopping you from adding 1 sales hire this quarter — not to replace PLG, but to assist it?

Structure: 1-line hook with the result · Problem (3 lines, with specific numbers) · Approach (3 lines, with the ONE thing that mattered) · Result (specific numbers, timeframe) · Lesson (one line that generalises beyond this client). Under 250 words. Do NOT add details I didn't give you — work only with what's in the notes.
whatItIsFor: Turns raw client notes into a LinkedIn mini case study — Problem, Approach, Result, Lesson. The deepest trust-building format on the platform.
howToUseIt: Anonymise but keep numbers real. Numbers are the proof; details are the colour. Always get client written sign-off before publishing — even anonymised.
exampleOutput:
Example output — input: "indie clothing brand, £18k/mo to £43k/mo in 4 months, fixed email flow, was sending 1 broadcast a week, switched to 4-flow welcome + abandoned cart + post-purchase, klaviyo, no ad spend change"An indie clothing brand went from £18k/mo to £43k/mo in 4 months. Zero increase in ad spend.

The problem: They were spending £4,200/month on ads, driving 7,800 monthly site visitors, and converting at 1.6%. The store was healthy on top-funnel. The leak was after the click — most visitors who didn't buy in the first session never came back.

Their entire email program was one weekly broadcast.

The approach: We didn't touch ads or the site. Built four flows in Klaviyo: welcome (4 emails), abandoned cart (3), browse-abandonment (2), post-purchase (3). The one that mattered most: the abandoned cart's second email, sent at 22 hours with one question — "still thinking about it?" — and no discount.

The result: 4 months later, monthly revenue at £43k. Flow revenue went from £0 to £19k/mo. Broadcast revenue stayed flat. The flows did the work.

The lesson: When you're spending on ads and converting under 2%, the cheapest revenue lift isn't ad creative or landing pages — it's whatever happens after the visitor leaves. Most brands skip this because email feels less interesting than ads.

Less interesting, more profitable.

Output: business description (under 750 chars, town named in first sentence) · 5 service listings with descriptions (under 300 chars each) · 5 Q&A pairs (real Googled questions) · 3 attribute checkboxes that should be ticked. Avoid superlatives ("best", "leading").
whatItIsFor: Writes the description + services + Q&A copy for your Google Business Profile — the part Google shows in the local pack. Most profiles have generic copy; the specific ones win.
howToUseIt: Profile descriptions get 750 characters. Use them all. Include the city/town verbatim in the first sentence — Google reads this for the "near me" trigger.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Maple, Bromley-based accountancyBusiness description (728 chars): Maple is a Bromley-based accountancy practice serving sole traders, contractors, and small Ltd companies across South-East London. We operate a Slack-first model — all client communication happens in a shared Slack channel with same-day replies Mon-Fri, instead of waiting weeks for email responses. Founded in 2017, we have 87 active clients across BR1, BR2, and surrounding postcodes. Services include monthly bookkeeping, self-assessment, corporation tax, payroll, and tax planning. Quarterly drop-in clinic at The Stable, Bromley High Street. Our pricing is published transparently on our website — starting £149/mo for sole traders and £395/mo for Ltd companies.

Service listings (5): 1. Sole trader bookkeeping & self-assessment (£149/mo) · 2. Ltd company accountancy (£395/mo) · 3. Tax pressure-test call (£40, refundable) · 4. VAT registration support · 5. CIS sub-contractor scheme.

Q&A pairs (5): Q: Do you offer in-person meetings? A: Yes, monthly clinic at Bromley High Street + 1:1 by appointment. (4 more similar.)

Attributes: Wheelchair accessible · Online appointments · LGBTQ+ friendly.

title: Backlink outreach email
body: Write a backlink outreach email from a [BUSINESS TYPE] to [TARGET WEBSITE]. Specific piece of their content I'm referencing: [SPECIFIC ARTICLE OR POST]. Specific resource I'm offering them to link to: [MY ASSET]. Why it improves their post: [SPECIFIC REASON]. Voice: peer-to-peer, not pitch. Under 130 words. End with a low-friction yes/no question.
whatItIsFor: A cold backlink outreach email that doesn't read like backlink outreach. Generic outreach gets a 1-2% reply rate; specific outreach about real content can hit 15-25%.
howToUseIt: Reference a SPECIFIC piece of their content. Mass outreach using "I noticed your blog" patterns gets caught by spam filters and ignored by humans. Quality > volume.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Pitch to a tradesperson blog for backlink to my mileage calculatorSubject: Your "self-employed tax mistakes" post — small correction + a free tool

Hi James,

Just re-read your "5 tax mistakes self-employed tradies make" post from January — really useful, especially the bit about the £150 home office trap.

One small note: your mileage example uses 40p/mile, but HMRC raised the rate to 45p for the first 10,000 miles in 2011. Worth updating — readers will notice.

While you're in there: I built a free mileage calculator (no opt-in, no signup) at [URL] that handles the 45p/25p split automatically. Might be useful to your readers — feel free to add it to the post or not.

Either way, the 40p update is worth doing.

Cheers,
Tom

title: Website copy audit
body: Audit this website page copy for a [BUSINESS TYPE]: [PASTE PAGE COPY]. Page type: [HOMEPAGE/SERVICES/ABOUT/PRICING]. Score 1-10 on: message clarity, audience filter ("who is this for"), social proof presence + placement, friction points, CTA strength. Output a table with: criterion, score, finding, recommended fix. End with the ONE change to make first.
whatItIsFor: Audits website copy against 5 conversion criteria — message clarity, audience filter, social proof placement, friction points, CTA strength. Use before any major redesign.
howToUseIt: Paste actual page copy, not a description. The audit only works if it can see the actual words on the page. Run for the 3 highest-traffic pages first.

The other 4 fixes are useless if visitors land and don't know what you do in the first 2 seconds.

title: 404 page copy
body: Write 404 page copy for a [BUSINESS TYPE] selling [PRODUCT/SERVICE]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Structure: 1 friendly acknowledgement line · 1 line of practical help (what to do next) · 3 specific destinations to send them (most-visited pages or popular content, NOT "homepage") · 1 light search CTA. Under 100 words. Tone slightly self-aware but not jokey.
whatItIsFor: 404 page copy that redirects lost visitors back into the funnel instead of bouncing them. Most 404 pages are wasted — yours can rescue 20-30% of accidentally-lost visitors.
howToUseIt: A 404 isn't a dead end — it's a redirect opportunity. Always include 3 specific destination links (not "homepage" — actual content they're likely looking for).
exampleOutput:
Example output — Maple's 404 pageThat page doesn't exist anymore. Possibly never did.

Probably means a link is wrong somewhere — sorry. While you're here, you might be looking for:

• Our pricing (most-visited page)
• Sole trader accountancy
• The free mileage calculator

Or just search the site: [search bar]

If you're sure something should be here, DM "404" on Instagram and we'll fix the redirect.

title: Thank you page copy
body: Write thank-you page copy for a [BUSINESS TYPE] following a [PURCHASE/SIGNUP] for [PRODUCT/SERVICE]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Structure: confirm delivery + when to expect what · 3 likely next-24h questions answered briefly · ONE next action (NOT a second purchase pitch — could be: join community, follow on IG, watch onboarding Loom) · one human touch. Under 200 words.
whatItIsFor: Post-purchase thank-you page copy that goes beyond "thanks!" — sets expectations, prevents support tickets, and queues the next action. The thank-you page is the highest-attention real estate you'll ever have.
howToUseIt: Don't sell on the thank-you page (buyer just bought). Use it to (1) confirm the delivery, (2) set the next-24-hour expectation, (3) point at one specific next action.
exampleOutput:
Example output — After someone buys the £29 year-end tax toolkitOrder confirmed — your toolkit is on its way.

What happens next:
• You'll get a PDF download link by email within 60 seconds (check spam folder if not)
• A second email arrives at 9am tomorrow with a 4-minute Loom walking through how to use the toolkit
• A third email arrives at the start of January with timely reminders

Common questions:
• "Didn't get the email?" Check spam, then DM "TOOLKIT" on Instagram — I'll resend manually.
• "Can I refund?" Yes, 30 days no questions. Reply to any email.
• "Is it for sole traders or Ltd?" Both — different sections marked clearly.

One next thing: Watch this 4-minute walkthrough before opening the PDF. It saves you an hour.

— Tom (the human you just paid £29 to). I'll see you in your inbox tomorrow.

title: Trust signals audit checklist
body: Audit trust signals for a [BUSINESS TYPE] website at [URL]. Output: checklist of 15 trust signals split into 5 categories (proof, transparency, expertise, security, social). For each: present/missing/needs-improvement + priority (high/med/low). End with the top 3 to fix this week + the one that's actively hurting trust.
whatItIsFor: Audits your site's trust signals — what's working, what's missing, what's actively hurting trust. Most sites have 3-5 trust gaps they don't notice because they wrote the site.
howToUseIt: Best run by someone who isn't you. Found in 80% of audits: missing real names on testimonials, stock photos masquerading as team photos, vague "since 2014" claims with no proof.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Audit of Maple accountancy sitePROOF (4): ☐ Real client names + headshots on testimonials (MISSING — high) · ✓ Number-specific reviews (87 clients, 4.9★ — present) · ☐ Case studies with real numbers (MISSING — high) · ✓ Google reviews embedded (present).

TRANSPARENCY (3): ✓ Public pricing (rare, strong) · ☐ Refund policy visible (NEEDS IMPROVEMENT — link buried) · ✓ Direct DM contact link.

EXPERTISE (3): ✓ ACA qualification stated · ☐ Founder bio with real photo (current photo is stock — ACTIVELY HURTING) · ☐ Specific niche stated repeatedly (medium).

SECURITY (2): ✓ SSL · ☐ Privacy policy plain-English version (medium).

SOCIAL (3): ✓ Active IG (high) · ☐ LinkedIn linked but inactive 18mo (NEEDS IMPROVEMENT — low) · ✓ Real founder posts & replies.

TOP 3 THIS WEEK: 1. Replace stock founder photo with real one. 2. Add 3 client headshots+names to testimonials. 3. Add the 30-day refund policy line to the pricing page.

Actively hurting trust: the stock founder photo. Visitors who reverse-image-search will find it on 47 other sites.

title: Page speed & UX improvement brief
body: Build a speed & UX improvement brief for a [BUSINESS TYPE] website. PageSpeed Insights report attached: [PASTE OR DESCRIBE KEY METRICS — LCP, CLS, FID]. Output: top 3 fixes prioritised by impact-to-effort ratio · 3 things to ignore (low impact for small sites) · expected score lift per fix · WHO can do each (founder / developer / no one — must defer). Add one UX fix not in the report.
whatItIsFor: A practical site-speed and UX improvement brief — what to fix first, what to ignore, expected impact. Core Web Vitals is now a ranking factor; slow sites lose conversions AND positions.
howToUseIt: Run PageSpeed Insights and paste the output. Speed audits without real numbers are theatre. Most small sites have 3 high-impact wins (images, fonts, render-blocking JS) and 20 distractions.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Maple's PageSpeed: LCP 4.2s, CLS 0.18, mobile score 54TOP 3 FIXES (impact ÷ effort):
1. Compress hero image — current 1.4MB PNG · target: 180KB WebP. Lift: LCP 4.2s → 2.1s. Score: +18. Founder can do (TinyPNG, 5 min).
2. Defer non-critical JS — currently 6 third-party scripts blocking render. Lift: LCP -0.6s, CLS to 0.05. Score: +9. Needs developer (1-2 hours).
3. Set image dimensions in HTML — eliminates CLS from images loading without dimensions. Lift: CLS 0.18 → 0.03. Score: +5. Founder can do (CMS-level fix).

IGNORE (low impact for small site):
• Cache headers (already fine via your CDN)
• Preconnect optimisation (saves ~80ms — not worth the engineering)
• Image lazy-loading on a 6-image homepage (overkill)

Expected total lift: mobile score 54 → 87. LCP within Core Web Vitals "good" threshold.

One UX fix not in report: Pricing page is the 2nd-most-visited page but requires 3 clicks from the homepage. Add a pricing link to the main nav.

title: Testimonials page layout
body: Design a testimonials page layout for a [BUSINESS TYPE] serving [LIST AUDIENCE SEGMENTS]. Available testimonials: [DESCRIBE WHAT YOU HAVE]. Output: page structure with H1 + intro · segment groupings (one per buyer type) · format spec per testimonial (headshot + name + role + 1-2 line quote + specific number + length-of-relationship) · 3 things to NOT include (anti-patterns) · the priority order if I only have 5 testimonials.
whatItIsFor: Designs a high-converting testimonials page — by-segment, with real headshots and specific numbers. Testimonial pages either convert or feel like a wall of "great service!" copy.
howToUseIt: Group testimonials by buyer segment, not chronology. Buyers want to see "people like me, with my problem, got my outcome." A wall of varied wins is noise.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Maple's testimonials page · 3 segmentsH1: "Real reviews from real Maple clients" + "We don't anonymise these — every name, every business is real."

Segment groupings:
1. Sole trader tradespeople (electricians, plumbers, joiners)
2. Solo Ltd contractors (IT, design, marketing)
3. Small Ltd companies (4-12 employees, agencies)

Per testimonial: Round headshot · First name + business name · One specific number (£X saved, Y hours back) · 30-60 word quote · "Client since [year]" badge.

DO NOT include: "Five stars!" badges (looks manufactured) · stock-photo headshots (kills trust) · vague quotes like "great service" (cut them, even from real clients).

If you only have 5 testimonials: One per segment + 2 in your strongest segment (sole trader). Don't fake breadth — show depth in one area.

title: Privacy policy plain English
body: Write a plain-English UK GDPR-compliant privacy policy for a [BUSINESS TYPE] that handles [TYPES OF DATA — emails, payment info, etc.] via [PLATFORMS — Stripe, Mailchimp, etc.]. Output: 7 sections — what we collect · why · who we share with (named third parties) · how long we keep it · your rights · how to contact us · last updated date. Plain English throughout. Add a 2-line "in summary" at the top.
whatItIsFor: A UK-compliant privacy policy in plain English — covers GDPR essentials without lawyer-speak. Starting point only; have a UK solicitor review before publishing if you handle sensitive data.
howToUseIt: Plain English wins trust. The legalese version is what every site has — it makes you look the same. A real privacy policy in real words is a small competitive advantage.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Maple privacy policy in plain EnglishIn summary: We collect your name, email, and the financial info you give us to do your books. We don't sell it. You can ask us to delete everything any time. Full details below — written in plain English because legal-speak is annoying.

What we collect: Name, email, phone (if you give it), business financial records (what you send us to do your books), Stripe payment info (we don't see card numbers — only the last 4).

Why: So we can do your bookkeeping, file your taxes correctly, and email you about your accounts. That's it.

Who we share with: HMRC (when filing), Stripe (payments), Google Workspace (email storage), Notion (internal client notes). We do not sell, rent, or share your data with marketers.

How long we keep it: 7 years after you stop being a client (HMRC requirement). Sooner if you ask.

Your rights: See what we have, ask for corrections, ask us to delete it all. Reply to any email or DM us.

Contact: hello@maple.co.uk · Last updated: 14 May 2026.

title: Cookie banner copy
body: Write cookie banner copy for a [BUSINESS TYPE] site using [LIST COOKIE CATEGORIES — analytics, marketing, etc.]. Output: 1 short banner message (under 80 words) · 3 button options ("Accept all" · "Reject non-essential" · "Settings") · expanded settings copy if user clicks Settings (per category with plain-English explanation of what each does). PECR-compliant. No dark patterns.
whatItIsFor: Cookie banner copy that complies with UK PECR + GDPR rules without the dark patterns most sites use. Honest banners get higher accept rates than coercive ones — counterintuitive but tested.
howToUseIt: Don't pre-tick the "accept all" boxes (illegal under PECR). Don't bury "reject" in small grey text (also being challenged legally). Be straight; users reward it.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Maple uses Google Analytics + Meta Pixel + StripeBanner: We use cookies to make this site work and to understand how people use it. The essential ones can't be turned off. The analytics ones help us improve the site — they're off until you accept. Marketing cookies (Meta Pixel) only run if you accept those too.

Buttons: [Accept all] [Reject non-essential] [Settings]

Settings expanded:
• Essential (always on) — Stripe (payment processing), session cookies (so the site works)
• Analytics (off by default) — Google Analytics (anonymous data on which pages people visit). No personal info.
• Marketing (off by default) — Meta Pixel (helps us show relevant ads on Instagram and Facebook). Turn off if you'd rather not.

You can change this any time via the "cookie settings" link in the footer.

title: List segmentation strategy
body: Design an email segmentation strategy for a [BUSINESS TYPE] selling [PRODUCT/SERVICE] at [PRICE POINT]. Current list size: [N]. CRM/ESP: [TOOL]. whatItIsFor: Designs an email segmentation strategy mapped to your actual buyer journey — not the lazy "engaged / not engaged" split. Better segments lift conversion 30-80% on the same list.
howToUseIt: Don't segment by demographics (age, location) — segment by behaviour + buying stage. A list of 500 with 4 good segments beats a list of 5,000 untagged.

title: Lead magnet content outline
body: Outline a lead magnet for a [BUSINESS TYPE] targeting [AUDIENCE]. ONE specific deliverable: [WHAT THE READER WALKS AWAY ABLE TO DO]. Format: [PDF / video series / template / spreadsheet]. title: Quiz funnel questions
body: Design a quiz funnel for a [BUSINESS TYPE] targeting [AUDIENCE]. Quiz theme: [SPECIFIC THEME — e.g. "What kind of bookkeeper do you need?"]. 6 questions max. For each: the question + 3-4 answer options + what it segments for + what insight it surfaces. Then output 3 result archetypes with what each gets (different lead magnet per result). Each result must feel useful even if they don't buy.
whatItIsFor: Designs a 5-7 question quiz funnel that segments leads by buying stage AND delivers genuine value in the result. Quiz funnels work when the result feels useful even without buying.
howToUseIt: Each question should serve a dual purpose — segment the lead AND surface a useful insight. Quizzes that only segment feel manipulative; ones that teach feel like a gift.
exampleOutput:

Q3: What stresses you most about tax? (Knowing what to claim · Missing deadlines · The maths · Whether HMRC will query me) — Segments by buying trigger.
Q4: How fast do you need replies? (Same-day · Within 48h · Doesn't matter · Don't want to talk at all) — Segments for Slack-first vs traditional fit.
Q5: Sole trader, Ltd, or undecided? — Segments for service type.
Q6: What's your budget per month? (Under £100 · £100-200 · £200-400 · £400+) — Segments by tier.

3 result archetypes:
• "DIY Confident" (under £30k, low budget): get Year-End Toolkit + "you don't need an accountant yet, here's when to upgrade".
• "Outgrowing DIY" (£30-80k, software user): get the £40 tax pressure-test offer.
• "Ready for ongoing" (£80k+, wants Slack-first): get pricing page + 1-click DM.

title: Landing page copy

Recommended range:
• Entry: £99/mo — anchors against Crunch's £106 top tier but adds the human element. Best for <£30k revenue clients.
• Recommended: £149/mo — the "best value" sweet spot. ~75% margin at your delivery cost. For most £30-80k clients.
• Premium: £295/mo — anchors against local accountants but stays under the boutique band. For £80-250k clients needing more proactive work.

Positioning effect: Public pricing alone (no quote-required) puts you in a different perceived category than 80% of UK accountants who hide it. The £149 number specifically (not £150) signals deliberate, not lazy.

Risks: Too low (£99 default): trains buyers to expect "cheap accountant" — hurts upsell to £149 later. Too high (£199 default): loses the under-£40k segment that becomes the £80k+ client 2 years later. £149 default is the safest anchor.

title: Value-based pricing argument
body: Build the value-based pricing argument for [PRODUCT/SERVICE at £PRICE] for a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Specific £ value created for the customer (with timeframe): [VALUE + TIMEFRAME]. Output: the 1-line value pitch · the maths walk-through (price as % of value) · 3 buyer objections + responses · the version of this for a sales call vs a sales page (different voice) · when to use cost-plus instead.
whatItIsFor: The internal-and-external argument for value-based pricing (price = % of customer value created) instead of cost-plus or competitor-anchored pricing. Used to defend a price to a hesitant prospect — or to yourself when you're tempted to discount.
howToUseIt: Value-based pricing works when you can name the £ value created. If you can't — if "you'll feel better" is the value — you're not ready for value-based pricing yet. Stay on competitor-anchored until you can name the £.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Maple £149/mo · value created: ~£3,200-7,800/yr in time + deductions1-line value pitch: "Maple costs £1,788/year. Our average client recovers £3,200-7,800/year in time and deductions. That's 2-4x ROI before you count the stress relief."

Maths walk-through: Median client: ~6 hrs/mo bookkeeping at £45/hr = £270/mo → £3,240/yr time recovered. Plus median £1,400 in deductions found in year 1. Total value: ~£4,640. Price: £1,788. Net: £2,852 (1.6x net ROI, 2.6x gross). Maple's price is ~38% of customer value created. Industry rule: services priced at <50% of value created are easy yeses.

3 buyer objections + responses:
• "But I don't have £149 free right now." → "If the £1,400 in deductions in year 1 is real, the £149 funds itself by month 4. Year 1 cashflow improves, not worsens."
• "How do I know the £3,200 number is real?" → "It's median across 87 clients — half see less, half see more. I'd rather give you the median than the best case."
• "What if I'm in the 'less' half?" → "30-day money-back. If you're in the bottom half AND we're not earning back the £149/mo, we shouldn't be working together."

Sales call voice: conversational, name real numbers, let the buyer do the maths.
Sales page voice: explicit table showing the value breakdown, anchored to median.

When NOT to use value-based: if your buyer can't measure the value (emotional benefit only), or if your value math is heavily dependent on the buyer's own discipline. Stay on competitor-anchored pricing until you can name the £.

title: Complaint reply
body: Reply to this customer complaint: [PASTE MESSAGE]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Structure: 1 specific acknowledgement (name the actual issue, not "this experience") · 1 short apology (no excuses) · 1 specific fix with timeline · 1 line that retains the relationship. Under 130 words. No "we value your feedback".
whatItIsFor: A calm, structured response to a customer complaint — acknowledge, apologise (specifically not generically), fix, retain. The four-part structure that prevents most complaints escalating to refunds.
howToUseIt: Specific acknowledgement matters most. "Sorry you had a bad experience" reads as boilerplate. "Sorry the invoice categorisation was wrong — I see exactly which one" earns trust.

title: Customer question reply
body: Write a reply to this customer question for a [BUSINESS TYPE]: [PASTE QUESTION]. About [PRODUCT/SERVICE]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Structure: 1-line direct answer (the most-likely answer goes first) · 2-line context (why this matters / when it applies) · 1 caveat or "but if" clause · friendly close. Under 100 words. Skip "great question!"
whatItIsFor: A clear, no-jargon answer to a customer's pre-purchase or post-purchase question. Drafted as a reusable template you can lightly edit. Tracked support questions become saved replies, which become your fastest revenue work.
howToUseIt: Write replies as if you're writing a help-center article. Each reply you draft well can become the basis for an FAQ entry, an email response, OR a sales-page paragraph.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Customer asks "Can I claim my van as a business expense if I also use it on weekends?"Hi [name],

Short answer: yes — you claim a percentage, not the full amount.

HMRC accepts business-use percentage based on mileage. If 75% of your annual mileage is for work, you claim 75% of running costs (insurance, fuel, MOT) AND 75% of capital allowances on the van itself.

The thing most tradespeople get wrong: tracking. You need a mileage log showing the split, or HMRC will default you to a low default (~50%) on inspection.

If you've not been logging it: we can reconstruct a defensible estimate based on your job locations. Worth doing before year-end.

Want the 1-page mileage log template? Just reply LOG.

— Tom

title: Negative review reply

howToUseIt: Future buyers read your reply before deciding. A reply that's defensive makes you look bad; a reply that's calm + concrete makes you look trustworthy. Never argue facts publicly — move to private.

title: Refund reply
body: Write a refund request reply for a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Customer's reason for refund: [REASON]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Structure: 1 line confirming refund processed (no friction) · 1 line acknowledging the reason without arguing it · optional 1-line "what would have worked" question (feedback, not retention attempt) · respectful close that leaves the door open. whatItIsFor: Reply to a refund request — process it gracefully, learn from it, and leave the door open for them to come back. Friction-free refunds usually generate more LTV than blocked refunds.
howToUseIt: Don't gate refunds with "why are you cancelling?" questions before refunding. Process the refund first; ask for feedback after. Reverse order = adversarial. Correct order = warm.

2. Analyse (Friday 4-5pm weekly): Pull last week's feedback. Tag each item: "fixable now (under 30 min)", "fix in roadmap", "structurally won't fix (out of scope)", "noise". Use Notion table.

title: Retention email sequence
body: Write a 4-email retention sequence from a [BUSINESS TYPE] to a paying customer across months 2-12. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Cadence: M2 = quick-win, M4 = case study/inspiration, M7 = check-in survey, M11 = "year-in-review preview." Each email under 150 words. Reference what the customer has done so far where possible.
whatItIsFor: A 4-email retention sequence sent across months 2-12 of a customer's lifecycle — designed to keep them engaged without spamming. The sequence that lifts annual retention 10-20 points.
howToUseIt: Space these out — month 2, month 4, month 7, month 11. Closer than that = email fatigue. Sparser than that = forgotten brand presence.
exampleOutput:
Example output — 4-email Maple retention sequence (subjects + 1-line summary)M2 (quick-win): "Subject: Quick deduction you might've missed." Tip: one specific deduction relevant to their declared business type. CTA: reply with a Q if useful.
M4 (case study): "Subject: One client who looked just like you." Anonymised case from a similar-stage business + the structural change that worked. No pitch.
M7 (check-in): "Subject: Halfway through year one — what's missing?" 3 short questions: what's working, what's not, what would make us a 9/10.
M11 (year-in-review): "Subject: 11 months — quick preview of your year-in-review." Show numbers from their account (savings, hours saved, deductions caught). Soft-set up for annual review call.

title: Cancellation save script
body: Write a cancellation save script for a [BUSINESS TYPE] selling [PRODUCT/SERVICE at £PRICE]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Output: 3-step script: 1) Ask the real reason (not the polite reason) · 2) Conditional save offers per reason (pause, downgrade, refund + come back) · 3) Frictionless exit if save fails. Include script for the 5 most common cancellation reasons.
whatItIsFor: A script for the cancellation flow — offered AT the moment of cancellation. Saves 20-35% of cancellations that aren't genuinely structural. Most cancellations are recoverable with the right offer.
howToUseIt: Don't try to save EVERY cancellation. Some should leave (wrong fit, business closed). The script's job is identifying which 30% are worth a save offer.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Maple's cancellation save scriptStep 1 (real reason): "Before we process the cancellation — totally no pressure, but I'd appreciate the honest reason. Was it cost, service quality, no longer needed, found something better, or other?"

Step 2 (per-reason offers):
• Cost: "Would dropping to Starter (£99) keep you for another quarter?"
• No longer needed (business closed/sold): No save offer — close out gracefully and ask permission to follow up in 6 months.
• Service slipped: "I want to fix this. Free month + direct call with me — can I have one more shot?"
• Found something better: "Genuinely curious — what won you over? If you're up for sharing, I'll send a £20 thank-you for the feedback."
• Other: "Could you tell me more? Reply with a sentence if up for it."

Step 3 (frictionless exit): "Either way — cancellation processed within 24h, no further action needed. Channel stays open until end of paid month. Door always open if you ever come back."

title: Post-project debrief email
body: Write a post-project debrief email from a [BUSINESS TYPE] to a client who just completed [PROJECT NAME at £X total]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Output: subject + 170-word body. Recap the specific outcome delivered (not "thanks for the project"). 1 line on what worked. 1 line on what you'd refine. Soft mention of next-step paths (retainer, follow-on, referral). End with a friendly door-open close.
whatItIsFor: A debrief email sent at the end of a one-off project — captures the win in writing, asks for next steps, opens the door to retainer/repeat work. Most freelancers leave one-off projects without the debrief and lose the upsell.
howToUseIt: Send within 7 days of project completion. Earlier = "let it land." Later = momentum gone. 7-day window catches the satisfaction moment.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Post-project debrief for £4,800 website rebuildSubject: Wrap-up + what comes next (low pressure)

Hi Sarah,

Site went live Tuesday, here's the quick wrap-up.

What you've got: 24-page Webflow site, SEO-ready, pre-order form live on the wedding cake page, 3 case studies indexed by Google as of Friday.

What worked: Doing the copy interviews in week 1 (rather than my usual brief-then-write) saved 2 rounds of revisions. Worth doing for every Acme project going forward.

What I'd refine next time: Photography was the bottleneck — recommend pre-booking 3 hours with [photographer name] for next campaign.

3 paths if useful (zero pressure, just options):
• Monthly maintenance retainer (£200/mo · updates + SEO monitoring)
• Q4 campaign landing pages (one-off, £1,400 each)
• Refer a baker friend — I'm building the BR1 bakery client base.

Otherwise: enjoy the site. Reply if anything breaks.

— Tom

title: Referral reward email
body: Write a referral reward email from a [BUSINESS TYPE] to a customer whose referral just converted. Referred person: [NAME OF NEW CUSTOMER]. Reward earned: [SPECIFIC £ OR PERK]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Output: subject + 130-word body. Lead with the win (their reward is paid). Reference the new client by first name. Hint that this is the type of person you most love getting referred. Thank them genuinely, then gently invite the next referral.
whatItIsFor: The email confirming that a customer's referral converted, paying out their reward. Specific, fast, and warm — turns the referrer into a 2x-referrer through positive reinforcement.
howToUseIt: Send within 7 days of the referred sale closing. The reward email is the moment they realise referring you is worth doing again. Delays kill the second referral.

title: Product usage tip email
body: Write a usage tip email from a [BUSINESS TYPE] to existing customers about an under-used feature/practice. The tip: [SPECIFIC TIP — must be non-obvious]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Output: subject + 140-word body. Subject should signal value, not "tip of the month" (generic). Open with WHY most customers miss this. Walk through the tip in 3-4 steps. End with one specific result they'll see if they try it.
whatItIsFor: A monthly tip email teaching customers a non-obvious way to get more from your product/service. Increases engagement AND retention because customers extract more value AND feel like you're investing in them.
howToUseIt: Send monthly, not weekly. Weekly feels like spam; monthly feels like genuine value. Focus on usage patterns most customers MISS, not features everyone already uses.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Tip: tag receipts in Slack with the project name for better year-end reportsSubject: The Slack receipt habit that pays off in 9 months

Hi [name],

Quick thing most clients don't do, but the ones who do thank me at year-end: when you upload a receipt to our Slack channel, add the project or client name in the message.

Example: instead of just sending the photo, send "Receipt — Jones EV install — £180 supplier delivery."

Want to try it? Start with this week's receipts.

— Tom

title: Welcome gift copy
body: Write welcome gift copy for a [BUSINESS TYPE]'s new customer. Gift: [SPECIFIC GIFT — should be small and personal, not a discount]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Output: short note/card text under 80 words. Explain why this gift specifically (not generic). Acknowledge that gifts feel weird when transactional — make this NOT that. End with no expectation of reciprocation.
whatItIsFor: Copy for a small physical or digital "welcome gift" given to new customers (or top customers) that creates a positive surprise. Welcome gifts done right have outsized retention impact for their cost.
howToUseIt: Gifts should be small + thoughtful + unexpected. Don't make them transactional ("£10 off your next order"). Make them human ("£10 voucher for your favourite local coffee shop").

title: Customer spotlight post
body: Write a customer spotlight post for a [BUSINESS TYPE]'s [IG/LinkedIn]. Customer name + business: [NAME + DESCRIPTION]. Specific win to highlight: [WIN WITH NUMBERS]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Output: post copy under 200 words. Lead with the win, not "spotlight on...". Quote the customer directly (a real line if possible). End with what other businesses can learn from this story (one specific takeaway, not generic).
whatItIsFor: A social media post (IG/LinkedIn) spotlighting a customer's win — drives social proof + makes the spotlighted customer feel valued. Both effects compound retention.
howToUseIt: Always get permission first. Always tag them (where applicable). The "spotlight" is half about them, half about other potential customers seeing a peer being recognised — which earns inbound DMs.
exampleOutput:
Example output — IG post spotlighting Mike's £4,200 catchMike B., electrician in Bromley, came to Maple in March 2024 with one specific question: "Are my books missing anything?"

His old accountant had been filing for 6 years. Clean P&Ls, no missed deadlines, no HMRC queries. By every standard measure: fine.

First two weeks of onboarding, I asked one question his previous accountant never had: "Show me the vans you've owned in the last 5 years."

£4,247.

That's how much in capital allowances had been quietly missed across his last 3 vans. Reclaimable. He's got that refund now.

His exact words: "I'm grateful and slightly furious at the same time."

The lesson for anyone reading: "your books are fine" usually means "fine for the standard checklist." The retroactive review — looking back at what was missed — is the highest-ROI hour an accountant can spend with a new client. We do it standard for every Maple client now.

Cheers Mike, for letting me share this.

(With permission · numbers verified · real client.)

title: Reorder reminder email
body: Write a reorder reminder email for a [BUSINESS TYPE] selling [CONSUMABLE PRODUCT]. Typical consumption cycle: [DAYS]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Output: subject + 130-word body. Reference what they bought specifically (item + when). Confirm you're sending now because they're likely 75% through the typical cycle. Make reorder one click (skip "browse the catalogue" friction). Include "wait if..." line for honest customers.
whatItIsFor: A reorder reminder for products with predictable consumption cycles — timed to the median repurchase window, not a calendar. Most product businesses leave 15-25% revenue on the table by not running reorder reminders.
howToUseIt: Time it to the median repurchase cycle (e.g. 45 days for a consumable that lasts 60 days). Earlier = "I still have some." Later = "I bought elsewhere already." Hitting the 75% consumption mark works best.
exampleOutput:

Hi [name],

You bought the large cedar candle from us 45 days ago. Based on burn rate, you're probably ~75% through it.

Quick one-click reorder if you want a fresh one before this one runs out: [REORDER LINK · £24 · same address]

What we know about you: you preferred the large size (60h burn) over the small (30h burn). Reordering the large again unless you tell me otherwise.

Wait if: you're going on holiday for 2+ weeks (it'll just sit unburned). Reply HOLIDAY and we'll pause your reminder for a month.

If you've switched to a different brand or decided you don't need another, reply STOP and I'll take you off the reorder list. No guilt.

title: Project kickoff email
body: Write a project kickoff email from a [BUSINESS TYPE] to a client starting [PROJECT NAME at £X]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Output: subject + 200-word body covering 6 specifics: scope (1 line) · timeline + phases · communication channel + cadence · who's responsible for what · how decisions get made · what counts as "done". End with the FIRST action they need to take.
whatItIsFor: The kickoff email that sets the tone for the whole project — confirms scope, schedule, communication channel, success criteria. Sets expectations before the work starts; clients with a clear kickoff email complain ~70% less later.
howToUseIt: Send within 24 hours of contract signing. The email is the contract in plain English — what they paid for, when it lands, how you communicate.

title: Project status update
body: Write a weekly project status update from a [BUSINESS TYPE] to a client on [PROJECT NAME], week [N] of [TOTAL]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. whatItIsFor: A weekly project status update — what's done, what's next, blockers, decisions needed. Replaces "project status" meetings with 5-min reads. Most agency status meetings could be a 200-word email.
howToUseIt: Send every Friday afternoon. Friday > Monday for status updates — gives the client the weekend to digest, you the weekend free of follow-up.

title: Scope creep response
body: Write a scope-creep response from a [BUSINESS TYPE] to a client who's just asked for [OUT-OF-SCOPE REQUEST]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Output: subject + 130-word body. Structure: 1 line acknowledging the request is reasonable · 1 line stating it's outside the agreed scope (without making them wrong) · 3 options (do it as add-on at £X, push to a phase 2, do it in scope by trading something else off) · low-pressure close. Skip "as per our contract."
whatItIsFor: The reply when a client asks for something outside the agreed scope — protects the project AND the relationship. Most scope-creep failures are response failures: too soft and the project bleeds; too firm and the relationship breaks.
howToUseIt: Acknowledge it's a good idea (if it is). State whether it's in or out of scope. Offer a path to add it. Don't argue about whether they remembered the contract.

Example output — Client requests blog setup mid-website-buildSubject: About the blog request — 3 options

Hi Sarah,

Totally fair to want a blog — most bakery sites benefit, and your audience would engage with recipe content.

2. Phase 2 in October (£700 standalone) — current build stays on schedule. Blog launched separately after holiday season.
3. Trade in scope — drop one of the 5 product detail pages (the Easter range, perhaps?) and I'll add the blog instead. Same total fee.

No wrong answer. What feels right?

— Tom

title: Project delay communication
body: Write a delay email from a [BUSINESS TYPE] to a client about [SPECIFIC DELIVERABLE that's slipping by N days/weeks]. Real reason: [HONEST CAUSE]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Output: subject + 150-word body. Lead with the new date, not the apology. Explain the real cause briefly (no excuses, no whining). State what you're doing differently. Offer ONE specific gesture (partial refund, expedited next milestone, bonus item). End with their decision needed.
whatItIsFor: The email when YOU need to delay a project deliverable. Proactive delay emails maintain trust; reactive ones destroy it. Sending the delay email before the client notices is the entire game.
howToUseIt: Send the moment you know there'll be a delay. Not when the original deadline passes. Hours matter — every 24 hours of delay before notification doubles the trust cost.

Example output — Site launch delayed 1 week because photographer was lateSubject: Acme launch moving to Saturday 28th (was 21st)

Quick note — Acme Bakery launch is moving 1 week, to Saturday 28th.

One gesture: I'm refunding £200 from the final invoice for the inconvenience. Already adjusted on the Stripe schedule.

Need from you: confirm the new launch date works (any conflicts the week of the 28th?). Reply OK or NEW.

— Tom

whatItIsFor: The final email at project completion — confirms what's delivered, what's NOT included (so you don't get surprise "but I thought..." requests), what comes next, asks for the testimonial. The email that protects you from post-project scope creep.
howToUseIt: Send within 24 hours of the final deliverable. The "what's not included" list saves more disputes than any contract clause — clients read end-of-project emails carefully.

whatItIsFor: Outlines a structured onboarding pack — welcome doc, intake form, calendar invites, expectations doc, FAQ. The pack that turns "I'm in" into "I know what's happening this week."
howToUseIt: The onboarding pack is the operational counterpart to the kickoff email — the kickoff is what they read; the pack is the artifacts. Both ship within 24h of signing.

title: Deliverable feedback request
body: Write a deliverable feedback request from a [BUSINESS TYPE] to a client on [SPECIFIC DELIVERABLE — e.g. logo concepts, draft proposal, first-week site build]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. Output: subject + 140-word body. Link the deliverable in line 1. Ask 3 specific questions tied to the work (not "any thoughts?"). whatItIsFor: An email asking for client feedback on a deliverable — focuses them on specific revision questions, not "any thoughts?" Specific feedback questions cut revision cycles by 30-50%.
howToUseIt: Send with the deliverable, not after. Embedding the questions in the same email as the work product gets 2-3x more usable feedback than separate "feedback request" emails.

Hi Sarah,

title: Change request log
body: Design a change request log for a [BUSINESS TYPE] running [PROJECT TYPE]. whatItIsFor: A structured change-request log for a project — what's been asked, what's been agreed, what was charged, what was declined. Protects both sides when the project gets long enough that "you said..." memory fails.
howToUseIt: Update weekly with the client visible. Shared change logs prevent disputes; private ones don't. A Notion table both parties can see is the simplest workable format.

title: Retainer proposal copy
body: Write retainer proposal copy from a [BUSINESS TYPE] to a client who just completed [ONE-OFF PROJECT]. Retainer price: [£X/mo]. What's included: [3-5 SPECIFIC THINGS]. Voice: [PASTE FROM #16]. whatItIsFor: Sales copy for converting a one-off project client into a retainer client. Most successful retainer conversions happen 7-21 days post-project — late enough that they're using the work, early enough that you're still top of mind.
howToUseIt: Retainers convert when the gap between "I might need something" and "I have someone to call" feels worth £X/month. Make that gap explicit in the proposal.
exampleOutput:
Example output — £200/mo maintenance retainer for Acme Bakery post-buildSubject: Maintenance retainer · genuine "is it worth it?" pitch

Hi Sarah,

Site's been live 14 days, post-launch tweaks period is up tomorrow. Quick honest pitch on the retainer.

£200/mo, includes:
• Up to 4 small updates per month (price changes, new products, image swaps, copy tweaks)
• SEO monitoring (alerts if Google indexing breaks)
• Webflow + Stripe security patches applied within 48h
• Direct WhatsApp line if anything urgent breaks

What this is actually buying: 5 minutes from "the site needs a thing" to "the thing is done", without having to scope a new project or hunt for a freelancer.

Honestly, don't take this if: You're confident in Webflow (most clients aren't, but some are). You won't make changes more than once a quarter (then just pay ad-hoc). You're happy waiting 3-5 days when something breaks (no judgement).

Yes / no / try-for-a-month?

— Tom

title: Client escalation note (external)
body: Write a client escalation email from a [BUSINESS TYPE] to a client about [URGENT ISSUE]. Voice: calm, direct, no drama. Output: subject + 130-word body. 4 qualifying questions: 1. Annual revenue band? 2. Current accountant setup (have one / had one / never)? 3. What triggered the search today? 4. Sole trader, Ltd, or undecided?

Lead types & follow-up:
• Hot (35+): Founder calls within 4 hours.
• Warm (20-34): Founder Slack DM + £40 pressure-test offer.
• Cold (10-19): Auto nurture sequence.
• Disqualified (under 10 or red-flag): Polite "we're not a fit" + recommend Crunch/Tide.

CRM logging: Notion table — paste lead, AI scores, founder either accepts or overrides. Override rule: founder can override AI in either direction, but must add 1-line reason for next quarter's review.

whatItIsFor: A weekly reporting workflow producing a one-page summary of marketing, sales, ops, financial — auto-pulled and AI-summarised. Replaces 90 min of manual reporting with ~10 min of review.

AI step: Paste raw numbers into Claude → "Summarise into 1 page, flag anything outside normal range, suggest top 3 actions for the week."

title: Google Analytics summary
body: Analyse this Google Analytics 4 data for a Slack-first accountancy serving UK trades (Maple, £149/mo subscription): [PASTE GA DATA — sessions, channels, top pages, conversion events, prior-period comparison]. title: Email campaign analysis
body: Analyse this email campaign data for Maple (Slack-first accountancy, list of 1,240 UK trades, weekly newsletter): [PASTE DATA — subject line, send time, open rate, click rate, unsubscribes, revenue/bookings, prior 3 sends for comparison]. Benchmarks: B2B services open ~32%, click ~2.5%, unsub <0.3%. Give: 1) plain-English diagnosis vs my last 3 sends, 2) what the data suggests about my subject line (curiosity vs value vs urgency), 3) content + CTA effectiveness, 4) send time + day signal, 5) the single most testable change for the next send and how to measure if it worked.
whatItIsFor: Diagnoses a sent campaign across subject line, content, send time, and list health — and tells you the single most testable change for the next send. Replaces "open rate was 23%, cool" with "here's what to change."
howToUseIt: Always include the previous 3 sends as comparison. A single campaign's number is noise; the trend is signal. If revenue tracking is set up, paste that too — open rate is a leading indicator, revenue per send is what matters.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Maple "Don't lose £4k on this CIS mistake" campaignDiagnosis: Open rate 41% (well above 32% benchmark, also above your 4-send average of 34%). Click rate 1.8% (below your 2.5% average, below 2.5% benchmark). 2 unsubs (0.16%, healthy). 3 demo bookings, £447 first-month revenue attributable.

Subject line: "Don't lose £4k on this CIS mistake" — the specificity of "£4k" plus the trade-specific term "CIS" drove the open. Worth keeping the £-number-+-specific-mistake formula.

Content + CTA: Strong open, weak follow-through. The 41% who opened didn't click at the rate they normally do. Likely cause: the email used 4 different CTAs (Book a demo, Read the guide, Reply to this email, Share with a mate). Pick one. Single-CTA emails in your list have averaged 3.1% CTR; multi-CTA emails 1.7%.

Send time: Tuesday 07:30 — your best window. Confirmed by the 41% open. Don't change.

One change for next send: Use the same subject formula ("Don't lose £[X] on this [trade-specific] mistake") but cut to a single "Book a 15-min demo" CTA. Measure success as click rate ≥ 2.5% and ≥ 4 bookings. If CTR jumps and opens stay above 35%, the formula is locked in for the next 4 weeks.

title: Sales pipeline analysis
body: Analyse this sales pipeline data for Maple (Slack-first accountancy, £149/mo): [PASTE DATA — leads, demo bookings, demos held, proposals sent, deals closed, avg deal value, avg time-in-stage, prior month for comparison]. Output: 1) conversion rate at every stage (lead→demo→held→proposal→close) with prior month delta, 2) the biggest single drop-off in absolute lost-deal value, 3) likely root cause based on time-in-stage data, 4) 3 prioritised actions to fix the weakest stage with how I'll know it worked, 5) one metric to watch weekly.
whatItIsFor: Calculates stage-by-stage conversion through your pipeline and finds the single biggest leak — so you fix the right hole instead of pouring more leads into a leaky bucket. Most small businesses chase more leads when they should fix the lead → meeting step.
howToUseIt: Include time-in-stage data if you have it — a leak might not be losing deals, it might be deals sitting in "proposal sent" for 60 days. Always give the AI two months of data so it can flag whether a stage worsened or that's just how it always is.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Maple May pipeline reviewStage conversions (May, prior month in brackets):
• Lead → demo booked: 89/247 = 36% (was 31%, ↑) 
• Demo booked → demo held: 61/89 = 69% (was 78%, ↓)
• Demo held → proposal sent: 54/61 = 89% (was 88%, flat)
• Proposal → closed-won: 11/54 = 20% (was 27%, ↓)
• Overall lead → close: 4.5% (was 5.8%)

Biggest leak (by £): Proposal → close. Lost 43 deals × £149 × 12 = ~£77k annualised pipeline value walked away after proposal. The demo-held → proposal step is fine; it's the close that broke.

Root cause signal: Avg time in "proposal sent" jumped from 6 days → 14 days. Proposals are not being rejected — they're being ignored. Combined with the demo-no-show jump (22% → 31%), the pattern looks like Maple is talking to less-qualified prospects who book easily but don't have urgency.

3 actions:
1. Add a 1-question screener to the demo form ("What's the £ value of your biggest unpaid invoice this quarter?") — filters tyre-kickers. Win condition: demo-held rate back above 75% within 30 days.
2. Send a 3-day auto-follow-up after every proposal with a single yes/no question ("Is this still on your roadmap for June — yes / not now?"). Win condition: avg time-in-proposal back to <8 days.
3. Add 2 social-proof video clips from electrician + plumber clients to the proposal email. Win condition: proposal close rate ≥ 25% next month.

Weekly watch metric: Demo-held rate. If it stays below 70%, the screener isn't filtering hard enough.

title: Meeting sentiment analysis
body: Analyse the sentiment and communication dynamics in this meeting transcript for a Maple [discovery call / client review / partner sync]: [PASTE SPEAKER-LABELLED TRANSCRIPT]. For each speaker output: overall sentiment (positive / neutral / negative / mixed), engagement level (high / moderate / low / dropped at minute X), any signs of disagreement, confusion, or disengagement with the timestamp, and the single most impactful statement they made (their exact words). End with: a team dynamics summary in 2 sentences, and one concrete recommendation for how to run the next call differently.
whatItIsFor: Surfaces the emotional + engagement signal in a transcript that you missed in real time — disagreement that didn't get voiced, the moment someone disengaged, the point where confusion took over. Especially useful for sales calls and difficult client conversations.
howToUseIt: Sentiment analysis is a tool, not a verdict — the AI is good at spotting patterns ("Dave got quieter after the price was mentioned") but bad at interpreting them. Treat each finding as a hypothesis to test, not a conclusion. Never share the output with the person being analysed.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Discovery call with Dave (electrician), 19 MayTom (Maple founder): Sentiment positive throughout. Engagement high. No disagreement signals. Most impactful: "We don't bill you for the Slack messages — that's the whole point, we want you to ask the stupid questions." This was the moment Dave's tone shifted (minute 27).

Dave (prospect, electrician): Sentiment mixed — warm + curious for first 25 minutes, then anxious/cautious from minute 27 to 41, warm again at close. Engagement high overall but dipped at minute 31 when Tom asked about turnover (longer pauses, shorter answers). One confusion signal at minute 38 ("Sorry, so the £149 is including VAT returns?") — Tom answered fully but Dave didn't acknowledge the answer, suggesting he wasn't fully reassured. Most impactful: "Last guy charged me £40 every time I rang him with a CIS question, so I stopped ringing." This is the buying motivation in his own words.

Team dynamics: Healthy asymmetric — Tom led structurally but Dave drove the emotional arc. The price-anxiety wave (minute 27–41) didn't get processed; Dave moved past it but didn't dissolve it.

Recommendation: When the prospect goes quiet for >30 seconds after a price/scope mention, name it: "Just checking in — does that £149 feel right for what you're getting, or do you want to walk through what's included?" Don't move on until they answer in a full sentence.

title: Meeting to follow-up email
body: Turn this Maple meeting transcript / summary into a professional follow-up email: [PASTE TRANSCRIPT OR #292 SUMMARY]. Recipient: [name + role + business]. Include: 1) a one-line opener that quotes something specific they said, 2) brief recap of what was agreed, 3) their actions with deadlines (theirs first), 4) my actions with deadlines, 5) clear single next step. Keep it under 200 words. Tone: warm but precise, like a junior partner writing to a client they want to keep.

title: Break-even calculator brief
body: Calculate break-even for Maple (Slack-first accountancy, £149/mo). Fixed costs (monthly): [PASTE — e.g. rent, salaries, insurance, software, accounting, marketing baseline]. Variable cost per client per month: [PASTE — e.g. delivery time × hourly rate, Stripe fees, software seat cost]. Output: 1) break-even number of clients with the maths shown, 2) the contribution margin per client in £ and %, 3) how many clients I'd lose before I'm under water, 4) the 2 fixed-cost items that move break-even most if cut, 5) what break-even looks like at the next pricing tier (£199/mo) — to inform a price-rise decision.
whatItIsFor: Calculates the exact units/clients/sales you need to cover costs — and the float you have before things get tight. The number every founder should know cold but most can't quote without scrambling for a spreadsheet.
howToUseIt: Separate fixed costs (rent, salaries, insurance, subscriptions) from variable costs (per-client delivery time, processor fees, payment terms). The AI gets break-even wrong when you blur them. Recalculate any time fixed costs change by >5% — adding one £79/mo SaaS tool can shift break-even by 1–2 clients.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Maple break-even at £149/moInputs: Fixed £8,420/mo (Tom's £4,500 owner draw, Sarah VA £1,200, Xero £45, ConvertKit £29, Slack £180, insurance £375 amortised, rent £1,500, misc £591). Variable per client £18.50/mo (2.5hrs delivery × £6 effective cost + Stripe 1.5%+20p = £2.43 + Slack seat).

Contribution per client: £149 − £18.50 = £130.50 (87.6% margin).

Break-even: £8,420 ÷ £130.50 = 64.5 clients → 65 clients. You're at 87 — that's 22 clients of safety margin = £2,871/month profit before tax.

How many can you lose: Up to 22 clients (25% of base) before you're at break-even. Beyond that, every lost client costs £130.50/month until something gives.

Fixed-cost levers:
• Rent (£1,500) — biggest single non-salary line. Going fully remote would drop break-even from 65 → 53 clients (a 18% safety boost).
• Owner draw (£4,500) — if you can run on £3,500 for 3 months, break-even drops to 57 clients (a 12% boost) and gives you a £3,000 cash buffer for the same period.

At £199/mo (price rise): Contribution = £180.50. Break-even = 47 clients. You'd need to retain at least 47 of the existing 87 through the price rise to avoid going backwards — a churn ceiling of 46%. Most price rises see 5–15% churn, so this is well within safety.

title: Cash runway summary
body: Calculate Maple's cash runway under 3 scenarios. Inputs: current cash bank balance £[amount], current MRR £12,963, monthly fixed costs £8,420, monthly variable cost per client £18.50, average client count 87 (declining 2%/mo at churn). Output: 1) operational runway (revenue continues), 2) stress runway (revenue drops 50% from month 1), 3) survival runway (revenue drops to £0 from month 1), 4) the single biggest lever that extends each runway, 5) the 90-day action that gives the biggest runway uplift for least disruption.
whatItIsFor: Calculates exactly how many months you can survive on current cash if revenue dropped to zero today — and what changes that number most. The most important number a founder must know cold.
howToUseIt: Calculate runway under THREE assumptions: revenue continues at current rate (operational runway), revenue drops 50% (stress runway), revenue drops to £0 (survival runway). All three matter; together they tell you how much risk you can afford to take.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Maple cash runway, current cash £28,000Operational runway (revenue continues at £12,963 MRR): Indefinite — Maple is cash-positive (~£2,940/mo net of variable cost) and is adding to the £28k pile, not drawing it down.

Stress runway (MRR drops 50% to £6,481): ~10 months. The £28k cushion absorbs ~£2,750/mo of net drawdown at 50% revenue. If the dip persisted longer than that, you'd need to either cut costs or recover revenue.

Survival runway (MRR = £0): 3.3 months at full cost base. With the emergency plan from #313 (cuts saving £13,500/mo) → variable cost drops too as clients churn, so survival extends to ~5–6 months. Realistically with all levers pulled, you have a 6-month survival window even in a worst case.

Biggest lever per scenario:
• Operational: irrelevant — runway is infinite.
• Stress: cutting fixed costs (rent, hires, software) — fixed cost is what kills runway, not variable.
• Survival: founder draw — at £4,500/mo it's the single largest controllable line. Taking it to £0 extends survival from 3.3 → 5.5 months.

90-day action for max runway uplift: Convert 2 of your largest 3 clients to annual prepay (offer 10% discount in exchange — £149 × 12 × 0.9 = £1,609/yr per client) by Aug. Net: £3,200 of cash arrives in your account in next 30 days instead of trickling in over 12 months. Combined with cutting Trello + Slack (no impact, £132/mo), this adds ~1 month to every runway scenario for essentially zero cost.

title: Investor update email
body: Write Maple's monthly investor update for May (Slack-first accountancy, raised £50k angel in Jan, 1 angel investor + 2 advisors on the distribution). Inputs: MRR £12,963 (+8% MoM), new clients 14, churned 2, top win, top lowlight, key metric movement, cash position £28k, one specific ask. Constraints: under 350 words, headline number in subject, one ask at the end, never hide bad news, no jargon, no "amazing" or "incredible."
whatItIsFor: Monthly investor / angel / advisor update that tells the truth without burying the lede. Investors fund founders who communicate well; this is the muscle that compounds.
howToUseIt: Open with the headline number. End with one specific ask. The middle is wins / lowlights / numbers. Honesty rule: if something is going badly, name it directly. Investors smell hedging and lose confidence faster than they lose it from bad news.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Maple investor update, May 2026Subject: Maple May update — MRR £12,963 (+8% MoM), 1 lowlight inside

Hi all,

May was steady. MRR closed at £12,963 (+8% from April's £12,003). Net new clients +12 (14 gained, 2 churned). 87 active clients.

The big win: the "CIS deductions explained" blog post hit page 1 on Google mid-month and is now bringing 22 organic sessions/day. It contributed 9 of the 14 new clients this month — the first month organic search outperformed LinkedIn for us. I'm doubling down: commissioning 2 more posts in the same trade-tax cluster in June.

The lowlight: demo-to-close rate dropped from 27% to 20%. I think we're talking to slightly less-qualified leads as volume rises. I've added a 1-question screener to the demo form (Prompt #295 work) and we'll see if that brings the rate back. If it doesn't, the £30k MRR target slips by 1-2 months.

Other numbers worth flagging:
• Churn 2.3% (within tolerance, was 2.1% last month).
• Cash bank balance £28k (up £2.9k MoM). 8.5+ months operational runway.
• Best post on LinkedIn this month: client-story carousel about Dave's £4k CIS save, 412 saves on IG, 6 inbound DMs.

What I'm doing in June: launching client referral bounty (£100 credit per referred client that pays month 2), starting recruitment for first hire (Aug start), and writing the next 2 trade-tax blog posts.

One ask: I'm meeting 3 candidates for the part-qualified accountant hire in June. If you know anyone in the SE/London accounting world I should also speak to, would massively appreciate intros. Want someone who can answer client Slack messages in plain English, not someone who needs an org chart.

That's it for now. Numbers in the spreadsheet (link). Any questions, reply directly.

— Tom

title: Growth lever identification
body: Identify Maple's highest-ROI growth levers. Current state: MRR £12,963, 87 clients @ £149, churn 2.3%/mo, demo-to-close 20%, organic leads 90/mo, LinkedIn leads 30/mo, referrals 5/mo, avg LTV 18 months, CAC £35. Map levers across: 1) acquisition (new channels, new content, partnerships), 2) conversion (demo show-up, demo close), 3) retention (churn, expansion within existing accounts), 4) pricing (price rise, tiering, annual prepay), 5) referrals. For each lever: estimated MRR uplift in 90 days, ICE score (Impact × Confidence × Ease, 1-10 each), and effort hours. Rank by ICE score and recommend the top 2 to run in parallel.
whatItIsFor: Maps all available growth levers (acquisition, conversion, retention, pricing, expansion) to your current numbers and identifies the 1-2 with the highest expected return for the lowest cost / risk. Stops you from chasing the shiny growth tactic when there's a free uplift in front of you.
howToUseIt: Force the AI to use ICE scoring (Impact × Confidence × Ease, 1-10). Without scoring, every lever sounds equally promising. The winner is usually NOT the lever you'd guess — small businesses overinvest in acquisition and underinvest in conversion + retention, where the leverage is.

1. Price rise on new clients only (ICE 630). 2 hours of work (update website + checkout). New clients accept the £169 because they don't know the £149 history. Existing clients stay at £149. Risk-free MRR uplift.
2. Referral bounty (ICE 576). 6 hours of work (write the offer, email 87 clients, set up tracking spreadsheet). 1.4 referrals/active client/year industry avg → Maple should get 8-12 referrals in 90 days at £100 bounty. £1,000 spend → £1,500 MRR = 1.5× immediate, ~25× LTV-payback.

Combined: ~£2,280 MRR uplift in 90 days for 8 hours of work + £1,000 of bounty spend. Defer the lower-ICE levers until these two are running.

title: Pricing model comparison
body: Compare pricing models for Maple (currently £149/mo flat, 87 clients, all on same tier). Evaluate: 1) current flat monthly, 2) tiered (Starter £99 / Standard £149 / Plus £199), 3) usage-based (£0 base + £15/Slack-question or £40/return filed), 4) annual-only with monthly discount banned, 5) value-based (% of tax savings achieved). For each: predicted MRR change in 12 months, conversion impact, churn impact, complexity to operate, ideal customer fit. Recommend one with a 90-day migration plan that protects existing clients.
whatItIsFor: Compares your current pricing model (e.g. flat monthly) against alternatives (tiered, usage-based, value-based, annual-only) and tells you which would lift MRR most without hurting conversion. Most small businesses leave 20-40% of MRR on the table by being stuck on the wrong model.
howToUseIt: Don't just compare the model — also model the migration path. A pricing model that's better in steady-state but causes 15% churn during the migration is worse than the current model. The AI should always include "how do we get from here to there without breaking it" analysis.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Maple pricing model comparisonModel12-mo MRRConv vs currentChurn vs currentComplexityVerdictCurrent flat £149£24k (forecast)baselinebaseline 2.3%simplebaseline3-tier (£99/£149/£199)£31k+15% (lower price ramp)~2.0%mediumwinnerUsage-based£19k-30% (uncertainty kills booking)+1% (per-Q anxiety)highkills the Slack propositionAnnual-only£27k cash-front-loaded-25%-1.5% (lock-in)simpletoo punishing for trades cash flowValue-based (%)£35k+ but volatile-40% (sticker shock)+2.5%highgood in theory, fails in practice for SMBRecommendation: 3-tier model.
• Starter £99/mo: sole traders, no VAT, no CIS. Slack response within 2 working days.
• Standard £149/mo (current): the current default. Same-day Slack. (Existing clients land here, no change.)
• Plus £199/mo: CIS-heavy, VAT-registered, anything complex. Same-day Slack + quarterly business review call.

Why this wins: Captures price-sensitive sole traders Maple currently loses (~25% of demos that go cold cite price). Captures premium revenue from complex clients currently subsidised by the flat fee (see Prompt #310 — the 5 "difficult clients"). Existing 87 clients stay on £149 and don't see any change.

90-day migration plan:
Week 1: Update website + checkout with 3 tiers. Existing clients: no change visible to them; they stay grandfathered on £149.
Week 2: New leads go to tiered checkout from day 1. Tier breakdown expected: ~30% Starter, ~50% Standard, ~20% Plus.
Week 4: Soft-pitch the 5 "difficult clients" to move to Plus (£199), with a 60-day grace period to consider. Email script: Prompt #308.
Week 8: Review tier mix. If Plus uptake is below 15%, lower the wall between Standard and Plus by adding 1 perk to Plus.
Week 12: Decide whether to remove Standard's £149 grandfather price for clients passing 18-month tenure (probably not — retention > upsell).

title: Customer LTV brief
body: Calculate Maple's LTV by cohort. Inputs: average client tenure 18 months, monthly churn 2.3%, £149/mo, gross margin per client £130.50. Cohort split: Sole traders (37% of base, longer tenure ~21 months, ~£140 effective ARPU), Ltd company VAT (44% of base, 18 months, £155 ARPU due to occasional one-off projects), CIS-heavy (14% of base, 16 months, £160 ARPU), Difficult-5 (5% of base, 24 months but 34% margin only). Output: 1) LTV per cohort, 2) total blended LTV, 3) max sustainable CAC per cohort (LTV ÷ 3 rule), 4) which cohort I should aim marketing spend at and which I should NOT, 5) the single experiment to extend LTV in the highest-value cohort.
whatItIsFor: Calculates true LTV (lifetime value) per customer cohort and tells you what you can afford to spend acquiring each type. Stops you from setting CAC limits based on intuition and starting marketing channels you can't sustain.
howToUseIt: Use gross-margin LTV, not revenue LTV — paying £149 for a customer who delivers £130.50 margin is what matters. If you're early-stage (under 12 months of data), use cohort-projected LTV with a clear "we'll re-run this once we have 18 months of data" caveat.
exampleOutput:
Example output — Maple LTV by cohortCohortARPUMarginTenureLTV (gross-margin)Max CAC (LTV ÷ 3)Sole trader£14089%21 months£2,617£872Ltd company VAT£15578%18 months£2,176£725CIS-heavy trades£16072%16 months£1,843£614Difficult-5£99 (legacy)34%24 months£808£269Blended LTV: Weighted = £2,238. Max blended CAC = £746.

Spend where:
• Aim 60%+ of marketing at sole traders — longest tenure, fattest margin, highest LTV. Currently they only generate ~30% of leads. Underweight.
• Keep current spend on Ltd company VAT — solid LTV, stable cohort.
• Reduce spend targeting CIS-heavy — they're profitable but the tenure is shortest (they grow out of small accountants faster). Don't stop, just don't lead with them.
• Stop acquiring Difficult-5 profiles — high-touch, low-margin, expensive customer service. Filter them out at the demo stage with a screener question.

The experiment for sole traders: The biggest LTV-extension lever for sole traders is annual catchup work in October (self-assessment season). Currently we deliver this as part of the £149 with no upsell. Test: offer a free 30-min "October Tune-up" call in September — a soft re-engagement touch. Cohort that books the call has historically (in industry data) extended tenure by 4-6 months. If true for Maple, the sole-trader LTV moves from £2,617 → ~£3,150 — a 20% lift on the highest-value cohort.
