title: Passive income idea audit
body: Audit this passive income idea for a [BUSINESS TYPE] owner with [HOURS PER WEEK] of free time and [STARTING BUDGET]: [IDEA]. Score it 1–10 on: setup time, time-to-first-revenue, monthly maintenance hours, scalability, and realistic 12-month revenue. Flag the 3 most common ways this idea fails for solo operators. End with a verdict: pursue now / park for later / do not start. Be specific and skeptical, not aspirational.
whatItIsFor: Stress-tests a specific passive income idea against the realities of solo operators — setup time, revenue lag, scaling ceiling, and common failure modes. Use it before spending a single hour or pound on the idea.
howToUseIt: Pick one specific idea, not a category. Be brutally honest about your free hours and starting budget — soft inputs produce useless verdicts.

title: Side hustle to business planner
body: I run [SIDE HUSTLE TYPE] earning [CURRENT MONTHLY REVENUE] in [HOURS PER WEEK]. My main job pays [MAIN JOB INCOME]. I want this to be my full income in [TIMEFRAME]. Build a phased transition plan with: revenue milestones I need to hit before leaving my main job, what to systemize first, hiring/contractor decisions, tax and legal setup priorities by phase, and the 3 biggest risks I should plan for. Give me a specific revenue floor I must reach in each phase before moving to the next.
whatItIsFor: Builds a phased transition plan from side hustle to main business, anchored to specific revenue milestones rather than vague "when I feel ready". Use it 6–18 months before you'd consider quitting your main job.
howToUseIt: Be brutally honest about current revenue and hours — the plan only works if the numbers are real. The output gives you a revenue floor to hit at each phase before scaling up.

title: Exit strategy brief
body: I run a [BUSINESS TYPE] doing [ANNUAL REVENUE] at [PROFIT MARGIN], with [OWNER HOURS PER WEEK]. I want to exit in [TIMEFRAME]. Map my realistic exit options (sale to competitor, employee acquisition, lifestyle wind-down, succession to family/staff). For each option: typical multiple, prep work required, owner involvement during handover, likely buyer profile, and biggest risk. End with one recommended exit path and a month-by-month prep checklist for the 6 months before listing.
whatItIsFor: Maps your realistic exit options based on revenue, profitability, and owner involvement — then recommends one path with a 6-month prep checklist. Use it 12–24 months before any planned exit.
howToUseIt: The "owner involvement" hours number is the most important input. If you're irreplaceable, valuation drops sharply — the plan reveals what to delegate first.

title: Business valuation narrative
body: Write a 1-page valuation narrative for a [BUSINESS TYPE] doing [ANNUAL REVENUE] at [PROFIT MARGIN], with [CUSTOMER COUNT], and [KEY DEFENSIBLE ASSET — e.g. proprietary process, exclusive supplier deal, recurring contracts]. Audience: a potential acquirer. Sections: business at a glance, defensible moat (3 lines max), revenue concentration risk, the growth lever the buyer would inherit, and a recommended valuation range with reasoning. Tone: confident, specific, no hype. Do not invent numbers I haven't given you.
whatItIsFor: Generates a one-page narrative an acquirer or investor would read — focused on moat, risk, and growth lever, not vanity metrics. Use it to pressure-test how investable your business actually is.
howToUseIt: Use real numbers, not aspirational. The "growth lever" section reveals whether you've built something a buyer can scale, or a job in disguise.

title: Job description writer
body: Write a job description for a [ROLE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE] based in [LOCATION]. Employment type: [FULL-TIME/PART-TIME/CONTRACTOR]. Core responsibilities: [LIST 3–5 TASKS]. Must-have skills: [LIST]. Nice-to-have: [LIST]. Salary range: [RANGE]. Reports to the founder. Make it direct and jargon-free — write for a specific person, not an HR filter. End with 3 interview questions we'll ask at the shortlisting stage.
whatItIsFor: Writes a clear, honest job description for your first or next hire that attracts the right person without HR jargon or corporate filler.
howToUseIt: Fill in the role specifics. The more concrete your task list, the better the output — vague inputs produce generic job ads that attract the wrong candidates.

title: Behavioural interview question generator
body: Generate 10 behavioural interview questions for a [ROLE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Structure: 3 questions testing technical competence for this role, 3 testing client or customer communication, 2 testing self-management and working independently, and 2 revealing attitude to mistakes and feedback. For each question add a brief "strong answer would include" note for the interviewer. Keep questions under 25 words each.
whatItIsFor: Generates 10 behavioural interview questions for a specific role that will actually reveal whether someone can do the job — not just whether they interview well.
howToUseIt: Name the role and the 3–4 qualities that matter most. The prompt structures questions across technical skill, client handling, self-management, and attitude to failure.

title: Onboarding plan builder
body: Build a structured onboarding plan for a new [ROLE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Create 3 phases: Day 1 (orientation and access), Week 1 (foundations and observation), Month 1 (independent contribution). For each phase: list specific tasks, who is responsible for each, what tool or resource is used, and what "done" looks like. Include the 5 questions this person should be able to answer by end of month 1 to confirm they're properly onboarded.
whatItIsFor: Creates a structured Day 1 / Week 1 / Month 1 onboarding plan so that new hires feel set up rather than thrown in — and you don't repeat the same induction from scratch each time.
howToUseIt: Specify the role and the most critical things they need to know first. The output gives you a reusable template, not a generic checklist.

title: Team culture document writer
body: Write a team culture document for a [BUSINESS TYPE] with [TEAM SIZE] people. Sections to include: how we work (hours, communication norms, decision-making), what we care about, what we don't do or accept, how we handle mistakes, and what success looks like in this team. Tone: [TONE — e.g. direct, warm, informal]. Maximum 1 page. No buzzwords. No aspirational waffle — only things we actually do.
whatItIsFor: Writes a 1-page culture guide that tells a new hire what you expect and how your team works — without buzzwords or corporate mission-statement filler.
howToUseIt: Answer the tone and size inputs honestly. The result is a culture document that reads like something a real founder wrote, not an HR handbook.

title: Performance review template
body: Write a quarterly performance review template for a [ROLE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Include: what went well (with prompts for specific examples), what needs to improve (with specific evidence), 3 goals for next quarter with measurable outcomes, support the business commits to providing, a 1–5 rating scale with a clear description of each level, and space for the employee's own assessment. The format should feel like a productive conversation, not an appraisal tribunal.
whatItIsFor: Creates a quarterly review template for small teams without formal HR processes — structured enough to be useful, simple enough to actually run.
howToUseIt: Name the role and your business type. The output is a 2-way review template (not a one-way judgement) that you can reuse every quarter.

title: Delegation readiness checker
body: I am a [BUSINESS TYPE] owner currently doing these tasks myself: [LIST 8–12 TASKS]. Evaluate each task on 3 dimensions (1–5): (1) Only I can do this, (2) It can be documented and repeated, (3) The value freed up if I delegate it. Rank the top 5 tasks to delegate first. For each: name what role should own it, what I'd need to document before handing off, and the fastest way to start the handover this week. Be direct about what I'm holding onto unnecessarily.
whatItIsFor: Identifies which tasks you should hand off next, based on whether they can be delegated, documented, or eliminated — freeing time for higher-leverage work.
howToUseIt: List 8–12 tasks you currently do yourself. The output gives you a delegation priority list and what to do about each item.

title: Contractor vs employee decision guide
body: I'm a [BUSINESS TYPE] considering hiring [ROLE] for approximately [HOURS PER WEEK] hours per week doing [SPECIFIC TASKS]. They would [WORK FROM THEIR OWN PREMISES / WORK ONSITE WITH ME]. I'm based in the UK. Analyse this arrangement against the main contractor vs employee tests: right of substitution, mutuality of obligation, and control. Give me: (1) risk rating for treating them as a contractor (Low/Medium/High), (2) estimated true cost comparison (contractor rate vs employee with employer NI, pension, holiday pay), (3) a recommendation with caveats. Flag the top 2 risks I should discuss with an employment adviser before proceeding.
whatItIsFor: Analyses a specific role against the key contractor/employee tests so you don't accidentally create an IR35 or employment law risk.
howToUseIt: Describe the role and working arrangement honestly. The output gives you a risk rating and recommendation — verify with an employment adviser before acting.

title: Team meeting agenda builder
body: Create a recurring [FREQUENCY — weekly/fortnightly] team meeting agenda for a [TEAM SIZE]-person [BUSINESS TYPE]. Meeting length: [DURATION IN MINUTES]. Include: standard agenda items for every meeting, time allocated to each section, who leads each section, how to handle overruns without losing the next section, and what gets captured as an action item (vs what is just noted). Add 3 rules for keeping the meeting on track that everyone agrees to upfront.
whatItIsFor: Builds a structured, time-boxed recurring meeting agenda that produces decisions rather than discussions — and ends on time.
howToUseIt: Input your team size, meeting frequency, and the typical topics you cover. The output is a reusable template with strict time allocations.

title: Difficult conversation script writer
body: Write a script for a conversation between a small business owner and a [ROLE] about [SPECIFIC ISSUE]. The goal is [DESIRED OUTCOME]. Tone: direct but fair. Include: opening statement (specific, not vague), the specific behaviour and its impact with one concrete example, what needs to change and by when, how we'll review it, and a close that keeps the relationship intact. Also include 3 possible responses the employee might give and how to handle each without backing down or escalating unnecessarily.
whatItIsFor: Writes a script for a hard conversation with a team member — one that's direct and fair without being a performance tribunal or an avoidant non-conversation.
howToUseIt: Describe the specific issue, not a general frustration. The more concrete the situation, the more useful the script.

title: Freelancer project brief writer
body: Write a project brief for a freelancer doing [DELIVERABLE] for a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Include: project overview (2 sentences), specific deliverables with success criteria for each, what is NOT included (scope exclusions), timeline with key milestones, how revisions work (number of rounds, turnaround), file or handover requirements, communication expectations (how often, which channel), and payment milestones. End with a sign-off line. Maximum 1 page.
whatItIsFor: Writes a clear, scoped project brief for a freelancer that prevents scope creep before it starts — because vague briefs produce missed expectations, revision spirals, and overspend.
howToUseIt: Describe what you need delivered and the constraints. The output is a brief you can send before any work starts, that both parties sign off.

title: Hiring funnel designer
body: Design a hiring funnel for a [ROLE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Include: top 3 channels to post the role (be specific — not just "job boards"), CV screening criteria (must-have vs nice-to-have), phone screen questions (5 max, 20 minutes), any task or test brief, final interview structure, and communication at each stage. Write the rejection email for the CV stage and the phone screen stage. Target: complete the process within [X WEEKS].
whatItIsFor: Designs the complete candidate pipeline from job post to offer — with stages, criteria at each stage, and templated rejection messages so nothing slips through the cracks.
howToUseIt: Specify the role and your target timeline. The output is a full recruitment process you can run without an HR team.

title: Exit interview analyser
body: Here are exit interview responses from [NUMBER] departing employees at my [BUSINESS TYPE]: [PASTE RESPONSES OR SUMMARISE EACH]. Identify: (1) the top 3 recurring themes across responses, (2) specific management, process, or culture issues named more than once, (3) the gap between what we say we are and what employees experienced, (4) the one change most likely to have retained 2 or more of them. Be direct — don't soften the findings. End with 3 actionable recommendations ranked by likely retention impact.
whatItIsFor: Extracts real patterns from exit interview responses — so you understand why people actually leave rather than why they say they're leaving.
howToUseIt: Paste or summarise the exit interview responses. The output identifies actionable patterns — not comfort-food findings.

title: Salary benchmark researcher
body: Research current salary benchmarks for a [ROLE] in [LOCATION] with [EXPERIENCE LEVEL] experience, working [FULL-TIME/PART-TIME] at a [COMPANY SIZE]-person [INDUSTRY] business. Provide: median salary, lower and upper quartile, common additional benefits offered at this level, typical notice period for this type of role, and the top 3 non-financial factors that attract strong candidates to this type of role. Flag any significant variation by sector or region that I should be aware of.
whatItIsFor: Researches current market rates for a specific role so you offer a competitive salary without over- or under-paying — either of which costs you.
howToUseIt: Be specific about experience level and location. Generic inputs produce generic ranges. Cross-reference the output with live job boards before making an offer.

title: 90-day new hire integration plan
body: Build a 90-day integration plan for a new [ROLE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Structure in 3 phases: Days 1–30 (learn and observe), Days 31–60 (contribute with support), Days 61–90 (own independently). For each phase: specific learning goals, first projects or tasks, weekly check-in format, what success looks like at the end of that phase, and what would be a concern. End with the 3 questions we should both be able to answer confidently by day 90.
whatItIsFor: Creates a specific integration timeline for a new hire with milestones and success criteria — so both you and they know what "settled in" looks like.
howToUseIt: Specify the role and the most important things they need to own independently by day 90. The output is a phased plan you can review together at each stage.

title: Knowledge transfer plan
body: Create a knowledge transfer plan for [PERSON/ROLE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE] who holds critical expertise in [KNOWLEDGE AREA]. Goal: document this knowledge so another team member or successor can operate without them. Include: format for capturing (video walkthrough, written SOP, live coaching), session structure and time estimate, who receives the knowledge and in what sequence, how to test transfer has worked (not just "did you watch the video?"), and the 3 highest-risk things that would be lost if this person left tomorrow.
whatItIsFor: Moves critical business knowledge out of one person's head — before they leave, before they get ill, and before that knowledge walks out the door permanently.
howToUseIt: Identify the person and the knowledge area. The output gives you a structured transfer plan with formats and a timeline.

title: Reference check question generator
body: Generate 8 reference check questions for a [ROLE] candidate at a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Structure: 2 questions probing specific claims they made in the interview ([SPECIFIC CLAIMS TO PROBE]), 2 uncovering how they handle pressure or conflict at work, 2 checking actual output quality beyond "were they good to work with", 1 on rehire eligibility, and 1 open question. For each question, add a note on what a vague or deflecting answer signals.
whatItIsFor: Generates specific reference check questions that reveal what a reference won't volunteer unless you ask directly — giving you real information, not a polished endorsement.
howToUseIt: Name the role and 2–3 claims the candidate made in their interview. Good reference checks probe specific evidence, not general impressions.

title: Redundancy communication guide
body: I need to make a [ROLE] redundant at my [BUSINESS TYPE] due to [GENUINE BUSINESS REASON]. They have been with us for [LENGTH OF TIME] and are [FULL-TIME/PART-TIME]. Write: (1) the initial at-risk notification letter, (2) what to cover in the consultation meeting, (3) the formal redundancy confirmation letter, (4) the statutory redundancy pay calculation (UK formula), and (5) the 3 most common mistakes small businesses make that create unfair dismissal risk. Note: all letters are for solicitor review before sending.
whatItIsFor: Writes fair, legally-aware communication for a small business making a role redundant — without using lawyers for the drafting, but with enough awareness to know when you need one.
howToUseIt: Provide the situation specifics honestly. Always verify the output with an employment solicitor before sending any formal communication.

title: Employee KPI setter
body: Set 5 KPIs for a [ROLE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Each KPI must be: specific (clear definition of what counts), measurable (a number or %, not a feeling), within the employee's control, reviewed [MONTHLY/QUARTERLY], and linked to a business outcome. For each KPI include: the metric, current baseline if I provide one ([BASELINES]), target, how it's measured, and what reward or consequence is triggered when hit or missed. Avoid vanity metrics and inputs disguised as outcomes.
whatItIsFor: Creates role-appropriate performance metrics for non-corporate teams — specific, measurable, and actually motivating rather than surveillance-style tracking.
howToUseIt: Name the role and any current performance issues or gaps. The output gives you 5 KPIs with baselines, targets, and measurement methods.

title: Probationary review structure
body: Create a probationary review structure for a [ROLE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE] with a [LENGTH] probation period. Include: a mid-probation check-in (key questions and scoring guide), an end-of-probation assessment (evaluation criteria and rating), and the specific wording for three outcomes: confirming employment, extending probation, and ending employment during probation. For each outcome include what to document to protect the business legally. Note: wording is for solicitor review before use.
whatItIsFor: Creates a mid-probation and end-of-probation review structure so that poor fits are identified early — and strong hires are retained by being told clearly that they're doing well.
howToUseIt: Specify the role and probation length. The output gives you a structured review for both check-ins, plus the exact wording for extending, confirming, or ending probation.

title: Founder-to-manager transition guide
body: I am a [BUSINESS TYPE] founder with a [TEAM SIZE]-person team. I still personally do or check the following tasks: [LIST TASKS]. Map my transition from operator to manager: (1) which 3 tasks to fully release in the next 30 days, (2) what I need to document or train before I can let go of each, (3) how many hours I'll free up per week, (4) what I should be spending that time on instead (be specific — not just "strategy"). Flag where I'm most likely to slip back into doing rather than managing, and what to do when that happens.
whatItIsFor: Helps a founder stop doing tasks they should be delegating by mapping the transition from "doing everything" to actually leading the business.
howToUseIt: List the tasks you still do personally that your team theoretically handles. Be honest — include the ones you've "handed off" but still check on constantly.

title: SOP writer
body: Write a standard operating procedure (SOP) for [PROCESS NAME] at a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Format: title, purpose (1 sentence), who this applies to, tools and resources needed, numbered step-by-step instructions (specific enough that someone with the relevant skills could complete this without further guidance), what to do if something goes wrong at each key step, and a 6-month review date. Maximum 1 page. Plain English — no jargon.
whatItIsFor: Turns any repeatable business process into a clear step-by-step SOP that a new team member could follow on day 1 without asking you questions.
howToUseIt: Describe the process as you currently do it. Don't filter or clean it up — the raw version produces a more accurate SOP.

title: Process audit tool
body: Here is my current process for [PROCESS NAME] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]: [DESCRIBE OR PASTE EACH STEP IN ORDER]. Audit it for: (1) steps that are redundant or could be eliminated, (2) steps that could be automated using tools I likely already have, (3) steps where errors most commonly occur (or are most costly), (4) steps that only I can do vs steps that can be owned by someone else, and (5) the total time this process takes vs how long it should take. Rate the overall process efficiency 1–10 and give me a revised leaner version.
whatItIsFor: Identifies redundant, bottlenecked, or broken steps in an existing business process before you document it and bake the inefficiency in permanently.
howToUseIt: Describe or paste your current process as-is. The output flags what to cut, automate, or fix before you document it.
tokens: DESCRIBE OR PASTE EACH STEP IN ORDER

title: Tool consolidation planner
body: I pay for these tools: [LIST TOOLS WITH MONTHLY COSTS]. My business is a [BUSINESS TYPE] and my core workflows are: [DESCRIBE KEY WORKFLOWS]. Audit for: (1) overlapping features across tools I already pay for, (2) tools I could replace with features in something I already use, (3) tools I can likely cut without replacing, and (4) tools I definitely need to keep. Calculate the total monthly saving available. Give me a priority order: highest saving + lowest switching friction first. Flag any migration risks.
whatItIsFor: Audits your current software subscriptions to find overlapping features, unused tools, and consolidation opportunities — typical savings: £150–£400/month.
howToUseIt: List every tool you pay for with the monthly cost. Include ones you "might use one day." The output gives you a priority consolidation plan.

title: Client intake system designer
body: Design a complete client intake system for a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Cover: (1) first enquiry response (within what timeframe, via which channel, what it says), (2) qualification step (form or call — which is right for this business and why), (3) proposal or quote delivery, (4) contract and payment, (5) onboarding handover. For each stage: who handles it, what tool, what the client receives, and the maximum time before it moves to the next stage. Include one automated message template per stage.
whatItIsFor: Designs a complete end-to-end client intake process from first enquiry to signed contract — so every new client gets the same experience and nothing falls through the gaps.
howToUseIt: Describe how clients currently find and contact you. The output maps a better process using tools you likely already have.

title: Business continuity plan
body: Build a business continuity plan for a [BUSINESS TYPE] where the main operator is unavailable for up to [TIMEFRAME] due to illness or emergency. Cover: (1) who handles client communication (with exact message wording), (2) which tasks can pause vs must continue, (3) which tasks a VA or temporary contractor could pick up quickly, (4) critical access requirements (list the types of access — not actual passwords), (5) the one action to take in the first 24 hours of an emergency, and (6) what documentation needs to exist before this plan is useful. Make it practical — I should be able to hand this to someone in 15 minutes.
whatItIsFor: Answers the question "what happens if I'm unavailable for two weeks?" before it becomes an emergency. Most small businesses have no answer to this — it's the single biggest operational risk.
howToUseIt: Be specific about your client commitments and deadlines. The output is a practical plan, not a theoretical document.

title: Documentation gap finder
body: Here are the key functions in my [BUSINESS TYPE]: [LIST 10–15 BUSINESS FUNCTIONS]. For each function rate whether it's documented (Fully / Partially / Not at all). Then identify: (1) the top 3 undocumented processes that would cause a crisis if I were unavailable, (2) which processes a new team member would need on day 1, (3) the fastest format to document each (10-min video, 1-page written SOP, or decision flowchart). Output a documentation priority list sorted by business risk.
whatItIsFor: Identifies business processes that exist only in your head — then prioritises which ones to document first based on the risk if you're unavailable.
howToUseIt: List all the key functions in your business honestly, including the informal ones. The output tells you where your single points of failure are.

title: Quality control checklist builder
body: Create a quality control checklist for [DELIVERABLE TYPE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Include: technical accuracy checks (specific to this deliverable type), brand consistency checks, client brief alignment checks, proofreading and formatting steps, the approval workflow before sending, and what to do if a quality issue is discovered after delivery. Format as a checkable list with a pass/fail gate at the end. A deliverable that fails the gate does not go out.
whatItIsFor: Creates a pre-delivery review checklist so that every client deliverable is checked before it goes out — eliminating the embarrassing errors that chip away at client trust.
howToUseIt: Describe the deliverable in detail. The output is a checkable list with a pass/fail gate — print it, use it every time.

title: Time audit analyser
body: Here is my typical week as a [BUSINESS TYPE] owner: [DESCRIBE HOW YOU SPEND YOUR TIME, INCLUDING MEETINGS, ADMIN, CLIENT WORK, MARKETING, AND ANYTHING ELSE YOU DO]. Analyse it for: (1) time that directly generates revenue, (2) time that could be delegated or automated, (3) time that serves no clear purpose, (4) the split between reactive vs proactive work. Estimate the percentage of my week that is high-leverage vs low-leverage. Give me a rebalanced ideal week schedule — being specific about what moves, what gets cut, and what I need to put in place to make the change.
whatItIsFor: Extracts where you're actually spending time and identifies the lowest-value activities to cut, delegate, or compress — giving you a rebalanced week that prioritises revenue-generating work.
howToUseIt: Describe your typical week honestly, including the time you waste. The output gives you a rebalanced schedule, not advice to "be more productive."
tokens: DESCRIBE HOW YOU SPEND YOUR TIME

title: Standard email response library
body: I am a [BUSINESS TYPE] who regularly receives these types of messages: [LIST 10 COMMON ENQUIRY OR MESSAGE TYPES]. Write a ready-to-use template reply for each. Each template must: start with the actual content (no "Thanks for reaching out" openers), answer the most common version of that question, use [FIRST NAME] as the personalisation placeholder, stay under 150 words, and end with one clear next step for the recipient. Tone: [TONE].
whatItIsFor: Creates 10 ready-to-send email templates for your most common enquiry types — so the inbox stops taking your mornings and every reply sounds consistent and professional.
howToUseIt: List the 10 types of enquiries or messages you reply to most often. Be specific — "pricing questions" is more useful than "general enquiries."

title: Supplier evaluation matrix
body: Create a supplier evaluation matrix for choosing a [SUPPLIER TYPE] for a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Include 8 scoring criteria weighted by importance (total must equal 100%). Suggested criteria to consider: price, delivery reliability, product/service quality, contract flexibility, payment terms, communication responsiveness, references or reviews, and minimum order or commitment size. Format as a table with columns for weighting and 3 vendor scores. Add 3 automatic disqualifiers — criteria that eliminate a vendor regardless of their overall score.
whatItIsFor: Creates a weighted scoring matrix to compare vendors on the criteria that actually matter for your business — not just price — so you stop making supplier decisions based on who replied fastest.
howToUseIt: Specify the supplier type and the factors most important for your business. The output gives you a pre-built matrix to fill in across 3 vendors.

title: Recurring task scheduler
body: Build a recurring task calendar for a [BUSINESS TYPE] with [TEAM SIZE] people. Include tasks that must happen: daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, and annually. For each task: who is responsible, how long it takes, which tool or system handles it, and the consequence of skipping it. Flag the 5 tasks most commonly forgotten by businesses like mine and explain the typical cost of each missed task.
whatItIsFor: Builds a master recurring task calendar so that nothing critical gets forgotten — critical in small businesses where one missed deadline can cost a client or a filing penalty.
howToUseIt: Describe your business type and the functions it involves. The output is a frequency-based master list you can add to your project management tool.

Summarise the top 3 risks and suggest what to negotiate before signing. Note: this analysis is for information — I will verify with a solicitor before signing.
whatItIsFor: Prompts Claude or ChatGPT to identify the riskiest clauses in a supplier contract before you sign — so you're not locked into terms you didn't notice until month 9.
howToUseIt: Paste the contract text or a summary of key clauses. The output flags the top risks — always verify with a solicitor before signing any significant contract.

whatItIsFor: Creates a simple weekly dashboard of 8–10 metrics that tell you in under 15 minutes whether your business is healthy — or heading for a problem before it becomes a crisis.
howToUseIt: Describe your business type and the key levers that drive your revenue. The output is a reusable weekly scorecard template.

title: Decision log template
body: Create a decision log template for a [BUSINESS TYPE] that can be completed in under 5 minutes per decision. Include 5 completed example entries for realistic business decisions at a [BUSINESS TYPE] that show how the template works in practice.
whatItIsFor: Creates a one-page decision record so that key business decisions can be revisited 6 months later — and you can understand why you made them, not just what you decided.
howToUseIt: Use this template whenever you make a significant decision — pricing changes, new hires, supplier switches, marketing experiments. Takes under 5 minutes to complete.

title: Meeting audit and reduction plan
body: Here are all my recurring meetings: [LIST MEETINGS WITH FREQUENCY AND DURATION]. For each meeting evaluate: (1) does it produce decisions or just share information, (2) does everyone there need to be present, (3) could it be replaced with a written update, async tool, or shorter meeting, (4) what would happen if it was cancelled for one month as an experiment. Give me a recommended meeting diet: which to keep as-is, which to shorten or restructure, which to replace, which to cancel. Include estimated hours saved per week.
whatItIsFor: Identifies which of your recurring meetings to cancel, shorten, or replace with async updates — typical output is 4–8 hours per week reclaimed for actual work.
howToUseIt: List every recurring meeting with duration and who attends. Include internal and client meetings. The output gives you a leaner meeting diet.
tokens: LIST MEETINGS WITH FREQUENCY AND DURATION

title: File naming and folder structure designer
body: Design a file naming convention and folder structure for a [BUSINESS TYPE] with [TEAM SIZE] people using [GOOGLE DRIVE / ONEDRIVE / DROPBOX]. Include: top-level folder structure (maximum 6 folders), sub-folder logic for client or project files, a naming convention with examples, version control approach, archive policy (when and where files move), and 5 non-negotiable rules for the team. Include a before/after example showing the difference between a chaotic and organised state for this type of business.
whatItIsFor: Creates a consistent file naming convention and folder structure for a small team so that anyone can find anything within 30 seconds — not 10 minutes of guessing.
howToUseIt: Describe your current chaotic situation honestly. The output is a practical system with rules the whole team can actually follow.

title: Project handover template
body: Create a project handover template for [PROJECT TYPE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Include: project overview and current status, what's been completed and what's outstanding, key contacts and their roles, tools and access required (list types, not actual credentials), open questions or risks, preferred communication channel for updates, deadline and remaining milestones, and a "day one actions" list for the person taking over. Specific enough that someone qualified could pick this up without a call.
whatItIsFor: Creates a standardised document for handing over a project to a team member or contractor so they can pick it up without a two-hour briefing call.
howToUseIt: Fill in the template for your specific project. The output is a document you can share and start using immediately.

title: Automation opportunity finder
body: Here are my regular business tasks: [LIST 15–20 TASKS]. For each task that could be automated, identify: the tool to use (Zapier, Make.com, Google Sheets automation, built-in tool feature, or email rule), the complexity to set up (Easy = <1hr / Medium = 1–4hrs / Advanced = >4hrs), the estimated time saved per week, and the trigger + action for the automation. Prioritise the top 5 by time saved ÷ setup complexity. I want quick wins first.
whatItIsFor: Identifies the 5 best automation opportunities from a list of your tasks — the ones that will save the most time with the least setup complexity.
howToUseIt: List your regular tasks including ones that feel too small to bother automating. Often those are the highest-leverage targets.

title: New process designer
body: Design a new process for [BUSINESS FUNCTION] at a [BUSINESS TYPE] where currently [DESCRIBE THE CURRENT SITUATION — e.g. "it's whoever remembers", "it's me every time", "there's no consistent approach"]. The process must have: a clear trigger (what starts it), a defined owner, no more than 8 steps, a consistent output every time, and a check that confirms it's been completed correctly. Format as a numbered step-by-step with the tool or template used at each step. Add a 30-day review note: what to check after running this process 10 times.
whatItIsFor: Builds a new business process from scratch when the current approach is "whoever remembers to do it" — producing a consistent, owned, checkable workflow.
howToUseIt: Describe the business function that has no process yet. Be honest about how it currently gets done (or doesn't).

title: Internal project brief template
body: Create an internal brief template for use at a [BUSINESS TYPE] when assigning work to [ROLE — e.g. designer, writer, developer, VA]. The template must include: project or task name, context (2 sentences maximum), the specific deliverable with success criteria, target audience and tone, constraints and must-avoids, reference examples or links (placeholder), deadline and format for delivery, who to contact if unclear, and a self-check the assignee completes before submitting. Include one completed example brief for [SPECIFIC TASK TYPE].
whatItIsFor: Creates a standard internal brief that a team member or contractor can pick up and act on without needing a call to understand what they're doing or why.
howToUseIt: Fill in the template for any piece of work you're assigning. The output is a brief that prevents the most common reasons for misaligned deliverables.

title: New product idea validator
body: Validate this product idea for a [BUSINESS TYPE]: [DESCRIBE IDEA WITH PRICE POINT AND TARGET BUYER]. Evaluate: (1) who specifically is buying this and why now, (2) what free or cheaper alternatives already exist, (3) whether the price point covers realistic acquisition cost at normal conversion rates, (4) the minimum evidence of demand I should see before building, (5) the 3 most common ways this type of product fails in its first year. Give a verdict: strong signal / weak signal / do not build. Suggest one fast way to test demand without building first.
whatItIsFor: Stress-tests a product idea against real market conditions before you invest any time building it — the fastest way to avoid building something nobody buys.
howToUseIt: Be specific about the idea. "An online course" is not specific. "A 4-week course on Instagram Reels for photographers charging £297" is specific enough to validate.
tokens: DESCRIBE IDEA WITH PRICE POINT AND TARGET BUYER

title: MVP scope definer
body: Define the MVP for this product: [DESCRIBE PRODUCT CONCEPT]. I have [TIMEFRAME] and [RESOURCES/BUDGET]. Identify: (1) the one core value the MVP must deliver (everything else is optional), (2) features that are must-have vs nice-to-have vs not-yet, (3) what the MVP explicitly does not include, (4) the fastest way to test the core value with minimal build, (5) 3 specific success criteria that confirm the MVP is working. Make the scope as small as possible — what is the least we can build that gets a genuine "yes, this is useful" from a real buyer?
whatItIsFor: Strips a product idea to its absolute minimum testable version — so you ship and learn rather than spend 3 months building a product that misses what people actually needed.
howToUseIt: Be honest about your resources. The output is deliberately aggressive — push back if something truly can't be cut, but challenge every objection before accepting it.

title: Product launch checklist
body: Create a product launch checklist for [PRODUCT TYPE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Audience: [EMAIL LIST SIZE / SOCIAL FOLLOWING]. Divide into: 4 weeks pre-launch (build and prepare), 2 weeks pre-launch (warm-up and test), launch week (execute), and 2 weeks post-launch (follow up and learn). For each phase include specific tasks, who is responsible, what tool, and what "done" looks like. Flag the 5 tasks most commonly missed by small business owners that cause launches to underperform.
whatItIsFor: Creates a pre/launch/post checklist so nothing critical is missed — especially the things that get dropped in the excitement of launch week.
howToUseIt: Specify the product type and your audience size. The output is a prioritised checklist, not a theoretical launch plan.

title: Feature prioritisation matrix
body: I'm building [PRODUCT/SERVICE] for [AUDIENCE]. Here are the features or improvements I'm considering: [LIST 10–15 FEATURES]. Score each on: customer impact (1–10), implementation effort (1–10), alignment with core product promise (1–10), and revenue impact (1–10). Calculate a weighted priority score. Rank them. Flag the 3 I should build first and the 3 I should cut from the roadmap entirely. Explain why the top 3 win, and why the bottom 3 aren't worth building now.
whatItIsFor: Decides what to build next using a value vs effort matrix — stops you building the most-requested features rather than the most impactful ones.
howToUseIt: List every feature or improvement you're considering. Include ones that have been requested. The output challenges your assumptions about what matters most.

title: Customer discovery interview guide
body: Write an 8-question customer discovery interview guide for [TARGET CUSTOMER] about [PROBLEM AREA / PRODUCT CONCEPT]. For each question: state the question, what you're trying to learn, and one follow-up if the answer is vague or theoretical. Questions must not lead the interviewee toward a specific answer. Include 3 questions about current behaviour, 3 about frustrations and workarounds, and 2 about context and motivation. Add an interviewer guide: how to open the call, handle silence, and close without pitching.
whatItIsFor: Generates a customer discovery interview script to uncover real problems before building a product — because the best features come from watching what people do, not asking what they want.
howToUseIt: Run 5–10 interviews before building anything. Record them (with permission). The output is a guide to stop you leading witnesses.

title: Product positioning statement
body: Write a product positioning statement for [PRODUCT NAME] by a [BUSINESS TYPE], priced at [PRICE], targeting [SPECIFIC CUSTOMER]. Follow this structure: "For [specific customer segment] who [specific problem], [Product name] is a [category] that [primary benefit]. Unlike [main alternative], we [key differentiator with evidence]." Then expand each element into one supporting sentence. Create 2 alternative versions with different differentiators and flag which is strongest and why.
whatItIsFor: Creates a clear, specific positioning statement that tells exactly who the product is for, what it does, and why it's different — without marketing waffle or claims every competitor could also make.
howToUseIt: Test the output against this question: could a direct competitor truthfully use the same statement? If yes, it's not differentiated enough yet.

title: Digital product outline builder
body: Create the complete outline for a [FORMAT — ebook/guide/workbook/template pack] called [TITLE] for [TARGET AUDIENCE]. Transformation promised: [SPECIFIC OUTCOME IN SPECIFIC TIMEFRAME]. Include: introduction (the promise and who this is for), 5–8 main sections with 3–4 subsections each, what the reader learns or gets in each section, a quick-win early in the document for skimmers, and a final action plan. Each section should build on the previous. Flag the 2 sections most likely to determine whether a buyer recommends the product to others.
whatItIsFor: Creates the full structure and chapter sequence for any digital product — ebook, guide, template pack, or workbook — before you start writing a single word.
howToUseIt: Be specific about the transformation. "Learn about AI" is not specific. "Save 5 hours per week on content creation within 30 days" is specific and gives the outline real direction.

title: Beta test plan writer
body: Write a beta test plan for [PRODUCT/SERVICE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Include: who to invite (profile, number of testers, what they get in return), what access they receive and for how long, the 5 specific questions you need answered during beta (frame them as learning goals, not satisfaction questions), how to collect feedback (survey, call, or usage observation), success criteria (the minimum threshold to proceed to full launch), and what would cause you to pause or pivot. Include a tester invite email template.
whatItIsFor: Designs a structured beta test that produces actionable feedback rather than polite compliments — because "I really liked it" tells you nothing about whether it will sell.
howToUseIt: Be clear about what you need to know from the beta — not just "is it good?" but "does it achieve the specific outcome promised?"

title: Pricing model explorer
body: I offer [PRODUCT/SERVICE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE] targeting [AUDIENCE] currently priced at [CURRENT PRICING STRUCTURE]. Compare these pricing models: one-time fee, monthly subscription, annual subscription (with a typical 20% discount), and tiered pricing (3 tiers). For each model: estimate average annual revenue per customer assuming [REALISTIC RETENTION RATES], churn risk, acquisition friction, and upsell opportunity. Recommend the one best model for my situation and explain the 2 biggest risks of switching to it.
whatItIsFor: Compares 4 pricing structures for the same offer and recommends the one with the best revenue potential and lowest churn risk for your specific situation.
howToUseIt: Include your current pricing and any constraints (e.g. platform limits, client expectations). The output gives you a model comparison with real numbers, not just theory.

title: Competitive product teardown
body: Analyse [COMPETITOR PRODUCT NAME OR DESCRIPTION] in the [MARKET/NICHE]. Based on what you know or this information I'm pasting: [PASTE REVIEWS, SALES PAGE COPY, OR DESCRIPTION]. Identify: (1) the core promise and who it's for, (2) what it delivers well (be fair), (3) the most common buyer complaints from reviews, (4) the gaps you could address that this product doesn't, (5) 3 specific positioning angles you could use to be "the alternative for people who [specific frustration]." End with the one thing this competitor does that you should learn from.
whatItIsFor: Reverse-engineers a competitor's product to understand what they're doing well, what's missing, and exactly where you can win against them.
howToUseIt: Name a specific competitor product or paste reviews and sales page copy. The output identifies gaps — real gaps based on what buyers complain about, not what you wish they complained about.

title: 12-month product roadmap builder
body: Build a 12-month product roadmap for [PRODUCT/SERVICE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Current state: [DESCRIBE WHERE THE PRODUCT IS NOW AND TOP 2–3 CUSTOMER COMPLAINTS]. Structure the roadmap as: Q1 (consolidate and fix core problems), Q2 (improve core experience), Q3 (add one differentiating feature), Q4 (expand or deepen based on Q3 learning). For each quarter: what specifically ships, the evidence that drives that priority, expected customer impact, and what would change this plan if the assumption is wrong.
whatItIsFor: Creates a 12-month product roadmap with logic for what ships when and why — stopping the cycle of building features reactively based on whoever complained most recently.
howToUseIt: Describe your product, current state, and the 1–2 biggest customer complaints or gaps. The output gives you a structured plan with the reasoning behind each quarter's focus.
tokens: DESCRIBE WHERE THE PRODUCT IS NOW AND TOP

title: Offer stack builder
body: I sell [CORE OFFER] at [PRICE] to [AUDIENCE]. Build a complete offer stack: (1) core deliverable (specific), (2) 3 complementary bonuses that increase the value of the core — not random extras, (3) a performance-backed guarantee with specific terms, (4) any legitimate urgency or scarcity element, (5) the full "worth vs price" summary. Write a one-paragraph offer description ready for a sales page or pitch. Only include urgency if it's real — never manufacture it.
whatItIsFor: Combines your core product with bonuses, guarantee, and urgency into a compelling offer package — increasing perceived value without raising price.
howToUseIt: Be honest about what bonuses you can actually deliver. Manufactured bonuses that add no real value hurt more than they help — buyers see through it instantly.

title: Course curriculum builder
body: Build a course curriculum for [COURSE TITLE] targeting [AUDIENCE] with a goal of [SPECIFIC TRANSFORMATION IN SPECIFIC TIMEFRAME]. Include: 5–7 modules with 4–5 lessons each, time estimate per lesson, the core skill or knowledge delivered in each lesson, how each module builds on the previous, one practical exercise per module, and a total course completion time estimate. Flag: the module students most commonly quit before finishing and how to reduce that risk. Flag the lesson most likely to produce an "aha moment."
whatItIsFor: Plans a complete course curriculum with modules, lessons, time estimates, and learning outcomes — so you build a course that gets finished, not one that sells once and sits on a hard drive.
howToUseIt: The transformation promise shapes everything. If it's vague, the curriculum will be unfocused. If it's specific, every lesson has an obvious purpose.

title: Service productisation guide
body: I currently offer [SERVICE DESCRIPTION] as a bespoke service priced at [CURRENT RATE STRUCTURE]. Productise this into a fixed-scope offer. Include: exact deliverable with format and timeline, scope exclusions (what's not included), who it's for (specific client type), who it's not for, the right price point with justification, how to position fixed-price vs bespoke (when does each make sense?), and the one objection buyers will raise. End with a 50-word product description ready for a sales page.
whatItIsFor: Turns a bespoke, quote-every-time service into a fixed-scope product that can be sold on a sales page without a discovery call — the fastest route to scalable revenue for service providers.
howToUseIt: Choose one specific service you deliver repeatedly. The goal is to standardise it enough to sell at a fixed price while still delivering real value.

title: Template product creator
body: I regularly create [DELIVERABLE TYPE] for clients at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Help me turn this into a sellable template product. Include: what the template covers and excludes, the format (Google Docs, Notion, Excel, Canva, etc.), who the buyer is and what transformation the template delivers, 3 price point options with rationale (free/lead magnet, paid entry, premium), where to sell it, how to market it to people who aren't already clients, and the one mistake template creators make that causes poor reviews.
whatItIsFor: Turns any recurring client deliverable into a sellable template — one of the fastest paths to passive income for service providers, because the work is already done for your clients.
howToUseIt: Pick the deliverable you create most often and like doing. The best template products are the ones you'd use yourself.

title: Upsell sequence designer
body: Design a 3-step post-purchase upsell sequence for buyers of [CORE PRODUCT] at a [BUSINESS TYPE]. For each step: what to offer (must logically extend the core purchase), when to offer it (immediately / 3 days / 7 days post-purchase), why the buyer wants it now, price point (typically 25–50% of core product), and the first paragraph of the offer message. Tone: helpful, not pushy. The offer should feel like "oh, that makes sense" not "oh, they just want more money."
whatItIsFor: Designs a post-purchase upsell flow that increases average order value without feeling like a used-car dealership — the upsell must feel like a logical next step, not a separate sales push.
howToUseIt: Specify the core product and what you'd naturally recommend next to someone who just bought it. The upsell should solve the next problem they'll face after using what they just bought.

title: Product FAQ generator
body: Generate 15 FAQs for [PRODUCT NAME] priced at [PRICE], sold by a [BUSINESS TYPE] to [AUDIENCE]. Include: 5 questions about what's included and results to expect, 3 about who it's for and who it isn't, 3 about delivery and refunds, 2 about comparisons to alternatives, and 2 about implementation time. For each question write an answer that is specific and honest — addresses the real hesitation behind the question, not a marketing spin version of it.
whatItIsFor: Generates the 15 questions buyers actually ask before purchasing — and the specific answers that convert hesitant buyers rather than dodge their real concerns.
howToUseIt: Think about the questions you receive by DM before people buy. Those are the real FAQs — not the ones you wish they'd ask.

title: Product retirement plan
body: I need to retire [PRODUCT NAME] at my [BUSINESS TYPE]. [NUMBER] customers have bought it. Reason for retirement: [GENUINE REASON]. Plan: (1) how to notify existing buyers (timing, channel, tone), (2) what to offer them instead (upgrade path, discount on replacement, or something else), (3) how to handle refund requests triggered by the announcement, (4) what to do with existing reviews and testimonials, (5) the public-facing message for anyone who finds the old sales page. Write the customer notification email and a brief public statement.
whatItIsFor: Sunsets an existing product without alienating buyers, triggering refund waves, or damaging your reputation — because how you retire a product is as important as how you launch it.
howToUseIt: Plan this 4–6 weeks before the retirement date, not the day before you switch the sales page off.

title: Product suite audit
body: Here are my current products and services: [LIST EACH WITH PRICE AND ONE-LINE DESCRIPTION]. Audit this suite for: (1) missing entry points — can a new buyer try before committing to a major purchase? (2) progression gaps — does buying product A naturally lead to wanting B? (3) overlaps — where do two products compete for the same buyer? (4) price ladder — is there a clear entry, mid, and premium tier? (5) the most confusing product in the suite and why. End with a recommended restructure with rationale.
whatItIsFor: Evaluates your existing product range for gaps, overlaps, and logical progression — so buyers have a clear journey from first purchase to your highest-value offer.
howToUseIt: List every product and service with its price and a one-line description of who it's for. The output will challenge your assumptions about how they fit together.
tokens: LIST EACH WITH PRICE AND ONE

title: Product name generator
body: Generate 10 name options for a [PRODUCT TYPE] targeting [AUDIENCE], priced at [PRICE], delivering [CORE OUTCOME]. For each name: identify the naming strategy (descriptive, aspirational, outcome-led, problem-led, or contrarian), how it reads in 3 seconds with no context, the buyer personality it appeals to most, and any obvious trademark or domain risks. Then pick your top 3 and explain your final recommendation. Avoid using: "ultimate", "blueprint", "secrets", "hack", "system", "game-changer", or "unlock" unless paired with something highly specific.
whatItIsFor: Generates 10 product name options with rationale for each — testing different naming strategies so you choose a name that communicates clearly, not just one that sounds good to you.
howToUseIt: Avoid names that require explanation. The best product name answers "what is this?" in under 3 seconds. Test your shortlist with 5 people who don't know your business.

title: Franchise readiness assessment
body: Assess whether my [BUSINESS TYPE] is ready to franchise. I've operated for [YEARS], revenue is [ANNUAL REVENUE], margin is [PROFIT MARGIN], and I have [NUMBER] current locations or pilots. Answer: (1) Is the model profitable without my personal client relationships? (2) Is every core process documented to a level a new operator could learn in [WEEKS]? (3) What's the minimum proof of concept required before seeking franchisees (industry standard for your type of business)? (4) What are the 3 biggest risks in my current model that would amplify across a franchise network? Give a readiness score out of 10 and a 6-month pre-franchise action checklist.
whatItIsFor: Determines whether a business model is systemised, profitable, and replicable enough to franchise — before spending on legal setup or approaching franchisees.
howToUseIt: Answer honestly. The three tests most businesses fail: profitability without the founder's personal relationships, documented processes, and proof of replicability in at least one other location or operator.

title: White-label service pitch writer
body: Write a one-page white-label pitch for my [SERVICE TYPE] to be resold by [TARGET PARTNER TYPE] under their own brand. Structure: (1) what their clients currently lack that my service provides, (2) how the white-label model works operationally (I deliver, they front it), (3) what the partner earns per sale or per retainer, (4) what the partner needs to commit to (minimum volume, onboarding time), (5) implementation timeline from agreement to first client. Write in plain business language. Include the opening message to send when first approaching a potential partner.
whatItIsFor: Writes a pitch for a complementary business to resell your service under their own brand — the fastest way to scale revenue without building your own sales team.
howToUseIt: The best white-label partners serve the same client type as you but don't do what you do. Focus on the value to their clients, not the administrative convenience for them.

title: Operations manual outline
body: Create an operations manual outline for a [BUSINESS TYPE] franchise or licensed model. Include chapters covering: brand standards, client-facing processes, back-office operations, quality standards and measurement, support and escalation from head office, marketing rules and local marketing guidance, compliance and legal requirements, and how to handle situations not covered by the manual. For each chapter: list 4–6 specific sections and estimate the number of pages. Total target: a manual that can be learned in [X days] by a new operator with relevant skills but no prior experience of this specific business.
whatItIsFor: Creates the chapter structure for a franchise or licensee operations manual — the document that lets someone else run your business to your standards without calling you every day.
howToUseIt: Write this before you have franchisees, not after. The process of writing it reveals the gaps in your own systems.

title: Reseller programme designer
body: Design a reseller programme for [PRODUCT/SERVICE] at a [BUSINESS TYPE]. Create 2–3 reseller tiers with different: commission or margin levels, minimum activity commitments, marketing support provided, and co-branding rules. Include: how to apply to become a reseller, a brief onboarding process, what happens to inactive reseller accounts, and 3 reasons a partner would choose to resell this rather than build their own alternative. Write a one-page reseller overview document ready to share.
whatItIsFor: Designs a tiered reseller or partner programme with clear margins, support levels, and onboarding — turning complementary businesses into a sales channel without hiring a sales team.
howToUseIt: Start simple — one tier, not three. Add complexity once you have 10+ active resellers and understand what they actually need.

title: IP protection checklist
body: Create an IP protection checklist for a [BUSINESS TYPE] preparing to scale, license, or franchise. Include: trademark registration (what to register, in which classes, in which territories), copyright protection for key assets, trade secret protections using NDAs and internal policies, domain and social media handle security, and what happens if someone copies the model. For each item: flag whether it can be DIY or requires a solicitor, estimated cost, and time to complete. Flag the 5 highest-risk IP gaps typical for a [BUSINESS TYPE].
whatItIsFor: Walks through the minimum IP protection steps before scaling or licensing a business — so you don't discover your brand name or proprietary method is unprotectable after you've built it into your entire model.
howToUseIt: Work through this before signing any licensing or franchise agreement. Flag anything marked "solicitor required" and address it before proceeding.

title: Franchisee selection criteria builder
body: Create a franchisee selection criteria framework for a [BUSINESS TYPE] franchise. Define: the profile of an ideal franchisee (skills, background, capital, and mindset), the red flags that predict poor performance (be specific — not just "low motivation"), the selection process from application to offer (stages and what each reveals), the questions to ask in the franchisee interview, and the minimum financial requirements (investment, working capital, and personal financial stability threshold). End with the 3 most common franchisee failures in this type of business and what the selection process should do to prevent each.
whatItIsFor: Defines what profile makes a successful franchisee in your specific model — and what red flags to screen out early, before you've signed someone up and discovered the problem.
howToUseIt: Base this on the skills and behaviours your business model actually requires, not on who you'd enjoy having lunch with. The two overlap less than most franchisors expect.

title: Franchise training programme builder
body: Build a new franchisee training programme for a [BUSINESS TYPE] franchise. The programme should cover everything a franchisee needs to operate independently within [TIMEFRAME]. Structure by: pre-arrival preparation (self-study materials), in-person training days (content, sequence, who delivers each section), shadowing period with an existing operator, solo practice with support available, and final sign-off criteria. Include: how to test that each module has been retained (not just delivered), and the 3 things a franchisee must be able to do independently before they're signed off.
whatItIsFor: Creates the structure for a new franchisee induction training programme — covering what to teach, in what order, and how to test that it's been retained rather than just delivered.
howToUseIt: Design for the person who knows nothing about your specific model — not for the person who reminds you most of yourself.

title: Licence agreement key clauses brief
body: Create a key clauses brief for a [TYPE OF LICENCE — software, brand, methodology, or content] licence agreement between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and [LICENSEE TYPE]. Cover the essential clauses: licence scope (what exactly is being licensed), exclusivity or non-exclusivity, territory, permitted use (and prohibited uses), royalty or fee structure, IP ownership (who owns what if the licensee improves or adapts the licensed material), term and renewal, termination rights (and what happens to the licensee's materials on termination), and confidentiality. Flag 3 clauses where small business licensors most commonly get burned.
whatItIsFor: Identifies the key clauses that must appear in any licensing agreement before a solicitor drafts it — so you arrive briefed and save billable hours rather than starting from scratch in the first legal meeting.
howToUseIt: Use this to brief a solicitor, not to replace one. Licensing agreements for anything other than simple affiliate arrangements need professional legal drafting.

title: Franchise marketing co-op guide
body: Create a marketing co-op policy for a [BUSINESS TYPE] franchise with [NUMBER] franchisees across [GEOGRAPHY]. Define: (1) how much each franchisee contributes to the central marketing fund (% of revenue or flat fee), (2) what the central fund can and cannot be spent on, (3) what franchisees can run locally without approval, (4) what requires head office sign-off before running, (5) how the fund is reported on quarterly so franchisees can see where their money goes, and (6) what happens if a franchisee runs unapproved marketing that damages the brand. Include a one-page policy summary franchisees sign at onboarding.
whatItIsFor: Defines how national and local marketing budgets split across a franchise network — preventing conflict between head office campaigns and franchisee local activity.
howToUseIt: Draft this before you have more than 3 franchisees. The absence of a clear co-op policy is one of the top sources of franchise disputes.

title: Territory conflict resolution script
body: Write a territory conflict resolution process and script for a [BUSINESS TYPE] franchisor dealing with a dispute between two franchisees over [SPECIFIC CONFLICT — e.g. online lead poaching, client approaching wrong location]. The process should include: a 48-hour cooling-off protocol, a structured fact-finding call with each franchisee separately, a decision framework the franchisor uses to determine who is in the right, the communication script for informing both franchisees of the decision, and the written record the franchisor keeps. The resolution must protect the brand, not just one franchisee. End with the 3 territory clauses every franchise agreement should include to prevent this dispute.
whatItIsFor: Provides a structured script and process for resolving disputes between franchisees over territory overlap or lead poaching — before they escalate into legal threats.
howToUseIt: Adapt the process to your franchise agreement's territory definitions. Having a documented process before a conflict happens is what prevents it becoming expensive.

title: Franchisee performance review template
body: Write a quarterly performance review template for a [BUSINESS TYPE] franchisee. Include sections covering: revenue vs target (and whether variance is operator-driven or market-driven), brand standards compliance (with specific observable metrics), client satisfaction indicators, local marketing activity, and the franchisee's own assessment of what head office could do better. Include a rating scale, a mandatory action plan for any section rated below 3, and the franchisor's escalation process if the same section is below 3 for two consecutive quarters. Tone: direct and constructive — not punitive, but not soft.
whatItIsFor: Creates a structured quarterly review template for assessing individual franchisee performance — so underperformance is addressed early and top performers are recognised before they start looking elsewhere.
howToUseIt: Run these quarterly, not annually. A yearly review is too infrequent to course-correct in a franchise where problems compound across a network.

title: Franchise disclosure document summary
body: Create a plain-English summary of what a Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD) or equivalent pre-contract disclosure for a [BUSINESS TYPE] franchise in the UK should contain. For each section: what it must cover, what a franchisee should check carefully, and what missing or vague content is a red flag. Sections to include: the franchisor's business history, litigation history, fees and costs (initial and ongoing), the franchisee's territory and exclusivity, what support the franchisor provides, renewal and exit terms, financial performance data for existing franchisees, and the franchise agreement summary. Flag the 3 sections most commonly used to obscure unfavourable terms.
whatItIsFor: Creates a plain-English summary of what a franchise disclosure document should contain — so you know what to ask your solicitor to draft, and what to check when reviewing a competitor's FDD.
howToUseIt: This is a briefing tool, not a legal document. Use it before your first meeting with a franchise solicitor to avoid spending billable time learning basics.

title: Royalty structure calculator brief
body: Help me design a royalty structure for a [BUSINESS TYPE] franchise. My typical franchisee has estimated monthly revenue of [RANGE] and estimated operating costs of [COST ESTIMATE]. I need the royalty to fund: [LIST WHAT HEAD OFFICE MUST COVER — e.g. national marketing, tech platform, support staff]. Evaluate 3 royalty models: flat monthly fee, percentage of gross revenue, and tiered percentage by revenue band. For each model: calculate what it yields at low, average, and high franchisee revenue, what it leaves the franchisee after royalty and costs, and the risk to the franchisor if revenue underperforms. Recommend one model with reasoning.
whatItIsFor: Defines the right royalty or fee structure for a franchise or licence model — balancing what franchisees can afford to pay while leaving them motivated, against what the franchisor needs to fund central operations and profit.
howToUseIt: Run this before setting your first royalty rate. The most common mistake is setting a percentage that looks small but wipes out franchisee profit at realistic revenue levels.
tokens: LIST WHAT HEAD OFFICE MUST COVER

title: Brand standards enforcement letter
body: Write a brand standards enforcement letter from a [BUSINESS TYPE] franchisor to a franchisee who has breached the following standard: [DESCRIBE THE BREACH]. The letter should include: the specific clause in the franchise agreement that has been breached, the observable evidence of the breach, the required corrective action and deadline, the consequence if the deadline is not met, and a closing line that leaves the door open for a call if the franchisee has questions. Tone: professional and firm — not aggressive. This is a first formal warning.
whatItIsFor: Writes a structured enforcement letter for a franchisee who is not meeting brand standards — firm enough to create a paper trail, measured enough to avoid unnecessarily escalating a fixable problem.
howToUseIt: Send this letter, not a phone call, so there is a written record. Always document what the breach was, what standard was breached, and what correction is required by when.

title: Franchise exit process document
body: Write a franchisee exit process document for a [BUSINESS TYPE] franchise. Cover 3 exit scenarios: (1) franchisee sells to an approved new operator, (2) franchisee hands the territory back to head office, (3) franchisee reaches term end and does not renew. For each: the notice period required, what happens to existing clients, how equipment or branded assets are handled, what the franchisee is paid (if anything), non-compete obligations post-exit, and the timeline from notice to clean separation. Flag the 3 issues that most commonly turn an exit into a dispute and how to prevent each.
whatItIsFor: Documents the step-by-step process for a franchisee exiting the network — whether selling to a new operator, handing back the territory, or completing the agreement term and not renewing.
howToUseIt: Give this to franchisees at onboarding, not when they ask to leave. The time to know the exit process is before someone needs it under pressure.

title: Multi-unit franchisee pitch
body: Write a multi-unit expansion proposal for a [BUSINESS TYPE] franchisee who currently operates [NUMBER] unit(s) with [PERFORMANCE METRICS — e.g. revenue, NPS, compliance record]. They are requesting [NUMBER] additional units in [TERRITORY]. The proposal should include: what performance threshold must have been met to qualify for multi-unit rights, the financial model for the additional units (investment required, break-even timeline, franchisor support during setup), reduced royalty or incentive for proven operators, operational capacity assessment (can they actually manage more units?), and what the franchisor requires in writing before approving. Include the qualifying criteria any franchisee must meet before multi-unit discussion begins.
whatItIsFor: Writes a pitch for a franchisee who wants to expand from one unit to multiple — a more complex conversation than initial recruitment because the franchisor must weigh proven performance against execution risk.
howToUseIt: Use this when a franchisee approaches you about a second unit, or when you want to proactively offer expansion to your top performers before they start looking at alternatives.

title: Licensee onboarding checklist
body: Create a licensee onboarding checklist for a [TYPE OF LICENCE] licence for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The checklist should cover: pre-start (before the licence is activated), week 1 (materials access and orientation), weeks 2–4 (supported first use), and ongoing (what the licensee is responsible for maintaining). For each item: who is responsible (licensor or licensee), what "done" looks like, and what to do if the item is blocked. End with the 5 questions a new licensee most commonly asks in the first 30 days — and the answers to include in the onboarding pack so they don't need to contact you for basics.
whatItIsFor: Creates a structured onboarding checklist for a new licensee — covering everything from agreement signing to first independent use of the licensed material, so nothing falls through the gap between "signed" and "operational".
howToUseIt: Walk through this with the licensee on a shared call, not by email. Misunderstandings at onboarding compound into disputes later.

title: Agency service agreement brief
body: Create a key clauses brief for a service agreement between my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE] and a [CLIENT TYPE]. Sections to cover: scope of work (what's included and what's explicitly excluded), deliverable format and approval process, payment terms and late payment consequences, IP ownership of work created, kill fee if the client cancels mid-project, revision limits, confidentiality, and what happens if timelines slip on the client's side. Flag the 3 clauses most commonly weaponised against small agencies and how to protect against each.
whatItIsFor: Defines the key terms a client-facing agency service agreement must contain — so you arrive at a solicitor prepared, or review a client's paper with clear eyes.
howToUseIt: Focus on the IP ownership clause and the kill-fee clause — these are the two most fought-over provisions in agency agreements.

title: White-label pricing calculator brief
body: Help me set a white-label pricing structure for my [SERVICE TYPE]. My current direct-client rate is [RATE]. My cost to deliver is [COST — time + expenses]. Design a wholesale pricing model for resellers that: gives them a 35–45% margin to sell at a price competitive in their market, keeps my wholesale rate above my cost floor, and does not undercut my direct-to-client pricing if they price aggressively. Include: the minimum order or commitment level that justifies the wholesale rate, whether to use flat wholesale prices or % discount off list, and how to handle a reseller who tries to undercut your direct rate publicly.
whatItIsFor: Helps you set white-label pricing that is competitive for the reseller, profitable for you, and doesn't undercut your direct-to-client rate — the three constraints that are harder to balance than they look.
howToUseIt: Model your direct-client rate first. White-label wholesale price must sit below that at a level that gives the reseller a 30–50% margin to sell at, without your wholesale rate being so low it erodes your own positioning.

title: Agency client onboarding workflow
body: Design a client onboarding workflow for my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE] serving [CLIENT TYPE]. The workflow should cover: what happens immediately after contract signing (within 24 hours), the onboarding call agenda and what to cover in it, what information you need from the client in week 1 to start work, how to handle a client who is slow to provide information (chaser sequence), and what the client should receive by end of week 2 to confirm the relationship is running well. Include a client-facing onboarding timeline I can send as a PDF or email attachment.
whatItIsFor: Creates a repeatable, professional client onboarding workflow that reduces back-and-forth, sets expectations clearly, and means your first impression after contract signing is organised rather than chaotic.
howToUseIt: The first 14 days after signing define the entire client relationship. Build this once and reuse it for every new client — don't improvise it every time.

title: Agency proposal template
body: Write a proposal template for a [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE] responding to a [CLIENT TYPE] who needs [SPECIFIC OUTCOME]. The proposal should include: a problem statement (written in the client's language, not ours), our recommended approach (3 phases max), what's included and what's explicitly excluded, timeline from approval to first deliverable, investment (with a monthly or project option), 2 short proof points (results or client quotes — I'll fill in the actual names), and a clear next step. Maximum 2 pages. No jargon. No "we are passionate about" statements.
whatItIsFor: Writes a client-ready proposal template for your agency that wins work without being a 20-page document — specific enough to show you understand the client's problem, short enough to get read.
howToUseIt: Fill in the [BRACKETED] sections with client-specific details before sending. Never send a generic proposal — a proposal that could apply to any client will be priced against every competitor.

title: Retainer agreement brief
body: Create a retainer agreement brief for my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE] with a [CLIENT TYPE] on a [MONTHLY FEE] retainer. The brief must cover: exactly what is included each month (list as specific deliverables or hours, not "ongoing support"), what happens to unused capacity (does it roll over or is it lost?), what counts as out-of-scope and how it's priced, the minimum retainer term and notice period to exit, review cycle (when do we renegotiate scope and price?), and what happens if the client regularly uses over their allocation. Flag the 3 retainer structures that most often lead to scope creep disputes.
whatItIsFor: Defines the key provisions for an agency retainer agreement — including the scope trap that most retainers fall into and how to prevent it before the first month is out.
howToUseIt: Retainer agreements need a monthly deliverable list or hour cap — not a vague "ongoing support" scope. Vague scope always expands in the client's favour.

title: Agency case study writer
body: Write a client case study for my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE]. Client details: [CLIENT TYPE AND SIZE]. Problem they came to us with: [PROBLEM]. What we did: [APPROACH IN 2–3 STEPS]. Result: [SPECIFIC RESULT WITH NUMBERS]. Time to result: [TIMEFRAME]. Format: 300 words maximum. Lead with the result in the headline. Write in third person. Include one direct quote placeholder I can fill in after client approval. End with a one-line CTA suitable for a website or sales deck.
whatItIsFor: Writes a punchy, results-led case study for an agency or service business — structured to answer the question a prospective client actually asks: "will this work for someone like me?"
howToUseIt: Always lead with the result, not the process. The best case studies are 300 words and get read. The worst are 1,000 words and skim-scrolled past in 4 seconds.

title: Client escalation protocol
body: Write a client escalation protocol for a [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE] with [TEAM SIZE]. Define: what triggers an escalation (specific client behaviours or signals, not just "when they complain"), who handles each stage (account manager → senior → founder), the response time commitment at each stage, what the escalation handler must do first (before defending or explaining), and how to document and close the escalation. Include the exact opening script for the first escalation call. Separate the internal protocol (what the team does) from the client-facing version (what clients are told).
whatItIsFor: Defines a clear internal escalation process for unhappy agency clients — so a complaint doesn't bounce around the team or land with the founder only when it's already turned into a refund demand.
howToUseIt: Share the client-facing version of this with new clients at onboarding — it signals a professional operation, not defensiveness.

title: Agency rate card builder
body: Build a rate card for my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE] targeting [CLIENT TYPE]. Include: standard day rate and half-day rate, a fixed-fee menu for your 3–4 most common project types (with what's included and excluded from each), a retainer tier structure (2–3 tiers with what's covered), rush fee policy (what counts as rush and how much it adds), and payment terms. For each rate, include a one-line description of what the client gets so the rate card can be sent without a covering explanation.
