Also include the 2 most common rate objections and the direct response to each.
whatItIsFor: Creates a structured rate card for an agency or freelance business — defining day rates, project rates, and rush fees in a format that can be sent to prospects without negotiating from scratch every time.
howToUseIt: Your rate card is an anchor, not a prison. State your rates confidently — prospects who immediately push back on rates are usually not your best clients.

title: Service package builder
body: Design a 3-tier productised service package for my [SERVICE TYPE] targeting [CLIENT TYPE]. For each tier: a clear name (not "Basic/Standard/Premium"), what's included (specific deliverables), what's excluded, price, delivery timeline, and who this tier is right for. Ensure the value difference between tiers is obvious — not just a volume increase but a qualitative step up. Include the most common mistake when designing service tiers and how to avoid it.
whatItIsFor: Designs a 3-tier productised service offer for an agency or consultant — making it easier for clients to buy, easier for you to scope, and easier to compare against competitors without racing to the lowest price.
howToUseIt: Productised packages work best when the deliverables are consistent between clients and don't need deep customisation each time. If every project is completely bespoke, a rate card works better than packages.

title: Agency capacity planner
body: Build a capacity model for my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE] with [TEAM SIZE AND ROLES]. Inputs: each team member's available hours per week (subtract admin, meetings, and non-billable time), average hours per [PROJECT TYPE OR CLIENT] per month, number of active clients currently, number we could take on before hitting 85% capacity (the safe ceiling before quality deteriorates). Build a table showing: current load, maximum safe capacity, the next hire trigger (at what client count does headcount become the bottleneck?), and what happens if one team member is sick for 2 weeks — how many clients are at risk?
whatItIsFor: Builds a simple capacity model to know how many clients you can take on before your team is at breaking point — so you stop saying yes past the point where quality drops.
howToUseIt: Run this quarterly, not just when you're already overwhelmed. The goal is to know your ceiling before you hit it.

title: Niche positioning statement
body: Write 5 positioning statement options for my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE] that serves [SPECIFIC CLIENT TYPE] and solves [SPECIFIC PROBLEM]. Each statement must: name the exact client type (not "businesses"), state the specific outcome (not "better results"), and imply the differentiation without listing features. After the 5 options, give me the criteria I should use to choose between them (e.g. which one would make the ideal client feel most seen). Maximum 2 sentences per statement.
whatItIsFor: Writes a sharp positioning statement for a agency or consultant that makes it immediately clear who you serve, what problem you solve, and why you and not someone else — in one or two sentences that can live on a website header, a LinkedIn bio, or a pitch intro.
howToUseIt: Test it by asking a prospect who just read it: "who do we serve and what do we fix?" If they can't answer both, rewrite it. Most positioning statements fail because they describe what you do, not who you help and what changes for them.

title: Agency growth roadmap
body: Build a 12-month growth roadmap for my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE] currently at [MONTHLY REVENUE] with [TEAM SIZE]. My 12-month revenue target is [TARGET]. Identify the 3 highest-leverage growth levers available (e.g. raise prices, add a new service, increase client count, reduce churn, launch a retainer model). For each lever: what it would add to monthly revenue if executed, what's required to activate it (time, hire, investment), and what the sequencing should be (which lever to pull first and why). End with a quarterly milestone plan showing what "on track" looks like at Q1, Q2, Q3, and Q4.
whatItIsFor: Creates a 12-month growth plan for a service business — from current revenue to a specific target — with the levers to pull, the order to pull them in, and the hires or investments each phase requires.
howToUseIt: Build this at the start of the year and review it quarterly. The plan isn't a prediction — it's a decision framework for where to spend time and money each quarter.

title: Agency monthly ops review template
body: Create a monthly operational review template for a [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE] with [TEAM SIZE]. Sections to include: revenue vs last month and vs same month last year, MRR (monthly recurring revenue) from retainers, churn (any clients who left, and why), active client health ratings (red/amber/green and what triggered each), pipeline status (number of proposals out, total value, expected close date), team capacity (% utilisation this month), and the 3 things the agency must focus on in the next 30 days based on the review. Include prompts under each section so I can answer them quickly each month rather than having to think about what to include.
whatItIsFor: Creates a monthly internal review template for an agency — covering financial performance, client health, team capacity, and pipeline — so founders stop running by feel and start running by data.
howToUseIt: Run this on the first working day of each month, not at the end when you're busy. Set a 90-minute block — no phones, no client work. The agency that reviews monthly grows faster than the agency that reviews annually.

title: Client offboarding process
body: Write a client offboarding process for my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE]. Cover: what happens in the final 2 weeks of the relationship (deliverables, handover documents, access removal), what to include in a handover pack so the client can continue without you, how to collect a testimonial or case study permission during the offboarding (not awkwardly, not too late), how to handle a client leaving under difficult circumstances (different protocol to happy exits), and what to document internally for future client relationships. Include the exact wording for the final offboarding email.
whatItIsFor: Designs a structured offboarding process for when a client relationship ends — so departing clients become referrers rather than detractors, and the agency leaves nothing behind that causes problems later.
howToUseIt: Run this every time a client leaves, regardless of the reason. The last impression is as powerful as the first — and a well-offboarded client often comes back.

title: White-label reseller pitch script
body: Write a white-label reseller prospecting sequence for my [SERVICE TYPE] targeting [RESELLER TYPE — e.g. accountants, marketing consultants, web designers]. The sequence covers: (1) the initial outreach message (email or LinkedIn — under 80 words), (2) a 4-day follow-up if no reply, (3) the pitch for a 20-minute discovery call (what to cover, in what order), (4) the one-page overview to send after the call. For each stage: what to personalise, what to never say, and the one thing most people get wrong at that stage.
whatItIsFor: Writes the prospecting message and follow-up sequence for approaching potential white-label resellers — the businesses that could resell your service under their own brand.
howToUseIt: Be specific about who you're approaching and why they're a natural fit. Generic "partnership opportunity" outreach is ignored. Specific "I know your clients need this" outreach gets replies.

title: Agency referral programme designer
body: Design a referral programme for my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE]. Define: who is eligible to refer (existing clients only, or also past clients and partners), what the referrer receives (cash, credit, gift — and at what trigger point), what the referred client receives as an incentive to try the service, how referrals are tracked (code, link, or named attribution), and how the programme is announced to existing clients without it feeling like a cold sales email. Include the announcement email and a short FAQ for existing clients. Keep it simple enough to manage manually with under 50 clients.
whatItIsFor: Designs a structured referral programme for an agency that rewards existing clients and partners for sending new business — without the programme feeling transactional or cheapening the relationship.
howToUseIt: The best referral programmes are simple and generous, not complex and stingy. Err on the side of a reward that surprises the referrer — they'll talk about it.

title: Agency KPI dashboard brief
body: Design a weekly and monthly KPI dashboard for a [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE] with [MONTHLY REVENUE]. Define the 8 most important metrics — covering revenue, client health, team, and pipeline — and for each: what it measures, how to calculate it, what the healthy range is, and what a bad number triggers (action, not just awareness). Separate into two views: a weekly 10-minute pulse check (3–4 metrics) and a monthly 60-minute deep review (all 8). Include one leading indicator (predicts future revenue) and one lagging indicator (confirms what already happened).
whatItIsFor: Defines which KPIs an agency should actually track — and builds the structure for a one-page dashboard that gives the founder a real picture of business health in under 10 minutes per week.
howToUseIt: Most agency owners track revenue and nothing else until something goes wrong. Build the dashboard before you need it — not after a client surprise or a cash flow shock.

title: Agency client reporting template
body: Create a monthly client report template for my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE]. The report must include: a one-line summary of the month (the most important thing that happened), 3–5 key metrics with comparison to last month and target, what performed well and why, what underperformed and what we're changing, one specific recommendation for next month, and the plan for the coming month. Format it to be readable in under 5 minutes. Maximum 1 page for the written sections. Include a table structure for the metrics. Write a note on what NOT to include in client reports.
whatItIsFor: Creates a monthly client report template that shows results clearly, highlights what's working and what isn't, and gives the client one clear recommendation — so they see the value of the retainer every month without you writing a novel.
howToUseIt: The report should take 30 minutes to complete, not 3 hours. If it's taking longer, you're over-explaining. Clients want to know three things: did it work, why or why not, and what's next.

title: Scope of work document
body: Write a Scope of Work document for a [PROJECT TYPE] project between my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE] and a [CLIENT TYPE]. Include: project objective (1–2 sentences), deliverables (specific, numbered list), what's excluded (be explicit — this prevents the most common disputes), timeline with milestone dates, revision policy, client responsibilities (what they must provide and when), how changes to scope are managed, and sign-off process. Use plain language. No legal jargon. The document should be readable in 3 minutes and signable the same day.
whatItIsFor: Writes a precise, client-ready Scope of Work document for a specific project — the document that prevents scope creep, protects your time, and gives both parties something to refer back to when "but I thought that was included" happens.
howToUseIt: Every project, no matter how small or how trusting the client relationship, should have a signed SOW. The friendlier the client, the more important this becomes — because the awkward conversation later is much harder with someone you like.

title: Agency team expansion plan
body: Create a team expansion plan for my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE] currently at [REVENUE] with [CURRENT TEAM]. I want to grow to [REVENUE TARGET] in [TIMEFRAME]. For each of the next 3 hires: define the role, the trigger point (what revenue or client volume justifies the hire), the estimated cost (salary or contractor day rate), how the hire pays for itself (what additional revenue capacity they unlock), and the order to hire in. Include a simple financial model showing what monthly revenue must be to justify each hire, assuming the hire takes 6 weeks to become fully productive.
whatItIsFor: Maps the next 2–3 hires for a growing agency — in order of priority, with the financial model to confirm you can afford each hire before making an offer rather than after.
howToUseIt: Hire slightly before you need the resource, not when you're already overwhelmed. An agency that hires reactively always underinvests in onboarding and gets worse output from the new hire.

title: Agency pitch deck outline
body: Create a pitch deck outline for my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE] for a [CLIENT TYPE] prospect. Include: the 8 slides to include (with the goal of each slide and what to put on it), what each slide must achieve for the prospect to move to the next one, what to cut from most agency decks that wastes time or feels like filler, and the single most important thing the last slide must do. Include a note on slide design principles for an agency that doesn't have a dedicated designer.
whatItIsFor: Creates a concise, high-converting pitch deck structure for agency new business — covering what to include on each slide and what to cut, so the deck gets read rather than skimmed and closed.
howToUseIt: The deck supports a conversation — it doesn't replace it. 8 slides maximum. If a prospect needs 20 slides to understand you, the positioning is the problem.

title: Subcontractor briefing document
body: Write a subcontractor briefing document template for my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE]. The brief should cover: client and project overview (2–3 sentences), the specific deliverable required (format, length, quantity), what good looks like (example or reference standard), what to avoid (specific to this client), deadline and revision policy, how to submit work, who to contact with questions and when, and payment terms. Include a sign-off section the subcontractor signs before starting. Write it so a new subcontractor with no prior relationship with the agency can complete the work correctly without a call.
whatItIsFor: Creates a project briefing document for freelancers or subcontractors working on client work — so they produce on-brief output the first time rather than requiring two rounds of corrections because "I didn't know that was the expectation".
howToUseIt: Write this before you brief, not during. Rushed briefing documents produce off-brief work and erode client trust when the subcontractor's output is blamed on the agency.

title: Agency service expansion brief
body: Evaluate whether my [AGENCY/SERVICE TYPE] should add [NEW SERVICE] as an offering. Assess: (1) Is there demonstrable demand from my current client base (how many have asked in the last 6 months)? (2) Can we deliver this to the same quality standard as our core service — or does it require skills we don't have? (3) What's the margin on the new service vs our current core? (4) Does adding it create upsell value (making existing clients more sticky) or does it dilute focus? (5) What's the minimum viable version of this service we could offer in 30 days to test demand before fully committing? Give a yes/no recommendation with reasoning.
whatItIsFor: Evaluates whether a new service line is worth adding to an existing agency — based on client demand, delivery capacity, margin, and whether it distracts from what's already working.
howToUseIt: Run this before agreeing to add a new service, not after a client has asked for it and you've said yes to keep them. New services added reactively almost always underdeliver and strain capacity.

title: YouTube channel strategy brief
body: Build a YouTube channel strategy for a [BUSINESS TYPE] targeting [AUDIENCE]. Define: the channel niche (what topic do we own, and how is it different from existing channels?), 3 content pillars with 5 example video ideas per pillar, the best video types for this audience (tutorial, case study, Q&A, documentary, list-style), recommended upload frequency based on my capacity of [HOURS PER WEEK], how long videos should be and why, and the call-to-action structure for every video (what do we send viewers to?). Flag the #1 mistake small business owners make when starting a YouTube channel.
whatItIsFor: Defines a focused YouTube channel strategy for a small business — niche, content pillars, video types, and upload cadence — based on what actually generates leads rather than vanity views.
howToUseIt: Strategy before content. A generalised channel that uploads inconsistently is invisible on YouTube. A niche channel with 50 videos and a clear audience beats a broad channel with 300.

title: YouTube video script writer
body: Write a complete YouTube video script for a [BUSINESS TYPE] on the topic: "[VIDEO TOPIC]". Target length: [8–12 MINUTES / 400–600 WORDS spoken]. Structure: (1) hook — the first 15 seconds that stop the scroll, (2) context — why this matters to the viewer, (3) the main content in 3–5 clear sections with transitions, (4) one worked example using a specific scenario, (5) CTA — what to do next (subscribe, DM, download, buy). Include [ON-SCREEN TEXT] notes for graphics or callouts. Tone: [TONE]. Write for spoken delivery — no bullet points, no numbered lists in the script.
whatItIsFor: Writes a complete YouTube video script — with a strong hook, structured content, on-screen text cues, and a CTA — for a small business owner who doesn't want to wing it on camera.
howToUseIt: Give the script to the AI and then edit it to sound like you — the AI gets the structure right, you make it sound human. Never read a script verbatim; use it as talking points with a natural delivery.

title: YouTube thumbnail concept generator
body: Generate 5 YouTube thumbnail concepts for a video titled "[VIDEO TITLE]" from a [BUSINESS TYPE] channel targeting [AUDIENCE]. For each concept: the on-screen text (maximum 5 words), the face expression or image direction (if the creator appears), the background colour and visual style, and why this concept would get a click from the target audience. Rank the 5 concepts from strongest to weakest click-through potential and explain the ranking. Include the one principle that separates high-CTR thumbnails from low-CTR thumbnails in this niche.
whatItIsFor: Generates 5 thumbnail concept options for a YouTube video — with text, image direction, and colour scheme — so you have design options before opening Canva.
howToUseIt: Thumbnails and titles drive clicks, not content quality. A great video with a weak thumbnail will underperform a mediocre video with a strong one. Spend as much time on the thumbnail as the intro.

title: YouTube SEO title and description writer
body: Write YouTube SEO metadata for a video about "[VIDEO TOPIC]" from a [BUSINESS TYPE] channel targeting [AUDIENCE]. Provide: (1) 3 title options optimised for YouTube search (under 60 characters, include the primary keyword), (2) a 150-word video description with the primary keyword in the first sentence, a 3-line summary, a CTA with a link placeholder, and 3 hashtags, (3) 15 relevant tags (mix of broad and specific), (4) suggested chapter timestamps if the video covers [THESE SECTIONS]. Explain which title option is strongest and why.
whatItIsFor: Writes a YouTube-optimised title, description, tags, and chapter timestamps for a video — so it gets found on YouTube search and Google, not just pushed to existing subscribers.
howToUseIt: Write this before filming, not after. The title should inform the hook and the script — if you can't write a strong title, the video concept probably needs sharpening.

title: YouTube content calendar builder
body: Build a 12-week YouTube content calendar for a [BUSINESS TYPE] channel targeting [AUDIENCE], publishing [FREQUENCY — e.g. once per week, every fortnight]. The calendar should cover 3 content pillars: [PILLAR 1], [PILLAR 2], [PILLAR 3]. For each video: a working title (searchable, specific), the content pillar, the primary keyword to target, the video type (tutorial / case study / Q&A / list), and the CTA. Alternate pillars across the weeks to maintain variety. Flag 2 "evergreen" videos in the calendar (topics that will still be relevant in 2 years) and 2 "timely" videos (topics with seasonal or news-driven relevance).
whatItIsFor: Builds a 12-week YouTube content calendar with specific video titles, pillar assignments, and publish dates — so you're never staring at a blank screen wondering what to film next.
howToUseIt: Plan 8 weeks ahead, film 4 weeks ahead, edit 2 weeks ahead. This buffer means a bad filming day doesn't blow your publishing schedule.

title: YouTube community post writer
body: Write 10 YouTube Community post templates for a [BUSINESS TYPE] channel targeting [AUDIENCE]. Include: 3 poll posts (questions that generate engagement and tell you what the audience wants to learn), 3 tip posts (one specific insight in under 100 words), 2 video preview posts (teasing an upcoming upload), 1 question post (ask a real question the audience encounters), and 1 behind-the-scenes post. Each post should end with a question or prompt to drive replies. Keep each post under 150 words.
whatItIsFor: Writes YouTube Community tab posts — the short-form content between videos that keeps the channel active, builds relationships with subscribers, and tells the algorithm the channel is engaged even between uploads.
howToUseIt: Post to Community 2–3 times per week. It takes 10 minutes per post and signals consistent activity to YouTube without requiring filming. Use it to preview upcoming videos, ask questions, share quick tips, and run polls.

title: YouTube subscriber conversion funnel
body: Design a viewer-to-client conversion funnel for a [BUSINESS TYPE] YouTube channel targeting [AUDIENCE]. Define: (1) the lead magnet that would make a viewer trade their email address immediately after watching (specific, high-value, relevant to the most popular video topic), (2) the in-video CTA (where in the video, exact wording, and what to show on screen), (3) the video description CTA (under 30 words, with a link placeholder), (4) the 3-email welcome sequence after they download the lead magnet, (5) the offer to present at the end of the welcome sequence. Make the funnel work on autopilot — no manual follow-up required.
whatItIsFor: Maps the journey from YouTube viewer to email subscriber to paying client — with the specific lead magnet, CTA placement, and follow-up sequence that makes the conversion happen without being pushy.
howToUseIt: Most YouTube channels generate viewers but not leads because they skip the middle step: a specific, compelling reason to hand over an email. Fix the funnel before spending more time on content.

title: YouTube Shorts repurpose plan
body: I have a YouTube video about [VIDEO TOPIC] that is [VIDEO LENGTH] minutes long covering these sections: [LIST SECTIONS]. Identify 3 YouTube Short clip opportunities (under 60 seconds each) from this video. For each Short: the specific moment in the video to clip (timestamp range), why it works as a standalone clip without the full video context, what on-screen text to overlay, the suggested title for the Short (under 50 characters), and the end CTA ("watch the full video for [SPECIFIC THING]"). Rank the 3 clips by expected Short performance.
whatItIsFor: Maps which parts of an existing long-form YouTube video can be clipped into YouTube Shorts — extending the reach of one piece of content to the short-form algorithm without creating new content from scratch.
howToUseIt: Every long-form video should generate 2–3 Shorts. Shorts feed the long-form channel's subscriber growth — the algorithms are linked. A Short that does well sends new viewers to your full videos.

title: YouTube channel audit checklist
body: Create a YouTube channel audit checklist for a [BUSINESS TYPE] channel. The checklist should cover: channel-level settings (about section, channel keywords, links, featured video), individual video health (title keyword placement, description optimisation, thumbnail design, end screen and cards), content strategy (pillar consistency, upload frequency, video length vs audience retention patterns), and conversion elements (lead magnet CTA, description links, community tab activity). For each item: what "passing" looks like, what "failing" looks like, and the priority fix if failing. Organise into: fix today (takes under 30 minutes), fix this week, and fix this month.
whatItIsFor: Audits an existing YouTube channel against the elements that drive discoverability, watch time, and subscriber conversion — so you fix the right things instead of just uploading more videos.
howToUseIt: Run this audit before you upload your next video. Fixing metadata, thumbnails, and CTAs on existing videos can double performance without filming a single new piece of content.

title: YouTube collaboration pitch
body: Write a YouTube collaboration pitch to send to a [COLLABORATOR TYPE — e.g. accountant with a finance channel] creator whose audience overlaps with my [BUSINESS TYPE] channel targeting [AUDIENCE]. The pitch should include: a specific reference to their content (not generic flattery), the collaboration idea (format, topic, value to both audiences), the practical arrangement (who hosts, who promotes, how it's filmed), what they gain from it (audience exposure, content, credibility), and a low-friction next step. Keep it under 150 words. Include a subject line for email outreach.
whatItIsFor: Writes an outreach pitch to another YouTuber for a collaboration — structured to make the value exchange clear to someone who gets dozens of these messages and ignores most of them.
howToUseIt: Pitch creators whose audience overlaps with yours but who are not direct competitors. A collaboration works when both audiences benefit — not when one channel parasitises another's subscriber list.

title: YouTube monetisation strategy brief
body: Design a monetisation strategy for a [BUSINESS TYPE] YouTube channel currently at [SUBSCRIBER COUNT] and [MONTHLY VIEWS]. I sell [PRODUCT/SERVICE] at [PRICE POINT]. Map 4 monetisation routes in order of priority for my current stage: (1) lead generation (how YouTube feeds my service pipeline), (2) digital product sales (what product would convert best from this audience), (3) AdSense (is it worth enabling, and when does it become meaningful?), (4) brand partnerships or sponsorships (realistic timeline and what to charge). For each route: what's required to activate it, realistic monthly revenue at my current traffic level, and what I need to do this week to start.
whatItIsFor: Maps the realistic monetisation options for a small business YouTube channel — from AdSense (almost always the wrong priority) to lead generation, digital products, and speaking opportunities that actually move the needle.
howToUseIt: Most small business YouTube channels should not chase AdSense. At 10,000 views per month, AdSense pays approximately £25–£40. The same viewers clicking through to a £150 product or a discovery call are worth 50–100x more. Build the funnel first.

title: YouTube Q&A video planner
body: Plan a Q&A YouTube video for my [BUSINESS TYPE] channel using these audience questions: [LIST 5–8 QUESTIONS]. Structure: (1) select the 4–5 strongest questions (criteria: most likely to be relevant to the widest audience, most searchable as standalone queries), (2) order them from most urgent to most strategic, (3) write the opening hook that teases the most compelling question, (4) for each question: a suggested answer structure (not the full answer — the framework for answering), (5) write the mid-video CTA (the natural point to mention the lead magnet without disrupting the flow). Suggest a title that would rank for at least one of the question topics.
whatItIsFor: Plans a Q&A-style YouTube video using real audience questions — the format that consistently produces strong audience retention and subscriber comments because viewers feel directly addressed.
howToUseIt: Source questions from: comments on existing videos, DMs, email subscribers, or community tab polls. Real questions from real people outperform invented questions every time — the specificity shows.

title: YouTube end screen and cards script
body: Write the end screen script and card placement plan for a [BUSINESS TYPE] YouTube video about [VIDEO TOPIC]. Provide: (1) the verbal call-to-action for the last 20 seconds of the video (what to say while the end screen is showing — including subscribe prompt, next video suggestion, and lead magnet mention), (2) the 2 end screen elements to show (subscribe button placement + recommended video), (3) the card placement recommendations (at what point in the video, what type — link card, video card, or playlist), and (4) the specific "recommended video" to link as the watch-next (from a [TOPIC LIST] of existing videos). Keep the verbal CTA under 40 words — viewers already know they can subscribe.
whatItIsFor: Writes the verbal prompts and on-screen suggestions for YouTube end screens and card placements — the in-video elements that drive subscribers, watch-next clicks, and lead magnet conversions.
howToUseIt: End screens appear in the last 20 seconds of a video. Cards can appear any time. Both are often ignored by small creators — which is why most channels have high view counts and low subscriber rates. Fix this for every video you've already uploaded, not just new ones.

title: YouTube comment reply templates
body: Write 12 comment reply templates for a [BUSINESS TYPE] YouTube channel covering these comment types: (1) a simple "great video" comment, (2) a question about the video topic, (3) a comment sharing the viewer's own experience, (4) a "can you do a video on X" request, (5) a politely wrong comment (where the viewer has misunderstood something), (6) a negative or dismissive comment, (7) a comment asking for free one-to-one help. For each: write the template (with [FILL IN] sections), and include a note on what to never say in YouTube comments as a small business owner.
whatItIsFor: Creates a set of comment reply templates for the most common YouTube comment types — so engaging with the community takes 20 minutes per week rather than being something that gets skipped.
howToUseIt: Reply to every comment in the first 48 hours — YouTube's algorithm rewards channels where the creator engages. One reply to a comment can generate 3 more replies from other viewers, which signals the algorithm that the content is driving discussion.

title: YouTube analytics review template
body: Create a monthly YouTube analytics review template for a [BUSINESS TYPE] channel. Define the 6 metrics to review each month (not just views — include watch time, CTR, average percentage viewed, subscriber gain per video, and traffic source breakdown), what "healthy" looks like for each metric for a channel at [SUBSCRIBER COUNT], what action to take when a metric is below healthy range, and what to look for in the traffic sources that signals content strategy is working. End with 3 questions to ask every month that guide the next month's content plan.
whatItIsFor: Creates a monthly YouTube analytics review template — so you know which videos are driving subscribers and leads, not just which ones got the most views, and you can make better content decisions each month.
howToUseIt: View count is a vanity metric on YouTube. Watch time, average percentage viewed, click-through rate, and subscriber conversion rate are what determine channel growth. Review these monthly — not just when a video goes viral.

title: YouTube live stream planner
body: Plan a YouTube live stream for my [BUSINESS TYPE] channel targeting [AUDIENCE]. Define: (1) the best live format for this audience (Q&A / workshop / case study / product demo — with rationale), (2) a specific topic and the hook that gets people to register or tune in live, (3) the promotional plan (what to post in the 7 days before the stream and where), (4) a 60-minute run-of-show (what happens in each 15-minute block), (5) how to handle live chat questions without losing the thread, (6) how to repurpose the recording into 2–3 pieces of on-demand content after the stream. Include the announcement post for the community tab.
whatItIsFor: Plans a YouTube live stream session for a small business channel — covering topic, format, promotional strategy, and how to repurpose the stream into on-demand content after the broadcast.
howToUseIt: Live streams perform well for Q&A, product demonstrations, and real-time workshops. They also tell YouTube you're actively creating, which can boost existing video recommendations. Repurpose every live stream into at least one edited on-demand video.

title: YouTube lead magnet landing page copy
body: Write the landing page copy for a lead magnet I'm offering to YouTube viewers of my [BUSINESS TYPE] channel. Lead magnet: [NAME AND DESCRIPTION]. The viewer arrives from a video about [VIDEO TOPIC] where I promised "[EXACT CTA WORDING FROM VIDEO]". The landing page must: match the promise of the video exactly, confirm what they get (specific, not vague), address the one doubt they might have before entering their email (is this worth my email address?), and include a simple email capture field. Write the headline, subheadline, 3-bullet benefit list, and a confirmation statement below the CTA button. Maximum 150 words total on the page.
whatItIsFor: Writes the landing page copy for a lead magnet linked from a YouTube video — converting YouTube viewers into email subscribers with a page that matches the specific promise made in the video.
howToUseIt: The landing page must match the video CTA exactly. If the video says "download the checklist", the landing page must show the checklist — not a general "subscribe for more tips" page. Mismatched CTAs kill conversion rates.

title: YouTube series planner
body: Plan a [3–5 PART] YouTube series for my [BUSINESS TYPE] channel on the topic of [SERIES TOPIC]. For each episode: the specific title (searchable, under 60 characters), the one question it answers, the hook that makes viewers watch this episode even without watching the previous one, the cliffhanger or lead-in to the next episode, and the runtime. Include a series trailer outline (60-second video that teases all episodes) and the best order to release them. Flag whether each episode works as a standalone video for new viewers who discover the series mid-way through.
whatItIsFor: Plans a multi-part YouTube series on a single topic — the format that drives the highest subscriber retention because viewers watch one video and then immediately want the next.
howToUseIt: Series work best when each video answers a specific question that leads naturally to the next. "Part 2" must deliver on a cliffhanger or an unanswered question from Part 1 — not just "more of the same topic".

title: YouTube sponsor outreach brief
body: Create a sponsorship media kit brief and outreach template for my [BUSINESS TYPE] YouTube channel with [SUBSCRIBER COUNT] and [MONTHLY VIEWS]. Audience profile: [AGE, ROLE, INTERESTS]. Define: (1) the sponsor types most likely to be relevant to this audience, (2) what a sponsor gets (placement options: intro mention, mid-roll, end card, description link, community post), (3) how to price each placement (CPM model vs flat rate — which works better at this scale and why), (4) the one-page media kit structure, (5) the cold outreach email to a potential sponsor (under 100 words). Include realistic rate expectations for the channel size.
whatItIsFor: Prepares a media kit and outreach brief for approaching potential sponsors for a YouTube channel — defining who your audience is, what a sponsor gets, and what to charge before you start conversations.
howToUseIt: Sponsorship is viable from around 2,000–5,000 subscribers if the audience is niche and valuable to advertisers. A niche channel with 3,000 highly relevant viewers is more valuable to a specialist advertiser than a broad channel with 30,000.

title: YouTube batch filming plan
body: Create a batch filming day plan for my [BUSINESS TYPE] YouTube channel. I want to film [NUMBER] videos in one day. My filming setup is [DESCRIBE — e.g. talking head, one camera, basic lighting]. The video topics are: [LIST TOPICS]. Plan: the ideal order to film (considering energy, outfit changes, and setup complexity), a preparation checklist for the week before filming, a filming day schedule with time blocks, what to check after each video before moving to the next, and the post-filming workflow (what needs to happen before the videos can be edited and uploaded). Flag the 3 things that most commonly derail a batch filming day.
whatItIsFor: Plans a single day of batch filming that produces 4–6 YouTube videos — so a small business owner can maintain a consistent publishing schedule without filming every week.
howToUseIt: Batch film once per month. All 4–6 videos scripted and fully prepared before the filming day — not improvised on the day. A filming day without prepared scripts produces 2 unusable videos and 3 hours of wasted time.

title: Podcast concept and format planner
body: Design a podcast concept for a [BUSINESS TYPE] targeting [AUDIENCE]. Define: (1) the show premise in one sentence (what specific problem does every episode address?), (2) the best format for this audience (solo expert / interview / co-host / case study — with reasoning), (3) episode length and cadence (weekly 20 min? biweekly 45 min? — based on what this audience has time for), (4) the show name (3 options — searchable, specific, memorable), (5) the first 10 episode topics, and (6) how the podcast feeds clients (what CTA converts a listener into a lead). Flag the #1 mistake small businesses make when starting a podcast.
whatItIsFor: Defines a focused podcast concept for a small business — niche, format, episode length, and release cadence — based on what the target audience actually listens to and what positions you as the go-to authority.
howToUseIt: Define the show concept before you buy equipment. The #1 mistake is starting with "I'll interview interesting people" — a format that produces no consistent SEO value and positions you as a connector, not an expert.

title: Podcast episode script writer
body: Write a complete podcast episode script for a [BUSINESS TYPE] episode on the topic: "[EPISODE TOPIC]". Target length: [15–25 MINUTES / 2,000–3,000 WORDS]. Format: (1) hook — the first 30 seconds that make the listener stay, (2) episode promise — what they'll know by the end, (3) main content in 3–4 sections with clear signposting ("Here's the first thing...", "Now, the second thing..."), (4) one worked example with a named fictional business, (5) the key takeaway in one sentence, (6) CTA — what to do next. Tone: [TONE — e.g. direct, warm, no jargon]. Write for spoken delivery — no bullet points, conversational sentences, and contractions throughout.
whatItIsFor: Writes a complete solo podcast episode script — with a strong hook, structured content in clear beats, and a natural-sounding close — for a host who wants to deliver confidently without rambling.
howToUseIt: Use the script as talking points, not a word-for-word read. Record a conversational version and then edit out the hesitations — not the other way around.

title: Podcast guest interview question writer
body: Write 12 podcast interview questions for a guest who is a [GUEST ROLE/EXPERTISE] appearing on a [BUSINESS TYPE] podcast for an audience of [AUDIENCE]. The questions should cover: (1) their backstory (1–2 questions — specific, not generic), (2) the specific expertise they're known for (4 questions — each one producing an actionable insight, not a vague opinion), (3) a contrarian or challenging question (1 question — the one most hosts don't ask), (4) a failure or mistake (1 question), (5) the one practical thing every listener can do this week based on their expertise, (6) where to find the guest after the episode. Include a note on the questions to send in advance vs keep as surprises.
whatItIsFor: Writes a structured set of interview questions for a podcast guest — going beyond the generic "tell us about your journey" to questions that produce specific, useful answers the audience can act on.
howToUseIt: Send the first 3 questions to the guest in advance — not all of them. Guests who over-prepare give rehearsed answers. The best conversations happen when the guest knows the direction but not every question.

title: Podcast guest pitch email
body: Write a podcast guest pitch email for my [PODCAST NAME] targeting [AUDIENCE] to invite [GUEST TYPE — e.g. a hiring consultant who runs a LinkedIn newsletter about first-time managers]. The email must: open with a specific reference to their work (not generic praise), state what angle the episode would cover and why it serves my audience, explain what the guest gets from the appearance (their specific audience benefit, not just "exposure"), outline the practical commitment (episode length, format, recording date range), and end with a low-friction reply option. Maximum 150 words. No flattery, no buzzwords.
whatItIsFor: Writes an outreach email to invite a specific guest onto a podcast — demonstrating that you've done your research, making the ask easy to say yes to, and not wasting the guest's time with a generic "love your work" pitch.
howToUseIt: Personalise the first 2 sentences specifically to the guest — no copy-paste opener. A personalised pitch that takes 3 minutes to write gets 5x the reply rate of a generic template.

title: Podcast show notes writer
body: Write show notes for a podcast episode of [PODCAST NAME] on the topic "[EPISODE TITLE]" featuring [GUEST NAME AND ROLE, OR SOLO]. The show notes must include: a 100-word episode summary (written for search — include 2–3 relevant keywords naturally), 5–6 key timestamps with descriptive labels (not just "intro" — what does each section cover?), 3 key takeaways in bullet format (actionable, specific), links mentioned in the episode (3 placeholders), a guest bio of 50 words (if applicable), and a CTA with a link placeholder. Format for a podcast website page or Substack post.
whatItIsFor: Writes SEO-optimised show notes for a podcast episode — with a summary, key timestamps, links, and a CTA — so each episode generates searchable content beyond the audio itself.
howToUseIt: Show notes are searchable. Google indexes podcast show notes pages, not audio. A well-written show notes page for a niche topic can drive organic traffic to your podcast for years.

title: Podcast listener conversion funnel
body: Design a listener-to-client conversion funnel for a [BUSINESS TYPE] podcast targeting [AUDIENCE]. Define: (1) the lead magnet that would make a listener trade their email (specific to the most popular episode topic, immediately useful), (2) the in-episode CTA (when in the episode, exact wording — under 25 words), (3) the show notes CTA (under 30 words with link placeholder), (4) a 3-email welcome sequence after download, (5) the offer to present at the end of the sequence. The funnel must work on autopilot — no manual follow-up from episode release to first offer presented.
whatItIsFor: Maps the journey from podcast listener to email subscriber to paying client — with the lead magnet, episode CTA, and welcome sequence that makes the conversion happen automatically.
howToUseIt: A podcast without a conversion funnel is a brand-building exercise with no measurable commercial output. Build the funnel for your first episode, not your fiftieth.

title: Podcast episode repurpose plan
body: Create a repurpose plan for my podcast episode on "[EPISODE TOPIC]". The episode covers: [LIST 3–4 KEY SECTIONS OR INSIGHTS]. My distribution channels are: [LIST — e.g. Instagram, LinkedIn, email newsletter, YouTube]. For each channel: identify 1–2 pieces of content that can be extracted from the episode (clip, quote, carousel, newsletter section), what to use verbatim from the transcript vs what to rewrite for platform, and the production time required per piece. Total output should be 8–12 pieces of content from one episode. Include a production order (what to create first based on time investment vs reach).
whatItIsFor: Maps every piece of content that can be extracted from a single podcast episode — so one hour of recording becomes a week's worth of content across multiple platforms without additional filming or writing.
howToUseIt: Repurpose from the episode transcript or a detailed outline — not from memory. The specifics (stats, quotes, frameworks) are what make repurposed content worth engaging with.

title: Podcast pitch to other shows
body: Write a podcast guest pitch for me to appear on [TARGET PODCAST TYPE — e.g. small business finance podcasts, women entrepreneur shows] as a [MY ROLE] from a [BUSINESS TYPE]. I can offer episodes on these topics: [LIST 3 TOPIC IDEAS]. The pitch email must: open with a specific reference to the target podcast (not generic), propose a specific episode topic with a clear audience benefit, establish credibility briefly (without a full bio), confirm practical requirements (I'm comfortable on Zoom, 30–45 minutes, I promote to my own audience), and end with a low-friction next step. Write a template I can personalise for each podcast, with clear [FILL IN] markers. Under 150 words.
whatItIsFor: Writes the outreach pitch to appear as a guest on other podcasts — the fastest way to reach a new, warm audience without building your own listener base from scratch.
howToUseIt: Pitch shows where the audience is one step away from being your client — not the biggest show in your field. A 500-listener niche show with your exact audience converts better than appearing on a 50,000-listener general business show.

title: Podcast episode title optimizer
body: Generate 5 podcast episode title options for an episode about "[EPISODE TOPIC]" on a [BUSINESS TYPE] podcast for [AUDIENCE]. For each title: make it under 60 characters, include the primary keyword, and target one of these angles: curiosity gap (what they don't know they don't know), specific outcome (a measurable result), contrarian (challenges a widely-held belief), urgency (why now matters), and direct statement (what it is). Rank the 5 titles by expected click rate and explain the ranking. Include the podcast app search keyword this episode should target.
whatItIsFor: Generates 5 title options for a podcast episode — optimised for listener curiosity and podcast app search — so the episode gets clicked on, not just uploaded.
howToUseIt: Test titles with your email list before publishing — the subject line of the episode announcement email is effectively a title test. The title that generates the most clicks becomes your episode title.

title: Podcast listener Q&A collector
body: Design a listener question collection system for my [BUSINESS TYPE] podcast with [APPROXIMATE LISTENER COUNT]. Include: (1) the 3 best collection channels for this audience (e.g. email reply, Instagram story, show notes form), (2) the exact wording of the question request (in-episode CTA and written prompt), (3) how to categorise and prioritise questions received (which to answer immediately vs batch into a Q&A episode), (4) a template for the monthly Q&A episode format using real listener questions, (5) how to credit the listener without revealing personal information. Include the exact in-episode request script (under 20 words).
whatItIsFor: Creates a system for collecting and using listener questions as episode topics — producing content the audience already wants rather than guessing what to cover next.
howToUseIt: The best podcast topics are questions listeners actually asked, not questions you think they should care about. Set up the collection method once and refer to it before every episode batch.

title: Podcast sponsorship pitch brief
body: Create a podcast sponsorship brief and media kit structure for my [PODCAST NAME] with [MONTHLY DOWNLOADS] and [AUDIENCE PROFILE — role, industry, income level]. Define: (1) the 3–5 sponsor types most relevant to this audience (be specific — not "brands" but exact company categories), (2) placement options and what each delivers (pre-roll 30 sec, mid-roll 60 sec, show notes link, dedicated episode), (3) pricing for each placement (CPM model vs flat rate — which suits this audience size and why), (4) the one-page media kit structure, (5) the outreach email template (under 100 words). Include realistic rate benchmarks for this download level.
whatItIsFor: Creates the media kit and pitch structure for approaching potential podcast sponsors — defining audience value, placement options, and pricing before entering sponsor conversations.
howToUseIt: A podcast with 1,000 highly targeted listeners in a specific professional niche can command sponsorship rates that a general lifestyle podcast with 10,000 listeners cannot. Know your audience's value before setting rates.

title: Podcast trailer script writer
body: Write a podcast trailer script for [PODCAST NAME] — a [FORMAT] show for [AUDIENCE] about [TOPIC]. The trailer should be 60–90 seconds when read at a natural speaking pace. Include: (1) who the host is (1 sentence — not a full bio), (2) who the show is for (specific, not everyone), (3) what a typical episode covers (with 2 specific episode examples), (4) why this show is different from others on the same topic, (5) a subscribe CTA. Tone: [TONE]. Write for spoken delivery — no lists, natural phrasing, and contractions throughout.
whatItIsFor: Writes a 60–90 second podcast trailer — the first thing new listeners hear before deciding to subscribe — that clearly explains who the show is for, what they'll learn, and why they should stay.
howToUseIt: The trailer is permanently pinned as the first episode. It is also the audio you use in promotional clips. Write it last — after you understand what the show actually covers — not before.

title: Podcast review request script
body: Write 5 podcast review request scripts for different episode positions — (1) end of the first episode, (2) end of the 10th episode, (3) mid-episode (subtle, non-interruptive), (4) a solo call-to-action episode insert, (5) a follow-up mention after a listener sends a DM or email. Each script: under 40 words, tells the listener specifically what to do (not just "leave a review"), and gives them a reason that benefits them (e.g. what a review helps the show do). Write in the host's natural voice — not corporate, not pleading.
whatItIsFor: Writes the in-episode review request that actually gets reviews — not a generic "please leave a review if you enjoy the show" that every listener ignores, but a specific, timed, low-friction request that converts.
howToUseIt: Reviews matter most in the first 90 days of a podcast's life, when they influence Apple Podcast chart placement. Ask for them in this window more aggressively than at any other time.

title: Podcast launch promotion plan
body: Create a 2-week podcast launch promotion plan for [PODCAST NAME] launching on [LAUNCH DATE]. I have [EXISTING AUDIENCE SIZE AND CHANNELS — e.g. 800 Instagram followers, 400 email subscribers]. Launch stack: [NUMBER] episodes ready. The plan must cover: what to post each day in the 14 days leading up to launch, which platform each post goes on, the email campaign (how many emails, what each covers), the personal outreach strategy (who to DM personally for the launch push), and the review-building push in week 1. Include the exact launch email subject line and the hook sentence for the Instagram launch post.
whatItIsFor: Maps the 2-week launch campaign for a new podcast — covering what to post, where, and when — so the show starts with momentum rather than 12 downloads (10 of which are the host).
howToUseIt: Launch with 3 episodes ready, not 1. Listeners who enjoy the first episode want to binge the second immediately. If there's no second episode, they won't return when it drops 2 weeks later.

title: Podcast transcript repurpose guide
body: Turn this podcast transcript into a long-form blog post for a [BUSINESS TYPE] website targeting [AUDIENCE] searching for information about [EPISODE TOPIC]. The blog post should: open with the primary keyword in the first sentence, use the episode's key sections as H2 headings (rewritten for search), keep the conversational insights but remove filler words and repetition, add 2–3 subheadings that target related search queries not covered in the episode, include the key takeaways as a bulleted list at the end, and end with a CTA matching the in-episode CTA. Target word count: 800–1,200 words. [PASTE TRANSCRIPT BELOW THIS LINE]
whatItIsFor: Turns a podcast transcript into a long-form blog post — capturing the SEO value of long-form written content from audio that otherwise generates no searchable text.
howToUseIt: Use auto-transcription (Otter, Descript, or Whisper) to generate a raw transcript, then use this prompt to turn it into a readable article. A raw transcript is not a blog post — it reads like a conversation, not a structured guide.

title: Podcast season planning brief
body: Plan a themed podcast season for [PODCAST NAME] on the overall theme: "[SEASON THEME]". The season should be [6–10 EPISODES] long, released [WEEKLY/BIWEEKLY]. For each episode: a specific title, the one question it answers, who delivers the insight (solo vs guest — and if guest, what type of expert), and how it leads naturally into the next episode. Include: the season trailer outline (60 seconds), the promotional hook for social media ("This season on [PODCAST NAME]..."), and the finale episode concept (what makes it a satisfying ending to the season).
whatItIsFor: Plans a themed podcast season — a series of 6–10 episodes around one coherent topic — which is easier to promote, easier for listeners to recommend, and more compelling for potential guests than a free-form episode list.
howToUseIt: Season-based podcasts convert listeners to subscribers faster because the theme makes it easier for a listener to say "you should listen to this — the whole series is about [THING YOU CARE ABOUT]". Design the season around one problem your ideal client is actively trying to solve.

title: Podcast analytics review template
body: Create a monthly podcast analytics review template for a [BUSINESS TYPE] podcast at [DOWNLOAD LEVEL]. Define the 6 metrics to review monthly — including downloads, episode completion rate, new subscriber rate, lead magnet clicks, and review count — with what "healthy" looks like at this download level, what triggers a content strategy change vs a promotion strategy change, and what 3 questions I should ask every month to improve the next month's content plan. Include a table structure for tracking the metrics month over month.
whatItIsFor: Creates a monthly podcast analytics review template — so you know which episodes drive subscriber growth and lead conversions, not just which ones get the most downloads.
howToUseIt: Downloads are the vanity metric of podcasting. Episode completion rate, new subscriber rate, and lead magnet clicks per episode are what tell you whether the podcast is working as a business tool.

title: Podcast email newsletter integration
body: Design a podcast-newsletter integration plan for my [BUSINESS TYPE] email list of [SIZE] targeting [AUDIENCE]. The plan should define: (1) how each podcast episode is announced in the newsletter (format, timing, what to include beyond a link), (2) the template for a "podcast week" newsletter issue (what replaces the usual content — a key excerpt? the full show notes?), (3) how to reference the podcast in non-podcast newsletter issues without it feeling like a push, (4) the subscriber re-engagement sequence when the podcast launches or returns from a break, (5) the metric that tells me the integration is working (what open rate or click rate on episode links is success?). Write the template for the standard "episode drop" email.
whatItIsFor: Designs how to integrate a podcast into an existing email newsletter — so each new episode is announced, the show notes drive website traffic, and newsletter subscribers become loyal listeners without a separate content workflow.
howToUseIt: The easiest podcast audience to build is your existing email list. Before investing in paid promotion or social media clips, convert the people who already trust you into listeners.

title: Podcast monetisation strategy (non-sponsorship)
body: Design a non-sponsorship monetisation plan for my [BUSINESS TYPE] podcast with [MONTHLY DOWNLOADS] targeting [AUDIENCE]. I currently offer [PRODUCTS/SERVICES AT PRICE POINTS]. Map 4 monetisation routes in order of priority: (1) podcast-to-client pipeline (how does the podcast generate service enquiries?), (2) a digital product that would convert listeners (specific to the most downloaded episode topic), (3) a premium podcast or members-only feed (would this audience pay, and for what?), (4) live events or workshops for the listener community. For each: estimated monthly revenue at current download levels, what to build or change this week to activate it, and the realistic timeline to first revenue.
whatItIsFor: Maps the non-sponsorship monetisation routes for a podcast — from premium content to consulting to digital products — for hosts who don't want to interrupt their episodes with ads or whose audience size doesn't justify sponsorship rates yet.
howToUseIt: For most small business podcasters, the best monetisation is not sponsorship — it's using the podcast as a trust-building tool that converts listeners into service clients or product buyers. Measure ROI in clients, not CPM.

title: Podcast feedback collection system
body: Design a listener feedback collection system for my [BUSINESS TYPE] podcast. Include: (1) a quarterly survey (8 questions maximum — which episodes they found most useful and why, what topics to cover, what format works for them, and what they wish was different), (2) the in-episode survey request script (under 30 words, not whining), (3) how to analyse and act on the responses (what to do with the top 3 insights), (4) a one-to-one interview approach for 3–5 "super listeners" each quarter, (5) what to share back with the audience after acting on their feedback. Write the full 8-question survey.
whatItIsFor: Creates a system for collecting structured listener feedback on a podcast — so content decisions are based on what the audience actually values, not what the host assumes they want.
howToUseIt: Run a listener survey every 6 months. The responses tell you what to keep, what to change, and which topics to cover next — and the survey itself reminds listeners the show exists and that the host cares.

title: PR story angle finder
body: Identify 5 newsworthy PR story angles for a [BUSINESS TYPE] with these recent developments: [LIST 2–3 BUSINESS UPDATES — e.g. revenue milestone, new service, client outcome, market trend you've noticed]. For each angle: the story frame (how to position this as news, not a press release), which publication type it fits (national business press, trade press, local press, consumer lifestyle), the hook sentence a journalist would use as their headline, and what data or evidence makes this story credible. Rank the 5 angles from most to least pitchable and explain why the top angle is the strongest.
whatItIsFor: Identifies the newsworthy story angles in your business that journalists actually want to write about — as opposed to the "we launched a new product" announcements that get ignored.
howToUseIt: Journalists don't cover businesses — they cover stories. The frame that turns your business news into a story is the one that connects your thing to something the journalist's audience already cares about.

title: Press release writer
body: Write a press release for my [BUSINESS TYPE] about [NEWS ANNOUNCEMENT]. Format: (1) headline (present tense, under 12 words, newsworthy), (2) dateline and opening paragraph (who, what, when, where, why — in under 60 words, front-loading the most important fact), (3) two supporting paragraphs with context and supporting data, (4) a direct quote from [SPOKESPERSON NAME AND TITLE] (provide the quote or I'll write a placeholder), (5) a "notes to editors" section including company boilerplate (2 sentences), contact name and email, and a high-resolution image availability note. Write in journalistic style — no marketing language.
whatItIsFor: Writes a journalist-ready press release — structured in the inverted pyramid format that editors expect, with a news hook, supporting evidence, and a company boilerplate — ready to send without an agency.
howToUseIt: A press release is not a marketing piece — it is a factual document written for a journalist who will use it as raw material. Every sentence must be something a journalist could quote. Remove all adjectives that describe how great you are.

title: Journalist pitch email writer
body: Write a journalist pitch email to [JOURNALIST NAME OR TYPE — e.g. "the small business editor at a regional newspaper"] about [STORY ANGLE]. The pitch must: open with a reference to the journalist's recent work (provide the article title or I'll write a placeholder), state the story in 2 sentences (what happened, why it matters to their readers), offer 3 things (an exclusive quote, data, or access to a case study), confirm availability for a call, and close with a low-friction next step. Maximum 150 words. Subject line options: 3 variants. No press release attached in the first email — explain why this is the right approach.
whatItIsFor: Writes a targeted pitch email to a specific journalist or editor — concise enough to be read in 90 seconds, compelling enough to generate a reply, and personalised enough to not look like a mass pitch.
howToUseIt: Pitch one story, one journalist, one publication at a time. Mass-blast pitching damages your reputation and wastes everyone's time. Research the journalist's last 5 articles before writing.

title: Media list builder brief
body: Define a media targeting strategy for a [BUSINESS TYPE] looking to generate press coverage about [STORY TOPIC]. For each of the following outlet categories, define: which specific publication types to target, what makes a journalist in this category a good fit for this story, and how to find the right journalist within a publication (beats, sections, keyword searches): (1) national business press, (2) industry/trade press for [INDUSTRY], (3) local/regional press, (4) freelance journalists covering [TOPIC], (5) business-focused podcasts and newsletters. For each: the realistic coverage value (credibility, SEO, audience reach) and the best time of year to pitch this outlet.
whatItIsFor: Defines the categories and specific publication types to target for a PR campaign — so you build a focused media list of 20–30 relevant journalists rather than a 500-contact spray-and-pray list that generates no coverage.
howToUseIt: A targeted list of 20 journalists who regularly cover your story type outperforms a 500-contact list every time. Build it manually and update it quarterly — journalists move between publications frequently.

title: Expert comment pitch writer
body: Write an expert comment pitch for my [ROLE AT BUSINESS TYPE] responding to a journalist who is writing about [JOURNALIST'S STORY TOPIC]. They asked for: [WHAT THE JOURNALIST REQUESTED — quote, expert opinion, data, case study]. My perspective on this topic: [YOUR ACTUAL POSITION OR INSIGHT]. The pitch should: respond directly to what was asked (not pitch my business), offer a quotable insight in 2–3 sentences, confirm my credentials briefly (1 sentence), and indicate availability for follow-up. Maximum 100 words total. Write 2 versions — one for email, one for Twitter/X DM (under 280 characters).
whatItIsFor: Writes a short "expert comment" pitch to journalists who are working on a story in your field — the fastest way to get quoted in a piece without pitching your own story.
howToUseIt: Monitor platforms like Qwoted, Response Source, or Twitter/X using journalist calls (#JournoRequest) and respond within 2 hours. Speed matters — journalists are working to a deadline and take the first credible expert who replies.

title: PR follow-up sequence
body: Write a 3-email follow-up sequence for a journalist pitch that received no reply. The original pitch was about [STORY TOPIC]. Email 1 (day 5 after the pitch): a brief, direct follow-up that adds one new data point or hook not in the original pitch. Email 2 (day 12): a short final nudge with a clear door-open for the future. Email 3 (day 20): a clean close that leaves the relationship intact for a future pitch. For each email: subject line, body under 80 words, and what not to do (common mistakes at each stage).
whatItIsFor: Writes a structured follow-up sequence for a pitch that received no reply — the sequence that gets responses without being annoying, persistent, or burning the relationship with the journalist.
howToUseIt: One follow-up is professional. Two is acceptable. Three is the limit. After three contacts with no reply, archive the journalist and move on — returning 6 months later with a different story.

title: Award application writer
body: Write an award application for my [BUSINESS TYPE] applying for [AWARD NAME OR CATEGORY — e.g. Best New Business, Small Business of the Year]. The application should respond to these typical questions: (1) describe your business and what makes it different (150 words), (2) what impact have you had on your clients/customers in the past 12 months (150 words — use specific numbers), (3) what challenge did you overcome and what did you learn (100 words), (4) what are your plans for growth (100 words). Write specifically and with evidence — no vague adjectives. Assume the judge knows nothing about the industry.
whatItIsFor: Writes a compelling award application for a small business — structured to stand out against entries from larger companies by leading with specific outcomes rather than feature lists or ambition statements.
howToUseIt: Judges read hundreds of entries. The ones that get shortlisted lead with a specific result in the first sentence, not a mission statement. Your business's impact on real people beats your growth plans every time.

title: Speaking opportunity pitch
body: Write a speaking pitch email to the organiser of [EVENT TYPE — e.g. a small business conference, a trade association annual meeting] to speak on the topic of [SPEAKING TOPIC]. The pitch must: propose a specific talk title and one-paragraph session description (written for an event programme), state what the audience will leave able to do (not just what they'll know), confirm my credentials for this specific topic (2 sentences), and include a link placeholder to my speaker page or previous speaking examples. End with a specific question to drive a reply. Maximum 200 words total.
whatItIsFor: Writes a pitch to speak at a conference, trade event, or industry panel — positioning you as the right expert for a specific topic without sounding like a sales pitch in speaker's clothing.
howToUseIt: Event organisers are looking for speakers who educate the audience, not promote themselves. The pitch that says "I'll teach your audience how to [SPECIFIC THING]" beats "I'd love to share my journey and insights" every time.

title: Media interview preparation guide
body: Prepare me for a [MEDIA TYPE — newspaper interview / podcast / TV segment / radio] on the topic of [TOPIC]. The publication/show is [NAME] and their audience is [AUDIENCE]. Create: (1) my 3 key messages (each in one sentence — the 3 things I want the audience to remember), (2) the "bridge" phrases I can use to redirect from a difficult question back to my key messages, (3) the 5 most likely challenging or hostile questions and my prepared answers to each, (4) the single most important thing to say if I only get 60 seconds, (5) 3 things not to say (phrases or claims to avoid with this audience). Include a note on the most common interview mistake made by subject-matter experts.
whatItIsFor: Prepares you for a media interview — newspaper, podcast, TV, or radio — with the key messages, difficult question responses, and bridging techniques used by experienced media spokespeople.
howToUseIt: Every media interview needs 3 key messages and a "bridge" technique for redirecting unwanted questions. Without preparation, interviews produce rambling answers that the journalist edits into the one quote you didn't want to give.

title: Bylined article pitch writer
body: Write a bylined article pitch to [PUBLICATION TYPE — e.g. a trade magazine, a business website] for a [BUSINESS TYPE] expert. Article topic: [TOPIC]. The pitch must: state the article premise (what specific angle will be argued or taught), explain why this publication's audience needs this information now (timely hook), confirm word count and turnaround time, briefly establish expertise (1 sentence, no résumé), and offer an alternative angle if the first is already assigned. Include the first 2 sentences of the article itself — the strongest hook available. Under 150 words total for the pitch.
whatItIsFor: Writes a pitch to a publication to contribute a bylined guest article — the format that positions you as a thought leader while giving the publication free expert content they need.
howToUseIt: A published byline in a relevant trade or business publication is worth more than 10 press mentions because you control the message. Pitch articles that teach something specific — opinion pieces with no actionable content rarely get accepted.

title: PR crisis message guide
body: Create a PR crisis message guide for a [BUSINESS TYPE] facing the following potential incident: [DESCRIBE THE SCENARIO — e.g. a client complaint that has gone public on social media, a data breach, a product recall]. The guide should include: (1) a holding statement for the first 4 hours (acknowledges the situation without admitting liability), (2) the full response statement for 24–48 hours later (after facts are confirmed), (3) the internal message to staff (what to say and what not to say to clients who ask), (4) a social media response template for public comments, (5) the 3 things you must never say in a crisis (and what to say instead). Write the holding statement ready to send.
whatItIsFor: Prepares holding statements, response messages, and stakeholder communications for a reputational incident — so you have something written before a journalist calls, rather than improvising under pressure.
howToUseIt: The first 4 hours of a public relations crisis determine 80% of the outcome. A prepared holding statement and a clear spokesperson policy means you don't say something you regret because a journalist called at 5pm on a Friday.

title: Thought leadership content calendar
body: Build a 12-week thought leadership campaign for a [BUSINESS TYPE] expert positioning themselves as the go-to authority on [CORE TOPIC]. The campaign should cover: the central thesis (the one contrarian or data-backed point that defines the position), and for each of the 12 weeks: one piece of owned content (LinkedIn post, article, or podcast episode), one earned media action (pitch, expert comment submission, or award application), and a brief note on how each week's owned and earned content reinforce each other. Include the 3-sentence positioning statement that opens every piece of content this campaign generates.
whatItIsFor: Creates a 12-week thought leadership content calendar — coordinating press pitches, bylined articles, LinkedIn posts, and podcast appearances into a coherent campaign around one core theme.
howToUseIt: Thought leadership works through repetition and consistency across channels. A single press mention generates awareness; 12 weeks of consistent, themed content on the same topic builds perceived authority.

title: Podcast media tour planner
body: Plan a 6-week podcast media tour for a [BUSINESS TYPE] expert promoting [NEW PRODUCT/SERVICE/BOOK/CAMPAIGN]. I want to appear on 8–12 podcasts in this period. Define: (1) the 3 categories of podcasts to target (with specific examples), (2) a different angle for each category (so the pitch isn't identical to every host), (3) the outreach timeline (when to pitch to get the appearances landing in the right weeks), (4) what to prepare once booked (speaker brief, topic options, promotional assets), (5) how to maximise each appearance beyond the episode itself (social clips, show notes blog post, email mention). Include the 3 talking points I should anchor in every appearance regardless of the specific angle.
whatItIsFor: Plans a "media tour" of 8–12 podcast guest appearances in a 6-week window — the format that generates the fastest credibility and audience growth without paid advertising.
howToUseIt: A media tour works because the cumulative effect of appearing on multiple shows in a short period creates the impression of ubiquity. When someone hears you on 3 different podcasts in 6 weeks, they assume you are the authority in your field.

title: Case study story writer
body: Write a case study for my [BUSINESS TYPE] about a client situation with the following details: Client: [CLIENT TYPE AND SIZE]. Problem: [SPECIFIC PROBLEM THEY CAME WITH]. What I did: [YOUR APPROACH IN 2–3 STEPS]. Result: [OUTCOME WITH SPECIFIC NUMBERS]. Timeframe: [HOW LONG IT TOOK]. Format: a 400-word narrative story (not a bulleted case study) written in third person. Lead with the result. Include a direct quote placeholder I can fill in after client approval. End with a one-sentence "what this means for a similar business." Avoid all marketing language and adjectives.
whatItIsFor: Writes a client case study structured as a compelling story — the format that works in press pitches, award applications, website pages, and sales calls because it shows proof through narrative rather than assertion.
howToUseIt: Always get explicit written permission from the client before publishing. A case study with numbers and a real client name is 10x more persuasive than an anonymised version — ask for permission before anonymising by default.

title: Newsjacking opportunity identifier
body: Identify 5 recurring news events or seasonal triggers where a [BUSINESS TYPE] expert could pitch for media comment. For each: the recurring event or trigger (e.g. Autumn Budget, academic year start, National Living Wage increase), which publications are most likely to cover it, the expert angle a [BUSINESS TYPE] professional could offer, and the window for pitching (how many days before or after the event). Include a Google Alert search string I can set up to be notified when each trigger occurs. Rank the 5 opportunities by likelihood of coverage.
whatItIsFor: Identifies current news stories where a small business expert can add a relevant comment or angle — the technique used by PR professionals to get their clients quoted in the news without pitching a story of their own.
howToUseIt: Newsjacking works on a tight window — you must pitch within 24–48 hours of a news story breaking. Set up Google Alerts for your topic and have your 3 key messages ready to deploy at short notice.

title: PR measurement framework
body: Create a PR measurement framework for a [BUSINESS TYPE] running a [CAMPAIGN TYPE — e.g. product launch, expert positioning, award campaign] campaign over [TIMEFRAME]. Define: (1) the 4–5 metrics to track (coverage volume, referral traffic, brand search volume, enquiries attributed to PR, and social media follower growth), (2) how to set up tracking for each metric (Google Analytics UTM parameters, search console, enquiry source tagging), (3) what success looks like at 4 weeks, 8 weeks, and 12 weeks, (4) what a "below expectations" result should trigger (change tactic vs change story), and (5) the single most important metric for a service business doing PR for the first time.
whatItIsFor: Defines how to measure the impact of a PR campaign — without relying on AVE (advertising value equivalent), the metric that sounds impressive but tells you nothing useful about whether the coverage is generating leads.
howToUseIt: Set up the tracking before the campaign launches. Coverage that cannot be traced to a business outcome is a vanity exercise. Track referral traffic, lead enquiries, and brand search volume — not clip counts.

title: Local press campaign brief
body: Create a local press campaign brief for a [BUSINESS TYPE] based in [LOCATION] seeking to increase local brand authority. The brief should include: (1) the 3 best local story angles for this business (with a different hook for the regional paper vs the local business magazine vs radio), (2) the top 5 local media outlets to target (types, not specific names — your local equivalents), (3) a local data point or statistic I could generate myself to anchor the story (how to collect it simply from my own client base), (4) the local community angle that makes this story specifically about [LOCATION] rather than anywhere in the UK, (5) a 6-month local PR calendar with 1 pitch per month. Write the pitch angle for month 1.
whatItIsFor: Plans a local press coverage campaign for a small business — the format with the highest success rate for local service businesses because regional journalists have genuine news holes to fill and respond well to local stories.
howToUseIt: Local press is the most underutilised PR channel for small businesses. A coverage mention in the local business press generates more qualified local leads than a national mention that no one in your area reads.

title: Journalist relationship building plan
body: Create a 12-month journalist relationship building plan for a [BUSINESS TYPE] targeting [NUMBER] journalist contacts at [PUBLICATION TYPES]. The plan should include: (1) how to identify and follow the right journalists (platforms, beats, signals), (2) the 3 low-effort ways to get on a journalist's radar before pitching (without being sycophantic or promotional), (3) a quarterly engagement cadence (what to do in months 1–3 / 4–6 / 7–9 / 10–12), (4) how to be useful to a journalist without pitching (data, expert quotes, introduction to a case study), (5) what to never do when building a journalist relationship. Include a concrete first-week action plan.
whatItIsFor: Maps a plan for building genuine relationships with 5–10 journalists over 12 months — so pitches go to known contacts who trust your expertise rather than cold emails that arrive with 300 others.
howToUseIt: PR is a relationship business. A journalist who has heard from you with useful, accurate information twice before a pitch will open your third email. A journalist who hears from you for the first time is sceptical by professional habit.

title: PR budget allocation guide
body: Create a PR budget allocation guide for a [BUSINESS TYPE] with a monthly PR budget of [BUDGET — e.g. £100/month, £300/month, or £0]. For each budget level: what to spend it on, what tools are worth paying for vs what has a free alternative, and what the budget unlocks in terms of PR activity and reach. Include: the free PR tools every small business should be using regardless of budget, the one paid tool most worth investing in first, and how to measure whether the PR spend is generating a return on investment.
whatItIsFor: Defines how to allocate a small PR budget across tools, monitoring, and amplification — so the money spent on PR actually extends reach rather than going to expensive PR software that a small business doesn't need.
