howToUseIt: Most small businesses can run an effective PR campaign for £0–£200/month. The expensive PR tools (Cision, Meltwater) are for large agencies — a Google Alert, a LinkedIn Premium account, and one press release distribution service replaces 90% of their functionality.

title: PR content calendar integration
body: Create a quarterly PR and content integration calendar for a [BUSINESS TYPE]. The calendar should show for each week: (1) the PR action (pitch, follow-up, byline submission, award deadline, or media monitoring), (2) the corresponding social media content that supports the same theme, (3) the email newsletter hook that ties in, (4) the amplification plan for when coverage drops (what to post, in what order, on which channels). Include the "coverage drop protocol" — the exact sequence of posts and emails to send on the day a press mention goes live.
whatItIsFor: Integrates PR activity into a quarterly content calendar — so press pitches, bylined articles, award deadlines, and media tour appearances align with social media content and email campaigns rather than running as a separate disconnected track.
howToUseIt: PR amplification requires coordinated social media and email activity on the day coverage drops. If the press mention goes live and no one knows to share it, half the potential reach is wasted.

title: Influencer partnership brief
body: Create an influencer partnership brief for a [BUSINESS TYPE] seeking to work with a [CREATOR TYPE — e.g. lifestyle micro-influencer, niche business creator] with [FOLLOWER COUNT RANGE]. The brief should define: (1) what you're asking them to create (format, platform, volume, timeline), (2) the key messages to include (and the messages not to include), (3) what they receive (free product, flat fee, commission, or combination), (4) content ownership and usage rights (can you repost, use in ads, or include in your website?), (5) approval process (do you see the content before it goes live?), and (6) the one metric you'll use to evaluate whether the partnership was worth repeating. Write the outreach message to send once the brief is ready.
whatItIsFor: Defines the terms of an influencer partnership — what you're asking the creator to do, what they receive, and what content you own — before starting the conversation rather than after it gets complicated.
howToUseIt: Influencer partnerships without a brief produce off-brand content that you can't use. Write the brief before the outreach — the creator should know what's expected before they say yes, not after.

title: Micro-influencer outreach email
body: Write a DM or email outreach to invite a [CREATOR TYPE] to collaborate with my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The message must: open with a specific reference to their content (provide me with a content detail or I'll use a placeholder), explain what the collaboration involves in 2–3 sentences, state what they receive upfront (no vague "exciting opportunity"), ask a low-pressure question that makes it easy to say yes without committing. Maximum 120 words. Write a DM version (under 80 words) and an email version (under 150 words with a clear subject line).
whatItIsFor: Writes the outreach message to approach a micro-influencer for a partnership — personal enough to show you've done research, professional enough to feel like a real business opportunity rather than a begging request.
howToUseIt: Personalise the first 2 sentences specifically to the creator — mention a specific piece of their content, not just a generic "love your posts". Creators receive hundreds of generic pitches; a specific reference gets opened.

title: UGC campaign brief writer
body: Create a UGC campaign brief for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The campaign should invite existing customers to share [TYPE OF CONTENT — e.g. how they use the product, their results, their before/after]. Define: (1) the campaign mechanic (hashtag, tag us, submit via form), (2) what participants receive (incentive, recognition, or entry into a prize), (3) the content brief for participants (what to film or photograph, what to say, what format), (4) how to announce the campaign (email, social, packaging insert), (5) how you'll use the content (repost rights, ad rights, testimonial), (6) the campaign duration. Write the campaign announcement post and the email to existing customers.
whatItIsFor: Creates a brief for a user-generated content campaign — asking existing customers to create and share content about your product in exchange for a small incentive or recognition.
howToUseIt: UGC campaigns work best when the barrier is low (one photo, not a professional video) and the incentive is genuine (a discount, not just "be featured on our page"). The content has to be worth creating even if they don't win.

title: Creator content brief
body: Write a creator content brief for a [CREATOR TYPE] producing [CONTENT FORMAT — e.g. a 30-second Reel, a 3-photo carousel, a testimonial video] for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The brief must cover: campaign goal (what this content should achieve), audience (who will see it and what they care about), mandatory content requirements (must-say, must-show), creative freedom (what the creator can decide), visual references (describe the style — not just "authentic"), prohibited content (what not to include), deliverable specifications (platform, aspect ratio, length, file format), timeline, and revision policy. Include the feedback process — how to request changes without demoralising the creator.
whatItIsFor: Writes a detailed creative brief for a paid creator or UGC producer — specifying the format, messaging, visual references, and approval process so the delivered content is on-brand and usable without 3 rounds of revision.
howToUseIt: A good creator brief is 1 page maximum. If it takes 3 pages to brief the content, the concept is too complicated. Simplify first, then brief.

title: Influencer contract key clauses
body: Create a key clauses brief for an influencer partnership agreement between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and a [CREATOR TYPE]. Cover: (1) deliverables (what, when, how many), (2) exclusivity (can the creator work with competitors during this period?), (3) usage rights (can you use the content in ads? For how long?), (4) FTC/ASA disclosure (how must they label the post as sponsored?), (5) kill clause (what happens if you or the creator wants to cancel before delivery), (6) revision and approval rights (how many rounds, what you can control), (7) content removal (can you ask them to remove a post, and in what circumstances?). Flag the 2 clauses small businesses most commonly skip and why they get burned.
whatItIsFor: Identifies the key clauses every influencer agreement should contain — so you're protected if a creator posts content you haven't approved, makes a claim you can't support, or disappears after receiving your product.
howToUseIt: For paid partnerships over £500, use a signed agreement. For gifting under £200, a clear DM trail confirming deliverables and usage rights is usually sufficient. Don't skip the usage rights clause regardless of partnership size.

title: Influencer performance tracker
body: Create an influencer performance evaluation framework for a [BUSINESS TYPE] that has run [NUMBER] creator partnerships in the past quarter. Define the 5 metrics to evaluate for each partnership (beyond reach and likes), what "good" looks like for each metric at this business stage, how to calculate cost per acquisition from a creator campaign, the decision criteria for which creators to rebook vs not, and how to use the performance data to brief the next round of creators differently. Build a simple scoring table I can complete within 30 minutes per creator.
whatItIsFor: Creates a framework for evaluating whether an influencer partnership delivered a return — beyond vanity metrics like reach and likes, to the metrics that actually tell you if it moved the business.
howToUseIt: Evaluate every partnership within 30 days of the content going live. Creators who delivered sales at a reasonable cost per acquisition get repeat partnerships. Creators who delivered reach but no action get one campaign only.

title: Gifting programme designer
body: Design a gifting programme for my [BUSINESS TYPE] with a product value of [£ AMOUNT]. The programme should define: (1) who qualifies for gifting (follower count, engagement rate, niche alignment — be specific), (2) how many gifting packages to send per month at my current budget, (3) what to include in the gifting package beyond the product (personalised note, usage guide, discount code for their followers), (4) how to follow up without being pushy (sequence if they don't post), (5) how to track posts and calculate the true cost of the programme. Include the DM request to send after someone posts about the product organically (converting an organic mention into an ongoing relationship).
whatItIsFor: Designs a structured gifting programme — sending product to creators without a paid fee in exchange for organic, honest reviews — for a small business that can't afford paid influencer campaigns yet.
howToUseIt: Gifting is not free marketing — factor in product cost, shipping, and time to manage it. A gifting programme that generates no posts is a donation programme. Track post rate before scaling.

title: Affiliate creator programme designer
body: Design a creator affiliate programme for my [BUSINESS TYPE] offering [PRODUCT/SERVICE] at [PRICE]. Define: (1) commission rate and structure (flat per sale vs percentage, with reasoning), (2) cookie duration (how long after a click does the creator get credit for a sale), (3) minimum payout threshold and payment schedule, (4) what promotional materials to provide (links, banners, discount codes), (5) which platform to use to manage tracking (Rewardful, ShareASale, Gumroad affiliate — free and paid options), (6) how to recruit the first 10 affiliates and what to say in the invite. Include the welcome message to send to a new affiliate and the #1 reason affiliate programmes fail for small businesses.
whatItIsFor: Designs a creator affiliate programme — giving creators a commission on sales they generate, which aligns their incentive with yours and scales without upfront cost per creator.
howToUseIt: Affiliate programmes work best for digital products and physical goods with a margin above 40%. Service businesses are harder to affiliate because the "conversion" is a booked call, not a purchase — commission structures need careful design.

title: Influencer vetting checklist
body: Create an influencer vetting checklist for a [BUSINESS TYPE] evaluating [CREATOR TYPE]. The checklist should cover: follower count vs engagement rate (what's healthy for each tier), audience quality signals (do comments look genuine?), content quality and consistency (posting frequency, content type, production level), brand alignment (does their aesthetic and audience match ours?), previous partnership disclosures (do they label ads correctly?), audience geography (are their followers in the right country?), and red flag signals (bought followers, pod engagement, sudden follower spikes). Include a simple 1–10 scoring system with a minimum score to proceed with outreach.
whatItIsFor: Creates a quick vetting checklist to evaluate whether a creator is a genuine fit before spending money on a partnership — catching inflated follower counts, low-quality audiences, and brand misalignment before the brief is sent.
howToUseIt: Run every potential creator through this checklist before making contact. A creator with 50,000 followers and a 0.3% engagement rate has a worse audience than a creator with 5,000 followers and 6% engagement.

title: User testimonial collection system
body: Design a testimonial collection system for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The system should cover: (1) when to ask (the exact trigger moments in the client journey), (2) how to ask (email, DM, in-person — with the exact wording), (3) the 3 questions to prompt a specific testimonial (not just "what did you think?"), (4) how to collect video testimonials from clients who aren't tech-savvy, (5) how to store, organise, and use testimonials across website, social, and sales conversations, (6) how to get permission to use a testimonial publicly. Write the email to send to a happy client asking for a testimonial.
whatItIsFor: Creates a systematic process for collecting video and written testimonials from happy customers — so you always have fresh, specific social proof rather than relying on 3 testimonials from 2 years ago.
howToUseIt: Ask for testimonials at the moment of peak satisfaction — not after the emotion has faded. The best time to ask a client for a testimonial is the same day they tell you it worked.

title: Brand ambassador programme brief
body: Design a brand ambassador programme for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Define: who qualifies to become an ambassador (minimum engagement criteria, proof of genuine product use, content quality standard), what ambassadors receive (monthly product, commission, exclusive access, co-creation opportunities), what they commit to (monthly post volume, content type, exclusivity if any), how to onboard a new ambassador (30-day welcome sequence), how to manage a community of ambassadors (communication channel, monthly briefing, feedback loop), and the exit criteria (what behaviour removes someone from the programme). Write the ambassador welcome email and the recruitment post for Instagram.
whatItIsFor: Designs a brand ambassador programme for loyal customers or industry peers — a long-term creator partnership model that generates consistent content and advocacy without the inconsistency of one-off influencer campaigns.
howToUseIt: Ambassadors are not influencers — they are your genuine fans who also create content. The difference is motivation: an influencer creates for the fee, an ambassador creates because they actually love the product. Build this programme from customers who have already posted about you organically.

title: UGC ad creative brief
body: Write a UGC ad creative brief for a creator producing a [FORMAT — 30-second Reel / 60-second video / photo set] to be run as a paid Meta ad for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The brief must specify: the hook (exact opening line or visual that will appear in the first 2 seconds), the problem to reference (what the viewer is experiencing that this product solves), the product demonstration (what to show and how), the social proof element (a specific result or statistic to include), the call to action (exact CTA to use verbally and/or in on-screen text), and what NOT to do (the 3 things that make a UGC ad feel like an ad). Include the technical specs for Meta Reels ads.
whatItIsFor: Writes a brief for UGC content specifically designed to run as a paid ad — the format that consistently outperforms polished studio ads because it looks native to social media feeds rather than like an advertisement.
howToUseIt: UGC ads work because they get past the viewer's "this is an ad" filter. Brief the creator to produce content that would look identical to an organic post — no logo bugs, no corporate overlays, no music that screams ad.

title: Influencer campaign debrief template
body: Create an influencer campaign debrief template for a [BUSINESS TYPE] that has completed a [CAMPAIGN TYPE — gifting / paid partnership / UGC] campaign with [NUMBER] creators. The debrief should cover: campaign objective and whether it was met, performance summary (by creator and overall), what content performed best and why, the creators to rebook and the reasoning, the creators not to rebook and the specific reason, what to brief differently next time, budget analysis (cost per acquisition vs target), and 3 specific actions for the next campaign. Write the template with prompts so it can be completed in 30 minutes.
whatItIsFor: Creates a structured end-of-campaign debrief for an influencer programme — capturing what worked, what didn't, and the specific decisions to make differently next time.
howToUseIt: Run this debrief within 7 days of campaign close, before the learnings fade. A debrief document created within a week is 3x more accurate and actionable than one created retrospectively at the end of a quarter.

title: Influencer event collaboration plan
body: Plan an influencer event for my [BUSINESS TYPE] targeting [CREATOR TYPE]. The event format: [IN-PERSON / VIRTUAL / HYBRID]. Goal: generate [NUMBER] pieces of content across [PLATFORMS] and build relationships with [NUMBER] creators who will become long-term ambassadors. The plan should cover: event concept and theme, number of creators to invite (and how to select them), the event run-of-show with content moments built in, what to prepare for creators to post from the event, the follow-up sequence after the event (when to reach out, what to offer next), and how to measure whether the event achieved its goal. Write the event invitation to send to creators.
whatItIsFor: Plans an influencer event — bringing creators to an in-person or virtual brand experience — producing content in a controlled environment and building genuine relationships that sustain long-term advocacy.
howToUseIt: Event-based influencer campaigns produce higher-quality content than product-only gifting because creators spend 3+ hours with the brand rather than receiving a package in the post. The content is more specific, more enthusiastic, and more trustworthy.

title: UGC rights management brief
body: Create a UGC rights management system for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The system should cover: (1) how to monitor mentions and UGC across [PLATFORMS], (2) the exact DM request to send when you want to use someone's content (getting permission in writing), (3) a simple tagging system for storing approved UGC (organised by platform, content type, and usage right granted), (4) the distinctions between "can repost on social", "can use in paid ads", and "can use on website/email" — and how to confirm which rights have been granted, (5) what to do if a creator retracts permission after you've used the content. Write the DM permission request script.
whatItIsFor: Defines how to manage usage rights for UGC content — from requesting permission to organising approved content for use in ads, emails, and website pages — so you don't use content without permission or miss repurposing opportunities.
howToUseIt: Every time a customer tags you or mentions your brand publicly, that's a potential ad creative. Without a clear rights management process, most of it is unused or misused. Set up the process before you need it, not when a lawyer's letter arrives.

title: Niche creator discovery system
body: Create a niche creator discovery system for a [BUSINESS TYPE] looking for [CREATOR TYPE] with [FOLLOWER RANGE]. The system should include: (1) the 5 most effective search methods for finding niche creators without paying for a platform (hashtag research, competitor tagging analysis, comment section discovery, TikTok search, Instagram Reels browse), (2) the specific search terms and hashtags to use for [NICHE], (3) how to qualify creators quickly (the 60-second assessment), (4) a tracking spreadsheet structure for building a prospect list, (5) how to organise outreach in batches (how many per week, in what order). Write the 5 hashtags most likely to surface relevant creators for [NICHE].
whatItIsFor: Creates a systematic method for finding niche creators who are a genuine audience fit — without paying for expensive influencer platforms or relying on random DMs.
howToUseIt: The best creators for a small business are often people with 2,000–15,000 highly engaged followers in a very specific niche. They're harder to find than celebrities but easier to work with, more affordable, and more effective for niche products.

title: Creator collaboration content calendar
body: Create a 3-month influencer and brand content calendar for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. I have [NUMBER] creator partnerships live per month and post [FREQUENCY] times per week on my own account. The calendar should: align creator content drops with brand content on the same theme, plan brand content that amplifies creator posts (e.g. repost story, complementary Reel), avoid scheduling gaps where creator content lands without brand support, and flag the 3 weeks where creator content plus brand content creates the strongest combined impact. Include the week-by-week schedule for month 1 in detail.
whatItIsFor: Plans a 3-month content calendar coordinating creator content with your own posts — so influencer drops land alongside organic content that amplifies them rather than sitting alone in a gap with no supporting context.
howToUseIt: Influencer content landing the same week as your own organic social content on the same theme creates a compounding effect. A creator's post plus your own brand post plus a story repost is 3x more impactful than the creator's post alone.

title: Influencer outreach tracking system
body: Design a creator outreach tracking system for a [BUSINESS TYPE] managing [NUMBER] outreach contacts per month. The system should include: (1) the spreadsheet columns to track (creator handle, platform, follower count, engagement rate, pitch date, pitch status, response, partnership status, content live date, performance metrics), (2) the pipeline stages from "identified" to "active partner" to "past partner", (3) how to set reminders for follow-ups without calendar overload, (4) what to record after a partnership ends (for future reference), (5) how to use the tracking data to improve the next month's outreach (what patterns to look for). Write the column headers and descriptions for the tracking sheet.
whatItIsFor: Creates a simple tracking system for managing influencer outreach — so pitches don't fall through the gaps, follow-ups happen on time, and partnership history is recorded for future campaigns.
howToUseIt: Track in a Google Sheet, not memory. A creator you approached 6 months ago and never followed up with is a missed relationship. A creator who said "not now" is a future opportunity if you note the date and reason.

title: Influencer budget planner
body: Design an influencer budget plan for a [BUSINESS TYPE] with [MONTHLY BUDGET — e.g. £200, £500, or £1,000]. Allocate the budget across: gifting (product cost), paid partnerships, and commission programme management. For each allocation: how many creators it covers, what to expect in return (volume and type of content), realistic performance benchmarks (reach, clicks, sales), and the priority if budget must be cut. Include the best channel split for this budget size and the one thing most small businesses overspend on at each budget level.
whatItIsFor: Allocates a small influencer marketing budget across gifting, paid partnerships, and commission to maximise coverage for the spend — rather than putting all the budget into one large creator who delivers one post and disappears.
howToUseIt: A £500/month budget spread across 5 micro-influencers produces more diverse content and coverage than one £500 macro-influencer post. Test before committing — allocate 30% to testing new creators and 70% to proven partners.

title: Creator welcome pack writer
body: Write a creator welcome pack for creators partnering with my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The pack (1–2 pages, PDF format) should include: a brief brand story (2–3 sentences — who we are and why we exist), the product overview (what it does, who it's for, what makes it different), 3 content suggestions (specific — not "just be creative"), what to avoid (brand conflicts, claims we can't support, style not aligned with our aesthetic), how to tag us and which hashtags to use, discount code details if applicable, and how to get in touch with questions. Tone: warm, peer-to-peer — not corporate instructions. Write it as if speaking directly to a friend who is going to try the product.
whatItIsFor: Creates a professional welcome pack for new influencer partners — covering brand background, usage guidelines, content examples, and everything a creator needs to produce on-brand content without a 30-minute briefing call.
howToUseIt: A welcome pack sent with a gifting package raises the quality of the content produced. Creators who understand what you're about and why the product exists make better, more authentic content than creators who received a box with no context.

title: Community strategy brief
body: Design a community strategy for a [BUSINESS TYPE] targeting [AUDIENCE]. Define: (1) the community premise (what does a member get from belonging that they can't get elsewhere?), (2) the best platform for this audience (Facebook Group, Discord, Circle, email community, WhatsApp — with reasoning), (3) the engagement model (free vs paid, open vs moderated, weekly vs always-on), (4) the content calendar for the community (how often to post, what types of posts, who can post), (5) the first 30-day launch plan (how to go from 0 to first engaged members), (6) how the community generates revenue or leads for the business. Flag the #1 reason small business communities die within 3 months.
whatItIsFor: Defines the right community format, platform, and engagement model for a small business — before spending time building in the wrong place or trying to run a community that needs 10 hours per week when you have 2.
howToUseIt: Every community decision should flow from one question: "What problem does this community solve for the member — not for us?" A community that exists to benefit the brand is not a community; it's a marketing channel wearing a name badge.

title: Community welcome sequence writer
body: Write a community welcome sequence for new members of a [COMMUNITY TYPE] built around [TOPIC]. The sequence should include: (1) an automated welcome message sent immediately when they join (under 100 words, sets the tone, tells them what to do first), (2) a welcome post prompt (the one specific question to ask that gets the first contribution), (3) a day-3 personal DM from the community founder (if under 200 members), (4) the first 7 days of content the new member sees (week's worth of existing posts to make the community feel active), (5) the "start here" pinned post that orients a new member in under 3 minutes. Write the welcome message and the start here post.
whatItIsFor: Writes the welcome message, first-week content, and onboarding DM sequence for new community members — the critical first 7 days that determine whether a new member becomes an active contributor or a passive lurker.
howToUseIt: 80% of community members who lurk in the first 7 days without posting will never post. The welcome sequence is the activation mechanism. Make the first post required frictionless and specifically prompted.

title: Community engagement post templates
body: Write 20 community engagement post templates for a [COMMUNITY TYPE] about [TOPIC], covering 5 post types: (1) a question that generates opinions (4 posts), (2) a challenge or prompt that generates contributions (4 posts), (3) a "share your experience" post (4 posts), (4) a resource or tip post the founder shares (4 posts), (5) a community celebration or recognition post (4 posts). Each post: under 80 words, ends with a specific question or prompt. Write them so they work whether the community has 20 members or 2,000.
whatItIsFor: Creates a bank of engagement post templates for a community — the posts that generate responses, conversation, and a sense that the community is alive and worth being part of.
howToUseIt: Use these as weekly templates — rotating through types rather than posting the same question format repeatedly. A community that only asks "what's your win this week?" every Monday starts to feel like a homework assignment.

title: Paid community pricing and structure
body: Design a paid community pricing structure for a [COMMUNITY TYPE] about [TOPIC] targeting [AUDIENCE]. Define: (1) the value proposition in 2 sentences (what members get that they can't get for free), (2) 2–3 membership tiers with different price points and access levels, (3) the core content and features at each tier, (4) the pricing rationale (monthly vs annual, what discount for annual, and why), (5) the trial or guarantee structure (free trial, money-back, or first month at reduced cost), (6) the first 50-member pricing strategy (launch price vs standard price). Include the "no-brainer" reason to join at the entry tier.
whatItIsFor: Defines the pricing model, membership tiers, and value structure for a paid community — so members feel the fee is justified and the community generates predictable recurring revenue for the business.
howToUseIt: A paid community only works when the value is specific and demonstrable. "Access to a supportive community" is not a pricing justification. "Monthly Q&A with an expert, templates, and peer accountability" is.

title: Community moderation policy
body: Write a community moderation policy for a [COMMUNITY TYPE] about [TOPIC]. The policy should include: (1) community rules (5–7 clear rules, written in a warm but firm tone — not legalese), (2) what constitutes a violation at each severity level (warning, temporary suspension, permanent removal), (3) the moderation process (who moderates, how quickly, what the response is to each violation type), (4) how to handle conflict between members (the escalation steps), (5) the self-promotion policy (what is and isn't allowed — be specific), and (6) how members can report a concern. Write the rules as they would appear pinned in the community — member-facing, not internal policy language.
whatItIsFor: Creates clear community rules and a moderation policy — protecting the community culture from spam, promotion, and conflict without the founder having to intervene personally in every awkward moment.
howToUseIt: Post the rules on day 1 and enforce them consistently from day 1. A rule introduced in month 6 after the community has already accepted certain behaviours is much harder to enforce and creates resentment.

title: Community content calendar
body: Create a 4-week community content calendar for a [COMMUNITY TYPE] about [TOPIC]. I post [FREQUENCY — e.g. 5 days per week]. For each day: the post type (question / resource / challenge / recognition / discussion topic) and a specific post idea (not a placeholder — a real post I could publish). Include a recurring weekly structure (e.g. Monday: week starter question, Wednesday: resource, Friday: celebration/reflection). Flag the 2 days per week where high engagement posts should be scheduled (based on community behaviour for this audience type).
whatItIsFor: Plans a 4-week community content calendar — scheduling what the community manager posts each day so the community stays active without requiring constant improvisation.
howToUseIt: Batch-create community posts once a month. The posts you schedule are prompts, questions, and resources — not announcements. A calendar that is 80% questions and 20% resources works better than one that is 80% announcements.

title: Community launch plan
body: Create a community launch plan for [COMMUNITY NAME] — a [COMMUNITY TYPE] about [TOPIC] launching on [TARGET DATE]. The plan should cover: (1) pre-launch phase (4 weeks before) — building the waitlist and creating founding member energy, (2) soft launch (2 weeks before) — founding members only, seeding content, (3) public launch — announcement strategy across channels, (4) week 1 post-launch — maintaining momentum, (5) month 1 retention — the actions that keep founding members from going quiet. Write the waitlist landing page copy and the founding member DM invite.
whatItIsFor: Plans the launch of a new community — from the pre-launch waitlist through the founding member cohort to steady-state engagement — so the community feels active and valuable from day 1 rather than feeling like an empty room.
howToUseIt: Launch with at least 30 members already active, not 5. The "empty room problem" kills communities before they start. Use a waitlist, a founding member rate, and pre-seeded questions to simulate activity before the community officially opens.

title: Community newsletter writer
body: Write a weekly community newsletter template for [COMMUNITY NAME] — a [COMMUNITY TYPE] for [AUDIENCE]. The newsletter should include: (1) a personal note from the founder (2–3 sentences, specific to what happened in the community that week — not generic), (2) the 3 most valuable posts from the community this week (with a link to each), (3) the week's resource or tip, (4) this week's question or challenge to re-engage passive members, (5) an upcoming live event or feature announcement if applicable, and (6) a footer with community link. Maximum 400 words. Subject line options: 3 variants. Write the complete template with [FILL IN] markers.
whatItIsFor: Writes a weekly community newsletter — the email that keeps members who aren't logging in to the platform connected and reminded that the community exists and is worth returning to.
howToUseIt: Every community loses 40–60% of members to passive non-engagement within 90 days. The weekly email is the re-activation mechanism. Keep it short, personal, and link-heavy so clicking through to the community is one action away.

title: Community events planner
body: Plan a quarterly events programme for [COMMUNITY NAME] — a [COMMUNITY TYPE] about [TOPIC] with [MEMBER COUNT] members. Design: (1) 4–6 events over 13 weeks (types: live Q&A, workshop, challenge, member showcase, guest expert, AMA), (2) for each event: title, format, duration, the problem it addresses for members, how to promote it within the community, and what to do with the recording after, (3) the event promotion sequence (how many days in advance to announce, the reminder schedule), (4) how to measure whether an event worked (attendance rate, post-event engagement). Include the event announcement post for month 1's first event.
whatItIsFor: Plans a quarterly programme of community events — live sessions, workshops, and challenges — that increase active membership and give passive members a reason to re-engage.
howToUseIt: Events give passive members permission to return. A member who hasn't posted in 3 weeks will show up for a live Q&A. Design events that serve the lurker, not just the active contributor — the lurker is your biggest retention risk.

title: Community monetisation strategy
body: Design a monetisation strategy for [COMMUNITY NAME] — a [FREE / PAID] [COMMUNITY TYPE] about [TOPIC] with [CURRENT OR TARGET MEMBER COUNT]. Map 4 revenue routes: (1) membership fees (structure and pricing if not yet monetised, or how to grow ARPU if already paid), (2) product launches to the community (what products fit, how to offer them without it feeling like constant selling), (3) upsell to 1:1 or group programme (what the conversion path looks like from community member to higher-ticket client), (4) brand partnership or sponsored content (what sponsors would pay to reach this audience). For each route: estimated monthly revenue at current community size, what to build first, and the conversion rate benchmark to aim for.
whatItIsFor: Maps the revenue routes from a community — from membership fees to product launches, upsells, and affiliate partnerships — so the community generates a return that justifies the time investment.
howToUseIt: A community that generates no revenue is a hobby project. A community that generates revenue proportional to the time it takes to run is a business asset. Design the monetisation model before you build the community, not after you have 200 members and want to introduce fees for the first time.

title: Community health check framework
body: Create a monthly community health check framework for [COMMUNITY NAME] — a [COMMUNITY TYPE] about [TOPIC]. Define: the 5 metrics to review monthly (active member rate, engagement rate per post, new member vs churned member ratio, post diversity index, and satisfaction signals), what "healthy" looks like for each metric at [MEMBER COUNT], what a "declining" signal looks like for each, and the 3 actions to take when overall community health is flagged as declining. Include a simple scoring system I can complete in 20 minutes per month.
whatItIsFor: Creates a monthly framework for assessing community health — active member rate, engagement quality, churn, and satisfaction — so problems are caught in month 2, not month 8 when the community has quietly died.
howToUseIt: A community health check is not a post count. A community with 10 posts and 50 comments from 30 different members is healthier than a community with 50 posts from 3 members who are all the same person.

title: Community member spotlight series
body: Design a member spotlight programme for [COMMUNITY NAME] about [TOPIC]. Include: (1) the selection criteria (how to choose who to feature — not just the most active poster), (2) the 5 interview questions that produce compelling, specific answers, (3) the format (written Q&A / video / post / newsletter section), (4) how to use the spotlight content beyond the community itself (cross-posting, testimonials, case studies), (5) the outreach message to a member you want to feature, and (6) a 12-week spotlight schedule plan. Write the 5 interview questions and the DM to invite a member to participate.
whatItIsFor: Plans a recurring "member spotlight" series — featuring individual members' stories and wins — which builds loyalty, recognition, and social proof while generating content the featured member is likely to share externally.
howToUseIt: Member spotlights work as a retention tool (members who feel seen stay) and as an acquisition tool (spotlighted members share with their audience, bringing new members in). Run one per week in any active community.

title: Community conflict resolution protocol
body: Write a conflict resolution protocol for [COMMUNITY NAME] about [TOPIC]. The protocol should cover: (1) what counts as a conflict (vs a heated debate that doesn't require intervention), (2) the first-response script for a moderator witnessing a conflict in real time, (3) the private DM approach for both parties involved (separate conversations, same script), (4) the decision tree (what outcome is possible: resolution / cooling-off / removal), (5) how to communicate a resolution to the wider community without drawing more attention to the incident, (6) what to document for future reference. Write the moderator's opening message to each party in a conflict.
whatItIsFor: Creates a clear protocol for resolving conflict between community members — so disputes are handled consistently, fairly, and without the founder needing to adjudicate every disagreement personally.
howToUseIt: Handle all conflict in private first, public last. A conflict managed privately leaves both members in the community. A conflict escalated publicly almost always ends with one or both leaving and 10 others going quiet.

title: Community growth strategy
body: Create a 90-day growth strategy for [COMMUNITY NAME] about [TOPIC] currently stalled at [MEMBER COUNT] members. The strategy should identify: (1) why growth has stalled (the 3 most common causes for a community this size and type, and which likely applies here based on the context I provide), (2) the 3 acquisition channels most likely to work for this specific audience without paid ads, (3) a referral mechanism for existing members, (4) a content-led acquisition strategy (what to publish externally that attracts the right new members), (5) the retention improvement that unlocks growth (word-of-mouth only flows from happy existing members). Build a week-by-week plan for the first 4 weeks.
whatItIsFor: Creates a 90-day growth plan for a community that has stalled at a membership plateau — identifying the specific levers to pull to break through without paid advertising.
howToUseIt: Most communities plateau at 50–150 members because organic word-of-mouth from the founding cohort has exhausted and no new acquisition channel has been built. This prompt identifies what that channel should be.

title: Community exit survey
body: Create an exit survey for members leaving [COMMUNITY NAME] — a [PAID / FREE] [COMMUNITY TYPE] about [TOPIC]. The survey should include: (1) 6 questions maximum (what's the primary reason for leaving? was there a moment when you considered cancelling before now? what would have kept you? what was the most valuable part of the community? would you re-join if [X] changed? can we stay in touch?), (2) a follow-up sequence for different exit reasons (price vs value vs life change vs competitor), (3) the re-engagement offer to make at the point of exit, and (4) what to do with the aggregate data (how to review quarterly). Write the exit survey and the thank-you response email.
whatItIsFor: Creates an exit survey for members who cancel or leave a community — the data that tells you whether the community is losing members for fixable or unfixable reasons, and what to change before the next wave of churn.
howToUseIt: Send the exit survey within 24 hours of a cancellation, while the reason is still fresh. Members who churn due to "too busy" are often recoverable with a future re-engagement offer. Members who churn because the value wasn't clear have told you something structural that needs fixing.

title: Community partner programme
body: Design a community partner programme for [COMMUNITY NAME] — a [PAID / FREE] community about [TOPIC]. Define: who makes an ideal referral partner (what type of business or creator serves the same audience), what the partner receives (commission structure, co-marketing, exclusive access), what the referred member receives (discount or bonus), how to track referrals (link or code), the outreach approach for recruiting partners, and the partner welcome pack. Write the partner outreach message and the partner welcome email. Flag the 2 partner types most likely to generate the highest quality referrals for this community.
whatItIsFor: Designs a partner or affiliate programme for a community — so external businesses, creators, or educators promote the community to their audience in exchange for a commission or co-marketing benefit.
howToUseIt: A community partner programme turns your best relationships into a distribution channel. The partner recommends the community because they genuinely believe it helps their audience — not just because of the commission. Both conditions must be true for it to work.

title: Community survey and research tool
body: Write a quarterly member survey for [COMMUNITY NAME] about [TOPIC]. The survey should include: (1) NPS question (how likely are you to recommend this community to someone like you — 0–10 scale, with follow-up for score reasoning), (2) value assessment (which 3 elements of the community do you find most valuable — provide a ranked list), (3) content gap (what topic do you most want us to cover in the next 3 months?), (4) product interest (would you pay for X — specific product idea — if we built it?), (5) demographic snapshot (for audience insight). Maximum 8 questions. Under 5 minutes to complete. Include the survey invitation post and the results-sharing post (showing members what you learned and what you're changing).
whatItIsFor: Creates a quarterly member survey — gathering feedback, identifying what members value most, and surfacing what they'd pay for next — turning community engagement into product and content intelligence.
howToUseIt: A community is the highest-quality market research resource a small business has. Members who spend money and time with you will tell you exactly what they want next — if you ask the right questions in a format they'll complete.

title: Community leaderboard and gamification brief
body: Design a community recognition and gamification system for [COMMUNITY NAME] about [TOPIC] with [MEMBER COUNT] members. The system should: (1) recognise the right behaviours (quality contributions, helping others, consistent engagement — not just post volume), (2) be manageable by a solo community manager (not require a tech platform or 10 hours per week), (3) include 3–4 recognition tiers with different rewards, (4) explain how members progress between tiers, (5) describe how to announce and celebrate recognition in a way that feels genuine rather than manufactured. Write the community post announcing the recognition programme.
whatItIsFor: Designs a simple gamification system for a community — recognising contribution without making the community feel like a points accumulation game that rewards activity over quality.
howToUseIt: Gamification works when the reward signals genuine contribution (quality answers, helping members) not just volume (number of posts). A community where quantity is rewarded ends up full of low-value posts from members chasing points.

title: Community transition plan (free to paid)
body: Write a plan for converting [COMMUNITY NAME] from a free community to a paid model at [PRICE POINT]. The plan should cover: (1) the announcement timing and channel (how many weeks before, where to announce), (2) the grandfathering policy for existing free members (what deal do they get and for how long), (3) the announcement post (the exact message to existing members — transparent, not apologetic), (4) the objection responses for the most common pushbacks ("I thought this was free", "I can't afford it", "it's not worth it"), (5) realistic expectations for churn (what % of free members will not convert), and (6) the 30-day post-launch retention plan to keep those who do convert. Write the announcement post.
whatItIsFor: Plans the process of converting a free community to a paid model — handling the announcement, the grandfathering of loyal members, the objections, and the churn — without destroying the culture that was built during the free phase.
howToUseIt: Give free members at least 30 days' notice and a genuine reason to convert. The reason cannot be "we need the revenue" — the reason must be "paid membership means we can [SPECIFIC IMPROVEMENT] that free membership couldn't support".

title: Community cross-sell and upsell system
body: Design a cross-sell and upsell system for [COMMUNITY NAME] about [TOPIC] that sells [LIST OF PRODUCTS/SERVICES AT DIFFERENT PRICE POINTS]. The system should: (1) map which member questions or situations should trigger a product recommendation (and what to recommend in each case), (2) define the 3 places in the community where product recommendations are appropriate (vs where they'd feel pushy), (3) write the script for a natural product mention in a reply to a member question, (4) design a monthly "members-only offer" or early access event, (5) set a rule for how often to promote (maximum frequency — what's too much). Write the member question → product recommendation flow for your top 3 products.
whatItIsFor: Designs a non-pushy cross-sell and upsell system within a community — turning member conversations into natural product recommendations that feel helpful rather than salesy.
howToUseIt: The best community upsell happens when a member asks for something that a paid product already answers. Build the bridge between the question and the solution rather than broadcasting offers into the feed.

title: Event Concept & Format Planner
body: I run [BUSINESS TYPE] and want to host an event to [GOAL: generate leads / launch a product / build community / educate customers]. My target audience is [AUDIENCE DESCRIPTION]. My budget is approximately [£AMOUNT] and I prefer [online / in-person / hybrid]. Recommend the best event format, ideal duration, optimal timing, and one angle that would make it stand out from generic industry events.
whatItIsFor: Choosing the right event type for your goal — webinar, workshop, roundtable, or in-person.
howToUseIt: Fill in your goal and audience before running.

title: Event Landing Page Copy
body: Write a landing page for my event: [EVENT TITLE], happening on [DATE] at [TIME]. The event is for [TARGET AUDIENCE] and will teach them [MAIN OUTCOME]. Include: a headline, 3-sentence description, 4 bullet-point benefits, speaker bio section (placeholder), FAQ section with 3 Qs, and a CTA button label. Keep it under 350 words total. No hype — concrete and outcome-led.
whatItIsFor: Writing a sign-up page that converts browsers into registered attendees.
howToUseIt: Include your event title, date, and the core promise.

title: Email Invitation Sequence
body: Write a 3-email invitation sequence for [EVENT NAME] on [DATE]. My list is made up of [AUDIENCE TYPE] who typically care about [PAIN POINT]. Email 1 (14 days out): announce and create curiosity. Email 2 (7 days out): handle the "is this for me?" objection. Email 3 (1 day out): urgency + what they'll miss. Each email under 150 words. Include subject line for each.
whatItIsFor: A 3-email sequence to drive sign-ups from your existing list.
howToUseIt: Run 2 weeks before the event; adjust send dates in the output.

title: Social Promotion Copy Pack
body: Create a 5-post social media promotion plan for [EVENT NAME] happening in [X] days. Target platform: [INSTAGRAM / LINKEDIN / FACEBOOK]. Each post should use a different angle: (1) pain-point hook, (2) what attendees will walk away with, (3) speaker/host credibility, (4) social proof or behind-the-scenes, (5) final urgency. Include post copy (under 100 words each) and a CTA for each. No generic "join us" language.
whatItIsFor: Creating a week's worth of social posts to drive event registrations.
howToUseIt: Runs best 7–14 days before your event date.

title: Webinar Script Writer
body: Write a 60-minute webinar script for [TOPIC]. My audience is [AUDIENCE]. The 3 main teaching points are: (1) [POINT 1], (2) [POINT 2], (3) [POINT 3]. End with a pitch for [PRODUCT/SERVICE] priced at [£PRICE]. Structure: welcome + credibility (5 min) → context-setting (5 min) → teaching block 1 (12 min) → teaching block 2 (12 min) → teaching block 3 (12 min) → pitch (10 min) → Q&A (4 min). Write full narration for each block, not bullet points.
whatItIsFor: Creating a structured 45–60 minute webinar script with natural transitions.
howToUseIt: Fill in your topic and the 3 core teaching points before running.

title: Q&A Preparation Guide
body: I'm hosting an event on [TOPIC] for [AUDIENCE TYPE]. Generate the 10 most likely questions this audience will ask — including the 2 or 3 most sceptical or challenging ones. For each question, write a 2–3 sentence answer that is direct and credible, not defensive. Flag which 3 questions I should prepare the most for.
whatItIsFor: Anticipating and preparing strong answers to the hardest questions your audience will ask.
howToUseIt: Run before any live event, webinar, or panel appearance.

title: Attendee Welcome & Pre-Event Email
body: Write a post-registration welcome email for [EVENT NAME] on [DATE] at [TIME]. Include: confirmation of what they registered for, what to do before the event (one prep task), a teaser of what they'll learn, technical instructions (link, what to have ready), and a "can't make it live?" option. Keep it warm but efficient — under 200 words. Subject line included.
whatItIsFor: The confirmation email that reduces no-shows and builds anticipation.
howToUseIt: Send immediately on registration and again 1 hour before the event.

title: Live Event Engagement Plan
body: Design an engagement plan for a [LENGTH]-minute live [WEBINAR / WORKSHOP / ROUNDTABLE] on [TOPIC] for [AUDIENCE]. Include: 4 interaction moments (polls, questions, tasks), how to handle the chat without losing your place, what to do if no one responds to a question, and how to transition from teaching content into the pitch or CTA without it feeling like a gear-shift. Write this as a host's cheat sheet.
whatItIsFor: Keeping virtual attendees engaged throughout a live session.
howToUseIt: Plan this before your event and brief any co-host or moderator.

title: Post-Event Follow-Up Sequence
body: Write a 3-email post-event follow-up sequence for people who attended [EVENT NAME]. They heard a pitch for [PRODUCT] at £[PRICE]. Email 1 (same day): replay + key takeaways + offer. Email 2 (day 2): handle the top objection [OBJECTION]. Email 3 (day 3): final close with urgency. Each email under 150 words. Include subject line. No pressure tactics — just clear, useful, and direct.
whatItIsFor: Converting attendees into customers in the 72 hours after your event.
howToUseIt: Set up as an automated sequence triggered by event attendance.

title: No-Show Re-Engagement Email
body: Write an email to send to people who registered for [EVENT NAME] but didn't attend. Acknowledge they missed it without making them feel guilty. Offer the replay (if available). Give them one standalone insight from the event so they get immediate value. Include a CTA to [PRODUCT / OFFER]. Keep it under 120 words. Subject line included.
whatItIsFor: Reconnecting with people who registered but didn't attend — they're warm leads.
howToUseIt: Send within 24 hours of the event ending.

title: In-Person Event Run Sheet
body: Create a run sheet for a [LENGTH]-hour in-person [WORKSHOP / NETWORKING EVENT / MASTERCLASS] on [TOPIC] for up to [NUMBER] people at [VENUE TYPE]. Include: arrival/setup time, opening, all content or networking segments with durations, breaks, close, and post-event networking window. Add 3 logistics notes (room setup, equipment, catering) and 2 contingency notes for common things that go wrong. Format as a timed table.
whatItIsFor: A timed logistics plan for running an in-person workshop or networking event smoothly.
howToUseIt: Adapt the venue, duration, and segments to your event before finalising.

title: Speaker & Panellist Briefing Document
body: Write a speaker briefing document for [SPEAKER NAME / ROLE] who is presenting at [EVENT NAME] on [DATE]. Include: event overview and audience description, their allocated slot (time and duration), technical setup requirements, what to prepare (slide format, file type, deadline), what not to cover (to avoid overlap), 3 things the audience specifically cares about, and logistics (arrival time, parking, contact on the day). Keep professional and concise.
whatItIsFor: Giving guest speakers everything they need to deliver a polished session.
howToUseIt: Send 10–14 days before the event; include your own customisations.

title: Event Sponsorship Pitch
body: Write a sponsorship pitch for [EVENT NAME] on [DATE], expected attendance [NUMBER], audience profile: [AUDIENCE DESCRIPTION]. The sponsorship package I'm offering is [PACKAGE DETAILS: e.g. logo on materials, speaking slot, table at event, social mentions]. Investment: [£AMOUNT]. Write a 200-word pitch email and a one-paragraph summary of why this audience is valuable to the sponsor. Target sponsor type: [BUSINESS TYPE].
whatItIsFor: Approaching local or industry businesses to sponsor your event in exchange for visibility.
howToUseIt: Customise the audience data and benefits for each sponsor prospect.

title: Event Feedback Survey
body: Write a post-event feedback survey for [EVENT NAME]. Include: 1 rating question (overall experience, 1–10), 3 specific questions about content quality, delivery, and usefulness, 1 open question about what to improve, 1 question that captures a testimonial, and 1 question about future event interest. Keep the whole survey completable in under 3 minutes. Write the intro message too.
whatItIsFor: Collecting structured feedback to improve future events and surface testimonials.
howToUseIt: Send within 2 hours of the event ending while the experience is fresh.

title: Replay & Recording Sales Page
body: Write a short sales page for the recording of [EVENT NAME]. The recording is [LENGTH] and covers [KEY TOPICS]. Price: [£PRICE]. Target buyer: someone who missed the live event or wants to rewatch. Include: headline, 3-sentence description, 4 bullet-point topics covered, 1 testimonial placeholder, CTA button text, and a "what you get" section. Under 250 words total.
whatItIsFor: Selling on-demand access to a past event recording.
howToUseIt: Use within 48 hours of an event to capitalise on fresh interest.

title: Recurring Event Series Planner
body: I hosted a successful [EVENT TYPE] on [TOPIC] for [AUDIENCE]. I want to turn it into a recurring series. Help me: (1) name the series, (2) define a consistent format and cadence (monthly/quarterly/seasonal), (3) map out 6 episode/session topics that build on each other, (4) describe how to grow attendance from one session to the next, and (5) identify one monetisation option beyond ticket sales.
whatItIsFor: Turning a one-off event into a repeatable series with a growing audience.
howToUseIt: Run after a successful first event to plan the next 3–6 sessions.

title: Event Collaboration Pitch
body: Write a collaboration pitch to [BUSINESS NAME / TYPE] proposing a joint event. My business: [MY BUSINESS TYPE], audience: [MY AUDIENCE]. Their business: [THEIR BUSINESS TYPE], audience: [THEIR AUDIENCE]. Proposed event: [EVENT IDEA]. Explain the shared audience overlap, what each party contributes, how costs and promotion are split, and what both sides gain. Under 200 words. Email format.
whatItIsFor: Co-hosting an event with a complementary business to double your reach.
howToUseIt: Fill in both businesses before pitching; lead with the audience benefit.

title: Virtual Summit Planning Brief
body: Help me plan a virtual summit on [TOPIC] for [TARGET AUDIENCE]. I want [NUMBER] speakers over [NUMBER] days. Outline: (1) summit name and tagline, (2) speaker slot structure (how long, format), (3) lead capture strategy, (4) monetisation model (free access + paid all-access), (5) tech stack recommendation (3 tools max), and (6) a 6-week build timeline. My audience size is currently [NUMBER] email subscribers.
whatItIsFor: Planning a multi-speaker online summit to rapidly grow your email list.
howToUseIt: Use this as a project brief before you start approaching speakers or building the event page.

title: Event Upsell & Offer Design
body: I'm hosting an event on [TOPIC] for [AUDIENCE]. At the end I want to pitch [PRODUCT / SERVICE] at [£PRICE]. Help me: (1) design the pitch moment (how to transition into it naturally), (2) write the 90-second verbal pitch, (3) create a "fast-action" incentive for people who sign up before leaving, and (4) set up a simple order mechanism that works in a live event context (QR code, link, etc.). No pushy tactics — the offer should feel like the obvious next step.
whatItIsFor: Designing the product offer you make at or after an event to maximise revenue per attendee.
howToUseIt: Define your audience's next logical step before designing the offer.

title: Event ROI Calculator Prompt
body: Help me calculate the ROI of an event I just ran. Inputs: registration cost or ticket income [£AMOUNT], costs (venue, tech, promotion, my time at [£/hr] × [hours]) [£AMOUNT], number of attendees [NUMBER], number who purchased after [NUMBER], product price [£PRICE]. Calculate: total revenue, total cost, net profit, cost per attendee, revenue per attendee, and conversion rate. Then give me 3 specific changes to improve ROI at my next event based on these numbers.
whatItIsFor: Evaluating whether an event was worth the time and money — and what to change next time.
howToUseIt: Run this after the event closes and you have all the numbers.

title: Referral Programme Design
body: I run [BUSINESS TYPE] and want to launch a referral programme. My average transaction value is [£AMOUNT] and my margin is approximately [%]. Design a referral programme including: (1) the referral incentive for the referrer, (2) a welcome incentive for the referred customer, (3) how the referral is tracked (code, link, or name-drop), (4) when the reward is paid out, and (5) the 30-word message I'll send to existing customers to introduce it.
whatItIsFor: Designing the structure, incentive, and mechanics of a formal referral programme.
howToUseIt: Fill in your business type and margins before running so incentives are realistic.

title: Referral Ask Script
body: Write a referral ask script I can use verbally (in person or on a call) and a version for a follow-up text or email. My business is [BUSINESS TYPE]. The moment I'm asking: [e.g. right after completing a job / after receiving a 5-star review / at a 30-day check-in call]. The ask should feel natural, not scripted. The incentive I'm offering: [INCENTIVE]. Keep both versions under 60 words.
whatItIsFor: A natural, non-awkward way to ask happy customers for a referral.
howToUseIt: Use at the moment of highest satisfaction — after delivery, after a positive review, or after a compliment.

title: Referral Email to Existing Customers
body: Write a referral programme launch email to my existing customers. Business: [BUSINESS TYPE]. Offer: [REFERRAL INCENTIVE]. Tone: [TONE]. The email should explain: what the programme is, how it works (3 steps max), what they get, what their friend gets, and how to refer. Keep it under 200 words. Include subject line. Make it feel like a genuine thank-you, not a promotion.
whatItIsFor: Launching or re-launching a referral programme to your email list.
howToUseIt: Send to customers who have been with you 3+ months — they have enough experience to refer confidently.

title: Partner Referral Agreement Brief
body: Draft a referral partner agreement brief for a mutual referral arrangement between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and a [PARTNER BUSINESS TYPE]. Include: what each party agrees to refer, the referral fee or reciprocal arrangement, how referrals are tracked and acknowledged, what happens if a referred lead doesn't convert, and a 3-sentence "handshake summary" both parties can agree to verbally before a formal agreement is drafted.
whatItIsFor: Setting up a structured referral relationship with another business (not a customer).
howToUseIt: Use when approaching complementary businesses about referring each other's clients.

title: Referral Thank-You Message
body: Write a thank-you message to send to someone who just referred a new customer to my [BUSINESS TYPE]. The message should: feel personal and genuine, confirm I'll take good care of the person they referred, let them know what happens next, and remind them of the reward they'll receive if applicable. Write a text/DM version (under 60 words) and an email version (under 100 words). No templates that sound like templates.
whatItIsFor: Acknowledging a referral in a way that encourages the person to refer again.
howToUseIt: Send within 24 hours of receiving a referral — before the new customer has even booked.

title: Referral Programme Social Post
body: Write 3 social media posts promoting my referral programme for [BUSINESS TYPE]. Incentive: [REWARD]. Platform: [PLATFORM]. Each post should use a different angle: (1) the reward itself, (2) social proof (a thank-you to someone who referred), (3) a story-style post about why referrals matter to a small business. Each under 80 words. No cringe "share the love" language.
whatItIsFor: Promoting your referral programme organically through social media posts.
howToUseIt: Post quarterly — not constantly. Referral posts work best when they feel like news, not an ongoing plea.

title: Referral Programme for Service Businesses
body: Design a referral programme specifically for a service business: [BUSINESS TYPE]. I have [NUMBER] active clients. My recurring service costs [£AMOUNT/month or per job]. The challenge: [e.g. clients don't talk to each other / my work is private / clients are businesses not consumers]. Design a programme that accounts for this context — including the incentive, the ask moment, and how to make it easy for clients to refer without feeling like they're doing me a favour.
whatItIsFor: Adapting referral mechanics for service businesses where repeat bookings are the goal.
howToUseIt: Especially useful for tradespeople, consultants, cleaners, and anyone booked for ongoing services.

title: Referral Conversion Tracking System
body: Design a simple referral tracking system for a small business with [NUMBER] customers and no dedicated CRM. I need to track: who referred whom, when the referral was made, whether the new customer converted, when the reward was paid, and the total value of referral-sourced revenue this quarter. Give me the column headers for a tracking spreadsheet and explain how to keep it updated with minimal admin time.
whatItIsFor: Setting up a simple way to track which referrals converted — without complex software.
howToUseIt: Works in a spreadsheet; can be upgraded to a CRM later.

title: Referral Incentive Options Generator
body: My business is [BUSINESS TYPE] and I want to incentivise referrals but [REASON CASH DOESN'T FIT: e.g. it's a professional services firm / my margins are too tight / my clients are businesses and can't accept gifts]. Generate 6 referral incentive alternatives — at least 2 experiential, 2 reciprocal, and 2 recognition-based. Each should be practical and low-cost to deliver.
whatItIsFor: Finding the right referral reward when cash discounts don't fit your business model.
howToUseIt: Run when you know cash incentives aren't appropriate (e.g. professional services) or aren't moving the needle.

title: Referral Reactivation Campaign
body: I want to reactivate referrals from past customers who haven't referred in [TIMEFRAME]. Write a personal outreach message (email and text version) acknowledging the time gap, showing what's new or improved in my business, and re-inviting them to refer with a refreshed incentive. Business: [BUSINESS TYPE]. Updated incentive: [INCENTIVE]. Keep both versions under 120 words. Sound like a person, not a campaign.
whatItIsFor: Relaunching referrals to customers who used to refer but have gone quiet.
howToUseIt: Send to the top 20% of past referrers with a personal, specific message — not a bulk email.

title: Referral Programme FAQ Page
body: Write an FAQ page for my referral programme. Business: [BUSINESS TYPE]. Programme details: [INCENTIVE FOR REFERRER / INCENTIVE FOR REFERRED / HOW TO REFER / WHEN REWARD PAID]. Include 8 questions customers commonly ask about referral programmes. Keep answers under 3 sentences each. Friendly but professional tone. Format as Q&A pairs.
whatItIsFor: Answering common questions about your referral programme clearly — reducing friction at the point of referral.
howToUseIt: Add to your website, email footer, or DM it to people who ask how the programme works.

title: Referral Programme for E-Commerce
body: Design a referral programme for my e-commerce store selling [PRODUCT TYPE] at an average order value of [£AMOUNT]. Customers are [AUDIENCE TYPE]. I currently use [EMAIL PLATFORM]. Outline: (1) referral incentive structure, (2) how to deliver unique referral links, (3) when in the post-purchase journey to introduce the programme, (4) the email copy for the referral invite, and (5) one app or tool that would handle this with minimal setup.
whatItIsFor: Designing a referral system for an online shop where most customers never speak to you directly.
howToUseIt: Works best when integrated with your email platform (Klaviyo, Mailchimp) or a referral app.

title: Client Milestone Referral Trigger
body: I provide [SERVICE TYPE] and my clients typically feel best at [MILESTONE MOMENTS: e.g. when they see first results / when a project is delivered / at month 3]. Help me: (1) design a referral trigger for each milestone, (2) write the ask message for each trigger point, and (3) decide which milestone has the highest referral conversion potential and why. I want to automate the trigger where possible.
whatItIsFor: Timing your referral ask to a moment of peak customer satisfaction — not randomly.
howToUseIt: Map your customer journey first, then identify 2–3 natural "high-five" moments where clients feel best about working with you.

title: Referral Programme Audit
body: Audit my existing referral programme. Current setup: [DESCRIBE: incentive, how customers find out about it, how they refer, when reward is paid]. Results so far: [NUMBER of referrals in last 90 days] from [TOTAL CUSTOMER BASE]. Identify the 3 most likely reasons it's underperforming and give me 3 specific changes to make — ranked by expected impact. Be direct.
whatItIsFor: Diagnosing why an existing referral programme isn't generating enough referrals.
howToUseIt: Input your current programme details and metrics for a specific improvement plan.

title: Referral Network Map
body: Help me map my referral network. My business is [BUSINESS TYPE] and my customers include [CUSTOMER TYPES: e.g. solo freelancers, small business owners, parents, tradespeople]. Which types of customers in this mix are most likely to refer — and why? What occupation or life stage predicts high referral behaviour? Give me a ranked list of customer segments by referral likelihood, with a one-sentence reason for each and a suggested approach to activate each.
whatItIsFor: Identifying which of your customers and contacts have the largest referral networks — so you can prioritise your ask.
howToUseIt: Run this with your actual customer list in mind; treat the output as a framework, not a formula.

title: Referral Programme for Professional Services
body: I run a [PROFESSIONAL SERVICE TYPE] and want to generate more referrals without offering financial incentives (which may feel inappropriate or be regulated). Design a referral approach that: (1) makes it easy for happy clients to refer without feeling awkward, (2) keeps my professional positioning intact, (3) uses a recognition or reciprocity model instead of cash, and (4) includes a warm introduction template I can give to clients to send on my behalf.
whatItIsFor: Structuring referrals in a context where overt incentives could damage professional credibility.
howToUseIt: Particularly useful for accountants, solicitors, IFAs, therapists, and coaches.

title: Referral Content Strategy
body: I want to use content to generate referrals for my [BUSINESS TYPE] without making every post a "refer a friend" ask. Design a 4-week content plan (2 posts/week) that builds referral intent organically. Include: social proof posts, behind-the-scenes posts, shareable content, and one direct referral ask. Platform: [PLATFORM]. Audience: [AUDIENCE DESCRIPTION].
whatItIsFor: Using content to prime your audience to refer — without directly asking.
howToUseIt: Layer this into your regular content calendar rather than running it as a separate campaign.

title: Referral Programme Launch Sequence
body: Write a 3-touch launch sequence for a new referral programme. Business: [BUSINESS TYPE]. Channels: [EMAIL / SMS / SOCIAL]. Incentive: [INCENTIVE]. Touch 1: announcement (email, day 1). Touch 2: reminder with a success story or social proof (social post, day 5). Touch 3: personal follow-up to top 10 customers (SMS, day 10). Each piece should feel distinct, not repetitive. Write all three.
whatItIsFor: Launching a new referral programme with a 3-touch sequence that builds momentum in the first two weeks.
howToUseIt: Run the full sequence before switching to steady-state referral mentions in your regular communications.

title: Referral Performance Review
body: Review my referral programme performance for the last quarter. Inputs: total referrals received [NUMBER], referrals converted [NUMBER], average order value of referred customers [£AMOUNT], total rewards paid out [£AMOUNT], total revenue from referred customers [£AMOUNT]. Calculate: conversion rate, cost per acquired customer, return on referral investment. Compare these metrics to my non-referral acquisition cost [£AMOUNT per customer]. Then give me 3 specific decisions to make for next quarter.
whatItIsFor: Evaluating your referral programme's ROI every quarter and deciding what to adjust.
howToUseIt: Fill in the numbers from your tracking spreadsheet before running.

title: Referral Programme Policy Document
body: Write a referral programme policy document for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Programme details: [INCENTIVE / HOW TO REFER / ELIGIBILITY / WHEN REWARD PAID / EXCLUSIONS]. Keep it under 300 words. Plain English — no legal jargon. Cover: who can refer, what counts as a qualifying referral, when and how the reward is paid, what happens if there's a dispute, and how to opt out. Add a last-updated date placeholder.
whatItIsFor: Writing the formal terms and conditions of your referral programme clearly enough that disputes don't happen.
howToUseIt: Publish on your website and link from every referral communication.

title: Subscription Model Feasibility Check
body: I run [BUSINESS TYPE] and I'm considering adding a subscription or membership model. My current average transaction is [£AMOUNT] and customers typically buy [FREQUENCY]. Evaluate whether a subscription model makes sense for me by assessing: (1) whether the purchase frequency supports it, (2) what the recurring deliverable would be, (3) what the minimum viable subscriber count is to make it worthwhile, and (4) the biggest risk I need to mitigate. Give me a direct recommendation: launch, test, or skip.
whatItIsFor: Deciding whether a subscription model makes sense for your business before you build one.
howToUseIt: Be honest about your delivery capacity — subscriptions only work if you can deliver consistently.

title: Membership Tier Design
body: Design 3 membership tiers for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My audience ranges from [ENTRY-LEVEL CUSTOMER] to [HIGH-VALUE CUSTOMER]. Each tier should serve a genuinely different use case, not just offer more of the same thing. For each tier: name, monthly price, 5 specific inclusions, the type of customer it's for, and the main upgrade reason from tier 1 to 2 and 2 to 3. Make the middle tier the most valuable-feeling.
whatItIsFor: Creating 2–3 membership tiers that are genuinely differentiated — not just "more of the same".
howToUseIt: Most businesses oversell the mid-tier. Make each tier serve a different use case, not just a different budget.

title: Subscription Pricing Calculator
body: Help me price a subscription for [BUSINESS TYPE]. My cost to deliver the subscription to one subscriber per month: [£AMOUNT] (including my time at [£/hr] × [hours]). I want a net margin of at least [%]. Typical churn in my sector is around [%/month]. I'm targeting [NUMBER] subscribers in month 12. Calculate: minimum viable price, recommended price (with buffer), break-even subscriber count at that price, and year-1 revenue projection if I hit target.
whatItIsFor: Setting a sustainable subscription price that covers delivery costs, allows for churn, and leaves margin.
howToUseIt: Input your real cost to deliver the subscription per subscriber — not a guess.

title: Membership Launch Plan
body: Create a 4-week membership launch plan for [MEMBERSHIP NAME] at [£PRICE/month]. My current audience: [EMAIL LIST SIZE] subscribers + [SOCIAL FOLLOWING] on [PLATFORM]. My launch goal: [NUMBER] founding members. Include: pre-launch warm-up content (week 1), early-access window (week 2), main launch (week 3), and last-chance urgency (week 4). For each week: the content theme, key emails to send, and social posts to run.
whatItIsFor: Planning a launch sequence that fills your membership in the first 30 days without burning out your audience.
howToUseIt: A launch to an existing audience of 500+ is enough to get meaningful traction — you don't need a large list.

title: Membership Sales Page
body: Write a sales page for [MEMBERSHIP NAME] at [£PRICE/month]. The membership is for [TARGET AUDIENCE] who struggle with [PAIN POINT]. Key inclusions: [LIST 5 INCLUSIONS]. Include: headline, 3-sentence lead, pain agitation section (2 paragraphs), what's included section (bullet list), who it's for and who it's not for, 2 testimonial placeholders, FAQ (4 Qs), and CTA. Under 500 words. Outcome-led, no hype.
whatItIsFor: Writing a sales page that converts visitors into subscribers without relying on hype.
howToUseIt: Focus the page on the problem solved, not the feature list. Benefits over features.

title: Subscriber Welcome Sequence
body: Write a 5-email welcome sequence for new subscribers to [MEMBERSHIP NAME]. The sequence should: Email 1 (instant): confirm access + what to do first. Email 2 (day 2): how to get the most out of the membership. Email 3 (day 5): the most popular resource or quick win. Email 4 (day 10): community or connection prompt. Email 5 (day 14): check-in + handle early cancellation intent. Each email under 150 words. Direct, not fluffy.
whatItIsFor: Onboarding new subscribers so they understand what they've joined, use it immediately, and don't cancel in month 1.
howToUseIt: Set up as an automated 5-email sequence triggered by subscription purchase.

title: Churn Prevention Email
body: Write a churn prevention email for a subscriber to [MEMBERSHIP NAME] who hasn't engaged in [NUMBER] days. Don't be needy — be genuinely helpful. The email should: acknowledge they've been quiet (without guilt-tripping), remind them of one specific thing they might have missed, offer one direct way back in, and give them an easy exit if the timing isn't right. Under 120 words. Subject line included.
whatItIsFor: Re-engaging subscribers who show signs of churning before they cancel.
howToUseIt: Trigger when a subscriber hasn't logged in or engaged in 30+ days.

title: Membership Cancellation Flow
body: Design a cancellation flow for my [MEMBERSHIP NAME] subscription. When a member clicks cancel, I want to: (1) ask why they're leaving (short survey, 3 options + free text), (2) offer a relevant save based on their reason (e.g. pause option, lower tier, or bonus content), (3) confirm cancellation clearly if they still want to go, (4) send a post-cancellation email that leaves the door open. Write the copy for each step.
whatItIsFor: Designing the cancellation experience so you recover some leavers and learn from the rest.
howToUseIt: This is a flow, not just an email — map the decision points before writing the copy.

title: Annual Plan Upgrade Campaign
body: Write a campaign to upgrade monthly subscribers of [MEMBERSHIP NAME] (£[MONTHLY PRICE]/month) to an annual plan (£[ANNUAL PRICE]/year). The offer should: show the saving clearly, add a meaningful bonus for annual members, have a deadline, and not feel like a cash grab. Write: 1 email (under 150 words), 1 social post, and the landing page headline + 3 bullet points. Subject line included.
whatItIsFor: Converting monthly subscribers to annual plans — improving cashflow and reducing churn in one move.
howToUseIt: Run to subscribers who have been active for at least 2 months — they've had enough time to see value.

title: Membership Engagement Content Calendar
body: Create a 4-week member content calendar for [MEMBERSHIP NAME]. My members are [AUDIENCE]. I can produce [NUMBER] pieces of content per week. Include a mix of: educational content (how-to), quick win (template or tool), community engagement (question or challenge), and live/interactive (Q&A or workshop). For each item: content type, title, and format (post, video, doc, email). Keep the monthly workload realistic for a solo operator.
whatItIsFor: Planning a month of member-only content that keeps subscribers engaged and reduces churn.
howToUseIt: Vary content type each week — a mix of education, community, and quick wins performs best.

title: Membership Win-Back Campaign
body: Write a win-back campaign for former subscribers of [MEMBERSHIP NAME] who cancelled [60–90 days ago]. The campaign: 2 emails spaced 5 days apart. Email 1: update on what's new since they left + a genuine invitation to return. Email 2: a limited-time returning member offer. The tone should feel like a personal message, not a marketing campaign. Include subject lines. Each email under 120 words.
