whatItIsFor: Re-engaging former subscribers who cancelled — they already know the value, which makes them cheaper to convert than new leads.
howToUseIt: Run 60–90 days after cancellation; earlier feels desperate, later feels irrelevant.

title: Free Trial Conversion Sequence
body: Write a 4-email free trial conversion sequence for [MEMBERSHIP NAME] (trial period: [NUMBER] days, then £[PRICE]/month). Email 1 (day 1): orientation + the first thing to do. Email 2 (day 4): highlight the feature most trial users miss. Email 3 (day 7): social proof + anticipate cancellation objection. Email 4 (day [LAST DAY]): trial ending + reason to subscribe now. Each email under 130 words. Subject lines included.
whatItIsFor: Converting free trial users into paying subscribers before the trial ends.
howToUseIt: Set up as a timed automated sequence from trial day 1.

title: Member Spotlight & Case Study
body: Write a member spotlight for [MEMBERSHIP NAME] based on this information: member name/business [NAME], how long they've been a member [TIME], what they were struggling with before [PROBLEM], what they've achieved since joining [RESULT], and their favourite thing about the membership [QUOTE]. Format as a 200-word story with a pull quote. Write it warmly but factually — no exaggeration. Include a social-shareable version (under 80 words).
whatItIsFor: Showcasing member success stories to retain existing members and attract new ones.
howToUseIt: Collect the story via a short interview or Google Form, then use this prompt to write it up.

title: Membership Pricing Page
body: Write a pricing page for [MEMBERSHIP NAME] with [NUMBER] tiers. For each tier: name, monthly price, annual price (if offered), and inclusions. I also want: a comparison table showing what each tier includes, a "most popular" callout on the middle tier, a money-back guarantee statement, and an FAQ section (3 questions). Make the copy direct — tell people exactly what they're paying for and why it's worth it.
whatItIsFor: Writing the pricing section of your website or sales page in a way that makes the value obvious and the decision easy.
howToUseIt: Present the annual plan first — it anchors the monthly price as the cheaper option.

title: Subscription Box Product Curation Brief
body: I'm planning a monthly subscription box for [TARGET AUDIENCE] at £[PRICE/month]. The theme is [THEME]. Help me curate a sample box for month 1 including: 5–7 items that fit the theme, their estimated wholesale cost, total cost of goods (including packaging at approximately [£AMOUNT]), margin at my chosen price, and a "hero item" that will make subscribers post about it. Then suggest a surprise element that differentiates it from Amazon.
whatItIsFor: Planning the contents of a physical subscription box for maximum perceived value and customer delight.
howToUseIt: Works for product-based businesses adding a physical subscription to their offer.

title: Membership Pause Policy
body: Write a membership pause policy for [MEMBERSHIP NAME]. Include: how long someone can pause (minimum and maximum), what they retain access to during a pause, what happens at the end of the pause period, how to activate a pause, and the email to send when someone chooses to pause. The policy should be generous enough to be genuinely useful but not so easy to abuse that members pause indefinitely. Keep the policy under 150 words. Write the pause confirmation email too.
whatItIsFor: Offering a pause option instead of full cancellation — recovering members who would otherwise leave permanently.
howToUseIt: Introduce this at the point someone clicks "cancel" — present it as a genuine alternative, not a trick.

title: Membership Community Guidelines
body: Write community guidelines for [MEMBERSHIP NAME]'s private member community. The community is for [AUDIENCE TYPE]. Guidelines should cover: what kinds of posts are welcome, what's not allowed (without sounding like a legal document), how to ask for feedback respectfully, how to promote your own business (if allowed, with limits), and what happens if guidelines are broken. Keep it under 300 words. Friendly but clear — not corporate.
whatItIsFor: Setting the cultural norms for a private member community from day one — before you need to moderate anything.
howToUseIt: Post this in your community welcome channel and reference it in the onboarding email.

title: Membership Revenue Dashboard
body: Design a monthly revenue dashboard for my [MEMBERSHIP TYPE] subscription business. I want to track the 5 most important metrics, no more. For each metric: name, definition, how to calculate it, what a healthy benchmark looks like, and what action to take if it's below benchmark. Format as a table. My current situation: [SUBSCRIBERS], [MONTHLY REVENUE], [MONTHLY CHURN RATE], [NEW SUBSCRIBERS THIS MONTH].
whatItIsFor: Tracking the 5 metrics that actually matter for subscription businesses — without drowning in data.
howToUseIt: Review monthly; these 5 numbers tell you everything you need to act on.

title: Membership Upgrade Email
body: Write an upgrade email for members on [TIER 1 NAME] (£[PRICE]/month) inviting them to upgrade to [TIER 2 NAME] (£[PRICE]/month). The email should: acknowledge what they've been getting from the current tier, introduce the upgrade specifically in terms of what they'd gain (not just a feature list), handle the price increase naturally, and include a limited-time incentive if appropriate. Under 150 words. Subject line included.
whatItIsFor: Moving members from a lower tier to a higher tier at a moment of peak satisfaction.
howToUseIt: Send to lower-tier members who have been active for 60+ days — they've proven they engage with the membership.

title: Membership Affiliate Programme Setup
body: Design an affiliate programme for [MEMBERSHIP NAME] (£[PRICE]/month). Include: commission structure (% or flat fee per referral), how long the cookie window lasts, how and when affiliates get paid, what marketing materials to provide, and the email I'll send to existing members inviting them to become affiliates. Keep the programme simple enough to run without dedicated software (at least initially).
whatItIsFor: Recruiting members to promote your membership to their own audiences in exchange for a commission.
howToUseIt: Your best affiliates are often your most engaged members — they know the value and can speak to it authentically.

title: B2B Ideal Client Profile Builder
body: I provide [SERVICE / PRODUCT] to businesses. My 3 best clients so far are [DESCRIBE: industry, size, why they're great]. Help me build an Ideal Client Profile (ICP) that includes: company size (employees and revenue), industry and niche, decision-maker role and title, what problem they have that I solve, what they've tried before that hasn't worked, what makes them a bad fit, and 3 qualifying questions I should ask on a first call. Format as a one-page reference sheet.
whatItIsFor: Defining your most profitable B2B client segment so you stop wasting time on bad-fit leads.
howToUseIt: Base this on your best existing clients — not hypothetical "dream clients".

title: Cold Outreach Email (B2B)
body: Write a B2B cold outreach email for my [SERVICE / PRODUCT] targeting [RECIPIENT JOB TITLE] at [COMPANY TYPE]. The email should: open with a specific, personalised observation (leave a [PERSONALISATION] placeholder), state the problem I solve in one sentence, give one concrete result (use [RESULT] as placeholder), make a low-commitment ask (a 15-minute call, not a pitch). Under 100 words. Subject line included. No "I hope this email finds you well."
whatItIsFor: Writing a cold email that gets responses — without sounding like a mail-merge spam campaign.
howToUseIt: Personalise the first sentence for each recipient before sending.

title: LinkedIn Outreach Message
body: Write a LinkedIn connection request message and 2-message follow-up sequence for reaching [JOB TITLE] at [COMPANY TYPE]. I provide [SERVICE]. My goal is a discovery call. Message 1 (connection request): under 30 words, no pitch. Message 2 (after connection accepted, day 2): a low-pressure opener that references something relevant. Message 3 (day 7): a soft ask if no reply. All three messages must feel like a human wrote them.
whatItIsFor: A connection request message and follow-up DM sequence that opens B2B conversations without being pushy.
howToUseIt: Send the connection request first with no pitch — wait for acceptance before following up.

title: B2B Discovery Call Script
body: Write a 30-minute B2B discovery call script for [SERVICE TYPE]. Structure: opening (2 min), current situation questions (8 min), problem and impact questions (8 min), goals and priorities (7 min), close and next step (5 min). Include 3–4 specific questions per section and notes on what to listen for. Add a "red flag" column: things that signal this is a bad-fit prospect. Format as a structured cheat sheet.
whatItIsFor: Running a structured 30-minute first call that qualifies the prospect and advances the sale — without feeling like an interrogation.
howToUseIt: Print this and use it as a reference sheet, not a word-for-word script.

title: B2B Proposal Template
body: Write a B2B proposal for [SERVICE] for [CLIENT TYPE]. The client's situation: [PROBLEM THEY DESCRIBED]. What I'm proposing: [SOLUTION OVERVIEW]. Investment: [£PRICE]. Include these sections: (1) context — what we heard, (2) our approach — 3 phases or steps, (3) what you'll have at the end — outcomes not deliverables, (4) investment and payment terms, (5) why us — 3 credibility statements, (6) next steps. Under 500 words total. Professional but not corporate.
whatItIsFor: Writing a proposal that reads as a solution document, not a quote sheet.
howToUseIt: Proposals should reflect what the client told you on the discovery call — never send a generic one.

title: ROI Business Case Generator
body: Build a business case for [PRODUCT / SERVICE] at [£PRICE] for a [COMPANY TYPE] with [NUMBER] employees. The problem it solves: [PROBLEM]. Quantify the cost of the problem (time saved, errors reduced, revenue protected). Calculate: annual cost of current situation, annual cost of the solution, net annual saving or gain, and payback period. Present as a one-page business case a decision-maker could forward to their CFO.
whatItIsFor: Building the financial case for a B2B prospect to justify purchasing your product or service internally.
howToUseIt: B2B buyers often need to convince a manager or finance director — this gives them the numbers to do it.

title: B2B Follow-Up Email Sequence
body: Write a 4-email follow-up sequence after sending a proposal to a B2B prospect. They said they'd "get back to me next week" but haven't. Email 1 (day 5 after proposal): gentle check-in with a value add. Email 2 (day 10): address a likely objection. Email 3 (day 17): offer a smaller first step if budget or commitment is the concern. Email 4 (day 24): polite final follow-up — leave the door open. Each under 80 words. Subject lines included.
whatItIsFor: Following up after a proposal or meeting without becoming annoying — persistence without desperation.
howToUseIt: Adapt the timing based on what the prospect said about their decision timeline.

title: Objection Response Library (B2B)
body: Generate a B2B sales objection response library for [SERVICE TYPE]. Include responses to these 6 objections: (1) "Your price is too high", (2) "We're already using a competitor", (3) "We need to think about it", (4) "We don't have budget right now", (5) "I need to check with [other stakeholder]", (6) "We've tried this before and it didn't work". For each: a 2-sentence response that acknowledges the concern, asks a probing question, and advances the sale without being pushy.
whatItIsFor: Preparing credible, non-defensive responses to the objections B2B prospects raise most often.
howToUseIt: Keep this as a live reference document; add new objections and responses as you encounter them.

title: Procurement & Tender Response Brief
body: I'm responding to a tender for [PROJECT TYPE] from [ORGANISATION TYPE]. Their stated evaluation criteria are: [LIST CRITERIA]. My business: [DESCRIPTION]. Write an executive summary for my tender response (under 300 words) that: addresses each criterion directly, leads with outcomes not activities, includes 2 relevant case study references, and closes with a clear statement of what makes us the right choice. No jargon. No padding.
whatItIsFor: Structuring a response to a formal tender or Request for Proposal (RFP) to stand out from generic submissions.
howToUseIt: Read the tender document carefully before running this prompt — input the specific evaluation criteria they've listed.

title: B2B Case Study Writer
body: Write a B2B case study based on these facts: Client type: [ANONYMISED OR NAMED DESCRIPTION]. Problem they had: [PROBLEM]. Solution I provided: [SOLUTION OVERVIEW]. Result: [MEASURABLE OUTCOME]. Timeframe: [DURATION]. Format: situation → complication → solution → result → client quote (placeholder). Under 250 words. Make the result specific and the story vivid — no generic "they saw great results" language.
whatItIsFor: Turning a client result into a structured case study that sells without sounding like a sales brochure.
howToUseIt: Collect the facts first — client type, problem, solution, result. Then run this prompt to shape the story.

title: B2B Pricing Strategy Brief
body: Help me set B2B pricing for [SERVICE / PRODUCT]. My cost to deliver it: [£AMOUNT] (time + overheads). The value it delivers to the client: [DESCRIBE OUTCOME AND ESTIMATED FINANCIAL BENEFIT]. Current price: [£AMOUNT]. Competitors charge: [RANGE]. Analyse: am I underpriced, fairly priced, or overpriced relative to value? Give me a recommended price, a premium version at higher price, and the one-sentence justification I'd use if a prospect pushes back on cost.
whatItIsFor: Setting B2B pricing that reflects value delivered rather than time spent — and defending that price under pressure.
howToUseIt: Run before your next proposal; use the output to recalibrate if you've been undercharging.
tokens: DESCRIBE OUTCOME AND ESTIMATED FINANCIAL BENEFIT

title: B2B Account Management Check-In
body: Write a quarterly account management check-in agenda and email template for B2B clients of [SERVICE TYPE]. The check-in call is 45 minutes. Include: (1) a pre-call email to set context and ask them to rate satisfaction before the meeting, (2) a 4-section call agenda (review results → uncover concerns → identify new needs → agree next quarter), and (3) a post-call follow-up email summarising actions. Keep each piece concise and professional.
whatItIsFor: Running a structured quarterly check-in with existing B2B clients to protect renewals and find upsell opportunities.
howToUseIt: Schedule these proactively — don't wait for the contract renewal conversation to discover dissatisfaction.

title: B2B Referral Activation (from Existing Clients)
body: Write a B2B client referral activation script and email for [SERVICE TYPE]. I want to ask satisfied clients to introduce me to specific types of companies. The ask: I'm looking for introductions to [TARGET COMPANY TYPE] who are dealing with [PROBLEM]. Write: (1) a verbal script for a call (under 60 seconds), (2) an email version (under 100 words), and (3) a templated warm introduction email I can pre-write and offer to send on their behalf so they just have to forward it.
whatItIsFor: Systematically asking B2B clients to introduce you to other potential clients — at the right moment and in the right way.
howToUseIt: Ask for introductions specifically, not referrals generally — "Do you know anyone?" is too vague.

title: B2B Competitive Positioning Brief
body: I'm regularly compared to [COMPETITOR NAME / TYPE] during B2B sales conversations. My business: [DESCRIPTION]. My strengths vs the competitor: [LIST 3 DIFFERENCES]. Where the competitor is stronger: [BE HONEST]. Write: (1) a one-paragraph positioning statement I can use verbally when the comparison comes up, (2) 3 questions I can ask that naturally surface why my strengths matter to this prospect, and (3) a situation where I should acknowledge the competitor is probably the better fit.
whatItIsFor: Clarifying how to position yourself when prospects are comparing you directly against a named competitor.
howToUseIt: Never badmouth competitors — position around your strengths and their gaps without being defensive.

title: B2B Sales Deck Outline
body: Create a B2B sales deck outline for [SERVICE / PRODUCT] targeting [COMPANY TYPE]. The deck is for a 20-minute in-person or Zoom presentation. Structure: slide 1 agenda, slide 2–3 the problem, slide 4–5 our solution, slide 6 proof (case study or result), slide 7 how we work together (process), slide 8 investment, slide 9 FAQ pre-emption, slide 10 next step. For each slide: title, 3 talking points, and the one thing the audience should feel or think by the time you move on.
whatItIsFor: Structuring a presentation or pitch deck for a B2B sales meeting that moves a prospect forward.
howToUseIt: Keep the deck under 12 slides; most good sales decks are 8–10 slides maximum.

title: Contract Renewal Campaign
body: Write a B2B contract renewal campaign for [SERVICE TYPE] with clients on [CONTRACT LENGTH] contracts. The campaign starts 90 days before renewal. Include: Email 1 (day 0): results summary + "let's talk about next year". Email 2 (day 14): renewal proposal with any price changes explained. Email 3 (day 30): address hesitation if no response. Email 4 (day 60): final renewal push with a decision deadline. Each email under 150 words. Subject lines included.
whatItIsFor: Proactively securing B2B contract renewals 60–90 days before expiry — not scrambling at the last minute.
howToUseIt: Start the conversation at 90 days before renewal — it's too late at 30 days if there's dissatisfaction.

title: B2B Customer Onboarding Plan
body: Design a 90-day B2B client onboarding plan for [SERVICE TYPE]. The plan should include: a welcome action in week 1 (information gathering + intro call), a quick win deliverable in weeks 2–3, a mid-point check-in in week 6, and a 90-day review meeting. For each milestone: what we do, what the client does, what gets delivered, and what a successful outcome looks like. Write it as a client-facing document I can send with the signed contract.
whatItIsFor: Structuring the first 90 days of a new B2B client relationship to build trust, deliver early wins, and set the right expectations.
howToUseIt: Send this to the client on day 1 — showing them the plan immediately reduces anxiety and increases confidence.

title: B2B Upsell & Expansion Script
body: I provide [SERVICE] to [CLIENT TYPE]. I want to upsell [ADDITIONAL SERVICE] to existing clients. Write: (1) a verbal script for introducing the upsell naturally in a check-in call (not a pitch — a conversation), (2) an email version for clients I can't reach by phone, and (3) a one-paragraph justification of why this add-on makes sense for their business specifically. Avoid making it sound like a money grab. Lead with their problem, not my product.
whatItIsFor: Identifying and pitching additional services to existing B2B clients — the lowest-cost way to grow revenue.
howToUseIt: Only pitch expansion when you have evidence of the need — not as a standard upsell attempt.

title: B2B Testimonial Collection System
body: Design a B2B testimonial collection system for [SERVICE TYPE]. Include: when to ask (the ideal moment in the client relationship), the 4 questions to ask to get a useful testimonial (covering problem, solution, result, and recommendation), how to make it easy (survey or email format), and what to do with the testimonial once collected (where to use it, how to get approval). Write the testimonial request email too.
whatItIsFor: Getting specific, usable testimonials from B2B clients — not generic "great to work with" quotes.
howToUseIt: Ask at a peak satisfaction moment, and give them the questions — don't expect them to write freeform.

title: Lost Deal Debrief
body: Help me debrief a lost B2B deal. The deal: [SERVICE / PRODUCT], [£VALUE]. Prospect: [TYPE OF COMPANY]. Why we lost (if known): [REASON GIVEN]. What I think the real reason was: [YOUR ASSESSMENT]. Run me through a structured debrief including: (1) what qualification signals I missed early, (2) what I should have done differently at each stage, (3) whether this prospect is worth re-approaching in future (and when), and (4) one change to make to avoid losing similar deals.
whatItIsFor: Learning from deals you didn't win — most sales teams don't do this and repeat the same mistakes.
howToUseIt: Run this within a week of losing a deal while the details are still fresh.

title: Affiliate Programme Design
body: Design an affiliate programme for [PRODUCT / SERVICE] at [£PRICE]. My margin is [%]. I want affiliates to be motivated to promote actively. Include: commission structure (% or flat fee), cookie duration, payout frequency and minimum, qualifying criteria (who can become an affiliate), what marketing materials to provide, and how to handle disputes or fraud. Also tell me the minimum conversion rate an affiliate needs to achieve to make promotion worthwhile for them.
whatItIsFor: Designing the structure of an affiliate programme before you launch it.
howToUseIt: Commission needs to be high enough to motivate action but sustainable at scale — run the maths first.

title: Affiliate Recruitment Email
body: Write a cold outreach email recruiting affiliates for [PRODUCT / SERVICE] at [£PRICE] with [%] commission. Target affiliate type: [e.g. lifestyle bloggers / business coaches / podcast hosts]. The email should: open with a specific observation about their audience (leave [PERSONALISATION] placeholder), explain what the product is in one sentence, state the commission and earning potential clearly, make it low-effort to say yes. Under 150 words. Subject line included.
whatItIsFor: Approaching potential affiliates — creators, bloggers, and complementary businesses — to join your programme.
howToUseIt: Personalise the opening for each recipient; note something specific about their audience or content.

title: Affiliate Welcome Pack
body: Write an affiliate welcome pack for [PRODUCT NAME]. The pack should include: a welcome message, a 3-step "start promoting today" guide, the 3 highest-converting promotion methods with brief how-to for each, their unique affiliate link (placeholder), key product facts they need to know, commission and payout details, and who to contact with questions. Format as a document they can bookmark and return to. Under 400 words total.
whatItIsFor: Onboarding new affiliates with everything they need to start promoting effectively from day one.
howToUseIt: Send within 24 hours of approval; affiliates who don't promote in the first two weeks rarely do.

title: Affiliate Promotional Email Template
body: Write an affiliate promotional email template for [PRODUCT NAME] at [£PRICE]. This email will be sent by affiliates to their own lists, so it should be written in a personal, first-person voice that could belong to any creator in [NICHE]. The email should: open with a personal story or relevant observation, explain why this product is useful in their own words, include key benefits (not features), and have a clear CTA with the affiliate link placeholder. Under 200 words. Subject line included. Add a note telling affiliates to personalise [BRACKETED SECTIONS].
whatItIsFor: Giving affiliates a ready-to-send email they can send to their list with minimal customisation.
howToUseIt: Write this in the affiliate's voice, not yours — they need to sound like themselves, not your marketing team.

title: Affiliate Social Post Templates
body: Write 3 social media post templates that affiliates can use to promote [PRODUCT NAME] at [£PRICE] on [PLATFORM]. Each template should use a different angle: (1) problem-focused, (2) personal recommendation, (3) outcome-focused. Each under 80 words with [AFFILIATE LINK] placeholder. Write them to sound like a person sharing something useful, not an ad. Include editing notes in brackets telling the affiliate what to personalise.
whatItIsFor: Giving affiliates social post templates they can adapt for their audience — so they promote without spending hours writing.
howToUseIt: Provide 3 templates in different styles; affiliates will gravitate to the one that suits their content voice.

title: Affiliate Performance Review
body: Help me review affiliate programme performance. I have [NUMBER] affiliates. In the last 30 days: total clicks [NUMBER], total sales [NUMBER], total commission paid [£AMOUNT], revenue generated [£AMOUNT]. Top 3 affiliates by sales: [LIST]. Bottom 5 by activity: [LIST or "inactive"]. Analyse: (1) overall programme ROI, (2) what the top affiliates are doing differently, (3) how to activate the inactive ones, and (4) whether the commission structure is motivating enough. Give me 3 actions to take this week.
whatItIsFor: Analysing which affiliates are generating results and which need support or removal from the programme.
howToUseIt: Run monthly; focus resources on your top 20% of affiliates who drive 80% of sales.

title: Reseller Partnership Agreement Brief
body: Write a reseller partnership agreement brief for [PRODUCT / SERVICE] being sold through [RESELLER BUSINESS TYPE]. Include: what the reseller is authorised to sell and how, the reseller margin or discount they receive, minimum sales commitments (if any), branding and co-branding rules, support responsibilities (who handles client queries), and the exit terms if either party wants to end the arrangement. Write it as a plain-English brief, not a legal contract.
whatItIsFor: Setting up a formal reseller relationship with a business that will sell your product or service to their clients.
howToUseIt: Resellers are different from affiliates — they typically add value or bundle your product with their own offer.

title: Joint Venture Pitch Brief
body: Write a joint venture pitch to [POTENTIAL PARTNER BUSINESS TYPE]. I run [MY BUSINESS TYPE]. The proposed JV: [DESCRIBE: e.g. co-create a course / run a joint promotion / bundle our products]. Revenue split proposed: [e.g. 50/50 / 60/40]. Who does what: [RESPONSIBILITIES]. Pitch should explain: why our audiences are complementary, what each party contributes, what each party earns, and the minimum commitment required. Under 200 words. Email format.
whatItIsFor: Proposing a joint venture — where two businesses create something together and share the revenue.
howToUseIt: Lead with what's in it for them — not what you want to gain.

title: Partner Newsletter Collaboration
body: Write a newsletter collaboration pitch to [NEWSLETTER / BUSINESS NAME] proposing either a swap (we each feature the other) or a paid sponsorship of their newsletter. My audience: [DESCRIPTION AND SIZE]. Their audience: [DESCRIPTION AND SIZE]. My offer: [WHAT I WANT FEATURED]. Write both: (1) a swap pitch (equal value exchange), (2) a paid sponsorship pitch (I pay them [£AMOUNT] to feature me). Keep both under 120 words. Email format.
whatItIsFor: Arranging a newsletter swap or sponsorship with a complementary business to reach each other's audiences.
howToUseIt: Works best with partners who have a similar audience but no competitive overlap — and who publish regularly.

title: Affiliate Programme Terms & Conditions
body: Write affiliate programme terms and conditions for [PRODUCT / BUSINESS NAME]. Cover: who is eligible to be an affiliate, what is and isn't permitted in promotions (e.g. no paid search on brand terms, no misleading claims), how commissions are calculated and when they're voided, fraud and abuse policy, payment terms, and how to terminate the relationship. Under 400 words. Plain English — no legalese. End with a last-updated date placeholder.
whatItIsFor: Writing clear, enforceable programme rules that protect you from fraud and abuse — in plain English.
howToUseIt: Publish publicly and require acceptance at sign-up; reference it in your affiliate welcome email.

title: Strategic Partnership Proposal
body: Write a strategic partnership proposal for a potential arrangement between my [BUSINESS TYPE] and [PARTNER BUSINESS TYPE]. The partnership I'm proposing: [DESCRIBE: joint product, distribution agreement, co-branding, shared team resource, etc.]. Each party contributes: [WHAT EACH SIDE BRINGS]. Expected outcome for both: [SHARED BENEFIT]. Duration proposed: [TIMEFRAME]. Include: executive summary, proposed structure, success metrics, financial arrangement, and next steps. Under 500 words. Professional document format.
whatItIsFor: Proposing a deeper, longer-term business partnership beyond a simple referral or affiliate arrangement.
howToUseIt: Use when the potential value is significant enough to justify a formal proposal document, not just an email.

title: Affiliate Re-Engagement Campaign
body: Write a 2-email re-engagement campaign for inactive affiliates of [PRODUCT NAME]. These affiliates joined [X] days ago but haven't promoted yet (or haven't promoted in 90+ days). Email 1: check-in + offer a done-for-you asset. Email 2 (7 days later): a simple challenge ("share this one thing this week") with a bonus incentive. Subject lines included. Each email under 100 words. Friendly and non-shaming tone.
whatItIsFor: Reconnecting with affiliates who joined your programme but have never promoted or haven't promoted in 90+ days.
howToUseIt: Don't assume they don't want to promote — often they just don't know where to start or got busy.

title: Affiliate Contest & Incentive Campaign
body: Design an affiliate contest for [PRODUCT NAME] running for [NUMBER] weeks. Prize structure: [PRIZE 1 for top affiliate, PRIZE 2 for second, PRIZE 3 for third, or participation bonus]. Metric to compete on: [sales count / revenue / new customers]. Write: the contest announcement email to all affiliates, a mid-contest leaderboard update email, and a winner announcement email. Keep each under 120 words. Make it feel exciting without being gimmicky.
whatItIsFor: Running a time-limited affiliate contest to spike promotion activity and reward your top performers.
howToUseIt: Run quarterly or around a product launch — too frequent and the incentive loses its edge.

title: Affiliate Disclosure Language
body: Write affiliate disclosure language for [PRODUCT / PROGRAMME NAME] that affiliates can use across: (1) blog posts or written content, (2) Instagram or social media captions, (3) email newsletters, (4) YouTube video descriptions. The language should comply with UK ASA (Advertising Standards Authority) guidelines — making it clear that a commission is earned. Write a version for each format. Keep each version under 30 words. Professional but not robotic.
whatItIsFor: Giving affiliates clear, compliant disclosure language they can copy into their content.
howToUseIt: Include this in your affiliate welcome pack — non-disclosure puts both you and the affiliate at legal risk.

title: Partner Co-Marketing Brief
body: Create a co-marketing campaign brief for [MY BUSINESS] and [PARTNER BUSINESS] jointly promoting [OFFER / EVENT / PRODUCT]. Our combined audience reach: [ESTIMATED NUMBERS]. Campaign duration: [TIMEFRAME]. Include: (1) shared messaging and positioning, (2) what each party creates and promotes, (3) content calendar (who posts what and when), (4) shared goals and how we'll measure them, and (5) what to do if the partnership isn't delivering equal value. Keep as a practical 1-page brief.
whatItIsFor: Planning a co-marketing campaign with a partner where both businesses promote the same thing to their audiences simultaneously.
howToUseIt: Best when both audiences are of similar size — asymmetric co-marketing needs a different structure.

title: Affiliate Content Brief
body: Write a content brief for affiliates promoting [PRODUCT NAME] via [CONTENT TYPE: blog review / YouTube video / Instagram Reel / podcast mention]. Include: the angle to take, key points to cover, what claims to avoid (accuracy requirements), the ideal audience description, the CTA to use, where to put the affiliate link, and the ideal length or duration. Keep the brief under 300 words so affiliates will actually read it.
whatItIsFor: Briefing affiliates to create specific content types — not just "write about it however you want".
howToUseIt: Structured briefs produce much better affiliate content than open-ended encouragement.

title: Commission Structure Comparison
body: Help me choose the right commission structure for my affiliate programme. Product: [DESCRIPTION]. Price: [£AMOUNT]. Margin: [%]. My goal: [e.g. maximise volume / attract top affiliates / reward loyalty]. Compare 4 models: (1) flat fee per sale, (2) percentage per sale, (3) tiered (higher % at higher sales volume), (4) recurring (% of subscription revenue monthly). For each: explain how it works, calculate the affiliate earnings at 10, 50, and 100 sales, and rate it for my goal. Recommend one model with reasoning.
whatItIsFor: Deciding between different commission models — flat fee, percentage, tiered, or recurring.
howToUseIt: The right model depends on your product type and how you want affiliates to behave.

title: Affiliate Exit Interview
body: Write an affiliate exit interview email for [PROGRAMME NAME]. The affiliate is leaving or has gone completely inactive. The email should: acknowledge their decision without guilt-tripping, ask 4 honest questions about their experience (commission, product fit, marketing support, personal timing), make it easy to respond (multiple choice + one open question), and leave the door open for them to return. Under 150 words. Subject line included.
whatItIsFor: Understanding why affiliates leave your programme so you can improve retention and the programme structure.
howToUseIt: Send when an affiliate cancels or goes 90+ days without any activity.

title: Partner Event Co-Sponsorship Brief
body: Write a co-sponsorship brief for an event co-sponsored by [MY BUSINESS] and [PARTNER BUSINESS]. Event: [EVENT NAME AND FORMAT]. Each party contributes: [FINANCIAL / CONTENT / PROMOTION]. Each party receives: [BENEFITS]. The brief should cover: how the event is branded (co-branding rules), who controls what, how attendee data is shared (or not), and a post-event debrief plan to evaluate whether to repeat it. Format as a practical working document.
whatItIsFor: Co-sponsoring an event with a partner to share costs and share reach — without either party doing all the work.
howToUseIt: Best for in-person networking events, webinars, or virtual summits where both brands appear side by side.

title: Affiliate Programme Launch Announcement
body: Write a launch announcement for my new affiliate programme for [PRODUCT / BRAND]. Target recruits: existing customers, email subscribers, and social followers. The announcement should cover: what the programme is, who it's for, commission details, how to apply (or get their link), and what support they'll receive. Write: (1) an email to existing list (under 200 words), (2) a social post (under 80 words), and (3) a reply email for when someone says "tell me more." Subject lines included.
whatItIsFor: Announcing the launch of a new affiliate programme to your existing audience — your best affiliates are often already in your community.
howToUseIt: Email first, then follow up with a social post; leads from your own audience convert at 2–3x the rate of cold outreach.

title: Discovery-to-Proposal Bridge
body: I just had a discovery call with a potential client. Here are my notes: [PASTE NOTES — include the problem they described, what they've tried, their goal, their timeline, and any concerns they raised]. Help me: (1) identify the 3 most important things they care about, (2) write an opening paragraph for my proposal that mirrors their language back to them (use their words, not mine), and (3) suggest the framing for my solution — how to position what I do in terms of their specific situation.
whatItIsFor: Translating what a prospect told you in a discovery call into a proposal that mirrors their language and priorities back to them.
howToUseIt: Take notes during your discovery call, then feed them directly into this prompt.

title: Service Business Proposal Template
body: Write a complete proposal template for [SERVICE TYPE] targeting [CLIENT TYPE]. Include these 8 sections: (1) About this proposal — context and client problem, (2) Our approach — how we work, (3) Scope of work — what we'll do (5–7 deliverables), (4) What we need from you — client responsibilities, (5) Timeline — milestones with approximate weeks, (6) Investment — fee and payment terms, (7) Why us — 2 credibility statements and 1 case study placeholder, (8) Next steps — how to accept and start. Professional, outcome-focused language throughout. Under 600 words.
whatItIsFor: A reusable proposal structure for service businesses that can be adapted for any client engagement.
howToUseIt: Fill in the client-specific sections before every proposal — don't send a generic version.

title: Creative Pitch Deck Brief
body: Help me plan a pitch deck for a creative project: [PROJECT TYPE] for [CLIENT TYPE]. The pitch is [NUMBER] slides, presented in [DURATION]. I need to communicate: our creative vision, our process, our relevant experience, and a clear reason to choose us. Outline each slide with: title, what it communicates (one sentence), what to show vs what to say, and a note on what the client should feel at that moment. No generic "about us" slide — earn trust through the work, not biography.
whatItIsFor: Planning a pitch deck for a creative project (brand, campaign, architecture, design) where vision matters as much as process.
howToUseIt: Creative pitches should show more and tell less — this prompt helps you decide what to show.

title: Project Scope of Work Writer
body: Write a scope of work document for [PROJECT TYPE] for [CLIENT TYPE]. Include: project overview (2 sentences), what is included (itemised list of 6–8 deliverables), what is explicitly excluded (3–4 items), revision policy (number of rounds, what counts as a revision vs a new request), timeline and milestone overview, and what happens if scope changes are requested mid-project. Professional but plain English — under 400 words.
whatItIsFor: Writing a detailed scope of work that protects you from scope creep while being clear to the client.
howToUseIt: Every project engagement should have a signed scope before work begins — verbal agreements don't hold.

title: Price Increase Proposal Letter
body: Write a price increase letter for existing [SERVICE TYPE] clients. Current price: [£AMOUNT]. New price: [£AMOUNT] (effective [DATE]). Reason: [HONEST REASON — e.g. cost of delivery has increased / I'm reducing client numbers to improve quality / market rate adjustment]. The letter should: acknowledge the relationship, explain the increase without over-apologising, state the new price and effective date clearly, and confirm what they're keeping. Under 200 words. Professional and warm.
whatItIsFor: Communicating a price increase to existing clients in a way that protects the relationship.
howToUseIt: Give 60–90 days' notice; frame around value delivered, not your own costs.

title: Value-Based Proposal Framing
body: Help me reframe a proposal from a time-based to a value-based structure. Current proposal: [DESCRIBE YOUR CURRENT DRAFT — deliverables, price, time estimate]. The value I deliver: [DESCRIBE THE OUTCOME AND ITS FINANCIAL OR STRATEGIC WORTH TO THE CLIENT]. Rewrite the proposal positioning so: (1) price appears after the value is established, (2) the outcome is described in the client's terms (not deliverables list), and (3) there's a clear comparison to what it would cost them to not solve the problem.
whatItIsFor: Restructuring a proposal so the price is anchored to the value delivered — not the time spent.
howToUseIt: Replace "days × day rate" proposals with outcome-focused pricing using this structure.
tokens: DESCRIBE THE OUTCOME AND ITS FINANCIAL OR STRATEGIC WORTH TO THE CLIENT

title: Grant Application Executive Summary
body: Write an executive summary for a grant application for [BUSINESS NAME / TYPE] applying for [GRANT NAME / TYPE]. The project I'm seeking funding for: [DESCRIBE]. Funding requested: [£AMOUNT]. What the money will be used for: [USES]. Expected outcome: [MEASURABLE RESULTS]. Funder's priorities (from the grant guidelines): [LIST 2–3 PRIORITIES]. The summary should address the funder's priorities directly, state the funding request clearly, and describe the impact in measurable terms. Under 250 words.
whatItIsFor: Writing the opening section of a grant application that makes assessors want to read the rest.
howToUseIt: The executive summary is often the only part assessors read fully — make it count.

title: Speaking & Pitch Proposal
body: Write a speaking proposal for [EVENT NAME / TYPE] proposing my talk on [TOPIC]. My audience for this talk: [EVENT'S AUDIENCE]. My talk title: [TITLE]. Key takeaways for attendees (3 bullet points): [LIST]. My credibility for this topic: [EXPERIENCE / BACKGROUND]. Format required: [KEYNOTE / PANEL / WORKSHOP]. Duration: [LENGTH]. The proposal should lead with audience value, include a brief bio, and end with a clear offer to provide more information. Under 250 words.
whatItIsFor: Applying to speak at a conference, event, or podcast as a business development strategy.
howToUseIt: Lead with audience value, not personal promotion — event organisers reject pitches that are obviously sales vehicles.

title: Investor Pitch One-Pager
body: Write a one-pager investor or lender pitch for [BUSINESS NAME]. Include: problem and market opportunity, our solution, business model (how we make money), traction to date (revenue, customers, key milestones), the ask (amount and use of funds), and why now. Keep it under 350 words. Factual and specific — no projections without evidence, no "we're revolutionising" language. Format as a clean document with clear section headers.
whatItIsFor: Summarising your business opportunity for an investor or lender in a format they'll actually read.
howToUseIt: This is a teaser, not a full business plan — the goal is to get the meeting, not close the investment.

title: Contract Proposal for Ongoing Retainers
body: Write a retainer proposal for an existing client of my [SERVICE TYPE]. Currently working with them on: [EXISTING ARRANGEMENT]. Proposed retainer: [£AMOUNT/month] for [SCOPE OF ONGOING WORK]. The proposal should: explain the business case for them (consistency, priority access, cost saving vs ad hoc), state what's included in the retainer, define what happens with out-of-scope work, and include the payment and notice terms. Under 300 words. Position it as a favour to them, not a request from me.
whatItIsFor: Proposing a shift from one-off projects to a recurring retainer arrangement with an existing client.
howToUseIt: Pitch retainers when you have 3+ months of successful project work with a client — not to a new prospect.

title: Multi-Option Proposal Structure
body: Create a 3-option proposal structure for [SERVICE TYPE] for [CLIENT TYPE]. Option 1 (essential): minimum viable scope at [£PRICE]. Option 2 (recommended): full scope at [£PRICE]. Option 3 (complete): expanded scope at [£PRICE]. For each option: list 4–6 inclusions, state what they'll have at the end, and explain who each option is best for. Add a comparison table and a note on which option you recommend and why.
whatItIsFor: Presenting 3 versions of a proposal (good / better / best) so the client chooses a scope, not whether to hire you.
howToUseIt: Design options so the middle one is the most attractive — and so the top option makes the middle look like a bargain.

title: Proposal Follow-Up & Close Script
body: Write a follow-up message for a proposal I sent [NUMBER] days ago for [SERVICE] at [£PRICE] that hasn't had a response. The message should: check in without pressure, offer to answer any questions, and give a gentle next step. Write 3 versions: (1) email, (2) WhatsApp/text, (3) LinkedIn message. Each under 60 words. Include subject lines for the email version. No "just checking in" openers.
whatItIsFor: Checking in on a proposal that's gone quiet — without sounding desperate or pushy.
howToUseIt: Wait 5 business days after sending a proposal before following up — then follow this sequence.

title: Tender Evaluation Criteria Mapping
body: I'm responding to a tender for [PROJECT TYPE]. The evaluation criteria are: [PASTE THE CRITERIA AND WEIGHTINGS IF GIVEN]. For each criterion: (1) summarise what the assessor wants to see, (2) identify the strongest evidence I can provide from my experience [PASTE RELEVANT EXPERIENCE NOTES], (3) suggest the structure of my response section (what to lead with, what evidence to cite, what to avoid). Output as a table: criterion | what they want | my evidence | recommended response structure.
whatItIsFor: Ensuring your tender response addresses every evaluation criterion — scored, not just mentioned.
howToUseIt: Create this map before writing — then write one response section per criterion.
tokens: PASTE THE CRITERIA AND WEIGHTINGS IF GIVEN

title: Proposal Rejection Response
body: Write a response to a client who has just rejected my proposal for [SERVICE] at [£PRICE]. Their stated reason: [REASON GIVEN]. My goal: leave the door open without appearing desperate, understand the real reason if possible, and keep the relationship warm. Write a short email (under 100 words) that: thanks them genuinely, asks one question to understand the decision better, and ends positively. No sales pitch in the response.
whatItIsFor: Responding to a "no" in a way that preserves the relationship and positions you for a future opportunity.
howToUseIt: Reply within 24 hours — a gracious response is remembered when circumstances change.

title: Partnership Proposal Email
body: Write a partnership proposal email to [PARTNER BUSINESS TYPE]. I run [MY BUSINESS TYPE]. The partnership I'm proposing: [DESCRIBE]. What they gain: [BENEFIT TO THEM]. What I gain: [BENEFIT TO ME]. The email should: open with a relevant observation about their business (leave [PERSONALISATION] placeholder), propose the partnership clearly in 3 sentences, state what each party does, and ask for a 20-minute call. Under 150 words. Subject line included.
whatItIsFor: Proposing a commercial partnership to another business — in an email format that gets a response.
howToUseIt: Lead with their benefit, not yours — and make the ask specific and low-effort.

title: Proposal Objection Pre-Emption
body: I'm writing a proposal for [SERVICE TYPE] at [£PRICE]. The 4 objections prospects most commonly raise are: (1) [OBJECTION 1], (2) [OBJECTION 2], (3) [OBJECTION 3], (4) [OBJECTION 4]. Write a "Questions you might have" section for the proposal that addresses each objection directly, honestly, and without over-explaining. Keep each answer under 3 sentences. Format as Q&A pairs. Tone: confident but not defensive.
whatItIsFor: Addressing common objections inside the proposal itself — before the prospect even raises them.
howToUseIt: Add a "Questions you might have" section to any proposal where price, timing, or proof are likely concerns.

title: Unsolicited Proposal Brief
body: I want to send an unsolicited proposal to [COMPANY TYPE]. I've identified this specific problem in their business: [PROBLEM — based on publicly available information, their website, job ads, or social media]. My proposed solution: [SOLUTION]. Help me: (1) write the opening email that gets the proposal read (under 80 words), (2) outline the proposal structure (4 sections max), and (3) write the one-paragraph business case — why they should care and why now. Don't pitch cold — lead with the insight.
whatItIsFor: Sending a proposal to a company that hasn't asked for one — but where you can clearly see an opportunity.
howToUseIt: Unsolicited proposals only work when the problem you've identified is real and visible — not a manufactured opportunity.

title: Proposal Design Brief
body: Create a design brief for a proposal document for [BUSINESS TYPE]. The proposal will be [NUMBER] pages, delivered as a PDF. Include: the overall visual tone and feel (reference words), colour palette recommendation (3 colours max), font pairing suggestion, section layout for each page, use of visuals (when to use graphs, case study images, or icons vs text-only pages), and 3 design mistakes to avoid in proposals. Keep it practical — this brief will be handed to a designer or used in Canva.
whatItIsFor: Planning the visual presentation of a proposal — not just the copy, but the document design that makes it feel professional.
howToUseIt: Use this when briefing a designer, or when building your own proposal in Canva or Notion.

title: Proposal Acceptance & Kickoff Flow
body: Design the proposal acceptance and project kickoff flow for [SERVICE TYPE]. The client has just said yes. Map out: (1) the confirmation email (what to send immediately), (2) the invoice sequence (what to send and when), (3) the contract or agreement (how to send it and what to use), (4) the onboarding form or information request, and (5) the kickoff call agenda. Write the text for items 1 and 5. Keep the process feeling organised but warm.
whatItIsFor: What happens the moment a client says yes — the next steps that make the relationship start well.
howToUseIt: Have this flow ready to send within 2 hours of receiving acceptance; delay erodes confidence.

title: Proposal ROI Summary Section
body: Write an ROI summary section for a proposal for [SERVICE TYPE] at [£PRICE]. The client's current situation: [DESCRIBE — e.g. spending X hours on Y, missing Z revenue, risk of ABC]. What my service changes: [DESCRIBE OUTCOME]. Quantify: annual cost of the problem, annual value of the solution, net gain in year 1, payback period. Present this in the proposal as a simple "What this investment returns" section. Under 150 words. Don't overstate — only use numbers you can reasonably defend.
whatItIsFor: Adding a financial ROI calculation to a proposal so the investment justifies itself on paper before the client has to decide.
howToUseIt: Place this section immediately before the investment figure — it makes the price feel smaller by anchoring it to the return.

title: Crisis Response Framework Builder
body: Help me build a crisis response framework for [BUSINESS TYPE]. Identify the 5 most likely crises for a business like mine (e.g. public complaint, product failure, data breach, negative press, key person unavailable). For each crisis: (1) early warning signs to watch for, (2) first response steps (who does what in the first 2 hours), (3) the stakeholders I need to communicate with and in what order, and (4) a recovery action. Format as a reference sheet I can access quickly when needed.
whatItIsFor: Creating a crisis response plan before you need one — so you're not writing your response in a moment of panic.
howToUseIt: Run once per year as part of your business planning; update when your business significantly changes.

title: Public Complaint Response (Social Media)
body: Write a public response to this social media complaint about my [BUSINESS TYPE]: "[PASTE COMPLAINT TEXT]". The response should: acknowledge the issue without admitting liability before you have the facts, demonstrate genuine concern, move the conversation private, and not be defensive or dismissive. Under 60 words. Professional but human — not a corporate script.
whatItIsFor: Responding to a public complaint on social media in a way that defuses the situation and shows good faith to onlookers.
howToUseIt: Always acknowledge publicly, resolve privately — never debate specifics in the public thread.

title: Negative Review Response Writer
body: Write a response to this negative review of my [BUSINESS TYPE]: "[PASTE REVIEW]". The response should: acknowledge what they experienced (not what actually happened), not be defensive, show you take quality seriously, offer a resolution where appropriate, and end in a way that leaves other readers with confidence in your business. Under 100 words. Warm and professional.
whatItIsFor: Writing a response to a negative Google, Trustpilot, or platform review that recovers credibility — for the reviewer and anyone reading.
howToUseIt: Respond within 48 hours. Your response is read by future customers more than the review itself.

title: Service Failure Apology Email
body: Write an apology email to a customer following [SERVICE FAILURE: describe what went wrong]. My business: [BUSINESS TYPE]. What happened: [FACTS]. What I'm doing to fix it: [REMEDIATION]. What I'm doing to prevent it recurring: [PREVENTION]. The email should: apologise clearly and specifically, explain what went wrong briefly (without making excuses), state exactly what I'm doing to fix it, and include a goodwill gesture. Under 200 words. Subject line included.
whatItIsFor: Writing a direct apology to an affected customer after a service failure — before they complain publicly.
howToUseIt: Send within 24 hours of knowing about the failure. Proactive apologies retain customers; reactive ones don't.

title: Business Continuity Plan Brief
body: Help me create a business continuity plan for my [BUSINESS TYPE] with [NUMBER] employees/contractors. I need to document: (1) what happens to client delivery if I'm unavailable for 1–2 weeks, (2) who has access to what systems and logins (framework — I'll fill in specifics separately), (3) which contracts or obligations have urgent deadlines, (4) who clients should contact in my absence, and (5) a one-page handover brief I could give someone to manage in my absence. Write the template for each section.
whatItIsFor: Documenting what happens to your business if you're suddenly unavailable — illness, family emergency, or burnout.
howToUseIt: Every solo or small business owner needs this. Write it when things are fine — not when they're not.

title: Data Breach or Privacy Incident Response
body: Help me respond to this data incident: [DESCRIBE WHAT HAPPENED — e.g. customer email list accidentally sent to wrong recipient, website form data exposed, payment data accessed by unauthorised person]. My business: [TYPE]. Affected data: [DESCRIBE]. Number of people affected: [NUMBER]. Write: (1) an internal incident log entry, (2) a customer notification email, and (3) the key questions I need to answer to assess whether ICO reporting is required. Note: this is a communication draft only — I will seek legal advice on regulatory obligations.
whatItIsFor: Responding to a data breach or privacy incident in line with UK GDPR requirements — clearly and quickly.
howToUseIt: Under UK GDPR, you must report breaches to the ICO within 72 hours if they pose a risk to individuals — this prompt helps you draft the communication, not legal advice.

title: Difficult Client Escalation Letter
body: Write a formal letter to a client whose [BEHAVIOUR: e.g. repeated out-of-hours demands / non-payment / abusive communication / scope creep demands] has become unsustainable. My business: [TYPE]. What has happened: [DESCRIBE FACTUALLY]. What I'm asking them to change: [SPECIFIC REQUEST]. Consequence if not addressed: [e.g. I'll need to end the contract]. The letter should be: professional, factual, non-emotional, and give them a clear path to resolution. Under 250 words. Formal salutation and sign-off.
whatItIsFor: Communicating formally with a client whose behaviour or demands have gone beyond what's reasonable — before terminating the relationship.
howToUseIt: Document all interactions before writing this letter; keep it factual and keep a copy.

title: Contract Termination Letter
body: Write a contract termination letter for [SERVICE TYPE] ending the relationship with [CLIENT TYPE]. Reason for ending: [REASON — choose: end of natural term / non-payment / mutual decision / behavioural issues / business change]. Notice period: [LENGTH]. Outstanding work status: [WILL COMPLETE / WILL NOT COMPLETE]. Outstanding payments: [DETAILS OR "NONE"]. The letter should: state the decision clearly, reference the relevant contract clause, confirm what's outstanding, and close professionally. Under 200 words. Formal format.
whatItIsFor: Ending a client relationship professionally — with clear terms and no loose ends.
howToUseIt: Always follow the notice period in your contract; if there is no contract, give reasonable written notice.

title: PR Crisis Statement
body: Write a public statement for [BUSINESS NAME] responding to [CRISIS TYPE]. What happened: [DESCRIBE FACTUALLY]. What we're doing about it: [ACTIONS]. What we're doing to prevent it recurring: [PREVENTION]. The statement should: acknowledge the situation clearly, avoid language that admits specific liability (use "we are sorry for the impact" rather than "this was our fault"), show accountability and action, and be in plain English. Under 200 words. No corporate spin.
whatItIsFor: Drafting a public statement for a business crisis that has attracted media or public attention.
howToUseIt: Before publishing, review with a legal adviser for any liability implications — this prompt gives you the structure and language, not legal clearance.

title: Cash Flow Crisis Action Plan
body: I'm facing a potential cash flow crisis. My situation: [DESCRIBE: e.g. a large client has delayed payment / I have a tax bill I can't cover / revenue dropped unexpectedly]. Current cash position: [£AMOUNT]. Projected gap: [£AMOUNT] in [TIMEFRAME]. Help me create a 30-day action plan covering: (1) immediate cash actions (what to collect, defer, or renegotiate), (2) who to call this week, (3) short-term revenue options (new offers, fast-close opportunities), and (4) what to do if the gap can't be closed. Be direct — I need practical options, not reassurance.
whatItIsFor: Creating a structured response to a sudden cash flow problem before it becomes an existential business crisis.
howToUseIt: Run as soon as you see a cash flow gap forming — earlier intervention = more options.

title: Key Person Risk Assessment
body: Help me assess key person risk for my [BUSINESS TYPE] with [NUMBER] staff/contractors. For each of the following people in my business: [LIST NAMES OR ROLES], assess: (1) what they solely own or control, (2) what would break if they were unavailable for 2 weeks, (3) the impact on revenue, (4) the mitigation action needed, and (5) whether I should consider key person insurance for them. Format as a risk table with a priority rating (High / Medium / Low) for each role.
whatItIsFor: Identifying the single points of failure in your business — people whose loss or absence would immediately damage operations.
howToUseIt: Run annually; act on the highest-risk items immediately.

title: Supplier Failure Response Plan
body: Help me plan for the failure of my critical supplier: [SUPPLIER TYPE / WHAT THEY SUPPLY]. What they provide: [DESCRIPTION]. How central they are: [e.g. sole supplier / primary supplier]. What happens to my business if they fail with 0, 7, and 30 days' warning. Include: (1) emergency alternatives (where to source in 48 hours), (2) what to communicate to affected customers and when, (3) how to stock or buffer against this risk in future, and (4) the one contract clause I should add to all supplier agreements to protect me.
whatItIsFor: Responding to a key supplier failing, going bust, or suddenly becoming unavailable — before it cascades into a customer problem.
howToUseIt: Identify your top 3 critical suppliers and run this prompt for each as a preparedness exercise.

title: Bad Debt Recovery Plan
body: Help me recover [£AMOUNT] owed by [CLIENT TYPE] for [SERVICE / PRODUCT]. Invoice date: [DATE]. Due date: [DATE]. Current status: [DAYS OVERDUE]. Previous contact: [DESCRIBE WHAT YOU'VE DONE SO FAR]. I want to [KEEP THE RELATIONSHIP / DO NOT NEED TO KEEP THE RELATIONSHIP]. Write a 4-step escalation sequence: (1) a polite reminder, (2) a firm follow-up with a deadline, (3) a final notice before formal action, and (4) a letter before action. Include subject lines for each step.
whatItIsFor: Recovering unpaid invoices without damaging the relationship (if you want to keep it) or without backing down (if you don't).
howToUseIt: Start the recovery process at day 7 overdue — don't wait 60 days to act.
tokens: DO NOT NEED TO KEEP THE RELATIONSHIP

title: Business Insurance Gap Analysis
body: Help me identify insurance gaps for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Current coverage I have: [LIST POLICIES — e.g. public liability, professional indemnity, employer's liability]. My business activities: [DESCRIBE — e.g. client site visits, online products, physical goods, data handling, sub-contractors]. Based on my activities, identify: (1) risks not covered by my current policies, (2) the 3 most financially dangerous uninsured risks, and (3) the insurance products I should discuss with my broker. Note: this is for guidance — always verify coverage with a qualified insurance broker.
whatItIsFor: Identifying risks your business is exposed to that your current insurance doesn't cover.
howToUseIt: Run annually before renewing your insurance policies — use the output in conversation with your broker.

title: Reputational Recovery Plan
body: Help me build a reputational recovery plan for my [BUSINESS TYPE] following [CRISIS TYPE]. What happened: [DESCRIBE]. Damage caused: [e.g. negative press coverage, drop in reviews, customer complaints, lost clients]. The recovery plan should cover: (1) a 30-day immediate response phase, (2) a 90-day rebuilding phase, and (3) a 6-month normalisation phase. For each phase: 3 specific actions, who they're targeted at, and how to measure progress. Be realistic about timeline — reputation recovery is slow.
whatItIsFor: Rebuilding trust and reputation after a business crisis that has caused public or customer damage.
howToUseIt: Start this plan only after the immediate crisis has been addressed — reputation recovery is a medium-term effort.

title: Grant Opportunity Identifier
body: I run [BUSINESS TYPE] in [LOCATION: town/county/region] with [NUMBER] employees and approximately [£AMOUNT] annual turnover. My business is [YEARS] old. I'm looking to fund [PROJECT: e.g. equipment purchase / staff training / premises upgrade / export development / digital transformation]. Based on this profile, what types of UK grant programmes am I most likely to qualify for? List the grant categories (not specific URLs), the typical funding range, who administers them, and what I should research first. Note: grant availability changes — I'll verify current programmes directly.
whatItIsFor: Identifying which grants and funding programmes your business is most likely to qualify for.
howToUseIt: Fill in your business details accurately — eligibility criteria are specific and worth checking before applying.

title: Grant Eligibility Pre-Check
body: I want to apply for [GRANT NAME]. The eligibility criteria state: [PASTE THE CRITERIA FROM THE GRANT GUIDELINES]. My business: [DESCRIBE — include size, sector, location, age, project type, previous funding received]. Assess: (1) which criteria I clearly meet, (2) which criteria I may not meet, (3) which criteria are ambiguous and need clarification from the funder, and (4) an overall likelihood rating (Strong / Moderate / Unlikely) with a one-line reasoning. Be honest — I don't want to waste my time on an application I won't win.
whatItIsFor: Quickly assessing whether your project genuinely qualifies for a specific grant before investing time in a full application.
howToUseIt: Paste the grant's eligibility criteria from the funder's website directly into this prompt.
tokens: PASTE THE CRITERIA FROM THE GRANT GUIDELINES

title: Grant Application Question Writer
body: Write a grant application answer for this question: "[PASTE THE GRANT QUESTION]". The question is from [GRANT NAME]. My answer should address: [PASTE THE SCORING CRITERIA IF GIVEN, or describe what the funder values]. My relevant information: [PASTE YOUR FACTS — project details, evidence, impact]. Word limit: [NUMBER] words. The answer should be: specific, evidence-led, structured (problem → solution → impact), and written in plain English. Do not pad or repeat.
whatItIsFor: Writing compelling answers to individual grant application questions — the part most applicants rush and lose marks on.
howToUseIt: Paste one question at a time. Read the scoring guidance before writing — if you can see what the assessor is looking for, write to that.
tokens: PASTE THE SCORING CRITERIA IF GIVEN

title: Grant Impact Statement
body: Write an impact statement for a grant application. My project: [DESCRIBE]. The funding amount requested: [£AMOUNT]. Describe the expected impact under 3 categories: (1) direct outputs (what we will create or deliver), (2) direct outcomes (what will change as a result), and (3) wider benefits (who else benefits, how, and when). Use measurable language — numbers, percentages, timescales. Acknowledge what won't happen without the funding. Under 250 words.
whatItIsFor: Writing the impact section of a grant application — demonstrating what will change as a direct result of funding, in measurable terms.
howToUseIt: Funders score impact heavily. Be specific and realistic — overstating impact is flagged by assessors.

title: Business Loan Application Narrative
body: Write a business loan application narrative for [BUSINESS NAME] ([BUSINESS TYPE]). We are applying for [£AMOUNT] over [TERM] for [PURPOSE]. Include: business overview (2 sentences), what the loan will fund (specific and itemised), why now (the opportunity or need driving the timing), how we'll repay (revenue projection basis), and what security or track record supports the application. Under 400 words. Honest and factual — banks can see through optimistic projections.
whatItIsFor: Writing the supporting narrative for a business loan application — the section banks and lenders care about most after the numbers.
howToUseIt: Banks lend to people they trust with a plan they understand — write this to answer their real questions.

title: Crowdfunding Campaign Brief
body: Help me plan a crowdfunding campaign for [PROJECT / PRODUCT] on [PLATFORM: Kickstarter / Crowdfunder / Seedrs / other]. Funding target: [£AMOUNT]. My existing audience: [EMAIL LIST SIZE + SOCIAL FOLLOWING]. Campaign duration: [NUMBER] days. Include: (1) campaign title and one-line pitch, (2) reward tier structure (4–5 tiers), (3) a 4-week promotion plan (what to do before and during the campaign), (4) the three content types that convert best on [PLATFORM], and (5) what % of my target I need to raise from my own network before going public.
whatItIsFor: Planning a crowdfunding campaign that reaches its target — not just a product listing nobody shares.
howToUseIt: Crowdfunding succeeds through community before it launches — plan the audience before the campaign.

title: Match Funding Evidence Pack
body: I am applying for a grant that requires [%] match funding. Total project cost: [£AMOUNT]. Grant requested: [£AMOUNT]. My match funding contribution: [£AMOUNT] from [SOURCE: e.g. own reserves / bank loan / other grant]. Write: (1) a match funding declaration paragraph (for the application form), (2) a list of the evidence documents I should attach, and (3) a brief explanation of how the match funding is confirmed and available. Keep it formal and specific — funders disqualify applications where match funding evidence is weak.
whatItIsFor: Preparing the documentation and narrative to evidence your match funding contribution to a grant application.
howToUseIt: Many grants require you to match-fund a percentage — this prompt helps you present your match funding credibly.

title: Project Budget for Grant Application
body: Help me build a project budget for a grant application for [PROJECT TYPE] with a total cost of [£AMOUNT]. The grant being applied for: [GRANT NAME]. I need the budget to cover: [LIST ITEMS AND ROUGH COSTS]. For each budget line: suggest the correct category (capital / revenue / staff / overhead), confirm what evidence I'll need to support it, and flag any lines that funders typically question or disallow. Output as a budget table with a column for grant-funded amount and match-funded amount.
whatItIsFor: Building a credible, itemised budget for a grant application that stands up to scrutiny.
howToUseIt: Get at least 2 supplier quotes before presenting any cost line — assessors check for market rates.

title: Funder Research Brief
body: Help me research [FUNDER NAME] before applying for their [GRANT NAME] grant. Based on their publicly available information (which I will paste below), help me identify: (1) their 3 stated priority areas, (2) the types of projects they have funded recently (if known), (3) the language and framing they use that I should reflect in my application, and (4) any application mistakes common to this funder that I should avoid. [PASTE FUNDER INFORMATION HERE — annual report excerpts, grant guidelines, funded project descriptions].
whatItIsFor: Researching a grant funder before applying — understanding their priorities makes your application more competitive.
howToUseIt: Read the funder's last 2–3 annual reports and recent grant awards before running this prompt.

title: Grant Rejection Analysis
body: I received a grant rejection for [GRANT NAME]. My application: [BRIEF SUMMARY OF WHAT I APPLIED FOR]. The feedback provided: [PASTE FEEDBACK — or describe "no feedback given"]. Help me: (1) identify the most likely reasons for rejection based on the feedback or common patterns, (2) assess whether the project is re-applicable under this grant or a different one, (3) suggest 3 specific improvements to the application before resubmitting, and (4) identify what evidence or credibility I need to build before applying again.
whatItIsFor: Turning a grant rejection into useful feedback that improves your next application.
howToUseIt: Always request assessor feedback after rejection — most funders will provide it.
tokens: BRIEF SUMMARY OF WHAT I APPLIED FOR

title: SME Loan vs Grant Decision Framework
body: Help me decide the right funding approach for [PROJECT]. Project cost: [£AMOUNT]. My business: [TYPE, AGE, REVENUE]. Timeline: I need the funding in [TIMEFRAME]. I am willing to give up equity: [YES / NO]. My available time for applications: [HOURS]. Compare: (1) grant (likely timeline, application effort, success probability), (2) business loan (likely rate and term, application effort, speed), (3) equity (if relevant), and (4) self-funding from cash flow or savings. Recommend one primary option and one backup. Be direct.
whatItIsFor: Deciding whether to seek a grant, a loan, or equity funding for a specific business need — before spending time on any application.
howToUseIt: The right funding type depends on the project, your business stage, and how much of your time the application is worth.

title: Apprenticeship Funding Brief
body: I run [BUSINESS TYPE] with [NUMBER] employees and an annual payroll of approximately [£AMOUNT]. I'm interested in hiring or upskilling someone using apprenticeship funding. The role or skills I'm looking to develop: [DESCRIBE]. Help me understand: (1) whether I pay the apprenticeship levy or qualify for co-investment, (2) what the government funding covers, (3) how much I'd pay (if anything), (4) the minimum and maximum duration of an apprenticeship in the UK, and (5) how to find an approved training provider for this type of role. Note: verify current rates with GOV.UK as funding rules change.
whatItIsFor: Understanding how to access apprenticeship levy funding (or employer incentives) to fund training for a new or existing hire.
howToUseIt: UK apprenticeship funding is significantly underused by small businesses — this prompt helps you understand what's available before speaking to a training provider.

title: R&D Tax Credit Eligibility Brief
body: Help me assess whether my business activities might qualify for UK R&D tax relief. My business: [TYPE]. Activities we've undertaken in the last financial year: [DESCRIBE — include any product development, new processes, software development, novel methods, or scientific/technical investigation]. I want to understand: (1) what HMRC considers to be qualifying R&D, (2) which of my activities most likely qualify, (3) which clearly don't qualify, and (4) the approximate financial benefit if [£X] of salary costs qualify. Note: always work with an accountant or R&D specialist for the actual claim.
whatItIsFor: Understanding whether your business activities may qualify for R&D tax relief — a significant underused benefit for innovating small businesses.
howToUseIt: This is a research prompt only — R&D claims must be made through your accountant or a specialist R&D adviser.

title: Enterprise Finance Guarantee Briefing
body: I run [BUSINESS TYPE] and have been declined or am unlikely to qualify for a conventional business loan because [REASON: e.g. limited trading history / no assets / thin credit file]. I need [£AMOUNT] for [PURPOSE]. Help me understand: (1) what government-backed loan guarantees (e.g. British Business Bank programmes) are designed for businesses like mine, (2) typical eligibility criteria, (3) which lenders participate, and (4) what I need to prepare before applying. Note: I'll verify current scheme details directly with the British Business Bank or a participating lender.
whatItIsFor: Understanding the UK Government-backed lending schemes available to SMEs who can't access conventional bank finance.
howToUseIt: Use as a research brief before a conversation with a participating lender — don't apply blind.

title: Post-Grant Reporting Brief
body: Help me prepare a grant progress report for [GRANT NAME]. The grant is for [PROJECT]. Original outputs promised: [LIST FROM APPLICATION]. Progress to date: [DESCRIBE WHAT HAS BEEN DONE]. Spend to date: [£AMOUNT] of [£TOTAL GRANT]. Any deviations from the original plan: [DESCRIBE OR "NONE"]. Write: (1) an executive summary (under 100 words), (2) a progress against outputs table, (3) a financial summary narrative, and (4) a note on any deviations and how they've been managed. Professional and factual — funders read dozens of these and reward clarity.
whatItIsFor: Preparing the progress and completion reports most grant funders require — and getting them right so you're not asked for extensions.
howToUseIt: Record project activity and evidence as you go — don't try to reconstruct it at reporting time.

title: CRM Setup Brief for Small Business
body: Help me set up a CRM for my [BUSINESS TYPE] with [NUMBER] active clients. I currently track customers in [CURRENT SYSTEM: e.g. spreadsheet / email / paper]. My main goals: [e.g. track where leads come from / follow up consistently / spot upsell opportunities / reduce churn]. Recommend: (1) the right CRM type for my size and budget (free / under £30/month / enterprise), (2) the 10 most important fields to track, (3) the pipeline stages I need, and (4) the 3 automations I should set up first. I am not technical — keep recommendations practical.
whatItIsFor: Planning the right CRM setup for your business — including which tool to use and what fields to track.
howToUseIt: Don't over-engineer it on day one — start with the minimum fields you'll actually use.

title: Customer Segmentation Framework
body: Help me segment my customer base for [BUSINESS TYPE]. I have approximately [NUMBER] active customers. Key data I have on them: [LIST WHAT YOU KNOW — e.g. purchase frequency, spend value, product type, location, business size, how they found me]. Design a 3–4 segment model based on this data. For each segment: a descriptive name, what characterises them, their estimated value to the business, and what I should do differently for each segment (communication, offer, frequency).
whatItIsFor: Dividing your customer base into meaningful groups so you can communicate and sell differently to each.
howToUseIt: Segmentation is most useful when it leads to different actions — if all segments get the same treatment, segmentation was wasted work.

title: Customer Lifetime Value Calculator
body: Help me calculate customer lifetime value (CLV) for my [BUSINESS TYPE]. Inputs: average purchase value [£AMOUNT], average purchases per year [NUMBER], average customer lifespan [YEARS], average gross margin [%]. Calculate: CLV, and what these numbers mean for my maximum customer acquisition cost (CAC). Also tell me: what a 10% improvement in retention would do to CLV, and what a 10% improvement in average order value would do. Format as a clear calculation with commentary.
whatItIsFor: Understanding how much a typical customer is worth to your business over time — which determines how much you can spend to acquire one.
howToUseIt: Calculate CLV before setting marketing budgets or acquisition costs — without this number, you're guessing.

title: Lapsed Customer Reactivation Campaign
body: Write a reactivation campaign for lapsed customers of my [BUSINESS TYPE] who haven't bought in [TIMEFRAME]. Include: a 3-email sequence (spaced 7 days apart), a win-back offer (use [INCENTIVE] as placeholder), and one final "are you still there?" email if no response after email 3. Each email under 120 words. Subject lines included. Don't guilt-trip — focus on what's new, different, or valuable to them now.
whatItIsFor: Re-engaging customers who haven't purchased in 6–18 months — they're cheaper to win back than acquiring new customers.
howToUseIt: Segment by recency — customers lapsed 6 months need a different approach than those lapsed 18 months.

title: Customer Data Audit
body: Help me audit the quality of my customer data. I'll describe my current data and you identify the gaps, risks, and priorities. My current data fields: [LIST WHAT YOU CURRENTLY RECORD]. My business: [TYPE]. What I want to use the data for: [e.g. targeted emails / renewal reminders / upsell campaigns / GDPR compliance]. Assess: (1) which fields I'm missing that matter most for my goals, (2) any GDPR compliance gaps I should be aware of, (3) data quality issues (duplicates, outdated info, missing consent), and (4) the 3 highest-impact improvements I should make first.
whatItIsFor: Reviewing the quality and completeness of your customer data — identifying gaps that are limiting your ability to sell and serve.
howToUseIt: Pull a sample of 20–30 customer records and assess them against this framework before investing in CRM or marketing automation.

title: GDPR Compliance Checklist for Small Business
body: Generate a GDPR self-assessment checklist for [BUSINESS TYPE] that collects and uses customer personal data for [DESCRIBE USES: e.g. email marketing / booking systems / payment processing]. Create a checklist of 15 practical items covering: lawful basis for data processing, privacy notice, consent records, data retention, data subject rights, breach procedures, and third-party processors. Format as a yes/no checklist with a brief explanation of each item and what to do if the answer is "no".
whatItIsFor: Reviewing your basic GDPR compliance — not a legal audit, but a practical check of the most common small business gaps.
howToUseIt: This is a self-assessment tool, not legal advice. For specific compliance questions, consult a data protection adviser.

title: Customer Purchase Pattern Analysis
body: Help me analyse customer purchase patterns for [BUSINESS TYPE]. Here is a summary of my sales data from the last [TIMEFRAME]: [PASTE OR DESCRIBE — e.g. top 10 products by units, common product combinations, repeat purchase intervals, average order frequency by customer type].
