Identify: (1) the most common product combinations that suggest cross-sell opportunities, (2) the average gap between first and second purchase (and what this means for timing follow-up), (3) any seasonal patterns worth planning for, and (4) the one customer behaviour pattern most worth acting on this quarter.
whatItIsFor: Identifying buying patterns in your customer data that reveal upsell, cross-sell, or timing opportunities.
howToUseIt: Even a 3-month sample of order data is enough to find patterns — you don't need a year of data to start.

title: CRM Pipeline Review Template
body: Create a weekly CRM pipeline review template for [SERVICE / PRODUCT TYPE] with an average deal value of [£AMOUNT] and a typical sales cycle of [DURATION]. The review should cover: pipeline health (total deals, total value, average age), deals to prioritise this week (selection criteria), deals to close off or deprioritise (criteria), follow-up actions needed (by deal), and a forecast for the next 30 days. Format as a structured template I can complete in 15 minutes every Monday morning.
whatItIsFor: Running a weekly pipeline review that identifies which deals to prioritise and which to close off.
howToUseIt: A 15-minute weekly pipeline review beats a monthly one — deals go cold fast at the SME level.

title: Customer Survey Design
body: Design a customer survey for [BUSINESS TYPE] to gather data on [GOAL: e.g. satisfaction / product preferences / reasons for lapsing / purchase barriers]. The survey should: take under 5 minutes to complete, include no more than 8 questions, use a mix of rating scales and open-ended questions, and collect one response that I can use as a testimonial. Write the complete survey including the intro message, all questions, and the thank-you message. Also suggest the best time to send it and the ideal incentive (if any) to improve response rate.
whatItIsFor: Designing a survey that collects genuinely useful data — not 20 questions nobody will finish.
howToUseIt: Keep it under 5 minutes; every extra question reduces completion rate by 10–15%.

title: NPS Follow-Up Action Plan
body: Help me create an action plan based on our NPS survey results. Our overall NPS: [SCORE]. Breakdown: Promoters (9–10): [NUMBER]. Passives (7–8): [NUMBER]. Detractors (0–6): [NUMBER]. Common themes from open-text responses: [PASTE OR SUMMARISE]. For each group: (1) what action to take in the next 7 days, (2) a follow-up message to send, and (3) a systemic improvement suggested by the feedback. Also: how to use our Promoters to generate referrals without being awkward about it.
whatItIsFor: Turning Net Promoter Score results into specific actions — not just a score you note and forget.
howToUseIt: NPS is only useful if you act on it. This prompt maps each response category to a different action.

title: Customer Journey Mapping Brief
body: Help me map the customer journey for [CUSTOMER TYPE] buying [PRODUCT / SERVICE] from [BUSINESS TYPE]. Map 6 stages: (1) Awareness (how they discover us), (2) Consideration (how they evaluate), (3) Purchase (how they buy), (4) Onboarding (first experience), (5) Ongoing use, (6) Advocacy or churn. For each stage: describe the customer's goal, their most common frustration, and the one thing I should do to improve this stage. Format as a table.
whatItIsFor: Mapping the end-to-end experience a customer has with your business — from first awareness to repeat purchase — so you can spot gaps and friction points.
howToUseIt: Map one customer type at a time — a corporate buyer and a consumer have completely different journeys.

title: High-Value Customer Retention Plan
body: Help me build a retention plan for my top [NUMBER] customers in [BUSINESS TYPE]. These customers represent approximately [£AMOUNT] / [%] of my annual revenue. My goal: reduce churn in this group from [CURRENT ESTIMATE]% to [TARGET]% over the next 12 months. Design a retention plan covering: (1) quarterly touchpoints, (2) early warning signals that a top customer might be at risk, (3) a fast-response process when risk is detected, and (4) a value-add programme that makes these customers feel different from average customers.
whatItIsFor: Building a personalised retention strategy for your top 20% of customers who generate 80% of revenue.
howToUseIt: Identify your top customers first (by revenue or profit), then build individual retention plans, not generic ones.

title: Email List Health Review
body: Help me review the health of my email list for [BUSINESS TYPE]. List size: [NUMBER]. Current average open rate: [%]. Current average click rate: [%]. Unsubscribe rate per campaign: [%]. Bounce rate: [%]. Last cleaned: [DATE / "never"]. Assess: (1) how my rates compare to benchmarks for my sector, (2) what the data tells me about list health, (3) a step-by-step list cleaning process, and (4) a re-engagement campaign for subscribers who haven't opened in 90+ days before removing them.
whatItIsFor: Assessing the health of your email list and planning a clean-up that improves deliverability and engagement rates.
howToUseIt: Run quarterly. A smaller, engaged list is worth more than a large, disengaged one — low open rates hurt your sender reputation.

title: Customer Feedback Loop System
body: Design a continuous customer feedback loop for [BUSINESS TYPE]. I want feedback collected automatically at key moments in the customer journey. Include: (1) 3 moments to trigger an automated feedback request and what to ask at each moment, (2) how to collect and store feedback (tool recommendation), (3) how to review feedback as a regular process (monthly cadence), and (4) how to close the loop with customers who give negative feedback. Keep the system simple enough to maintain solo.
whatItIsFor: Building a continuous feedback collection system so you always know what customers think — without running a survey every quarter.
howToUseIt: Set this up once; it then runs automatically. Review the aggregated feedback monthly.

title: Customer Data Privacy Policy (Plain English)
body: Write a plain-English privacy notice for [BUSINESS NAME] ([BUSINESS TYPE]). We collect: [LIST DATA TYPES — e.g. name, email, payment details, health information, IP address]. We use this data for: [LIST PURPOSES — e.g. delivering our service, email marketing, invoicing, analytics]. We share data with: [LIST THIRD PARTIES — e.g. payment processor, email platform, accounting software]. We keep data for: [RETENTION PERIOD]. The notice should cover lawful basis, data rights (access, deletion, correction), and how to complain to the ICO. Under 500 words. Clear and accessible — no legalese.
whatItIsFor: Writing a simple, readable privacy notice for your website that fulfils your UK GDPR obligation to inform customers what you do with their data.
howToUseIt: This is a starting point — have a solicitor or data protection specialist review it before publishing if you handle sensitive data.

title: Win-Back Email Based on Purchase History
body: Write a win-back email for a lapsed customer of my [BUSINESS TYPE] who last purchased [PRODUCT / SERVICE] [TIMEFRAME] ago. What they bought: [DESCRIBE LAST PURCHASE]. Why they might have lapsed: [REASON IF KNOWN / GUESSED]. What I want to offer them: [OFFER OR INCENTIVE]. The email should: reference their specific purchase (not generic), offer something relevant to what they bought before, and feel like it was written by a person who noticed they were gone. Under 120 words. Subject line included.
whatItIsFor: Writing highly targeted win-back emails using a customer's specific purchase history — far more effective than generic reactivation campaigns.
howToUseIt: Pull the customer's last 2–3 purchases and reference them specifically in the email — personalisation at this level stands out.

title: Upsell Opportunity Identifier
body: I want to upsell [NEW PRODUCT / SERVICE] to existing customers of my [BUSINESS TYPE]. My current product/service they use: [DESCRIBE]. The upsell: [DESCRIBE NEW OFFER]. Help me: (1) define the customer profile most likely to want the upsell (what signals in their behaviour or situation indicate readiness), (2) write a shortlist of qualifying questions to identify the best candidates, (3) write an outreach message for those candidates (email under 80 words), and (4) identify any customers who should NOT be approached for this upsell and why.
whatItIsFor: Systematically identifying which customers are most likely to buy an additional product or service — so you prioritise the right conversations.
howToUseIt: Run this before a sales push to an existing list; use it to prioritise outreach rather than spray-and-pray.

title: Customer Persona Builder from CRM Data
body: Help me build customer personas from my CRM data. I'll describe my top 3 customer segments: [DESCRIBE EACH GROUP — include demographics, purchase behaviour, how they found you, what they say in emails/calls, what they struggle with, what they love]. For each segment, build a persona including: name (fictional), background summary, primary goal, main frustration with businesses like mine, how they make decisions, what messaging resonates, and what would make them churn. One page per persona.
whatItIsFor: Building realistic customer personas from your actual CRM data — not hypothetical audience profiles.
howToUseIt: Data-based personas are dramatically more useful than invented ones — always base these on real customer patterns.

title: Customer Retention Scorecard
body: Design a customer retention scorecard for [BUSINESS TYPE] with [NUMBER] active clients. The scorecard should give each customer a health score (0–100) based on: recency of engagement, payment history, product usage, response to communications, and satisfaction rating. For each dimension: define what data to use, how to score it (0–20 points per dimension), and what score thresholds indicate risk (green / amber / red). Also: what action to take at each threshold.
whatItIsFor: Building a simple health score for each customer that tells you at a glance who's at risk before they cancel or churn.
howToUseIt: Assign the score monthly; flag any customer dropping below 60 points for immediate attention.

title: Customer Data Migration Plan
body: Help me plan a customer data migration from [CURRENT SYSTEM: e.g. spreadsheet / old CRM / paper records] to [NEW SYSTEM]. I have approximately [NUMBER] customer records. My main concern: [e.g. not losing contact history / maintaining GDPR compliance / not disrupting active customers]. Create a migration plan including: (1) data audit before migration, (2) field mapping (what goes where), (3) data cleaning steps, (4) migration sequence (what to migrate first), (5) testing and validation, and (6) rollback plan if something goes wrong. Keep it practical — I'm doing this without a developer.
whatItIsFor: Moving customer data from one system to another without losing records, breaking compliance, or disrupting service.
howToUseIt: Plan the migration before you start — data migrations that happen without a plan typically lose 10–20% of records and take 3× longer than expected.

title: AI Automation Opportunity Audit
body: Help me audit my business for AI automation opportunities. I run [BUSINESS TYPE] and my main daily/weekly tasks are: [LIST 10–15 TASKS — e.g. writing emails, booking appointments, answering FAQs, creating social posts, generating invoices, data entry, following up leads]. For each task, assess: (1) automation feasibility (High / Medium / Low / Not suitable), (2) the AI or automation tool best suited, (3) estimated time saved per week, and (4) the risk of over-relying on automation for this task. Rank by total impact (time saved × feasibility).
whatItIsFor: Identifying which tasks in your business are best suited for AI automation — before wasting time on the wrong ones.
howToUseIt: Be honest about what tasks are truly repetitive vs what requires your judgement — AI works best on the former.

title: AI-Powered Customer FAQ Bot Design
body: Help me design an AI customer FAQ bot for [BUSINESS TYPE]. My most common customer questions are: [LIST 10–15 QUESTIONS YOU GET REGULARLY]. For each question, write: (1) the ideal answer (concise, accurate, in brand voice), (2) a follow-up question the bot should ask if the customer wants more detail, and (3) a handoff trigger phrase (when the conversation should go to a human). Also recommend the simplest tool to build this for a non-technical small business owner.
whatItIsFor: Building a chatbot that answers your most common customer questions automatically — without coding.
howToUseIt: The quality of your FAQ bot is only as good as the questions and answers you feed it — spend time on the content before the tool.

title: Email Automation Workflow Builder
body: Design an email automation workflow for [BUSINESS TYPE] triggered by [TRIGGER EVENT: e.g. new sign-up / purchase / booking / form submission / no purchase in 60 days]. The workflow should have [NUMBER] emails over [TIMEFRAME]. For each email: trigger (when it sends), subject line, email body (under 120 words), and the goal of this specific email in the sequence. Also: what to do if someone replies (should it stop the automation? who sees the reply?). Keep the workflow practical for a small business using [PLATFORM: e.g. Mailchimp / Klaviyo / ConvertKit].
whatItIsFor: Designing an automated email workflow that sends the right email at the right time without manual intervention.
howToUseIt: Map the trigger before writing the emails — the trigger determines whether the automation is useful or annoying.

title: AI Content Repurposing Pipeline
body: Design an AI-assisted content repurposing pipeline for [BUSINESS TYPE] starting from [ORIGINAL CONTENT TYPE: e.g. blog post / podcast episode / webinar / long-form video]. Map how one piece of content becomes: (1) 3 social media posts, (2) 1 email newsletter section, (3) 1 short-form video script (Reel / Short), (4) 1 LinkedIn post, and (5) a quote graphic. For each format: which AI tool to use, which prompt to run (write the prompt), and how long each step takes a non-technical operator. Total pipeline should save at least 4 hours vs doing this manually.
whatItIsFor: Building a semi-automated system for turning one piece of content into 5+ different formats.
howToUseIt: The pipeline is most efficient when you do the "thinking" content once (long-form) and let AI do the repurposing.

title: Automated Booking & Appointment System Design
body: Design an automated booking system for [BUSINESS TYPE] offering [SERVICE TYPE]. I currently book appointments via [CURRENT METHOD: e.g. email / phone / manually]. I want to automate: availability display, booking confirmation, reminder emails/SMS, cancellation handling, and follow-up after the appointment. Recommend: (1) the right booking tool for my size and budget, (2) the confirmation and reminder sequence (with timing), (3) what happens when someone cancels, and (4) how to integrate this with my calendar and payment system.
whatItIsFor: Planning an automated booking system that eliminates back-and-forth scheduling emails.
howToUseIt: Removes 2–4 hours of admin per week for most service businesses — one of the highest-ROI automations available.

title: AI-Assisted Proposal Generator Setup
body: Help me design a semi-automated proposal generation system for [SERVICE TYPE]. The system should: (1) use a standardised post-call intake form (design the form fields), (2) include a master prompt I can run with the form data to generate a first-draft proposal, (3) take under 15 minutes from form submission to draft proposal. Write the intake form (10 fields max) and the master proposal prompt that uses the form data as inputs. The output should be a proposal that needs 10–15 minutes of personalisation, not a full rewrite.
whatItIsFor: Building a semi-automated proposal system that produces a personalised draft in under 10 minutes after a discovery call.
howToUseIt: The key is a good intake form or call notes template that captures the right information — the AI does the writing.

title: Social Media Scheduling Automation
body: Design a weekly social media automation system for [BUSINESS TYPE] posting on [PLATFORMS]. I want to go from spending [CURRENT TIME] per week to under 90 minutes. The system should cover: content batching (how to create a week's content in one session), AI tools for caption writing and image creation, scheduling tool recommendation, and a weekly template (what day to do what). Also: what content should NOT be automated (e.g. real-time engagement, genuine stories).
whatItIsFor: Setting up a weekly content scheduling system that reduces social media management to a 90-minute weekly block.
howToUseIt: Batch creation + scheduled posting is 3× more efficient than daily posting — this prompt helps you design the system.

title: Invoice & Payment Automation Setup
body: Help me design an automated invoicing and payment chasing system for [BUSINESS TYPE]. I invoice [FREQUENCY] and currently spend [HOURS] chasing late payments. The system should include: (1) invoice trigger and template (when and how invoices are sent), (2) automated payment reminders (timing and message), (3) overdue escalation (what happens at 7, 14, 30 days overdue), and (4) confirmation when paid. Recommend a tool that handles all of this if my current setup doesn't. Write the reminder message for the day-7 overdue email.
whatItIsFor: Automating your invoicing and payment chasing so late payments are caught early without awkward manual follow-ups.
howToUseIt: Most accounting software already has this capability — this prompt helps you use what you likely already have.

title: AI Writing Style Guide
body: Help me create a reusable AI writing style guide for [BUSINESS NAME / BRAND]. Analyse these samples of my existing writing (paste 3–5 examples of your best written content — emails, captions, website copy) and extract: (1) tone characteristics (5 adjectives), (2) sentence structure patterns, (3) vocabulary preferences (words I use / words I avoid), (4) structural patterns (how I open, how I close), and (5) formatting preferences. Then write this as a "writing brief" I can paste into any AI prompt to get consistent output.
whatItIsFor: Training AI tools to write in your brand's specific voice — so all AI-generated content sounds like you, not generic ChatGPT.
howToUseIt: This guide becomes the opening of every content prompt you run — paste it in before any writing task.

title: Lead Qualification Automation
body: Design an automated lead qualification system for [BUSINESS TYPE]. I currently receive approximately [NUMBER] enquiries per week. I want to automatically: collect key qualification information, score leads by fit, route qualified leads to my booking system, and send a polite decline to unqualified ones. Design: (1) the intake form (8 questions max), (2) the scoring criteria (what makes a lead qualified vs not), (3) the auto-response for qualified leads (book a call), and (4) the auto-response for unqualified leads (redirect gracefully).
whatItIsFor: Setting up an automated system to qualify inbound leads before they reach you — so you only spend time on the right ones.
howToUseIt: Works best when your lead volume is high enough to make qualification worth automating (10+ enquiries per week).

title: Automated Client Onboarding System
body: Design an automated client onboarding system for [SERVICE TYPE]. When a new client signs a contract, the system should: send a welcome email, collect onboarding information via a form, send the signed agreement, schedule the kickoff call, and send a pre-kickoff preparation email. Map the automation flow (trigger → steps → timing) and write the copy for: (1) the welcome email, (2) the onboarding form intro, and (3) the pre-kickoff email. Recommend the simplest tool stack to make this work without a developer.
whatItIsFor: Removing the manual work from client onboarding while maintaining a personal feel.
howToUseIt: The onboarding system should collect information, send documents, and set expectations — without you manually managing each step.

title: AI-Powered Report Generator
body: Write a prompt I can reuse every month to turn my [REPORT TYPE: e.g. social media metrics / sales data / website analytics] into a readable narrative report. The report is for [AUDIENCE: e.g. myself / a client / a board]. Data I'll paste in each month: [DESCRIBE THE DATA FORMAT — columns, metrics]. The report should: summarise performance vs last month, highlight 3 key findings, flag 1 concern or risk, and end with 2 recommended actions. Also write the master prompt I paste into Claude each month with the data.
whatItIsFor: Turning raw data (sales figures, website analytics, social metrics) into a readable narrative report automatically.
howToUseIt: Paste your raw data into this prompt and get a written report in seconds — useful for monthly client reports, internal reviews, or stakeholder updates.

title: Zapier/Make Workflow Design Brief
body: Help me design an automation workflow for [BUSINESS TYPE]. The problem I want to solve: [DESCRIBE — e.g. "when someone fills in my contact form, I want them automatically added to my CRM and sent a welcome email"]. Tools involved: [LIST YOUR APPS — e.g. Typeform, HubSpot, Mailchimp, Google Sheets, Slack]. Map the complete workflow as: trigger → filter conditions (if any) → action 1 → action 2 → action 3. Flag any steps that might fail silently and need error handling. Recommend whether to use Zapier or Make (n8n) for this specific workflow and why.
whatItIsFor: Planning an automation workflow before you build it in Zapier or Make — saving hours of trial and error.
howToUseIt: Map the "if X then Y" logic in plain English first. Only then open Zapier.

title: AI Customer Service Response System
body: Create an AI-assisted customer service response system for [BUSINESS TYPE]. My 5 most common customer service scenarios are: [LIST]. For each scenario: (1) write a template response (under 80 words), (2) identify the tone (apologetic / informative / firm / warm), (3) add a personalisation instruction ("[PERSONALISE: add the specific order number/name/date here]"), and (4) note when NOT to use the template and escalate to a human. Format as a quick-reference guide my team can use without training.
whatItIsFor: Building a library of AI-assisted response templates for your most common customer service scenarios — so your team responds consistently and quickly.
howToUseIt: Create templates for the top 10 scenarios; update quarterly as new issues emerge.

title: AI-Assisted Hiring Workflow
body: Design an AI-assisted hiring workflow for [ROLE TYPE] in [BUSINESS TYPE]. The workflow should cover: (1) AI-drafted job post (write it), (2) a structured application form (10 questions max), (3) a scoring rubric for shortlisting applications (what to weight and how), (4) a first-round interview question set (8 questions), and (5) a reference check question template. Flag where AI should assist and where human judgment must be applied. The goal: reduce hiring admin by 60% without reducing quality.
whatItIsFor: Using AI to speed up the hiring process — from job post to shortlisting — without losing quality.
howToUseIt: AI can draft, filter, and score — but final hiring decisions must be human. Use AI to eliminate the admin, not the judgment.

title: AI-Powered Knowledge Base Builder
body: Help me build an AI-assisted internal knowledge base for [BUSINESS TYPE] with [NUMBER] staff. I want to document: [LIST AREAS — e.g. how we handle client complaints / our onboarding process / common software issues / brand guidelines / pricing policies]. For each area: (1) write the knowledge base article title, (2) the structure I should follow for each article, and (3) a prompt I can run to generate a first draft of any article using information I paste in. Also recommend the simplest tool to host the knowledge base for a small team (under £20/month).
whatItIsFor: Building a searchable internal knowledge base for your team — so information is documented once and found fast.
howToUseIt: Start with your most frequently asked internal questions — the ones you answer repeatedly via Slack, email, or verbally.

title: AI Performance Review System
body: Design an AI-assisted performance review system for [BUSINESS TYPE] with [NUMBER] employees. Include: (1) a self-assessment form for employees to complete before the review (8 questions), (2) a manager review form (aligned to the same dimensions), (3) a prompt to run before each review that summarises the employee's year based on notes I paste in, and (4) the agenda for a 45-minute review meeting. Flag how to keep the process legally defensible (documented, consistent, based on observable behaviour).
whatItIsFor: Using AI to help you structure and run fair, consistent employee performance reviews — saving time while improving quality.
howToUseIt: AI drafts the framework and supporting materials; the manager conducts the conversation and makes the judgments.

title: AI-Powered Product Description Generator
body: Design an AI system for generating product descriptions for my [PRODUCT TYPE] shop on [PLATFORM: Shopify / Etsy / WooCommerce / other]. I list approximately [NUMBER] new products per [FREQUENCY]. Create: (1) a product information template (what details I fill in for each product before running the AI), (2) a master prompt that turns that template into a product description optimised for [GOAL: conversions / SEO / both], and (3) a checklist of things to review before publishing. The descriptions should be [LENGTH] and match my brand voice: [DESCRIBE IN 3 WORDS].
whatItIsFor: Creating an efficient system for generating high-quality product descriptions at scale — useful for shops with large or frequently changing inventory.
howToUseIt: Build a product information template first — the AI output is only as good as the structured input you give it.

title: AI Business Dashboard Design
body: Design a weekly business dashboard for [BUSINESS TYPE] that I can review in 10 minutes every Monday. Include: the 8 most important metrics to track (across revenue, customers, and operations), data sources for each metric (where to pull the number from), target or benchmark for each metric, and a simple weekly review prompt I can run in Claude after pasting in the week's numbers. Format the dashboard as a table I can build in Google Sheets or Notion.
whatItIsFor: Designing a simple AI-assisted business dashboard that gives you a weekly view of what's working and what isn't — in under 10 minutes per week.
howToUseIt: The dashboard works best when data feeds are automated — manual dashboards get abandoned.

title: AI-Powered Competitive Intelligence System
body: Design an AI-powered competitive intelligence system for [BUSINESS TYPE] monitoring [NUMBER] competitors: [LIST COMPETITOR NAMES / TYPES]. The system should track: pricing changes, new service or product launches, content strategy shifts, customer reviews, and hiring signals. For each competitor, specify: (1) where to find intelligence (website, social, review sites, LinkedIn, job boards), (2) how often to check, (3) what to record. Also write a monthly competitive review prompt I can run in Claude after gathering data from these sources.
whatItIsFor: Building a lightweight system to monitor what competitors are doing — so you can respond to market changes without spending hours researching.
howToUseIt: Set up the monitoring sources once; review outputs monthly. Most useful when you have 3–5 direct competitors.

title: Annual Seasonal Calendar Builder
body: Build a seasonal marketing and trading calendar for [BUSINESS TYPE] covering the full year. Include: (1) all UK seasonal opportunities relevant to my business (retail calendar moments, B2B cycles, industry-specific peaks), (2) the 3 highest-revenue periods and why, (3) the 3 quietest periods and what to do during them (build / save / promote), and (4) for each season: what to start planning 8 weeks before. Format as a month-by-month table with an action column. Prioritise by impact, not just date order.
whatItIsFor: Mapping your whole year of seasonal opportunities in one session — so nothing creeps up on you.
howToUseIt: Run in Q4 for the following year; mark the 3 highest-value periods in your business before starting.

title: Peak Season Campaign Planner
body: Create a full campaign plan for [BUSINESS TYPE] targeting [PEAK SEASON: e.g. Christmas / Valentine's Day / Back to School / Black Friday / Summer]. The season runs from [START DATE] to [END DATE]. My campaign goal: [GOAL — e.g. increase bookings by 30% / sell [X] units / generate [£X] revenue]. Include: week-by-week campaign phases (awareness → interest → conversion → urgency → close), content themes for each phase, email timing, social post cadence, and the one promotion or offer that will anchor the campaign. Start planning 8 weeks before the season.
whatItIsFor: Planning the full marketing campaign for your highest-value seasonal period — from awareness to close.
howToUseIt: Run 8–10 weeks before the season starts. The earlier you plan, the more of the peak you capture.

title: Quiet Period Revenue Strategy
body: My [BUSINESS TYPE] typically experiences a quiet period from [MONTH] to [MONTH]. Revenue typically drops to approximately [£AMOUNT] during this period vs [£AMOUNT] at peak. Help me create a quiet season strategy that: (1) identifies 2–3 revenue opportunities specific to this period, (2) plans one "build" project to complete (system, product, or content), (3) reduces fixed costs where possible without damaging capacity, and (4) prepares a plan that capitalises on the next peak faster. Be specific — not generic "focus on retention" advice.
whatItIsFor: Turning your slow season from a cash drain into a productive period that sets up the next peak.
howToUseIt: The best businesses use quiet periods strategically — not as downtime, but as build time.

title: Black Friday / Seasonal Sale Designer
body: Design a [SALE TYPE: Black Friday / Summer Sale / End of Season / anniversary] promotion for [BUSINESS TYPE]. I sell [PRODUCT / SERVICE] at [£PRICE]. My margin is [%]. I don't want to devalue the brand or train customers to expect discounts. Design: (1) the promotion mechanic (discount / bundle / bonus / early access — which works best for my business type), (2) the offer itself (specific and bounded), (3) the promotional timeline (pre-sale, sale, close), and (4) the messaging that frames the promotion as exclusive or logical, not desperate.
whatItIsFor: Designing a promotional sale that generates revenue without devaluing your brand or training customers to wait for discounts.
howToUseIt: Discounts should be time-limited, clearly justified, and part of a bigger strategy — not a permanent price reduction disguised as a sale.

title: Seasonal Stock & Capacity Plan
body: Help me plan stock and capacity for [BUSINESS TYPE] ahead of [PEAK SEASON]. Last year's peak: [DESCRIBE — e.g. sold X units / had Y bookings / revenue was £Z]. This year's expected growth: [%]. My lead time for stock or staffing changes: [TIMEFRAME]. Create: (1) a target stock or capacity level, (2) a reorder/rehire trigger point (the number that triggers action), (3) a contingency for demand exceeding forecast by 20%, and (4) a minimum stock/capacity floor to avoid wastage if demand is 20% below forecast.
whatItIsFor: Planning stock levels or service capacity to meet seasonal demand without overstocking or turning customers away.
howToUseIt: Base projections on last year's actual figures — even rough data is better than pure guesswork.

title: Seasonal Email Campaign Sequence
body: Write a [NUMBER]-email seasonal campaign sequence for [BUSINESS TYPE] targeting [SEASONAL MOMENT]. The sequence runs over [DURATION]. Email 1: [TIMING] — teaser. Email 2: [TIMING] — main offer. Email 3: [TIMING] — social proof or story. Email 4: [TIMING] — urgency/last chance. Email 5 (optional): [TIMING] — post-season thank you + bridge to next offer. Each email under 150 words. Subject lines included. Tone: [DESCRIBE — e.g. warm and excited / direct and no-fuss / playful].
whatItIsFor: Writing a complete email sequence for a seasonal moment — from teaser to post-season follow-up.
howToUseIt: Write the whole sequence before the season starts; schedule it in advance so you're not writing under pressure.

title: Post-Season Review Template
body: Help me run a post-season review for [BUSINESS TYPE] following [PEAK SEASON]. Provide a structured review template covering: (1) revenue vs target (and why it was above or below), (2) operational successes and failures, (3) customer feedback themes, (4) what I'd do differently with 4 extra weeks of preparation, (5) what I'd do the same next year, and (6) 3 specific actions to take before the next planning cycle. Format as a document I can fill in and save for next year's planning. Under 400 words of prompts.
whatItIsFor: Capturing lessons from a peak trading period while they're fresh — so next year's planning is based on reality.
howToUseIt: Do this within 2 weeks of the season ending, not months later when details have faded.

title: New Year / January Campaign Planner
body: Design a January campaign for [BUSINESS TYPE] that capitalises on New Year intent. My target customer's most common New Year resolution related to what I offer: [DESCRIBE]. My January offer: [OFFER OR INCENTIVE]. Campaign duration: first 3 weeks of January. Include: the campaign angle (link to resolution without being cliché), email subject lines for 3 emails (1 Jan, 7 Jan, 14 Jan), a social content theme for January, and the one piece of content that will perform best for me this month.
whatItIsFor: Planning a January campaign that capitalises on New Year motivation — instead of hibernating because "nobody buys in January".
howToUseIt: January is one of the highest-intent months for many categories. Be ready on 2 January, not 15 January.

title: Summer Slow-Down Survival Plan
body: My [BUSINESS TYPE] typically slows significantly in [SUMMER MONTHS]. Last year's revenue drop: approximately [%] vs average months. I have [NUMBER] staff / contractors to keep busy. Help me plan a summer survival strategy covering: (1) 3 revenue activities that work even when clients are on holiday, (2) how to use the slower period productively (what to build or fix), (3) a cash flow bridge plan if revenue drops more than expected, and (4) a September relaunch plan to accelerate recovery. Be realistic about what's achievable with a reduced-capacity client base.
whatItIsFor: Managing cash flow and maintaining revenue through the summer quiet period for businesses that slow down in July–August.
howToUseIt: Particularly useful for B2B service businesses where client decision-making slows significantly in summer.

title: Seasonal Pricing Strategy
body: Help me design a seasonal pricing strategy for [BUSINESS TYPE]. My current pricing: [DESCRIBE — flat rate or tiered]. My peak season(s): [MONTHS]. My quiet season(s): [MONTHS]. I want to: charge more at peak without losing customers, use quiet season pricing to stimulate demand rather than just cut prices, and be transparent with customers about how pricing works. Design: (1) a peak / off-peak pricing structure, (2) how to communicate the change, (3) an early booking incentive for peak periods, and (4) a quiet season offer that doesn't undercut the perceived value of peak pricing.
whatItIsFor: Setting prices that fluctuate with seasonal demand — so you earn more during peak periods without competing on price during quiet ones.
howToUseIt: Seasonal pricing only works if it's communicated clearly in advance and customers understand the logic.

title: Local SEO Optimisation Brief
body: Help me optimise the local SEO for [BUSINESS NAME], a [BUSINESS TYPE] located in [TOWN / AREA]. My target customer searches for [DESCRIBE SEARCH TERMS: e.g. "dog groomer near me" / "independent coffee shop Manchester"]. Audit these areas and give me a prioritised action list: (1) Google Business Profile optimisation (what to add/update), (2) website local SEO (page titles, content, schema), (3) local citation building (directories to list on), and (4) review strategy (how to get more Google reviews faster). Rank actions by estimated impact. I am not technical — keep all actions practical.
whatItIsFor: Improving how your physical business appears in local Google searches — the most direct driver of footfall for local businesses.
howToUseIt: Run this before doing any local SEO work — it tells you what to fix in priority order.

title: Visual Merchandising Brief
body: Create a visual merchandising brief for my [STORE TYPE]. My store is [DESCRIBE LAYOUT: e.g. open-plan / boutique / small frontage]. My highest-margin products are: [LIST 3–5]. My average transaction value is [£AMOUNT] and I want to increase it to [£AMOUNT]. Design: (1) window display concept for this season, (2) product placement strategy (where to put what and why), (3) a cross-sell display idea (grouping complementary items), and (4) a till-point upsell display. Include one cost I can eliminate by moving an underperforming display.
whatItIsFor: Planning in-store displays that guide customers towards higher-margin products and increase average transaction value.
howToUseIt: Refresh your visual merchandising plan every 4–6 weeks — static displays stop being noticed.

title: Footfall Campaign for Quiet Periods
body: Design a footfall campaign for my [STORE TYPE] to increase visits during [QUIET PERIOD: e.g. weekday mornings / January / school holidays]. My current footfall at this time: approximately [NUMBER] visitors/day. I want to reach [TARGET]. My existing customer base: [DESCRIPTION AND APPROXIMATE SIZE]. Design: (1) an offer or event that gives people a reason to visit specifically at this time, (2) how to promote it (channels and messaging), and (3) a way to capture data from people who do visit so I can market to them again. No "10% off everything" — I need something more creative.
whatItIsFor: Driving in-store visits during low-footfall times — weekday mornings, January, or off-season months.
howToUseIt: Target your existing loyal customers first — they're already inclined to visit and easier to motivate.

title: Google Business Profile Post Calendar
body: Create a 4-week Google Business Profile post calendar for [BUSINESS TYPE] located in [LOCATION]. Include 1 post per week covering these types: (1) a product or service spotlight, (2) an event or in-store moment, (3) a customer story or review highlight, (4) a seasonal or local-relevance post. For each post: write the copy (under 100 words), suggest a photo subject, and include a call-to-action button type (Call / Book / Visit). Posts should feel local and human — not corporate.
whatItIsFor: Planning a month of Google Business Profile posts that improve local search visibility and give customers a reason to visit.
howToUseIt: GBP posts have a 7-day lifespan before they're deprioritised — post at least weekly.

title: In-Store Event Planner
body: Plan an in-store event for [STORE TYPE] in [LOCATION]. My goal: [GOAL — e.g. introduce new product line / attract a new customer segment / drive sales in a quiet period / build community]. Budget: [£AMOUNT]. Expected attendance: [NUMBER]. Provide: (1) event concept and format, (2) promotion plan (who to invite and how), (3) the in-store setup needed, (4) what to sell or offer at the event, (5) how to capture leads or data from attendees, and (6) the follow-up action the next day.
whatItIsFor: Planning an in-store event that drives footfall, builds community, and generates social media content.
howToUseIt: Events don't need to be large — 12 engaged people is more valuable than 50 disengaged ones.

title: Retail Customer Loyalty Programme
body: Design a loyalty programme for my [STORE TYPE] with an average transaction value of [£AMOUNT]. I want to increase repeat visit frequency from [CURRENT FREQUENCY] to [TARGET FREQUENCY]. My margin is [%]. Design: (1) the programme mechanics (stamps / points / tiers / spend-based), (2) the reward (what they earn and when), (3) how to introduce it to existing customers, (4) how to handle the "nearly there" moment to drive the next visit, and (5) what data I'll collect from the programme. Make sure the reward cost is sustainable at scale.
whatItIsFor: Designing a loyalty programme that increases repeat visit frequency without training customers to only shop when there's a reward.
howToUseIt: Simple paper stamp cards still outperform complex digital systems for most independent retailers — don't over-engineer.

title: Competitor High Street Audit
body: Help me run a high street competitor audit for [BUSINESS TYPE] in [LOCATION]. I have [NUMBER] direct competitors within [DISTANCE]. For each competitor, I'll assess: window display, pricing visibility, staff greeting, product range, Google reviews, and social presence. Create: (1) a scoring rubric (1–5 per dimension), (2) a gap analysis (where I'm weakest vs competitors), (3) 3 differentiation opportunities nobody in my area is currently exploiting, and (4) the one thing I should change in the next 2 weeks to improve relative to competitors.
whatItIsFor: Understanding how you compare to nearby competitors from a customer's perspective — so you can differentiate on the things that matter.
howToUseIt: Walk the high street as a customer, not a business owner. Look at what draws you in — and what puts you off.

title: Click & Collect Campaign
body: Design a click and collect launch or promotion campaign for [STORE TYPE]. I currently have [ONLINE SHOP PLATFORM]. In-store collection point: [DESCRIBE]. Average online order value: [£AMOUNT]. Average in-store order value: [£AMOUNT]. The campaign should: promote the convenience benefit, give customers a reason to choose collection over delivery, and design the in-store collection experience to encourage an additional purchase. Write: the launch email, a social post, and a 30-word in-store collection point sign.
whatItIsFor: Launching or promoting a click and collect service to bridge your online and in-store customer base.
howToUseIt: Click and collect drives store visits from customers who wouldn't otherwise come in — and in-store upsells when they collect.

title: Retail Staff Training Script
body: Write a retail staff training script for [STORE TYPE] covering these 4 skills: (1) greeting customers without being pushy (the first 30 seconds), (2) asking open questions to understand what they need, (3) recommending a product with a reason (not just "this is popular"), and (4) handling "I'm just looking" and turning it into a conversation. For each skill: write the script with example dialogue, a do/don't comparison, and a 1-sentence principle. Keep total length under 600 words — this is for reading, not a manual.
whatItIsFor: Writing a training script for retail staff covering the core skills that directly affect sales and customer experience.
howToUseIt: Use for new staff inductions and as a refresher for existing team — record as a short video if you have remote or part-time staff.

title: Product Range Review Brief
body: Help me review the product range for my [STORE TYPE]. I'll share my sales data: [DESCRIBE OR PASTE — top 10 products by units, top 10 by revenue, slowest 10 by units, slowest 10 by margin]. Analyse: (1) which products to keep and invest in, (2) which to discontinue or reduce, (3) which product categories are under-represented relative to demand, and (4) one new product or category I should test based on what's working. Format as a decision table: Keep / Grow / Reduce / Exit.
whatItIsFor: Systematically reviewing your product range to eliminate underperformers and identify what to stock more of.
howToUseIt: Run quarterly. Most retailers are stocking too many products that earn too little — simplification improves both margins and the customer experience.

title: Shopify / E-Commerce Email List Growth Plan
body: Design an email list growth plan for my [STORE TYPE] that captures email addresses from physical store visitors. I currently have [NUMBER] email subscribers. I want to reach [TARGET]. Design 3 email capture methods that work in a physical store: (1) at the till, (2) via a loyalty scheme, (3) through an event or competition. For each method: write the script or sign copy, estimate the weekly capture rate, and describe how to segment new subscribers based on how they joined. Also: the first email to send within 24 hours of sign-up.
whatItIsFor: Growing your email list from your physical store — so you have a direct line to customers beyond their in-store visit.
howToUseIt: The in-store email capture moment is underused by most independent retailers — this prompt fixes that.

title: Shop Layout Optimisation Brief
body: Help me evaluate and improve the layout of my [STORE TYPE]. My floor plan: [DESCRIBE — include approximate dimensions, entrance location, till position, and current product zones]. My highest-margin products are located: [DESCRIBE CURRENT PLACEMENT]. My observation: [DESCRIBE WHAT YOU NOTICE — e.g. customers rarely go past the mid-point / the till queue blocks the gift section / the window display doesn't match what's inside]. Provide: (1) a depower zone audit, (2) 3 specific layout changes, (3) the optimal till placement for impulse purchases, and (4) one sightline to create from the entrance.
whatItIsFor: Evaluating your shop layout to improve the customer journey, dwell time, and average spend.
howToUseIt: Small layout changes — moving a display, changing a sightline — can increase revenue significantly without any stock or staffing cost.

title: Local Business Partnership Plan
body: Help me plan a local business partnership strategy for [STORE TYPE] in [LOCATION]. My target customer: [DESCRIBE]. Other businesses they also visit in my area: [LIST or describe]. Design: (1) 5 specific businesses I should approach for a partnership, (2) the partnership mechanic for each (referral card / joint event / cross-promotion / shared display), (3) the pitch I'd use to approach each business, and (4) how to measure whether the partnership is worth continuing after 90 days.
whatItIsFor: Building relationships with complementary local businesses that drive mutual footfall without competing.
howToUseIt: The best local partnerships are non-competitive with overlapping audiences — map your customer's whole shopping trip, not just your part of it.

title: Retail Social Media Strategy
body: Design a social media strategy for [STORE TYPE] in [LOCATION] that drives in-store footfall, not just followers. My current following: [NUMBER] on [PLATFORM]. My posting frequency: [CURRENT]. Content that's worked before: [DESCRIBE]. Provide: (1) 5 content categories with examples specific to a physical store, (2) a 4-week content calendar, (3) how to use Instagram Stories to show in-store life in real time, and (4) one local hashtag or community strategy to reach people in my area who aren't following me yet.
whatItIsFor: Building a social media approach that drives in-store visits — not just likes from people who'll never come through the door.
howToUseIt: Retail social media should always include a geographic hook and a reason to visit — not just beautiful product shots.

title: Returns & Refunds Policy Writer
body: Write a returns and refunds policy for [STORE TYPE] selling [PRODUCT TYPE]. The policy should cover: time window for returns, condition the product must be in, what proof of purchase is required, what happens with faulty vs unwanted items, exchanges vs refunds, how to initiate a return (in-store vs online), and any exclusions. Write in plain English — no legal jargon. Under 300 words. Also write a 30-word version for the till point and a 60-word version for the website returns page header.
whatItIsFor: Writing a clear, fair returns policy that builds customer confidence — and reduces the time you spend managing disputes.
howToUseIt: A clear policy reduces refund requests — customers are less likely to buy anxiously if they know their options upfront.

title: Retail KPI Dashboard
body: Design a weekly KPI dashboard for [STORE TYPE] with [NUMBER] staff. Include the 8 most important retail metrics, covering sales performance, customer behaviour, and operational efficiency. For each metric: definition, where to find the data, weekly target benchmark, and what action to take if it's below target. Format as a tracking table I can fill in each Monday. Also: the one metric most independent retailers forget to track that costs them revenue.
whatItIsFor: Identifying the 8 numbers that matter most for a retail business and tracking them weekly without drowning in data.
howToUseIt: Build this in a simple spreadsheet; review every Monday morning in 15 minutes.

title: Stockist Pitch Email
body: Write a stockist pitch email for my [PRODUCT TYPE] to an independent [RETAILER TYPE] in [LOCATION / REGION]. My product: [DESCRIBE — include price, margin for retailer, MOQ if any]. Why it fits their customers: [EXPLAIN]. Include: a strong opening that references something specific about their store (leave [PERSONALISATION] placeholder), the product pitch in 2 sentences, the commercial terms, and a low-commitment next step (send samples, arrange a call). Under 150 words. Subject line included.
whatItIsFor: Pitching your product to retailers who might stock it — expanding your distribution without building your own shop.
howToUseIt: Target independent retailers first — they make faster decisions and are more receptive to small-batch producers than large retailers.

title: Retail Staff Scheduling Framework
body: Help me design a staff scheduling framework for [STORE TYPE] with [NUMBER] staff (including [NUMBER] full-time and [NUMBER] part-time). My trading hours: [HOURS, DAYS]. My busiest periods (from transaction data or observation): [DESCRIBE]. My quietest periods: [DESCRIBE]. Current staffing cost as a % of revenue: [%]. Target: [%]. Design: (1) minimum staffing levels by time slot, (2) how to structure part-time hours to cover peak without paying for quiet periods, (3) a holiday and absence cover plan, and (4) the scheduling rule that would have the highest impact on reducing labour cost without affecting service.
whatItIsFor: Building a staff scheduling framework that aligns labour costs to actual trading patterns — so you're not over-staffed at quiet times or understaffed at peak.
howToUseIt: Pull your transaction data by hour and day before running this prompt — the scheduling should follow the revenue, not habit.

title: Shop Opening Hours Optimisation
body: Help me optimise the opening hours for my [STORE TYPE]. Current hours: [DESCRIBE]. Revenue by day of week (if known): [DESCRIBE]. Revenue by time of day (if known): [DESCRIBE]. Staff cost per hour: [£AMOUNT]. My break-even revenue per hour (staff + overheads): [£AMOUNT]. Analyse: (1) which hours are profitable and which are break-even or loss-making, (2) whether extending any hours would be profitable, (3) whether reducing any hours would save more than they earn, and (4) what my Google Business Profile data shows about when people search for me vs when I'm open.
whatItIsFor: Evaluating whether your current opening hours are aligned with when your customers actually want to shop — and finding the highest-ROI hour to add or remove.
howToUseIt: Pull your transaction data by day and hour before answering this prompt — decisions made without data usually extend the wrong hours.

title: Physical Store Online Integration Plan
body: Help me integrate my physical store and online presence for [STORE TYPE]. Currently: my online shop earns [£AMOUNT/month] and my in-store earns [£AMOUNT/month]. They operate relatively independently. Design an integration plan covering: (1) how to drive online customers to the store, (2) how to drive in-store customers online, (3) how to use my store as a content studio for online channels, (4) how to manage stock and pricing consistently across both channels, and (5) one physical-store-only experience that online can't replicate — and how to promote it as a differentiator.
whatItIsFor: Creating a coherent strategy that bridges your physical store and online presence — so each channel reinforces the other.
howToUseIt: The best independent retailers use their physical presence as their competitive advantage over online-only retailers — lean into it.

title: Menu Description Writer
body:
Write menu descriptions for the following dishes at [RESTAURANT NAME], a [CUISINE TYPE] restaurant targeting [CUSTOMER PROFILE, e.g. family diners / date-night couples / lunch trade workers].

Dishes:
[LIST DISH NAME + 3–5 KEY INGREDIENTS FOR EACH]

For each dish write:
- A 2-sentence menu description (sensory, specific, appetite-triggering — no generic adjectives like "delicious" or "amazing")
- A suggested upsell pairing (wine, side, dessert)
- A dietary flag line (V, VE, GF etc.) where applicable

Aim for a tone that matches [CASUAL / SMART CASUAL / FINE DINING].
whatItIsFor: Writing appetite-triggering dish descriptions for print menus, online ordering, or QR menus.
howToUseIt: List dish names and main ingredients — the prompt adds sensory language and upsell framing without overpromising.

title: Google Business Profile Post Calendar (Hospitality)
body:
Create a 4-week Google Business Profile posting calendar for [RESTAURANT/CAFÉ NAME], a [TYPE] in [LOCATION] open [OPENING HOURS].

Include:
- 1 post per week (Wednesdays work best for restaurant footfall searches)
- A mix of: specials highlight, event or theme night promo, behind-the-scenes, and a review-request post
- Each post: headline (under 60 chars), 2-sentence body, and a clear CTA (book, call, visit link)
- Reference [SPECIFIC DISHES OR EVENTS] where relevant

Tone: [CASUAL / WARM / UPSCALE]
whatItIsFor: Generating a month of GBP posts to drive reservations, footfall, and positive review prompts for restaurants and cafés.
howToUseIt: Run once per month, adapt dates, post directly to your GBP listing.

title: Table-Turn & Shift Optimisation Plan
body:
Act as a hospitality operations consultant. Analyse this shift data for [RESTAURANT NAME] and identify table-turn and revenue-per-cover opportunities.

Current data:
- Covers per service: [NUMBER]
- Average table dwell time: [MINUTES]
- Booking slots offered: [E.G. 6pm, 7pm, 8pm only]
- Average spend per cover: £[AMOUNT]
- Busiest night: [DAY]
- Quietest night: [DAY]
- Current revenue per service: £[AMOUNT]
- Staff on floor per service: [NUMBER]

Identify:
1. Where table turns are being lost (dwell time, slot design, or pacing)
2. What one scheduling or slot change would add most covers per week
3. What upsell or pre-order system would raise average spend without slowing service
4. A staffing-to-cover ratio recommendation for peak and off-peak shifts
whatItIsFor: Identifying where covers are being lost to slow table turns, poor booking slot design, or understaffing — and getting a structured fix plan.
howToUseIt: Fill in your current shift data honestly — the output surfaces specific bottlenecks rather than generic hospitality advice.

title: Supplier Negotiation Script (Food & Beverage)
body:
Write a supplier negotiation email and a follow-up call script for [RESTAURANT/CAFÉ NAME] approaching [SUPPLIER NAME], our [PRODUCT CATEGORY, e.g. meat / produce / coffee] supplier.

Context:
- Current monthly spend with this supplier: £[AMOUNT]
- Length of relationship: [MONTHS/YEARS]
- Issue: [E.G. 12% price increase / minimum order now too high / delivery unreliable]
- Desired outcome: [E.G. hold price for 6 months / reduce minimum order / fix delivery window]
- Our leverage: [E.G. we've been loyal for 3 years / we refer other venues / we pay within 7 days]

Email: professional, warm, specific — reference the relationship before raising the issue.
Call script: bullet-point format with an opening, 2 negotiation moves, and a close.
whatItIsFor: Drafting a professional negotiation email or call script to renegotiate supplier terms — price, delivery frequency, or minimum order — without damaging the relationship.
howToUseIt: Use before a contract renewal or when a key supplier raises prices. Adapt the tone to match your existing relationship.

title: Seasonal Menu Planning Brief
body:
Create a seasonal menu planning brief for [RESTAURANT/CAFÉ NAME] for the [SEASON] menu update.

Include:
- 3–4 seasonal ingredient themes to anchor the menu (UK-sourced where possible)
- 5 dish concept directions (starters, mains, desserts — brief 1-line concept for each)
- Food cost targets: target GP% [E.G. 70%], max plate cost £[AMOUNT]
- Launch date: [DATE] — work backwards with a prep timeline (final menu approved, staff briefed, photography, print)
- 2 dishes to retire from the current menu and why (based on: [LIST ANY LOW SELLERS OR MARGIN PROBLEMS])
- A specials strategy for the first 4 weeks post-launch to test new dishes before committing
whatItIsFor: Planning a seasonal menu update with a structured brief covering dish concepts, cost targets, and a launch timeline — before the chef or food development begins.
howToUseIt: Run quarterly before each seasonal menu change. Use the output as the brief you hand to your chef or food developer.
tokens: LIST ANY LOW SELLERS OR MARGIN PROBLEMS

title: Staff Rota Communication Template
body:
Write two hospitality staff communication templates for [RESTAURANT/CAFÉ NAME]:

1. Weekly rota release message (sent every [DAY] for the following [DAYS] of shifts):
- Confirm where to find the rota [E.G. WhatsApp group / Rota app / pinboard]
- Deadline for any swap or cover requests: [DAY/TIME]
- Emergency contact process for day-of absences
- Tone: direct and professional, not harsh

2. Shift-cover request message (what a team member sends when they need cover):
- Must include: shift date, shift time, what they need covered, why (optional), swap offered or not
- A simple approval flow: [MANAGER NAME] approves all swaps before confirmed

We have [NUMBER] staff across kitchen and front of house. Our main communication channel is [WHATSAPP / SLACK / OTHER].
whatItIsFor: Writing clear, professional staff rota communications and shift-change policies that reduce no-shows and last-minute chaos.
howToUseIt: Use this to create your standard rota release message and your shift-cover request process — set it once, reuse every week.

title: Food Producer Product Launch Plan
body:
Create a 6-week product launch plan for [PRODUCT NAME] by [FOOD PRODUCER NAME], a [PRODUCT TYPE, e.g. artisan jam / cold brew / granola] launching into [CHANNEL: farm shop / online DTC / deli wholesale / all three].

Product details:
- RRP: £[AMOUNT]
- Pack size: [SIZE]
- Key differentiator: [WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT FROM COMPETITORS]
- Target customer: [DESCRIPTION]
- Production capacity: [UNITS PER WEEK]
- Available budget for launch: £[AMOUNT]

Include:
- Positioning statement (one sentence)
- Pricing rationale (vs comparable products)
- Week-by-week launch activities across the 6 weeks
- 3 stockist pitch angles for approaching farm shops or delis
- A first-month revenue projection at [UNITS/WEEK] sell-through
whatItIsFor: Planning the launch of a new food product into retail, farm shop, or online DTC channels — covering positioning, pricing, and a 6-week launch sequence.
howToUseIt: Fill in your product details and target channel. Use the output as the launch brief for your first 6 weeks.
tokens: WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT FROM COMPETITORS

title: TripAdvisor / Google Review Recovery Plan
body:
Help me respond to negative reviews and build a 90-day review recovery plan for [RESTAURANT/CAFÉ NAME], currently rated [RATING] on [TRIPADVISOR / GOOGLE] with [NUMBER] reviews.

Our 3 most critical recent reviews:
[PASTE REVIEW 1]
[PASTE REVIEW 2]
[PASTE REVIEW 3]

For each review write:
- A professional, non-defensive public response (under 100 words, specific to the complaint, no template language)
- A private DM/email follow-up offer (if appropriate)

Then create a 90-day rating improvement plan:
- What systemic issue each review points to (if any)
- 3 operational fixes to address root causes
- A review-request system for happy guests (timing, method, wording)
- A target: what rating is realistic after 90 days and how many new reviews are needed
whatItIsFor: Responding to negative reviews professionally and designing a systematic plan to improve your review rating over 90 days.
howToUseIt: Paste your 3 most recent negative reviews and your current rating. The output gives you response drafts plus a structured improvement plan.

title: Hospitality Job Advert Writer
body:
Write a job advert for a [JOB TITLE] role at [VENUE NAME], a [VENUE TYPE] in [LOCATION].

Role details:
- Hours: [FULL TIME / PART TIME / SHIFTS]
- Pay: £[AMOUNT] per hour / per year
- Start date: [DATE]
- Key responsibilities: [LIST 3–4 MAIN DUTIES]
- Must-have experience: [LIST]
- What we genuinely offer (be specific — not "great team culture"): [E.G. 45-hour guaranteed week, no split shifts, Sunday always off, staff meal every shift, above-industry pay]

Write:
1. A 3-sentence opening that speaks to the candidate's career, not our need to fill a shift
2. A clear "you will" responsibilities list (5 bullets)
3. A "you have" requirements list (5 bullets — must-haves only, no fluff)
4. A "we offer" section that uses specifics (hours, pay, days off, perks) not adjectives
5. A short, direct CTA for how to apply
whatItIsFor: Writing job adverts for hospitality roles that attract experienced candidates rather than high-churn applicants — by leading with culture, clarity, and specific role details.
howToUseIt: Fill in role specifics and what makes your venue genuinely different. The prompt avoids generic "passionate team player" language.

title: Food Allergen Compliance Checklist Generator
body:
Create an allergen compliance operational checklist for [RESTAURANT/CAFÉ NAME], a [CUISINE TYPE] serving [NUMBER OF DISHES ON MENU] dishes across [DINE-IN / TAKEAWAY / BOTH].

Our highest-risk dishes (those most likely to affect allergen-sensitive guests):
[LIST 3–5 DISHES WITH THEIR MAIN ALLERGENS]

Generate:
1. A pre-service allergen briefing checklist (what the team checks before each service)
2. A guest enquiry protocol (what staff say and do when a guest declares an allergy)
3. A kitchen cross-contamination checklist (for preparation, equipment, and plating)
4. A staff training completion log format
5. A flag for the top 3 operational risks in a [CUISINE TYPE] kitchen

Note: frame this as operational best practice, not legal advice.
whatItIsFor: Generating a working allergen compliance checklist tailored to your specific menu — covering the 14 major allergens, cross-contamination risks, and staff training requirements.
howToUseIt: This does not replace legal advice but gives you a practical operational framework. Always verify with your local environmental health officer.

title: Catering Enquiry Response Template
body:
Write a catering enquiry response email template for [CATERING BUSINESS NAME], a [CATERING TYPE] business covering [GEOGRAPHY].

Our typical events: [E.G. corporate lunches, private garden parties, weddings, street food festivals]
Minimum booking value: £[AMOUNT]
Typical lead time needed: [WEEKS]
Deposit required: [%] of event total
Our key differentiator: [WHAT MAKES US DIFFERENT]

The email should:
1. Acknowledge the enquiry warmly but efficiently (not gushing)
2. Ask 3 qualifying questions to establish if we're the right fit
3. Set a clear next step (discovery call, site visit, or quote request form)
4. Mention the minimum booking value and deposit naturally — not apologetically
5. Keep it under 200 words
whatItIsFor: Responding to private catering and events enquiries in a way that qualifies the booking, sets expectations, and moves the prospect towards a confirmed deposit — without underselling.
howToUseIt: Adapt the template to your catering format (canapes, buffet, sit-down, street food). The key is to qualify budget early and guide towards a site visit or call.

title: Hotel / B&B Upsell Email Sequence
body:
Write a 3-email pre-arrival upsell sequence for [HOTEL/B&B NAME], a [TYPE] in [LOCATION].

Our upsell offers:
- Upsell 1: [E.G. room upgrade from standard to superior — £25/night extra]
- Upsell 2: [E.G. dinner reservation in our restaurant — no charge to book, just secure the table]
- Upsell 3: [E.G. hamper on arrival — local produce, £35]

Send timing:
- Email 1: Immediately after booking confirmation
- Email 2: 7 days before arrival
- Email 3: 2 days before arrival

Each email should:
- Have a clear subject line
- Be under 150 words
- Make the upsell feel like a helpful suggestion, not a sales push
- Include a single CTA link or response method
whatItIsFor: Writing a 3-email pre-arrival sequence for accommodation businesses to upsell room upgrades, dinner bookings, and experiences before the guest arrives.
howToUseIt: Set this up in your email system to trigger automatically after booking confirmation. Timing shown below.

title: Waste Reduction Plan (Food Business)
body:
Act as a food waste consultant. Help [RESTAURANT/CAFÉ NAME] reduce food waste across three categories.

Current situation:
- Weekly food spend: £[AMOUNT]
- Estimated waste %: [%] (industry average is 4–10% of food spend)
- Main waste categories: [E.G. over-ordering produce / plate waste from over-large portions / prep offcuts not used]
- Current stock system: [PAPER SHEETS / SPREADSHEET / POS SYSTEM / NONE]
- Menu change frequency: [WEEKLY / MONTHLY / QUARTERLY]

For each waste category:
1. Diagnose the likely root cause
2. Recommend one practical fix (not a technology overhaul — operational habits first)
3. Give a measurable target (e.g. reduce produce waste from 8% to 5% in 60 days)
4. Suggest one menu or specials strategy that converts waste into revenue
whatItIsFor: Identifying where food waste is costing your kitchen money and generating a practical reduction plan — covering prep waste, plate waste, and ordering waste.
howToUseIt: Fill in your current waste data honestly. Even estimates work — the output gives you measurable targets and a system to track improvement.

title: Hospitality Business Grant Application Narrative
body:
Write a grant application narrative for [BUSINESS NAME], a [HOSPITALITY/FOOD BUSINESS TYPE] applying for the [GRANT NAME OR TYPE] grant of £[AMOUNT].

Business details:
- Location: [TOWN/CITY]
- Years trading: [NUMBER]
- Current employees: [NUMBER FTE]
- Annual turnover: £[AMOUNT]
- What the grant will fund: [E.G. kitchen equipment / outdoor seating / food production equipment]
- How it will help the business: [SPECIFIC IMPACT — revenue increase, new jobs, new market]
- Community benefit: [E.G. local employment, tourism, food education, rural supply chain]
- Why now: [WHY THIS INVESTMENT IS NEEDED AT THIS STAGE]

Write in a factual, evidence-led tone. Avoid phrases like "passionate about food" or "vibrant community" — use numbers and specifics instead.
whatItIsFor: Writing the narrative section of a grant application for a hospitality or food business — covering business impact, job creation, community benefit, and financial need.
howToUseIt: Adapt to the specific grant criteria. This prompt generates the narrative text — you still need to verify eligibility and submit via the funder's process.
tokens: WHY THIS INVESTMENT IS NEEDED AT THIS STAGE

title: Hospitality Business Instagram Content Plan
body:
Create a 4-week Instagram content plan for [VENUE/BRAND NAME], a [HOSPITALITY TYPE] in [LOCATION].

Our current focus: [E.G. summer bookings / new menu launch / gift voucher sales / winter event promotion]
Our best-performing content so far: [E.G. behind-the-scenes kitchen / dish reveals / team posts]
Average posting frequency: [NUMBER] times per week
Key dates this month: [LIST ANY EVENTS, SEASONAL MOMENTS, OR MENU CHANGES]

For each week provide:
- 3 post ideas (format: static / carousel / reel) with a one-line concept
- 1 caption draft (for the post most likely to drive bookings or enquiries)
- 1 reel concept (hook, 3 beats, CTA) for the month

CTA goal: drive [BOOKINGS / DM ENQUIRIES / WEBSITE VISITS / VOUCHER SALES]
whatItIsFor: Creating a month of Instagram content specifically for restaurants, cafés, hotels, or food producers — covering post ideas, captions, and a reel concept that drives bookings rather than just likes.
howToUseIt: Run once per month as your content brief. Adapt post ideas to your current menu, events, and season.

title: Professional Services Positioning Statement
body:
Write a positioning statement for [FIRM NAME], a [TYPE OF FIRM: accountancy / legal / management consultancy / HR advisory / financial planning] firm based in [LOCATION].

Our specialisation: [E.G. we work exclusively with owner-managed businesses in the construction sector / we advise professional practices on practice management and succession]
Typical client: [DESCRIBE IN ONE SENTENCE]
What we do that most firms in our category don't: [BE SPECIFIC — not "we're proactive"]
Our fee model: [FIXED FEE / HOURLY / RETAINER / MIXED]
Biggest client outcome in the last 12 months: [ONE REAL RESULT — financial saving, time saved, risk removed, deal closed]

Write:
1. A one-sentence positioning statement (for the hero section of the website)
2. A 3-sentence expanded version (for the About page)
3. A 30-second verbal pitch version (for networking events)
whatItIsFor: Crafting a clear, differentiated positioning statement for your professional services firm — one that goes beyond "trusted, experienced, client-focused" and actually communicates why a client should choose you.
howToUseIt: Use this on your website homepage, LinkedIn, and pitch materials. Run it again annually as your positioning evolves.

title: Service Packaging & Fixed-Fee Menu
body:
Help me design a fixed-fee service menu for [FIRM NAME], a [TYPE] firm.

My most frequently delivered service: [DESCRIBE IN ONE SENTENCE]
Typical scope for a standard engagement: [WHAT'S INCLUDED]
What clients often add on later (scope creep): [LIST 2–3 COMMON ADDITIONS]
My current pricing model: [HOURLY / QUOTE-BY-QUOTE / HYBRID]
The problem with current pricing: [E.G. clients don't know what to expect / I underquote and overdeliver / difficult to compare us to competitors]

Design 3 service tiers:
- Foundation tier (entry-level, self-service or minimal touch)
- Core tier (full standard service, most popular)
- Premium tier (highest touch, broadest scope)

For each tier include:
- What's included (specific, not vague)
- What's excluded (clearly stated)
- A suggested fixed monthly or project fee
- The type of client each tier suits
whatItIsFor: Structuring your professional services into clear, fixed-fee packages that remove pricing anxiety for clients and improve your own revenue predictability.
howToUseIt: Start with your most commonly requested service and use this to design 3 tiers. Review annually as your delivery evolves.

title: New Client Engagement Letter Template
body:
Draft an engagement letter template for [FIRM NAME], a [TYPE OF PROFESSIONAL SERVICES FIRM], to be sent to new clients at the start of every engagement.

Standard engagement details:
- Service to be provided: [DESCRIBE]
- Fee basis: £[AMOUNT] per [HOUR / MONTH / PROJECT] + VAT
- Payment terms: [E.G. monthly in advance / 30 days from invoice]
- Scope limitations: [WHAT THIS ENGAGEMENT DOES NOT INCLUDE]
- Our responsibility: [WHAT WE WILL DELIVER]
- Client's responsibility: [WHAT THE CLIENT MUST PROVIDE AND WHEN]
- Termination: [NOTICE PERIOD EACH PARTY MUST GIVE]
- Professional indemnity: [PI COVER LEVEL IF RELEVANT]

Write in plain English — clear, professional, not intimidating. Include a client confirmation signature block.
whatItIsFor: Writing a professional, clear engagement letter that sets scope, fees, and responsibilities from day one — reducing scope creep and protecting both parties.
howToUseIt: This is a working template, not legal advice. Have your PI insurer or solicitor review the final version before use. Adapt the liability clause to your professional body's requirements.
tokens: WHAT THIS ENGAGEMENT DOES NOT INCLUDE
WHAT THE CLIENT MUST PROVIDE AND WHEN
NOTICE PERIOD EACH PARTY MUST GIVE

title: LinkedIn Thought Leadership Post (Professional Services)
body:
Write 3 LinkedIn post options for [YOUR NAME], a [JOB TITLE] at [FIRM NAME].

My specialty: [AREA OF EXPERTISE]
My target audience on LinkedIn: [WHO SHOULD ENGAGE WITH THIS — e.g. owner-managed business directors / HR managers in the hospitality sector]
Current topic I want to write about: [DESCRIBE THE TOPIC IN ONE SENTENCE — a common mistake, a recent client situation (anonymised), a regulatory change, a counterintuitive insight]
My goal: [INBOUND ENQUIRIES / REFERRAL PARTNER AWARENESS / SPEAKING OPPORTUNITIES / BRAND BUILDING]

For each post:
- A hook line (first sentence — no question marks, no "Unpopular opinion:", no "Let me tell you a story")
- 3–4 short body paragraphs (no bullet lists unless genuinely necessary)
- A CTA that invites conversation, not a pitch
- Under 250 words total

Tone: Direct, specific, shows expertise without lecturing. UK professional services voice — not American LinkedIn coach style.
whatItIsFor: Writing LinkedIn posts that demonstrate expertise and generate inbound enquiries — without sounding like a press release or a compliance update.
howToUseIt: Run weekly to generate 3 post options. Pick the one that matches your current client conversations. The prompt avoids the "hot take followed by 37 bullet points" format.
tokens: DESCRIBE THE TOPIC IN ONE SENTENCE

title: Proposal Template (Professional Services)
body:
Write a professional services proposal for [FIRM NAME] addressing an enquiry from [CLIENT NAME / TYPE OF BUSINESS].

Discovery call notes:
- Client's main problem: [DESCRIBE IN ONE SENTENCE]
- What they've tried so far: [IF KNOWN]
- Urgency: [TIMELINE OR DEADLINE]
- Decision maker: [WHO SIGNS OFF]
- Budget signals: [ANY INDICATION OF BUDGET]

Our proposed solution: [DESCRIBE WHAT YOU WILL DO]
Proposed fee: £[AMOUNT] + VAT
Timeframe: [HOW LONG THE ENGAGEMENT RUNS]

Proposal structure:
1. Opening: restate their situation in their language (shows you listened)
2. What we recommend and why (not what we do generally)
3. What's included in this engagement (specific deliverables + timeline)
4. What's not included (protect scope)
5. Investment (fee, payment terms, what happens if scope changes)
6. Next step (simple, single action to move forward)
whatItIsFor: Writing a professional services proposal that leads with the client's problem, presents your solution clearly, and makes it easy to say yes — rather than a document that lists your credentials for three pages before getting to the point.
howToUseIt: Fill in client-specific details after your discovery call. Never send a generic proposal — personalise sections 1 and 2 at minimum.

title: Client Retention Email Sequence (Professional Services)
body:
Write a 3-email re-engagement sequence for clients of [FIRM NAME], a [TYPE] firm, who haven't been in contact for [NUMBER] months.

Email 1 (send at 90 days): a check-in that adds value — share something useful (a regulatory update, a common mistake we're seeing, a relevant deadline coming up). Do NOT lead with "we haven't heard from you." Under 100 words.

Email 2 (send at 105 days): a soft question — "Is there anything we should be reviewing for you before [END OF TAX YEAR / QUARTER END / RENEWAL PERIOD]?" One question, nothing more. Under 60 words.

Email 3 (send at 120 days): a direct invite — offer a 20-minute review call, no charge, no agenda other than checking in. Under 80 words.

All three: professional, warm, no pressure. Subject lines included.
whatItIsFor: Writing a 3-email sequence to re-engage clients who haven't been in contact for 3+ months — without seeming needy or salesy.
howToUseIt: Set up as an automated trigger at the 90-day no-contact mark in your CRM.

title: Service Upsell Email (Existing Clients)
body:
Write a service upsell email from [FIRM NAME] to an existing client introducing [NEW SERVICE / ADDITIONAL SERVICE].

Client context: [DESCRIBE THE CLIENT'S CURRENT SITUATION OR RECENT EVENT THAT MAKES THIS RELEVANT]
Service being introduced: [DESCRIBE]
Why this service is relevant to them right now: [SPECIFIC REASON, NOT GENERIC]
Fee: £[AMOUNT] or [FEE BASIS]
Next step: [WHAT YOU WANT THEM TO DO]

The email should:
- Reference the specific situation (not a generic broadcast)
- Explain the service in one sentence
- State why now (specific trigger)
- Give a clear next step (call, reply, or link)
- Under 120 words
whatItIsFor: Introducing an additional service to an existing client who you know is facing a relevant situation — without it feeling like a pitch.
howToUseIt: Trigger this when a client event occurs: a hiring decision, a lease renewal, a business sale, a contract dispute starting.
tokens: S CURRENT SITUATION OR RECENT EVENT THAT MAKES THIS RELEVANT
WHAT YOU WANT THEM TO DO

title: Referral Programme Design (Professional Services)
body:
Design a referral programme for [FIRM NAME], a [TYPE] firm regulated by [PROFESSIONAL BODY IF RELEVANT].

Our typical client: [DESCRIBE]
Our best source of new clients currently: [E.G. existing clients / networking / LinkedIn]
What we can and cannot offer as a referral incentive: [E.G. we can offer a free service upgrade but not cash commission]
Our average client lifetime value: £[AMOUNT]
Target: [NUMBER] referrals per quarter from [NUMBER] active clients

Design:
1. A referral ask script (how we ask for introductions — what we say and when)
2. A thank-you protocol for received referrals (what happens when someone refers)
3. A compliant incentive structure (if any)
4. A way to make referring easy (what we give clients to share)
5. A quarterly tracking metric (how we measure referral performance)
whatItIsFor: Designing a structured referral programme for a professional services firm that generates qualified introductions from existing clients — without offering cash kickbacks that breach professional codes.
howToUseIt: Many professions restrict financial referral incentives. This prompt creates a compliant, relationship-based referral structure.

title: Annual Client Survey & Feedback System
body:
Write an annual client survey for [FIRM NAME], a [TYPE] firm, and a system for acting on the results.

What we want to learn:
- [E.G. are clients clear on the value we provide / do they feel heard / would they refer us / what could we do better]

Survey format: email with [NUMBER, e.g. 5–7] questions (not a form they have to log in to)
Response target: [%] of active clients

Write:
1. The survey email (subject line + introduction + 5–7 questions)
2. A results-review framework (how to categorise and act on responses)
3. A follow-up email for low-satisfaction responses (under 80 words, specific and non-defensive)
4. A quarterly team debrief agenda item based on the results
whatItIsFor: Running an annual client satisfaction survey that actually surfaces useful insight — not just a Net Promoter Score you file and forget.
howToUseIt: Send annually after year-end work is complete. Use the output to prioritise one operational change and one relationship investment per year.

title: Fee Increase Communication (Professional Services)
body:
