Write a fee increase letter for existing clients of [FIRM NAME], a [TYPE] firm.

Current fee: £[AMOUNT] per [MONTH / PROJECT / YEAR]
New fee: £[AMOUNT] (effective [DATE])
% increase: [%]
Honest reason: [E.G. first increase in 3 years, reflecting inflation and expanded scope of work / cost of compliance has increased / we are reducing our client base to improve quality]
What clients are keeping: [ALL THE SAME SERVICES / ANY IMPROVEMENTS OR ADDITIONS]

The letter should:
- Open with something specific we have done for this client in the past year (leave a placeholder for personalisation)
- State the new fee and date clearly in the first third
- Not over-apologise or justify at length
- Offer a brief call if they want to discuss
- Be under 200 words
whatItIsFor: Communicating a professional services fee increase to existing clients in a way that retains the relationship — by leading with value delivered, not cost justification.
howToUseIt: Give 60 days' notice minimum. Send to individuals, not as a mass email. Personalise the first paragraph.

title: Professional Services Website About Page
body:
Write the About page copy for [FIRM NAME], a [TYPE] firm.

Firm details:
- Founded: [YEAR]
- Team size: [NUMBER]
- Specialism: [WHAT YOU ARE KNOWN FOR]
- Type of client: [WHO YOU WORK BEST WITH]
- What you do differently: [ONE OR TWO SPECIFIC THINGS — not "client focus"]
- A real result from the last 12 months: [ANONYMISED CLIENT OUTCOME]
- Values: [LIST 2–3 — the ones that actually affect how you work, not mission statement language]

Structure:
1. Opening paragraph: who you help and what you're known for (not "welcome to our firm")
2. What makes you different (specific, not generic)
3. A real result or client story (anonymised)
4. The team (without a biography-heavy CV-style section)
5. CTA: what someone should do next

Under 350 words. Professional but human — not corporate brochure language.
whatItIsFor: Writing an About page for a professional services website that builds trust through specificity rather than through credential-listing.
howToUseIt: The best About pages answer: who do you help, what's different about how you do it, and why does that matter to the visitor. Not: how many years have you been trading.

title: Tender Pre-Qualification Questionnaire Response
body:
Help me draft narrative answers for a Pre-Qualification Questionnaire for [FIRM NAME] applying for a [CONTRACT TYPE] contract with [BUYER TYPE, e.g. local authority / NHS trust / large corporate].

Our firm:
- Size: [NUMBER] staff, annual turnover £[AMOUNT]
- Years trading: [NUMBER]
- Relevant contracts: [LIST 2–3 SIMILAR CONTRACTS DELIVERED]
- Key differentiator for this contract: [WHAT MAKES US SUITABLE]

PQQ sections to answer:
1. Relevant experience (max 300 words)
2. Capacity and resources available for this contract (max 200 words)
3. Quality assurance and complaints handling (max 200 words)
4. Equality and diversity approach (max 150 words)

Write each section as a factual, specific, evaluator-friendly narrative. Avoid filler phrases like "we are committed to excellence." Use numbers wherever possible.
whatItIsFor: Answering the standard sections of a Pre-Qualification Questionnaire (PQQ) for professional services firms applying for public sector or large corporate contracts.
howToUseIt: Fill in firm-specific data and let the AI draft the narrative answers. Always review against the actual PQQ before submitting.

title: Networking Event Follow-Up System (Professional Services)
body:
Write a 3-touch follow-up sequence for contacts met at [EVENT NAME / TYPE] by [YOUR NAME] from [FIRM NAME].

Contact types to follow up with:
- Type A: a potential direct client (they need what we do)
- Type B: a potential referral partner (they serve similar clients but in a different discipline)

For each contact type write:
- Touch 1 (within 24 hours): a LinkedIn connection request message AND a short personal email (choose one or both)
- Touch 2 (5–7 days later): a value-add follow-up — share something useful relevant to what they mentioned
- Touch 3 (30 days later): a check-in that opens a next step without being salesy

Keep each message under 80 words. Specific to what was discussed, not templated. Leave [TOPIC DISCUSSED] as a placeholder to personalise.
whatItIsFor: Turning networking contacts into lasting relationships through a structured follow-up system — not just sending a LinkedIn request and hoping for the best.
howToUseIt: Run this within 24 hours of any networking event. The 3-touch sequence works for both referral sources and prospective clients.

title: Case Study Template (Professional Services)
body:
Write a professional services case study for [FIRM NAME] based on this client situation:

Client: [ANONYMISED DESCRIPTION — sector, size, years with us]
Problem they came to us with: [DESCRIBE]
What we did: [SERVICE DELIVERED + APPROACH]
Outcome: [SPECIFIC, MEASURABLE RESULT — financial saving, risk removed, time saved, deal concluded]
Timeframe: [HOW LONG THE ENGAGEMENT TOOK]
Quote or sentiment (if approved): [OPTIONAL — paraphrase if not verbatim]

Format:
- Headline (under 12 words)
- Situation (2 sentences)
- Approach (2–3 sentences)
- Outcome (2 sentences — lead with the number)
- One key lesson (optional — what any similar business should know)

Under 250 words. Professional, specific, no filler. Suitable for a website case study page and for insertion into proposals.
whatItIsFor: Writing a professional services case study that demonstrates value without revealing confidential client details — a core business development asset.
howToUseIt: Write one case study per quarter for your strongest client outcomes. Use them on your website, in proposals, and at networking events.

title: Client Offboarding Letter
body:
Write an offboarding letter from [FIRM NAME] to a departing client.

Context:
- Client type: [DESCRIBE]
- Reason for leaving (if known): [E.G. internal restructure / going with a competitor / owner retiring]
- Length of relationship: [YEARS]
- Work we completed for them: [BRIEF LIST]
- What we need to hand over: [DOCUMENTS / DATA / CONTACTS]

The letter should:
1. Thank them sincerely for the relationship (specific, not generic)
2. Confirm what we will hand over and by when
3. Offer a reference or LinkedIn recommendation if appropriate
4. Leave the door open without being needy
5. Under 200 words, professional and warm
whatItIsFor: Writing a professional, warm offboarding letter when a client ends their engagement — leaving the relationship in good standing for future referrals or re-engagement.
howToUseIt: Send within 48 hours of a client notifying you they are leaving. Never respond defensively or try to "win them back" in the initial letter.

title: Freelance Rate Calculator Prompt
body:
Help me calculate a sustainable freelance rate for [YOUR FREELANCE DISCIPLINE].

My financial targets and constraints:
- Desired annual take-home pay: £[AMOUNT]
- Estimated business expenses (software, equipment, insurance, professional body): £[AMOUNT]/year
- Tax rate estimate: [%]
- Realistic billable weeks per year (subtract holidays, admin, CPD): [NUMBER] weeks
- Realistic billable days per week: [NUMBER] days

Calculate:
1. The minimum day rate needed to hit my target (show the working)
2. The project rate floor for a [SHORT / MEDIUM / LARGE] project (define each as [X] days)
3. What a 20% increase to my day rate would mean for my annual income (at the same billable volume)
4. How many clients I'd need at different rate levels to hit my target
5. A note on where I sit vs market rates for [DISCIPLINE / LOCATION]
whatItIsFor: Calculating a sustainable day rate or project rate based on actual costs, desired income, and realistic billable hours — rather than guessing what the market will bear.
howToUseIt: Run annually or when setting rates for a new service line. Use the output as your floor, not your ceiling.

title: Creative Brief Template Generator
body:
Create a creative project brief template for [YOUR CREATIVE DISCIPLINE] projects.

Include sections for:
1. Project overview (what they want made)
2. Goals (what success looks like — not "something that looks good")
3. Audience (who will see or use it)
4. Tone and style (3 adjectives max, examples of what they like/dislike)
5. Deliverables (file types, sizes, quantities — specific)
6. Timeline (desired deadline, any hard launch dates)
7. Budget (approved or approximate)
8. Stakeholders and approval process (who signs off, how many rounds are expected)
9. Reference materials (existing brand assets, competitor examples, inspiration)
10. What's out of scope (anything NOT included in this project)

Make each section a fill-in field with a 1-sentence instruction explaining WHY we need this information. Under 600 words total.
whatItIsFor: Writing a professional creative brief that aligns client expectations before work begins — reducing revision rounds and scope creep.
howToUseIt: Send this brief (with a 3-day deadline to complete it) before issuing any quote or beginning any work.

title: Portfolio Case Study Writer
body:
Write a portfolio case study for a [CREATIVE PROJECT TYPE] project.

Project details:
- Client type: [ANONYMISED — sector, size]
- Brief: what the client needed
- Challenge: the specific creative or strategic problem to solve
- Approach: what you did and why (the creative thinking, not just the output)
- Outcome: any measurable result — conversion uplift, engagement rate, award, client satisfaction
- Your role: [SOLE CREATOR / LEAD WITH TEAM / COLLABORATOR]

Format:
1. Project title (under 8 words)
2. Client context (1 sentence)
3. The brief (2 sentences)
4. The challenge (2 sentences — what made this genuinely difficult)
5. The approach (3–4 sentences — the creative reasoning, not a production log)
6. The result (2 sentences — lead with any number if available)

Under 250 words. Written from the creative's perspective — insightful, not self-congratulatory.
whatItIsFor: Writing the narrative section of a portfolio case study that explains the thinking behind creative work — not just what it looks like, but why it works.
howToUseIt: Write one for every major project. Use on your website, in proposals, and when pitching to new clients.

title: Difficult Client Conversation Script (Freelance)
body:
Write scripts for three difficult freelance conversations for a [CREATIVE DISCIPLINE] freelancer.

Situation 1: Client asks for "just one more change" that is clearly outside the agreed scope
Situation 2: Invoice is 21 days overdue, client has been unresponsive
Situation 3: Prospective client says "I've found someone who can do this for half your price"

For each situation write:
- An email version (under 100 words)
- A verbal script for a call or in-person conversation (bullet-pointed, key phrases to use)
- One phrase to AVOID (and why)

Tone: calm, professional, non-apologetic. You are not asking for a favour — you are enforcing a normal business agreement.
whatItIsFor: Navigating three common difficult freelance client conversations — scope creep requests, late payment, and "I know someone who could do this cheaper."
howToUseIt: Adapt to your situation. The goal is firm but non-confrontational — protect the relationship while protecting your boundaries.

title: Freelance Service Productisation Plan
body:
Help me productise a freelance service into a fixed-price offering.

Service to productise: [DESCRIBE YOUR MOST FREQUENTLY REQUESTED SERVICE]
Typical scope when done custom: [WHAT'S USUALLY INCLUDED]
What varies between clients: [THE BITS THAT CHANGE — e.g. number of pages, number of images, length of copy]
My current pricing for this service: [£AMOUNT — hourly or project]
Time it typically takes: [HOURS / DAYS]
Who buys this most often: [DESCRIBE TYPICAL CLIENT]

Create:
1. A productised version with a fixed, defined scope (what's in, what's out)
2. A product name that communicates the outcome, not the process
3. A price point with a brief rationale
4. A one-paragraph sales description (for a website or proposal)
5. A delivery timeline (from brief to delivery)
6. Three add-on options (to increase average order value without scope creep)
whatItIsFor: Turning a custom creative service into a fixed-scope, fixed-price product that can be sold repeatedly without re-quoting every time.
howToUseIt: Start with your most frequently requested service. Productise one thing before trying to build a full product suite.
tokens: DESCRIBE YOUR MOST FREQUENTLY REQUESTED SERVICE

title: Freelance Income Diversification Plan
body:
Help me identify and plan income diversification for a freelance [CREATIVE DISCIPLINE].

My current income:
- Primary: [DESCRIBE CLIENT WORK — e.g. brand identity projects]
- Average monthly revenue: £[AMOUNT]
- Slow months: [WHICH MONTHS ARE TYPICALLY QUIET]
- Skills I have but don't monetise: [LIST 2–3]
- Assets I've built: [E.G. audience / course content / templates / software knowledge]

Identify 3 income diversification options that:
1. Use existing skills or assets (no retraining required)
2. Can generate meaningful income within 6 months
3. Don't require more than [NUMBER] hours/week to maintain

For each option: a brief description, realistic revenue potential in year 1, what it takes to set up, and the single biggest risk.
whatItIsFor: Identifying 2–3 additional income streams beyond client work that suit a creative freelancer's existing skills — reducing feast-or-famine income volatility.
howToUseIt: Run once a year as part of business planning. Focus on one new stream at a time — building all three simultaneously rarely works.

title: Creative Freelance LinkedIn Profile Rewrite
body:
Rewrite my LinkedIn profile sections for my freelance [CREATIVE DISCIPLINE] business.

My current headline: [PASTE CURRENT HEADLINE]
My current about section: [PASTE OR DESCRIBE]

My actual situation:
- I work best with: [DESCRIBE IDEAL CLIENT]
- The main thing they hire me for: [SPECIFIC OUTCOME, NOT THE MEDIUM]
- A result I've achieved for a client: [SPECIFIC, MEASURABLE]
- What makes me different from other [DISCIPLINE] freelancers: [ONE SPECIFIC THING]
- My location and whether I work remotely: [LOCATION / REMOTE / HYBRID]

Rewrite:
1. A LinkedIn headline (under 220 characters — lead with outcome, not job title)
2. An About section (under 300 words — who you help, what you do, one result, a CTA)
3. A featured section post idea (what content would demonstrate your expertise without being a portfolio dump)
whatItIsFor: Rewriting a freelance creative's LinkedIn profile to generate inbound enquiries — not just showcase work, but communicate clearly who you help and what you deliver.
howToUseIt: LinkedIn profiles for creatives often lead with process and medium (photographer, designer) when they should lead with outcomes and clients (helping X kind of business achieve Y).
